The brick stupa dates to the **3rd c. BCE**.
xa: Sanchi is in **Raisen, MP**; UNESCO **1989**.
The **south torana** is credited to **Siri Satakarni**.
Sanchi is ranked the **largest stupa in India** (older note).

30.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
30.x: Bharhut is a Shunga-period stupa generally dated to the second century BCE. Devnimori is associated with the Western Kshatrapas, Dhamek with the Gupta period and Kesariya is a later large brick stupa in Bihar.
30.tq: Use dynasty–period matching to catch swapped builders.
xs: **Bharhut** is **Shunga**, **2nd c. BCE** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Devnimori** is **Western Kshatrapa** (c. **4th c. CE**); **Dhamek** is **Gupta** (c. **500 CE**).
**Kesariya** (Bihar) is known as the **largest brick stupa in India**, not a Satavahana stupa.
xa: Bharhut is called the **most ancient stupa in India**.
**Piprahwa** (UP) is among the earliest, with a relic vessel of the Buddha's kin.

30.s: Which of the following is the largest brick stupa in India according to the recent identification mentioned?
30.x: Kesariya in Bihar is identified as the largest brick stupa in India. Older references sometimes attributed this distinction to Sanchi.
30.tq: Handle a current distinction by separating the older textbook claim from the recent identification.
xs: **Kesariya** (Bihar) is the **largest brick stupa in India** — so option **(2)** is correct.
An older note gives **Sanchi** as the largest.
xa: The world's largest stupa is **Borobudur** (Indonesia).
**Vaishya Tekri** near Ujjain (est. **350 ft** diameter) may prove larger than Sanchi.

30.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the number of stupas traditionally built after the Buddha’s death?
30.x: Nine stupas are traditionally listed as having been built after the Buddha’s death, including those at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Kapilavastu and Kushinagar.
30.tq: Recall the exact count rather than the more familiar number of Buddhist Councils.
xs: **Nine stupas** were built after the Buddha's death — so option **(3)** is correct.
They were at **Rajagriha, Vaishali, Kapilavastu, Allakappa, Ramagrama, Vethapida, Pava, Kushinagar, Pippalivana**.
xa: **Piprahwa** (ancient **Kapilavastu**) has an inscribed relic vessel linked to the Buddha's kin.
A stupa with **bodily relics** is a **Dhatugarbha** stupa.

30.s: Which one of the following correctly presents the ranking of stupas by the geographical category specified?
30.x: Borobudur in Indonesia is identified as the largest stupa in the world, Sanchi as the largest in India, and Amaravati as the largest in Andhra Pradesh.
30.tq: Split the options by checking the geographical level of each ranking.
xs: The ranking is **World — Borobudur; India — Sanchi; Andhra Pradesh — Amaravati** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Bhattiprolu** is the **oldest** stupa in AP, not the largest; **Bharhut** is the **most ancient** in India.
xa: A newer note names **Kesariya** the largest **brick** stupa in India.
Borobudur is in **Indonesia**.

30.s: Bharhut is traditionally identified as the most ancient stupa in
30.x: Bharhut is identified as the most ancient stupa in India.
30.tq: Distinguish superlative claims by their geographical scope.
xs: **Bharhut** is the **most ancient stupa in India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It dates to the **Shunga** period, **2nd c. BCE**, in **MP**.
AP's oldest is **Bhattiprolu**, not Bharhut.
xa: **Borobudur** is the largest in the world; **Sanchi** the largest in India.
**Piprahwa** is also listed among the earliest stupas.

30.s: Vaishya Tekri, near Ujjain, is believed to be associated with which of the following?
o: A Mauryan third-century BCE stupa linked to Ashoka’s wife Devi
A Satavahana vihara built by Gautamiputra Satakarni
A Gupta-period chaitya linked to Kumaragupta
A Jain cave complex built by Kharavela
30.x: Vaishya Tekri is believed to contain a Mauryan third-century BCE stupa associated with Ashoka’s wife Devi and possibly identified with Kanakagiri Vihara.
30.tq: Combine the excavation site, period and patron-linked tradition.
xs: **Vaishya Tekri** is believed to be a **Mauryan 3rd c. BCE stupa** linked to **Ashoka's wife Devi** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is thought to be the **Kanakgiri Vihara**.

xs: **Guntupalli** is the **Siddharthaka Chaitya** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC G2 **2008**).

xa: Guntupalli is the only **rock-cut cave temple** and the **oldest chaitya** in AP.
It lies in **West Godavari / Eluru**.

30.s:
Which of the following is correctly matched?

1. Dhanyakataka—Amaravati
2. Sriparvata—Nagarjunakonda
3. Kanakagiri Vihara—Sarnath

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Dhanyakataka is Amaravati and Sriparvata is Nagarjunakonda. Kanakagiri Vihara is associated with Vaishya Tekri near Ujjain, not Sarnath.
30.tq: Use exact ancient-name and present-site pairs to reject the swapped location.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **Dhanyakataka** — **Amaravati**.
Pair 2 is correct: **Sriparvata** — **Nagarjunakonda**.
Pair 3 is wrong: **Kanakgiri Vihara** is linked with **Vaishya Tekri** near **Ujjain**, not Sarnath — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Sriparvata had Nagarjuna's **1,500-room vihara**, built by **Yajna Sri Satakarni**.
Dhanyakataka and Nagarjunakonda were the great **Ikshvaku-era** educational centres.

30.s: What did Hiuen Tsang observe about Sriparvata during the seventh century CE?
o: It had been converted into a Jain centre.
It contained only a royal palace and no monastery.
It had just been founded by the Ikshvakus.
30.x: Hiuen Tsang found Sriparvata without patronage in the seventh century CE.
30.tq: Test the traveller’s observation rather than the site’s earlier period of prosperity.
xs: **Hiuen Tsang** found **Sriparvata without patronage** (**7th** c.) — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was not newly founded then — its vihara had been built by **Yajna Sri Satakarni**.
xa: Sriparvata's acharya was **Bhavaviveka**.
The **Vishnukundins** were the **last** Andhra dynasty to patronise Buddhism.

30.s: Vijayapuri, the ancient name associated with Nagarjunakonda, was a Buddhist centre mainly during the
30.x: Vijayapuri was a Buddhist centre during the 3rd–4th centuries CE.
30.tq: Use the century range to distinguish the site from earlier Buddhist centres.
xs: **Vijayapuri** was a Buddhist centre in the **3rd-4th centuries CE** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is now **submerged under Nagarjuna Sagar** (GS **2025**).
xa: Nagarjunakonda was the **Ikshvaku capital**.
It has **30+ stupas** and a **Sinhalese vihara**.

30.s: As per the APPSC Group 2 (2012) key on Andhra Buddhist sect centres, which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
30.x: Per the APPSC G2 2012 key, Purvasaila was at Dhanyakataka (Amaravati), and both Aparasaila and Rajagirika at Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda). Salihundam was a later Mahayana-Vajrayana centre, not the Purvasaila centre.
30.tq: Go with the key: Purvasaila-Amaravati; Aparasaila and Rajagirika-Sriparvata.
xs: The wrong pair is **(4)**: per the key, **Purvasaila** was at **Dhanyakataka (Amaravati)**, not **Salihundam**.
The key gives **Aparasaila** and **Rajagirika** both at **Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda)**.
xa: Salihundam was a **Mahayana-Vajrayana** centre.
⚠ Some notes place **Rajagirika** at **Guntupalli** and **Uttaraseliya** at **Jaggayyapeta**; APPSC **2011** treated "Uttarasaila-Jaggayyapeta" as wrong — go with the keys.

30.s: Sarnath was nominated for the UNESCO list in 2025–26 and had been on which list since 1998?
30.x: Sarnath was on the UNESCO Tentative List since 1998 and was nominated for the UNESCO list in 2025–26.
30.tq: Distinguish the status of a tentative listing from final World Heritage inscription.
xs: Sarnath has been on the UNESCO **Tentative List** since **1998** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was nominated for the UNESCO list **2025-26**.
xa: **B R Mani**'s **2013-14** excavations showed activity at Sarnath **before Ashoka**.
The **Dhamek** stupa at Sarnath is **Gupta**, c. **500 CE**.

30.s:
Which of the following sites are included in the Buddhist circuit highlighted by the AP Tourism campaign ‘Discover Andhra’?

1. Amaravati
2. Bavikonda
3. Thotlakonda

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: The ‘Discover Andhra’ campaign focused on the Buddhist circuit comprising Amaravati, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda.
30.tq: Check the complete regional list before selecting a partial combination.
xs: The "**Discover Andhra**" circuit covers **Amaravati, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
The AP Tourism campaign ran in Feb **2026**.
xa: **2 Buddhist circuits** were planned (**2024-25**).
Thotlakonda and Bavikonda are hilltop monasteries (c. **200 BCE**) in **Visakhapatnam**.

30.s: Which literary work describes sea trade under the Reddi kings?
30.x: Srinatha’s Haravilasam describes sea trade under the Reddi kings.
30.tq: Match the author and work with the specific historical-economic theme.
xs: **Srinatha**'s **Haravilasam** describes **sea trade under the Reddi kings** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC G2 **2019**).
**Mahavamsa** is the source on **Mahadeva Bhikshu** taking Buddhism to Sri Lanka with **100,000** followers.
xa: Andhra's ancient ports with Buddhist links include **Ghantasala (Kantakasala)** and **Salihundam**.
The hilltop monasteries near **Visakhapatnam** had **Sri Lanka-SE Asia** trade links.

31.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Ajita Kesakambalin — Merit and demerit produced by every action
31.x: Makkhali Gosala taught Niyativada or fatalism. Purana Kassapa taught Akriyavada, Sanjaya Belatthiputta scepticism, and Ajita Kesakambalin materialism.
31.tq: Start with the teacher whose doctrine is most directly identifiable, then eliminate swapped doctrines.
xs: **Makkhali Gosala — Niyativada** is the correct pair: Gosala taught **Niyativada**, i.e. **fatalism**, the Ajivika creed — option **(1)**.
**Purana Kassapa** taught **Akriyavada** (no merit or demerit from actions), not scepticism.
**Sanjaya Belatthiputta** was the **sceptic/agnostic** who refused to affirm or deny; the **seven eternal elements** belong to **Pakudha Kaccayana**.
**Ajita Kesakambalin** was the **materialist**: the body of **four elements** dissolves at death and nothing survives.
xa: **Nigantha Nataputta** in the list of six teachers is **Mahavira** (Jain).
⚠ **Niyativada** = Gosala (fate); **Akriyavada** = Purana Kassapa; materialism = Ajita Kesakambalin / **Charvaka**.
Gosala is the usual exam answer for **Ajivika founder** (**UKPSC 2024**), though he was the **third chief** who popularised it.

31.s: Purana Kassapa’s doctrine of Akriyavada held that:
o: All actions are fixed by fate before birth
The body is composed of four elements and nothing survives
Reality consists of seven eternal elements
Actions produce neither merit nor demerit
31.x: Akriyavada, associated with Purana Kassapa, held that actions have no moral consequence; even killing or charity produces neither merit nor demerit.
31.tq: Match the technical doctrine with its distinctive implication.
xs: **Akriyavada** of **Purana Kassapa** held that actions produce **neither merit nor demerit** — option **(4)**.
Even **killing or charity** has no moral effect in this view.
Actions fixed by fate before birth is **Niyativada** of **Makkhali Gosala**; the **four-element** body is **Ajita Kesakambalin**'s materialism.
**Seven eternal, uncreated elements** is the doctrine of **Pakudha Kaccayana**.
xa: **Sanjaya Belatthiputta** taught **scepticism/agnosticism** — refusing to affirm or deny.
⚠ Do not confuse **Akriyavada** (Purana Kassapa) with **Niyativada** (Gosala, fate).
The views of the six teachers are reported by **Ajatashatru** to the Buddha in the **Samannaphala Sutta** (**Digha Nikaya**).

31.s: Nigantha Nataputta, one of the heterodox teachers contemporary with the Buddha, was:
31.x: Nigantha Nataputta is the name used for Mahavira in the account of the contemporary heterodox teachers.
31.tq: Discriminate between a teacher’s alternative name and the names of other sect leaders.
xs: **Nigantha Nataputta** is the name used for **Mahavira**, the Jain teacher — option **(1)**.
**Sanjaya Belatthiputta** was the sceptic, **Makkhali Gosala** the Ajivika fatalist and **Ajita Kesakambalin** the materialist.
xa: **Purana Kassapa** taught **Akriyavada**; **Pakudha Kaccayana** taught **seven eternal elements**.
Gosala spent about **six years** as **Mahavira's companion** before breaking away.
The **Bhagavati Sutra** (Jain Anga) gives the fullest account of **Gosala's quarrel with Mahavira**.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I (Teacher)
a. Gautama Buddha
b. Makkhali Gosala
c. Ajita Kesakambalin
d. Sanjaya Belatthiputta
List-II (Association)
i. Ajivika
 ii. Materialist
 iii. Teacher of Buddhism
 iv. Skeptic
The correct code is:
31.x: Gautama Buddha was the teacher of Buddhism, Makkhali Gosala led the Ajivika tradition, Ajita Kesakambalin represented materialism and Sanjaya Belatthiputta was associated with skepticism.
31.tq: Start from the sure teacher-association pairs and eliminate codes with a mismatched philosophical school.
xs: The correct code is **a–iii, b–i, c–ii, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Gautama Buddha** — teacher of Buddhism; **Makkhali Gosala** — **Ajivika**.
**Ajita Kesakambalin** — **materialist** (four elements dissolve at death); **Sanjaya Belatthiputta** — **sceptic**.
xa: **Purana Kassapa** — **Akriyavada**; **Pakudha Kaccayana** — **seven eternal elements**; **Nigantha Nataputta** — **Mahavira**.
Gosala's doctrine is **Niyativada** (fatalism).
**Charvaka** materialism is traced to the legendary founder **Brihaspati**, hence the name **Barhaspatya**.

31.s: In which text does Ajatashatru report the views of the six teachers to the Buddha?
o: Samannaphala Sutta of the Digha Nikaya
31.x: The Samannaphala Sutta, contained in the Digha Nikaya, presents Ajatashatru’s report of the views of the six teachers to the Buddha.
31.tq: Use the source-and-content pair rather than recognising only the title.
xs: In the **Samannaphala Sutta** of the **Digha Nikaya**, **Ajatashatru** reports the views of the six teachers to the Buddha — option **(2)**.
The **Bhagavati Sutra** is a **Jain Anga** on Gosala's quarrel with Mahavira; the **Majjhima Nikaya** records the Buddha's debates with Jains and Ajivikas.
The **Brihaspati Sutra** is the lost Charvaka original.
xa: Charvaka is known mainly through opponents, e.g. Madhava's **Sarvadarshanasangraha**.
**Ashokan edicts** (**7th Pillar Edict**) and **Barabar cave inscriptions** name the Ajivikas / record the caves gifted.
The six teachers include **Makkhali Gosala**, **Purana Kassapa**, **Ajita Kesakambalin**, **Pakudha Kaccayana**, **Sanjaya Belatthiputta** and **Nigantha Nataputta**.

31.s: The fullest account of Gosala and his quarrel with Mahavira is found in the:
31.x: The Bhagavati Sutra, a Jain Anga, provides the fullest account of Gosala and his quarrel with Mahavira.
31.tq: Identify the principal source by linking the text to its religious tradition and subject.
xs: The **Bhagavati Sutra**, a **Jain Anga**, gives the fullest account of **Gosala** and his quarrel with **Mahavira** — option **(2)**.
The **Sarvadarshanasangraha** (Madhava) refutes **Charvaka**; the **Seventh Pillar Edict** names the Ajivikas; the **Samannaphala Sutta** reports the six teachers' views.
xa: Gosala spent about **six years** as Mahavira's companion before breaking away.
Some notes call Gosala Mahavira's "**guru**"; **Jain texts** make him Mahavira's **disciple**.
The **Majjhima Nikaya** records the Buddha's debates with **Jains and Ajivikas**.

31.s:
Which of the following constitute important sources for the study of the Ajivikas?
1. Ashokan edicts
2. Barabar cave inscriptions
3. Bhagavati Sutra
4. Samannaphala Sutta
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
31.x: Ashokan edicts, Barabar cave inscriptions, the Bhagavati Sutra and the Samannaphala Sutta all provide evidence for the study of heterodox sects, including the Ajivikas.
31.tq: Check whether each listed source contributes evidence before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four — **Ashokan edicts**, **Barabar cave inscriptions**, **Bhagavati Sutra** and **Samannaphala Sutta** — are sources, so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
Ashoka's **7th Pillar Edict** names the Ajivikas; the **Barabar** inscriptions record caves gifted to them.
The **Bhagavati Sutra** has Gosala's quarrel with Mahavira; the **Samannaphala Sutta** reports Gosala's views among the six teachers.
xa: **Ashoka donated the Barabar caves** (Bihar) — among the **earliest rock-cut caves** in India (**UPPSC 2023**).
The 7th Pillar Edict (**Delhi-Topra**) names the Ajivikas with **Brahmanas**, the **Sangha** and **Nirgranthas**.
For Charvaka, the **Brihaspati Sutra** is lost; it is known via opponents such as the **Sarvadarshanasangraha**.

31.s: Who was the most important leader and populariser of the Ajivika movement?
31.x: Makkhali Gosala was the most important Ajivika leader and the third chief who popularised the movement.
31.tq: Distinguish the principal leader from other contemporary heterodox teachers.
xs: **Makkhali (Makkali) Gosala** was the most important Ajivika leader and its populariser — option **(2)**.
He was the **third chief** who popularised the sect, and is the usual exam answer for "founder" (**UKPSC 2024**).
**Pakudha Kaccayana** taught **seven eternal elements**, **Sanjaya Belatthiputta** **scepticism**, **Purana Kassapa** **Akriyavada**.
xa: Gosala's core doctrine: **Niyati** — all thoughts and actions fixed before birth; **no free will**.
The Ajivikas were popular under **Bindusara**; **Ashoka** gave them the **Barabar caves**.
They survived nearly **2,000 years**, until the **14th century CE**, in **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about Ajivika doctrine:
1. Human thoughts and actions were considered fixed before birth.
2. There was no free will in the Ajivika view.
3. Karma could be used to alter destiny.
4. All beings were regarded as powerless before fate.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Ajivikas believed in determinism, denied free will and held that beings were powerless before fate. They rejected karma as a means of changing destiny, so statement 3 is false.
31.tq: Spot the statement that reverses the deterministic doctrine.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: all thoughts and actions were **fixed before birth** (**Niyati**).
**Statement 2** correct: there was **no free will**.
**Statement 3** wrong: **karma was rejected** as a means to change destiny.
**Statement 4** correct: all beings were **powerless before fate**.
xa: The Ajivikas also held an **atomic theory** of matter that influenced later **Vaisheshika**.
Exam angle: determinism **and** austerity true; "order of rebirth can be changed" false (**RPSC 2024**).
⚠ In the comparison table, Jainism and Buddhism say **effort decides**; only Ajivika says **all is predetermined**.

31.s: Which statement correctly describes the association between Makkhali Gosala and Mahavira?
o: Gosala and Mahavira belonged to the same order throughout their lives.
Gosala spent about six years as Mahavira’s companion before breaking away.
Mahavira became Gosala’s disciple after accepting Niyati.
Gosala was the author of the Buddhist Vinaya and never met Mahavira.
31.x: Gosala spent about six years as Mahavira's companion before breaking away to lead the Ajivikas. Jain texts make Gosala Mahavira's disciple (some sources call him Mahavira's 'guru'), but never Mahavira a disciple of Gosala, and they did not stay in one order.
31.tq: Test the relationship and duration without confusing companionship with permanent common membership.
xs: **Gosala** spent **about six years** as **Mahavira's companion** before **breaking away** — option **(2)**.
They did not stay in one order; Jain texts make **Gosala Mahavira's disciple**, never Mahavira a disciple of Gosala.
Gosala was the **Ajivika** leader, not an author of any Buddhist text.
xa: Some notes call Gosala Mahavira's "**guru**" — a confusable point.
The **Bhagavati Sutra** (Jain Anga) gives the fullest account of their **quarrel**.
In the list of six teachers, Mahavira appears as **Nigantha Nataputta**.

31.s: Which Buddhist text records debates involving the Buddha, Jains and Ajivikas?
31.x: The Majjhima Nikaya records debates involving the Buddha, Jains and Ajivikas. The other texts serve different source functions.
31.tq: Match the text with the specific interaction it records.
xs: The **Majjhima Nikaya** records the Buddha's debates with **Jains and Ajivikas** — option **(4)**.
The **Sarvadarshanasangraha** (Madhava) refutes Charvaka; the **Bhagavati Sutra** is a Jain Anga on Gosala.
The **Samannaphala Sutta** is in the **Digha Nikaya**, where **Ajatashatru** reports the six teachers' views.
xa: The Ajivika core doctrine is **Niyati** (fate/determinism).
Gosala was Mahavira's companion for about **six years** before breaking away.
⚠ **Majjhima Nikaya** = debates; **Digha Nikaya** (Samannaphala Sutta) = Ajatashatru's report on six teachers.

31.s: The Ajivikas' theory about matter, which influenced the later Vaisheshika school, was
o: the doctrine that matter is unreal
the theory of seven eternal elements with no killer or killed
31.x: The Ajivikas held an atomic theory of matter that influenced the later Vaisheshika. The seven eternal elements belong to Pakudha Kaccayana, dependent origination (Pratityasamutpada) is Buddhist, and the Ajivikas did not hold that matter is unreal.
31.tq: Ajivika atomism -> Vaisheshika.
xs: The Ajivikas held an **atomic theory of matter**, which influenced the later **Vaisheshika** — option **(1)**.
**Seven eternal elements with no killer or killed** is **Pakudha Kaccayana**'s doctrine, not the Ajivikas'.
xa: Ajivika core doctrine: **Niyati** — fate/determinism, **no free will**, karma cannot change destiny.
Lifestyle: **extreme asceticism** — nakedness, lying on nails, walking through fire, sitting in large earthen pots.
Social base: **no caste discrimination**; appealed to warrior, industrial and mercantile classes.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ajivikas:
1. They practised extreme asceticism, including nakedness and lying on nails.
2. Their ascetics were often called Sudra sannyasins.
3. They practised caste discrimination and appealed mainly to Brahmanas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 on the Ajivika lifestyle are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the Ajivikas had no caste discrimination and appealed to warrior, industrial and mercantile classes. So 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
31.tq: Ajivikas: no caste discrimination (BPSC 2024 trap).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: **extreme asceticism** — nakedness, **lying on nails**, walking through fire.
**Statement 2** correct: organised ascetic groups often called **Sudra sannyasins**.
**Statement 3** wrong: there was **no caste discrimination**; they appealed to **warrior, industrial and mercantile** classes.
xa: Caste discrimination "false" was the key in **BPSC 2024**.
Other austerities: sitting in **large earthen pots**.
The Ajivikas were popular under **Bindusara** and received the **Barabar caves** from **Ashoka**.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding Ajivika patronage is correct?
o: Ashoka was an Ajivika for most of his life and converted Bindusara to the sect.
Bindusara was associated with the popularity of the Ajivikas, while Ashoka donated the Barabar caves to them.
Chandragupta Maurya constructed the Barabar caves exclusively for the Ajivikas.
The Barabar caves were built under the Pallavas for Jain monks.
31.x: The Ajivikas were popular under Bindusara, and Ashoka donated the Barabar caves to them. Ashoka was a Buddhist, and the caves were not constructed by Chandragupta Maurya.
31.tq: Apply the wrong-ruler and wrong-patron trap to distinguish Ashoka from Chandragupta Maurya.
xs: **Bindusara** saw the Ajivikas' popularity, and **Ashoka donated the Barabar caves** to them — option **(2)**.
⚠ "Ashoka was an Ajivika for most of his life" is wrong — Ashoka was a **Buddhist** who also gave caves to the Ajivikas.
⚠ The Barabar caves were made by **Ashoka**, not **Chandragupta Maurya** (**UPSC 2013** statement false).
The **Pallavas** are linked to the Puranic-Bhakti revival that caused the sect's **decline**, not to Barabar.
xa: Barabar caves (**Bihar**) are among the **earliest rock-cut caves** in India (**UPPSC 2023**).
Ashoka's **7th Pillar Edict** (Delhi-Topra) names the Ajivikas with Brahmanas, the Sangha and **Nirgranthas**.
The Ajivikas survived until the **14th century CE** in **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**.

31.s: The Barabar caves are significant in Indian architectural history because they are regarded as:
o: Among the earliest rock-cut caves in India
The earliest surviving cave paintings of the Gupta period
The first brick stupas built by the Kushanas
The earliest structural temples of the Pallava period
31.x: The Barabar caves are among the earliest rock-cut caves in India and were donated by Ashoka to the Ajivikas.
31.tq: Separate the architectural significance of a monument from later temple traditions.
xs: The **Barabar caves** are among the **earliest rock-cut caves** in India — option **(1)**.
They were donated by **Ashoka** to the **Ajivikas** (**UPPSC 2023**).
xa: The caves are in **Bihar**.
⚠ Made by **Ashoka**, not **Chandragupta Maurya** (**UPSC 2013** statement false).
⚠ Ashoka was a **Buddhist**, not an Ajivika, though he honoured them.
The **Barabar cave inscriptions** are a source for the Ajivikas.

31.s: Ashoka’s Seventh Pillar Edict mentions the Ajivikas along with:
31.x: The Seventh Pillar Edict of Ashoka, associated with Delhi-Topra, names the Ajivikas along with Brahmanas, the Sangha and Nirgranthas.
31.tq: Recall the exact group of religious communities named in the edict.
xs: The **Seventh Pillar Edict** (**Delhi-Topra**) names the Ajivikas with **Brahmanas, the Sangha and Nirgranthas** — option **(1)**.
It reflects the great respect for the Ajivikas in the **Maurya** era.
xa: **Ashoka** donated the **Barabar caves** (Bihar) to the Ajivikas.
The Ajivikas were popular under **Bindusara**.
The Ashokan edicts and Barabar inscriptions are key **inscriptional sources** for the sect.

31.s: The Ajivika tradition survived in parts of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu until approximately:
31.x: The Ajivikas survived for nearly 2,000 years and disappeared around the 14th century CE in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
31.tq: Use the date-range clue and select the historically precise endpoint.
xs: The Ajivikas survived until the **14th century CE** in **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**, then disappeared — option **(1)**.
That is a span of nearly **2,000 years**.
xa: Causes of decline: **Puranic-Bhakti revival** (e.g. under the **Pallavas**) and **loss of royal patronage**.
Peak patronage came under **Bindusara** and **Ashoka** (Barabar caves).
Founder in exam answers: **Makkhali Gosala** (**UKPSC 2024**).

31.s: Which of the following was a major factor in the decline of the Ajivika and other heterodox traditions?
o: The complete disappearance of urban centres in the sixth century BCE
The Puranic-Bhakti revival and the loss of royal patronage
The adoption of Ajivika doctrines by all Mauryan rulers
The replacement of all religious traditions by Charvaka materialism
31.x: The heterodox traditions declined with the Puranic-Bhakti revival, including under the Pallavas, and because they lost royal patronage.
31.tq: Identify the stated cause-and-effect relationship rather than an absolute generalisation.
xs: The **Puranic-Bhakti revival** and the **loss of royal patronage** caused the decline — option **(2)**.
The Bhakti revival is noted, for example, under the **Pallavas**.
The Shramana sects in fact arose amid **urbanisation** and **Magadhan patronage**, not a disappearance of cities.
xa: The Ajivikas lasted nearly **2,000 years**, until the **14th century CE**, in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Under the Mauryas they were popular under **Bindusara** and given the **Barabar caves** by **Ashoka**.
**Charvaka** left no surviving texts; it is known via opponents' refutations.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Charvaka school:
1. It is also called Lokayata.
2. It is also called Barhaspatya, after its legendary founder Brihaspati.
3. It is also called Niyativada.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Charvaka = Lokayata = Barhaspatya (after Brihaspati). Statement 3 is wrong: Niyativada (fatalism) is the Ajivika doctrine of Makkhali Gosala. So 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
31.tq: Niyati = Ajivika; Lokayata/Barhaspatya = Charvaka.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: Charvaka is also called **Lokayata** (**APPSC GS 2025**).
**Statement 2** correct: also **Barhaspatya**, after legendary founder **Brihaspati**.
**Statement 3** wrong: **Niyativada** (fatalism) is the Ajivika doctrine of **Makkhali Gosala**.
xa: Charvaka is **complete materialism**: body formed of matter, ends in matter.
It accepts only **perception (pratyaksha)** as a means of knowledge.
Its original **Brihaspati Sutra** is lost; known mainly via the **Sarvadarshanasangraha** of Madhava.

31.s: Which one of the following statements best expresses the materialist position of the Charvaka school?
o: Human actions are predetermined by fate and cannot be altered.
Matter is unreal and liberation alone is the aim of life.
The body is temporary but the soul is eternal and moves through rebirth.
The body is formed of matter and ends in matter, while material pleasure is the aim of life.
31.x: Charvaka is a complete materialist philosophy. It regards the body as material and kama, or material pleasure, as the highest value.
31.tq: Match the doctrine with the school that actually advocates it.
xs: Charvaka holds that the **body is formed of matter and ends in matter**, and **material pleasure** is the aim of life — option **(4)**.
**Kama** is the **highest value** in this complete materialism.
Predetermined fate is the **Ajivika** (Niyati) view; Charvaka denies any soul that survives the body.
xa: Body-soul view: "**The conscious body is the soul**" (**CGPSC 2024**).
Only **perception** is accepted; inference and Vedic testimony are rejected.
Aphorism: "Live happily as long as you live; **borrow and drink ghee**".

31.s:
With reference to the Charvaka view of the soul, consider the following statements:
1. The conscious body itself is regarded as the soul.
2. A separate soul survives after death.
3. No separate soul continues after the destruction of the body.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Charvaka identifies the conscious body with the soul and denies the survival of a separate soul after death. Therefore, statements 1 and 3 are correct, while statement 2 is false.
31.tq: Split the options by checking the paired claim and its direct negation.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1** correct: "**The conscious body is the soul**" (**CGPSC 2024** answer: Charvaka).
**Statement 2** wrong and **statement 3** correct: **no separate soul** survives death.
xa: Contrast: Jainism — **eternal jiva** in all things; Buddhism — **Anatta**, no permanent self.
Charvaka is **complete materialism**; aim of life = **material pleasure** (kama).
Aphorism: "once the body is **ash**, how can it return?"

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Charvaka epistemology:
1. It accepts direct perception as a means of knowledge.
2. It accepts the Vedas as an authoritative testimony.
3. It rejects inference as an independent means of knowledge.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Charvaka accepts perception but rejects both inference and the authority of the Vedas. Thus, statements 1 and 3 are correct.
31.tq: Find the statement that reverses the school’s stated position on authority.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1** correct: Charvaka accepts only **perception (pratyaksha)**.
**Statement 2** wrong: **testimony (Vedas)** is rejected; **statement 3** correct: **inference** is rejected.
xa: Contrast: **Nyaya** accepts four pramanas — perception, inference, comparison, testimony.
Exam angle: "which school accepts **only perception**" → **Charvaka**.
All four heterodox schools **rejected Vedic authority**.

31.s: The aphorism advocating happiness during life, borrowing and drinking ghee, and denying return after cremation is associated with which school?
31.x: The aphorism expresses the Charvaka rejection of an afterlife and its emphasis on material enjoyment during the present life.
31.tq: Recognise a school through its distinctive aphorism and central doctrine.
xs: The aphorism "Live happily as long as you live; **borrow and drink ghee**" belongs to **Charvaka** — option **(4)**.
It sums up **material pleasure** as the aim of life and denial of return after the body is **ash**.
The **Ajivikas** stressed fate and **extreme asceticism**, the opposite of this pleasure ethic.
xa: Charvaka is also called **Lokayata** and **Barhaspatya** (after **Brihaspati**).
"**The conscious body is the soul**" — no separate soul survives death.
Known mainly via opponents, e.g. Madhava's **Sarvadarshanasangraha**.

31.s: Which statement about the textual legacy of Lokayata is correct?
o: It survives exclusively through Jain monastic rules.
Its doctrines are preserved only in Ashoka’s edicts.
It left no surviving texts and is known mainly through critics.
Its complete original canon survives in the Brihaspati Sutra.
31.x: Lokayata left no surviving texts and is known mainly through the criticisms and refutations of opposing philosophical traditions.
31.tq: Distinguish direct surviving evidence from information preserved by opponents.
xs: **Lokayata** left **no surviving texts** and is known mainly through **critics** — option **(3)**.
Its original, the **Brihaspati Sutra**, is **lost**.
It is known mainly via opponents' refutations, such as Madhava's **Sarvadarshanasangraha**.
xa: Lokayata = Charvaka = **Barhaspatya** (**APPSC GS 2025**).
⚠ Ashoka's edicts name the **Ajivikas**, not the Charvakas.
Charvaka accepts only **perception** as a means of knowledge.

31.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Jainism — eternal jiva in all things
31.x: Jainism accepts an eternal jiva in all things. Buddhism teaches anatta, Ajivika teaches predetermined fate, and Charvaka rejects Vedic authority.
31.tq: Compare each school across the soul, fate and Vedas columns to detect reversals.
xs: **Jainism — eternal jiva in all things** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Ajivika** held **Niyati** — all predetermined, not effort; **Buddhism** taught **Anatta** — no permanent self.
**Charvaka** **rejected** Vedic authority.
xa: Karma: Jainism — **material bondage** removable by penance; Buddhism — **intention-based**.
Ajivika karma **cannot alter destiny**; Charvaka **denies** karma.
Charvaka soul view: **conscious body = soul**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the views of the four heterodox schools:
1. Jainism regards karma as material bondage removable by penance.
2. Buddhism treats karma as intention-based.
3. Ajivika doctrine holds that karma cannot alter destiny.
4. Charvaka accepts karma as the determining force of rebirth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Jainism treats karma as material bondage removable by penance, Buddhism views it through intention, and Ajivikas deny its power to alter destiny. Charvaka does not accept karma as a determining force of rebirth, so statement 4 is false.
31.tq: Compare the karma column and reject the statement importing rebirth into Charvaka materialism.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: Jainism — karma is **material bondage**, removable by **penance**.
**Statement 2** correct: Buddhism — karma is **intention-based**.
**Statement 3** correct: Ajivika — karma **cannot alter destiny**.
**Statement 4** wrong: Charvaka **denies karma**.
xa: Fate: Jainism and Buddhism — **effort decides**; Ajivika — **Niyati**, all predetermined.
Soul: Jainism — **eternal jiva**; Buddhism — **Anatta**.
Common ground of all four: **rejection of Vedic authority** and ritualism.

31.s: What was common to Jainism, Buddhism, Ajivika and Charvaka in relation to the Vedas?
o: All accepted the Vedas as the highest authority.
Only Charvaka rejected Vedic authority while the others accepted it.
31.x: All four schools rejected Vedic authority. This rejection formed part of the broader Shramana reaction against Vedic ritualism.
31.tq: Identify the common element in a comparison table rather than a school-specific distinction.
xs: **All rejected Vedic authority** — option **(4)**.
Rejection of **Vedic authority and ritualism** is the **common ground** of Jainism, Buddhism, Ajivika and Charvaka.
xa: This was the **Shramana reaction** of the **6th c. BCE**.
It arose amid **urbanisation** and **Magadhan patronage**.
They differed on karma: Charvaka **denied** it; Ajivika said it **cannot alter destiny**.

31.s: The Shramana reaction of the sixth century BCE developed in the context of:
o: The end of all political support for non-Vedic traditions
The exclusive revival of Vedic ritualism in the Deccan
The complete decline of cities and the disappearance of Magadha
31.x: The Shramana reaction, including Jainism, Buddhism, Ajivika and Charvaka currents, arose amid urbanisation and Magadhan patronage in the sixth century BCE.
31.tq: Link an intellectual development with its stated social and political context.
xs: The Shramana reaction arose amid **urbanisation and Magadhan patronage** — option **(1)**.
It belongs to the **6th c. BCE**, and its common ground was rejection of **Vedic authority and ritualism**.
xa: Significance: the **intellectual ferment** of the 6th c. BCE.
The Ajivikas later enjoyed **Mauryan** patronage under **Bindusara** and **Ashoka**.
Decline came with the **Puranic-Bhakti revival** and **loss of royal patronage**.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly contrasts Charvaka epistemology with Nyaya epistemology?
o: Charvaka accepts only perception, whereas Nyaya accepts four pramanas including inference, comparison and testimony.
Charvaka accepts four pramanas, whereas Nyaya accepts only perception.
Both Charvaka and Nyaya reject perception as a valid means of knowledge.
Both schools accept only Vedic testimony.
31.x: Charvaka accepts only perception. Nyaya recognises four pramanas: perception, inference, comparison and testimony.
31.tq: Use the contrastive structure to separate a perception-only system from a multiple-pramana system.
xs: **Charvaka accepts only perception**, while **Nyaya** accepts **four pramanas** — option **(1)**.
Nyaya's four: **perception, inference, comparison, testimony**.
Charvaka rejects **inference** and **testimony (Vedas)**.
xa: Perception is called **pratyaksha**.
Charvaka body-soul view: "**The conscious body is the soul**".
Charvaka is also called **Lokayata** (**APPSC GS 2025**).

31.s:
The significance of the Ajivika, Charvaka and other heterodox traditions includes which of the following?
1. They reflect the intellectual ferment of the sixth century BCE.
2. They illustrate religious pluralism during the Mauryan period.
3. They demonstrate that all ancient Indian schools accepted Vedic ritualism.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
31.x: These sects reflect the intellectual ferment of the sixth century BCE and the religious pluralism of the Mauryan period. They rejected, rather than universally accepted, Vedic authority and ritualism, so statement 3 is false.
31.tq: Reject the sweeping universal statement and retain the two supported significance points.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: the sects reflect the **intellectual ferment** of the **6th c. BCE**.
**Statement 2** correct: they illustrate **Mauryan religious pluralism**.
**Statement 3** wrong: these schools **rejected** Vedic authority and ritualism.
xa: Ashoka's **7th Pillar Edict** names the Ajivikas with Brahmanas, the **Sangha** and **Nirgranthas** — pluralism in action.
The Shramana reaction arose amid **urbanisation** and **Magadhan patronage**.
Comparative note: Charvaka's **perception-only** view vs Nyaya's **four pramanas**.

32.s: Who was the first Achaemenid ruler to campaign into the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent?
32.x: Cyrus, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, was the first Achaemenid ruler to campaign into the Indian north-west, particularly the Gandhara region.
32.tq: Distinguish the first campaign from the later annexation of territory.
xs: **Cyrus**, the founder of the Achaemenid empire (c. **558-530 BC**), was the first to campaign into the Indian **north-west** — option **(4)**.
His campaign touched the **Gandhara** region.
**Darius I** came later and annexed Punjab/Sindh as the **20th satrapy**; **Xerxes** used Indian soldiers against the Greeks.
xa: ⚠ **FIRST** into the north-west = **Cyrus**; **20th satrapy** = **Darius I**.
**Herodotus**: the Indian satrapy was the **most populous and fertile**, paying **360 talents of gold dust**.
That tribute was **one-third** of the empire's revenue.

32.s: Which Achaemenid ruler annexed Punjab and Sindh west of the Indus?
32.x: Darius I annexed Punjab and Sindh west of the Indus. This territory became the twentieth satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire.
32.tq: Match the ruler with the specific territorial achievement rather than with the earlier campaign.
xs: **Darius I** (c. **522-486 BC**) annexed **Punjab/Sindh west of the Indus** — option **(2)**.
It became the **20th satrapy** of the Achaemenid empire.
**Cyrus** only campaigned first into the north-west; **Xerxes** used Indian soldiers against the Greeks; **Darius III** was the king **Alexander** defeated.
xa: The Indian satrapy paid **360 talents of gold dust** = **one-third** of imperial revenue (**Herodotus**).
Ashokan edicts copy the **Darius** model — words **"lipi/dipi"**, third person shifting to first person.
The **satrapy system** of administration became known in the north-west.

32.s: According to Herodotus, the Indian satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire was notable for which combination?
o: Being the most populous and fertile, and paying 360 talents of gold dust
Being the smallest satrapy and supplying only horses
Being exclusively pastoral and paying no tribute
Being the least populous and paying silver tribute
32.x: Herodotus described the Indian satrapy as the most populous and fertile. It paid 360 talents of gold dust, stated to be one-third of the empire's revenue.
32.tq: Combine the descriptive and quantitative clues instead of selecting only one part of the statement.
xs: **Herodotus** called the Indian satrapy the **most populous and fertile**, paying **360 talents of gold dust** — option **(1)**.
That tribute was **one-third** of the empire's revenue.
xa: The satrapy was Punjab/Sindh **west of the Indus**, annexed by **Darius I** as the **20th satrapy**.
**Cyrus** (founder) was the first Achaemenid into the north-west.
**Xerxes** used Indian soldiers against the Greeks.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Persian influence in north-western India:
1. Kharosthi, derived from Aramaic, was written from left to right.
2. Ashoka's Kandahar edict used Aramaic.
3. The satrapy system of administration was known in the north-west.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Kharosthi was written from right to left. Statement 2 is correct: the Kandahar edict used Aramaic. Statement 3 is correct: the satrapy system was known in the north-west. So 2 and 3 only (C); A, B and D include the false statement 1.
32.tq: Kharosthi runs right to left, like its parent Aramaic.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** only are correct — option **(3)**.
**Statement 1** wrong: **Kharosthi**, derived from **Aramaic**, was written **right to left**.
**Statement 2** correct: Ashoka's **Kandahar edict** used **Aramaic**.
**Statement 3** correct: the **satrapy system** was known in the north-west.
xa: Ashokan edicts copy **Darius** — words **"lipi/dipi"**; third person opening, then first person.
Ashokan pillars resemble Persian ones in **polished surface** and **animal capitals**.
But they differ: **no base**, **inverted lotus**, **smooth** (not fluted) shaft.

32.s: Which features of Ashokan edicts are associated with the Darius model?
o: The terms lipi or dipi and an opening in the third person followed by a shift to the first person
Only the use of Greek language and a circular script
A purely oral form without written terminology
The exclusive use of Persian royal titles
32.x: Ashokan edicts reflect the Darius model through the terms lipi or dipi and the stylistic movement from third-person opening to first-person expression.
32.tq: Look for the option containing both distinctive textual features rather than a general claim of influence.
xs: Ashokan edicts copy **Darius** in the words **"lipi/dipi"** and in opening in the **third person** then shifting to the **first person** — option **(1)**.
This is part of the **Persian legacy** in north-western India.
xa: Script: **Kharosthi** (right to left) derived from **Aramaic**; the **Kandahar edict** used Aramaic.
Pillars: **polished surface** and **animal capitals** resemble Persian ones.
Administration: the **satrapy system** was known in the north-west.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Ashokan pillars and Persian pillars:
1. Ashokan pillars resemble Persian pillars in their polished surface and animal capitals.
2. Ashokan pillars generally have fluted shafts and a conventional base.
3. Ashokan pillars have smooth shafts and an inverted lotus, unlike the Persian form in the stated respects.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Ashokan pillars resemble Persian pillars in polished surfaces and animal capitals. They have no base, an inverted lotus and smooth rather than fluted shafts, making statement 2 false.
32.tq: Separate shared features from the specific architectural differences.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1** correct: resemblance in **polished surface** and **animal capitals**.
**Statement 2** wrong: Ashokan pillars have **no base** and a **smooth (not fluted) shaft**.
**Statement 3** correct: **smooth shaft** and **inverted lotus** set them apart.
xa: Edicts too copy **Darius** — "**lipi/dipi**", third-person opening.
**Kharosthi**, derived from **Aramaic**, ran **right to left**.
Persian contact (**6th-5th c. BC**) left a lasting **script and art** legacy.

32.s: At the time of Alexander's invasion, the north-western part of India was politically characterised by which condition?
o: A single empire under the Nandas
A federation led by the Achaemenids
Small independent states such as Taxila, Porus's Punjab and Gandhara
32.x: The north-west was divided into small independent states, including Taxila, Porus's Punjab and Gandhara, rather than being united under one central power.
32.tq: Identify the broad political pattern instead of focusing on one ruler.
xs: The north-west was split into **small independent states** — **Taxila**, **Porus's Punjab**, **Gandhara** — option **(4)**.
This meant **no united resistance** to Alexander.
**Magadha** in the east was under the **Nanda dynasty** (Dhana Nanda), not the north-west.
xa: Causes of success (**UPPSC 2003** key "1, 2 and 3"): **no central power**, **superior army**, help from **traitorous Indian rulers**.
**Ambhi** of **Taxila** was the **first to surrender**.
The invasion later destroyed these small states, clearing the way for **Chandragupta**.

32.s: Which feature of the Nanda kingdom is said to have deterred Alexander from marching farther east?
o: Its alliance with the Greek settlements
Its absence of a standing army
32.x: The huge army of the Nanda kingdom deterred Alexander from advancing farther east. Dhana Nanda was, however, unpopular because of heavy taxation.
32.tq: Match the strategic consequence with the specific military feature.
xs: The Nandas' **huge army** deterred Alexander's eastward march — option **(1)**.
**Fear of the Nanda army** was also a cause of the refusal at the **Beas**.
xa: The Nanda ruler was **Dhana Nanda**, Greek "**Agrammes/Xandrames**".
The Nandas were **unpopular** for **heavy taxation**.
Other causes of the Beas refusal: **war weariness**, **homesickness**, **disease**.

32.s: Which one of the following was NOT identified as a cause of Alexander's success in India?
o: The assistance of some traitorous Indian rulers
The absence of a central power
His highly effective system of administration in India
32.x: Alexander's success was attributed to the absence of a central power, his superior army and assistance from traitorous Indian rulers. His administration was not identified as a cause.
32.tq: Find the non-cause by distinguishing military and political advantages from administrative achievements.
xs: **His administration in India** was not a cause of success — option **(4)**.
The causes (**UPPSC 2003** key "1, 2 and 3") were **no central power**, **superior army** and help from **traitorous Indian rulers**.
xa: The north-west was split into small states (**Taxila**, **Porus's Punjab**, **Gandhara**) → **no united resistance**.
**Ambhi** of Taxila surrendered first and **helped** Alexander.
After conquest, the area was split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.

32.s: The Nanda ruler of Magadha whom Greek writers called 'Agrammes' or 'Xandrames' was
32.x: Greek writers called Dhana Nanda 'Agrammes' or 'Xandrames'; his huge army deterred Alexander, though he was unpopular for heavy taxation. Bindusara was a Maurya and Ajatashatru a Haryanka; Mahapadma Nanda is not the ruler named in the Greek accounts of Alexander's time.
32.tq: Agrammes/Xandrames = Dhana Nanda.
xs: Greek writers called **Dhana Nanda** "**Agrammes/Xandrames**" — option **(1)**.
He ruled **Magadha** of the **Nanda dynasty** at the time of Alexander's invasion.
**Bindusara** was a later Maurya, who received **Deimachus**, envoy of **Antiochus I**.
xa: The Nandas' **huge army** deterred Alexander's eastward march.
Dhana Nanda was **unpopular** for **heavy taxation**.
**Fear of the Nanda army** helped turn Alexander's army back at the **Beas**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Alexander's route into India:
1. He crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BC.
2. He entered India through the Khyber Pass in 326 BC.
3. He entered India through the Bolan Pass in 326 BC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BC and entered India through the Khyber Pass in 326 BC. The Bolan Pass is not associated with this route.
32.tq: Split the route into the mountain crossing and the actual entry route; the similar pass name is the trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: crossed the **Hindu Kush** in **327 BC** (**APPSC G2 2008** key: invaded 327 BC).
**Statement 2** correct: entered India through the **Khyber Pass** in **326 BC** (**APPSC-GS 2025**); so **statement 3** (Bolan) is wrong.
xa: **Battle of Hydaspes** with **Porus**: **326 BC**.
Campaign in India lasted about **19 months**.
Alexander died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.

32.s: Who was the first among the following Indian rulers to surrender to Alexander and subsequently assist him?
32.x: Ambhi, also called Omphis, the king of Taxila, was the first to surrender and helped Alexander.
32.tq: Test the precise response of a ruler, not merely his geographical association.
xs: **Ambhi** (Omphis), king of **Taxila**, was the **first to surrender** and helped Alexander — option **(3)**.
**Porus** resisted at the Hydaspes; **Abhisara** (Kashmir hills) submitted later; **Dhana Nanda** of Magadha was never reached.
xa: Exam angle: "first to submit" = **Ambhi**; "whose women fought" = **Massaga**.
The **Assakenoi** (capital **Massaga**, Swat valley) put up fierce resistance.
The **Malloi (Malavas)** fought him during the **retreat**.

32.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Porus — Kingdom between the Jhelum and Chenab
Assakenoi — Gandhara, with Pushkalavati as capital
32.x: The Assakenoi, or Ashvakas, had Massaga as their capital in the Swat valley. The other three associations are correct.
32.tq: Find the wrong ruler–territory or people–capital pairing among closely related north-western groups.
xs: **Assakenoi — Gandhara, with Pushkalavati as capital** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **Assakenoi (Ashvakas)** had their capital at **Massaga** in the **Swat valley**.
The other pairs are right: **Abhisara** — Kashmir hills; **Ambhi** — **Taxila**; **Porus** — between **Jhelum and Chenab**.
xa: At Massaga, **women took up arms** after heavy losses (**UPPSC 2013**).
Ambhi was the **first to surrender**; Abhisara **submitted**.
Porus resisted at the **Hydaspes** and was restored to his kingdom.

32.s: Which of the following groups fought Alexander during his retreat from the north-western region?
32.x: The Malloi or Malavas and other gana-sanghas fought Alexander during his retreat.
32.tq: Distinguish resistance during the retreat from submission or resistance at the initial advance.
xs: The **Malloi (Malavas)** and other **gana-sanghas** fought Alexander during his **retreat** — option **(4)**.
The **Nandas** of Magadha were never fought; their huge army only **deterred** his eastward march.
xa: On the retreat he withdrew down the **Indus**; **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.
Earlier resistance: the **Assakenoi** of **Massaga** and **Porus** at the Hydaspes.
He died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.

32.s: During Alexander's invasion, the women of which people took up arms after their men suffered heavy losses?
o: The people of Taxila under Ambhi
The subjects of Porus on the Jhelum
32.x: The Assakenoi (Ashvakas), with their capital at Massaga in the Swat valley, resisted fiercely, and their women took up arms after heavy losses (UPPSC 2013). Ambhi of Taxila surrendered first, Abhisara submitted, and Porus fought at the Hydaspes.
32.tq: Women fought Alexander = Massaga (Assakenoi).
xs: The **Assakenoi (Ashvakas)** of **Massaga** — their **women took up arms** after heavy losses — option **(1)**.
Massaga lay in the **Swat valley** (**UPPSC 2013**).
**Ambhi** of Taxila **surrendered first**, **Abhisara** submitted, and **Porus** fought at the Hydaspes.
xa: Porus was defeated but Alexander **restored his kingdom** (later enlarged).
UPPSC 2013 also: king defeated on the **Jhelum** = **Porus**.
The **Malloi (Malavas)** fought him during the retreat.

32.s: The Battle of Hydaspes was fought on the bank of which river?
32.x: The Hydaspes was the Jhelum, called Vitasta in Sanskrit. The battle was fought there in 326 BC.
32.tq: Discriminate between the Greek and Indian names of the same river.
xs: The **Hydaspes** is the **Jhelum**, Sanskrit **Vitasta** — option **(4)**.
The battle with **Porus** was fought there in **326 BC**.
⚠ The **Beas** is the Greek **Hyphasis** — Alexander's furthest point, not the battle site.
xa: **Bucephala** (after his horse) and **Nicaea** were founded near the battlefield.
**12 large stone altars** stand on the **northern bank of the Beas**.
Porus's kingdom lay between the **Jhelum and Chenab**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Battle of Hydaspes:
1. It was fought in 326 BC.
2. Alexander fought Porus in the battle.
3. Porus was executed after his defeat.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The battle was fought in 326 BC between Alexander and Porus. Porus was defeated but was not executed; Alexander restored and later enlarged his kingdom.
32.tq: Use the outcome as the trap while retaining the correct date and opponents.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statements 1 and 2** correct: **Alexander** fought **Porus** at the Hydaspes in **326 BC**.
**Statement 3** wrong: impressed by his bravery, Alexander **restored his kingdom** (later enlarged).
xa: Hydaspes = **Jhelum** = **Vitasta**; UPPSC 2013: king defeated on the Jhelum = **Porus**.
**Bucephala** and **Nicaea** were founded near the battlefield.
Porus (**Parvataka**) later allied with **Chandragupta** to expel the Greek satraps.

32.s: Which pair of settlements was founded by Alexander near the battlefield of the Hydaspes?
32.x: Alexander founded Bucephala, named after his horse, and Nicaea near the Hydaspes battlefield.
32.tq: Start from the distinctive name linked with Alexander's horse and identify its associated settlement.
xs: **Bucephala** (named after his horse) and **Nicaea** were founded near the Hydaspes — option **(2)**.
**Taxila** was Ambhi's kingdom and **Massaga** the Assakenoi capital — not Alexander's foundations.
xa: The Hydaspes battle with **Porus**: **326 BC**.
Greek settlements such as **Alexandria** and **Bucephala** were an effect of the invasion.
⚠ **Hydaspes** = **Jhelum**; **Hyphasis** = **Beas**.

32.s: Which of the following was NOT among the reasons for Alexander's army refusing to proceed beyond the Beas?
o: A treaty imposed by Dhana Nanda
32.x: War weariness, homesickness, disease and fear of the Nanda army contributed to the refusal. No treaty imposed by Dhana Nanda is identified as a reason.
32.tq: Find the option outside the stated cluster of military, physical and psychological causes.
xs: **A treaty imposed by Dhana Nanda** was not a reason — option **(2)**.
The causes were **war weariness**, **homesickness**, **disease** and **fear of the Nanda army**.
xa: The army refused to go beyond the **Beas (Hyphasis)**, his furthest point.
He set up **12 large stone altars** on its northern bank.
He then withdrew down the **Indus**; **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.

32.s: The Greek name Hyphasis refers to which river?
32.x: Hyphasis was the Greek name for the Beas, beyond which Alexander's army refused to advance.
32.tq: Discriminate between the Greek names of the rivers encountered during the campaign.
xs: **Hyphasis** is the Greek name of the **Beas** — option **(1)**.
It was Alexander's **furthest point**: his army refused to go beyond it.
The **Jhelum** was the **Hydaspes** (Sanskrit **Vitasta**).
xa: **12 large stone altars** were set up on the **northern bank** of the Beas.
Causes of refusal: war weariness, homesickness, disease, **fear of the Nanda army**.
⚠ **Hydaspes** = **Jhelum** = **Vitasta**; **Hyphasis** = **Beas**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Alexander's retreat:
1. He set up twelve large stone altars on the northern bank of the Beas.
2. He withdrew down the Indus while Nearchus led the fleet by sea.
3. His campaign in India lasted about 29 months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the campaign lasted about 19 months; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE. So 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
32.tq: Alexander in India: about 19 months.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: **12 large stone altars** on the **northern bank of the Beas**.
**Statement 2** correct: he withdrew down the **Indus** while **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.
**Statement 3** wrong: the campaign lasted about **19 months**.
xa: He died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.
Entry via **Khyber Pass** in **326 BC**; **Hydaspes** battle the same year.
Nearchus, the **admiral**, left a first-hand account.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the effects of Alexander's invasion:
1. The conquered area was divided into three parts under Greek governors.
2. Most states that had submitted were annexed directly and not returned to their rulers.
3. Greek settlements such as Alexandria and Bucephala were founded.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: three parts under Greek governors. Statement 2 is wrong: most states were returned to the rulers who had submitted. Statement 3 is correct: Alexandria and Bucephala were Greek settlements. So 1 and 3 only (B); A, C and D include the false statement 2 or leave out a true one.
32.tq: Three satrapies under Greeks; submitting rulers got their states back.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1** correct: the area was split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.
**Statement 2** wrong: most states were **returned to rulers who submitted**.
**Statement 3** correct: Greek settlements such as **Alexandria** and **Bucephala**.
xa: Direct **Greece-India contact** and new **land and sea routes** opened.
**Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** recorded Indian geography and society.
Small NW states were destroyed → cleared the way for **Chandragupta**.

32.s: Which was a major geographical and commercial consequence of Alexander's invasion?
o: It replaced all Indian routes with Persian routes
It restricted communication to the Himalayan passes
It opened direct contact and new land and sea routes between Greece and India
It ended all contact between Greece and India
32.x: The invasion opened direct contact between Greece and India and encouraged new land and sea routes.
32.tq: Apply the historical consequence to the question of connectivity and routes.
xs: The invasion opened **direct contact** and **new land and sea routes** between **Greece and India** — option **(3)**.
Greek settlements like **Alexandria** and **Bucephala** followed.
xa: **Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** recorded Indian **geography and society**.
The conquered area was split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.
Politically, it cleared the way for **Chandragupta**.

32.s: The accounts of Onesicritus and Nearchus are particularly important because they recorded information about:
o: The complete history of the Vedic period
The religious reforms of Ashoka alone
32.x: The accounts of Onesicritus and Nearchus recorded observations on Indian geography and society.
32.tq: Match the source with the type of information it preserved.
xs: **Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** recorded Indian **geography and society** — option **(2)**.
Both came **with Alexander** and left **first-hand accounts**.
xa: **Aristobulus** also accompanied Alexander.
**Arrian**, **Curtius**, **Plutarch**, Diodorus and Justin were **later** (Roman-era) writers.
**Indian sources are silent** on Alexander — the campaign is known only from Greek writers.

32.s: Which development did Alexander's invasion help make possible in north-western India?
o: The restoration of Nanda power over all India
The permanent rule of Porus over Magadha
The rise of Chandragupta after the Greek satraps were expelled
The establishment of Achaemenid control over Pataliputra
32.x: The invasion destroyed several small north-western states and cleared the way for Chandragupta, who expelled the Greek satraps with Porus, also called Parvataka, as an ally.
32.tq: Connect political disruption with the later emergence of a larger power.
xs: The invasion paved the way for the **rise of Chandragupta**, who **expelled the Greek satraps** — option **(3)**.
It destroyed the **small NW states**, clearing the way for him.
His ally was **Porus (Parvataka)**.
xa: Greeks name **Sandrokottas** (Chandragupta) as a contemporary — anchor of chronology (c. **322 BCE**).
The conquered area had been split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.
Alexander had **restored Porus's kingdom** after the Hydaspes.

32.s: Who among the following accompanied Alexander and left a first-hand account of his campaign?
32.x: Nearchus, Alexander's admiral, accompanied him and left a first-hand account. Arrian and Plutarch were later writers, while Deimachus was a later envoy.
32.tq: Use the distinction between eyewitness companions and later reconstructive writers.
xs: **Nearchus**, Alexander's **admiral**, came with him and left a **first-hand account** — option **(2)**.
**Plutarch** and **Arrian** were **later** Roman-era writers.
**Deimachus** was a later envoy of **Antiochus I** to **Bindusara** — he did not come with Alexander (**UPPSC 2015**).
xa: Other first-hand writers: **Onesicritus** and **Aristobulus**.
Nearchus led the **fleet by sea** during the return.
**Indian sources are silent** on Alexander.

32.s: Which of the following writers belonged to the later Roman-era group that reconstructed Alexander's campaign?
32.x: Arrian was a later writer who reconstructed the campaign. Nearchus, Onesicritus and Aristobulus accompanied Alexander and provided first-hand accounts.
32.tq: Separate later historians from the original companions by their status.
xs: **Arrian** was a **later (Roman-era) writer** who reconstructed the campaign — option **(4)**.
**Aristobulus**, **Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** came **with Alexander** and left first-hand accounts.
xa: Other later writers: **Curtius**, **Plutarch**, Diodorus, Justin.
**Deimachus** was envoy of Antiochus I to **Bindusara** (**UPPSC 2015**).
Indian sources are **silent** — only Greek writers record the campaign.

32.s: Deimachus is correctly described as:
o: Alexander's admiral who sailed down the Indus
A later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara
32.x: Deimachus was a later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara and did not accompany Alexander.
32.tq: Test the look-alike category of a Greek-associated name against the correct diplomatic role.
xs: **Deimachus** was a later **envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara** — option **(3)**.
He **did not come with Alexander** (**UPPSC 2015**).
Alexander's **admiral** who led the fleet was **Nearchus**; the Nanda ruler was **Dhana Nanda**.
xa: First-hand writers: **Nearchus**, **Onesicritus**, **Aristobulus**.
Later writers: **Arrian**, **Curtius**, **Plutarch**.
**Bucephala** was founded by **Alexander**, after his horse.

32.s: The name 'Sandrokottas' in Greek accounts has been identified with which Indian ruler?
32.x: Greek writers used the name Sandrokottas for Chandragupta Maurya, helping establish the chronology of the early Mauryas around 322 BCE.
32.tq: Use the Greek–Indian name equivalence as a chronology anchor.
xs: **Sandrokottas** is **Chandragupta Maurya** — option **(3)**.
Greeks name him as a **contemporary**, the anchor of early Indian chronology (c. **322 BCE**).
xa: Chandragupta expelled the **Greek satraps** with **Porus (Parvataka)** as ally.
Alexander's invasion is the **first dated event** of Indian history.
**Dhana Nanda** was called **Agrammes/Xandrames** by the Greeks.

32.s: Which statement best expresses the historical significance of Alexander's invasion for Indian chronology?
o: It is regarded as the first dated event of Indian history and helps fix Mauryan chronology through Greek accounts.
It establishes the exact dates of all Gupta rulers.
It proves that Indian chronology was based only on Persian inscriptions.
It provides the first complete indigenous chronology of the Vedic age.
32.x: Alexander's invasion is regarded as the first dated event of Indian history, and Greek accounts help fix the chronology of the Mauryas.
32.tq: Select the precise significance rather than an exaggerated claim about all Indian chronology.
xs: Alexander's invasion is the **first dated event of Indian history**; Greek accounts **fix Mauryan chronology** — option **(1)**.
Greeks name **Sandrokottas** (Chandragupta) as a contemporary (c. **322 BCE**).
xa: **Indian sources are silent** on Alexander.
Key dates: Hindu Kush **327 BC**; Khyber Pass and Hydaspes **326 BC**; death at **Babylon** **323 BCE**.
First-hand Greek writers: **Nearchus**, **Onesicritus**, **Aristobulus**.

32.s: Which comparison between Persian contact and Alexander's invasion is correct?
o: Alexander's campaign created the lasting script legacy, whereas Persian contact had no artistic influence.
Persian contact left a lasting script and art legacy, whereas Alexander's nineteen-month campaign left little political mark.
Both contacts permanently replaced all Indian political institutions.
Neither contact influenced writing, art, routes or chronology.
32.x: Persian contact during the sixth–fifth centuries BC left lasting influences on script and art, while Alexander's nineteen-month campaign left almost no lasting political mark.
32.tq: Compare the duration and long-term nature of the two foreign contacts without reversing their effects.
xs: **Persian contact** left a lasting **script and art** legacy, while Alexander's **19-month** campaign left **almost no political mark** — option **(2)**.
Persian contact belongs to the **6th-5th c. BC**.
xa: Script legacy: **Kharosthi** from **Aramaic**, written right to left.
Art legacy: Ashokan pillars' **polished surface** and **animal capitals**.
Alexander's legacy was mainly **contact and routes**, Greek settlements, and **chronology**.

33.s:
Kautilya is also known by which of the following names?
1. Chanakya
2. Vishnugupta
3. Megasthenes
4. Pushyagupta
33.x: Kautilya is also known as Chanakya and Vishnugupta. Megasthenes was a Greek envoy, while Pushyagupta was a governor associated with the Sudarshana lake.
33.tq: Separate alternative names of a historical figure from other Mauryan-period personalities.
xs: Kautilya is also **Chanakya** and **Vishnugupta**, so **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
**Megasthenes** was the Greek author of the **Indica**.
**Pushyagupta** was Chandragupta's **governor** who built the **Sudarshana lake** (Junagadh inscription).
xa: Kautilya wrote the **Arthashastra** on **statecraft** (APPSC-GS 2023 match).
It was rediscovered by **R. Shamasastry** (Mysore, **1905**; published **1909**).
It has **15 books (adhikaranas)**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the Arthashastra:
1. It was rediscovered by R. Shamasastry at Mysore in 1905.
2. It consists of 15 books called adhikaranas.
3. It was first published in 1837.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: it was published in 1909; 1837 is the year James Prinsep deciphered the Ashokan edicts. So 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
33.tq: Shamasastry: found 1905, published 1909; Prinsep: 1837.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: **R. Shamasastry** rediscovered it at **Mysore** in **1905**.
**Statement 2** correct: it has **15 books (adhikaranas)**.
**Statement 3** wrong: it was published in **1909**; **1837** is when **James Prinsep** deciphered the Ashokan edicts.
xa: ⚠ Found **1905**, published **1909** — both by **Shamasastry**.
Author: **Kautilya** = **Chanakya** = **Vishnugupta**.
Topics include **slavery rules**, the **Saptanga** state, revenue and courts.

33.s: The Arthashastra is often compared with Machiavelli's The Prince primarily because both are associated with
o: realist politics and the use of ends to justify means
33.x: Both works are commonly compared for their realist approach to politics and their emphasis on ends-justify-means reasoning.
33.tq: Identify the basis of comparison rather than merely recalling the names of the two works.
xs: Both stand for **realist**, **ends-justify-means** politics — option **(1)**.
The Arthashastra is a treatise on **statecraft** — administration, economy, espionage, taxation, diplomacy, welfare.
xa: Author: **Kautilya** (Chanakya, Vishnugupta).
Rediscovered by **R. Shamasastry** in **1905**.
Structure: **15 books (adhikaranas)**; covers the **Saptanga** state.

33.s: Which literary source is primarily associated with administration, economy, espionage and taxation?
33.x: Kautilya's Arthashastra deals with administration, economy, espionage and taxation.
33.tq: Match a work with its central subject rather than its author alone.
xs: The **Arthashastra** deals with **administration, economy, espionage and taxation** — option **(1)**.
**Mudrarakshasa** is a drama on the Nandas' overthrow; **Indica** is Megasthenes' Greek account; **Parishishtaparvan** is Jain, on Chandragupta's conversion.
xa: Arthashastra also covers **diplomacy** and **welfare**.
Compared with **Machiavelli's The Prince**.
It has **15 books (adhikaranas)**, rediscovered by **Shamasastry**.

33.s: The original work of Megasthenes known as Indica is
o: preserved in its complete original form at Pataliputra
inscribed on the pillars of Ashoka
available only as a Jain manuscript from Shravanabelagola
lost, with fragments preserved by later classical writers
33.x: The original Indica has been lost. Its fragments survive in the works of Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny and Arrian.
33.tq: Distinguish an original lost work from later quotations and compilations.
xs: The original **Indica** is **lost**; fragments survive in later classical writers — option **(4)**.
Those writers are **Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny and Arrian**.
xa: Indica covers Mauryan **society, administration** and **Pataliputra**.
It is the **first foreign work** to mention the **Andhras** (**30** fortified towns).
Errors: **gold-digging ants**, **seven castes**, **no slavery** claim.

33.s: Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra by the name
33.x: Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra as Palibothra, also rendered in some accounts as Polibrotha.
33.tq: Discriminate between the Greek form of a place-name and Indian place-names from other contexts.
xs: Megasthenes called Pataliputra **Palibothra** — option **(1)**.
**UKPSC 2025** spelt it "**Polibrotha**".
xa: He described the **palace** (remains at **Kumrahar**) and the **city boards**.
The **80-pillared hall** at **Kumrahar** near Patna is part of the Pataliputra ruins.
Indica's fragments survive in **Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny, Arrian**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Megasthenes' account of Indian society:
1. He described society as divided into seven classes.
2. He noted endogamy and hereditary occupations.
3. His description exactly followed the fourfold varna classification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Megasthenes described seven classes and noted endogamy and hereditary occupations. His classification was not the fourfold varna system, making statement 3 incorrect.
33.tq: Spot the reversed comparison between the seven-class description and the fourfold varna scheme.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: Megasthenes described **seven classes** (castes).
**Statement 2** correct: he noted **endogamy** and **hereditary occupations**.
**Statement 3** wrong: his list is **not the fourfold varna**.
xa: The seven: **philosophers, farmers, soldiers, herdsmen, artisans, overseers, councillors**.
The seven "castes" and no-slavery claim are known **misreadings**.
He also wrongly claimed **no slavery**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the limitations of Megasthenes' Indica:
1. It contains uncritical folklore such as the gold-digging ants.
2. Strabo, following Megasthenes, said that Indians did not know writing.
3. Megasthenes correctly reported that slavery was widespread in Mauryan India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: both are known errors of the Indica tradition. Statement 3 is wrong: Megasthenes claimed there was no slavery, which is contradicted by the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts that mention dasas. So 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
33.tq: Megasthenes' 'no slavery' claim is a known misreading.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** only are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1** correct: **uncritical folklore** such as **gold-digging ants**.
**Statement 2** correct: **Strabo**, following him, said Indians **did not know writing**.
**Statement 3** wrong: Megasthenes claimed **no slavery**; the **Arthashastra** and **Ashokan edicts** mention **dasas**.
xa: He also described **seven classes**, not the fourfold varna.
The original **Indica** is lost; known through **fragments**.
⚠ Despite errors, it is the **first foreign mention** of the **Andhras**.

33.s: Which foreign writer was the first to mention the Andhras, crediting them with 30 fortified towns and an army of 1,00,000 infantry?
33.x: Megasthenes' Indica is the first foreign work to mention the Andhras, with 30 fortified towns and 1,00,000 infantry besides cavalry and elephants. Deimachus was Antiochus I's envoy to Bindusara; Strabo and Arrian only preserved fragments of the Indica.
33.tq: First to mention Andhra forts = Megasthenes (APPSC G2 2002); 30 forts.
xs: **Megasthenes** in the **Indica** first mentioned the **Andhras** — option **(1)**.
He credited them with **30 fortified towns** and **1,00,000 infantry** (plus cavalry and elephants).
**Strabo** and **Arrian** only preserve fragments of the Indica.
xa: **APPSC G2 2002**: who first mentioned Andhra forts = **Megasthenes**.
⚠ Some notes print "**80 forts**" — a misprint; the correct figure is **30**.
⚠ **80** is the **pillared hall** at **Kumrahar**, not the forts.

33.s: Who wrote the Sanskrit drama Mudrarakshasa, which describes the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya?
33.x: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa. The drama deals with the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya.
33.tq: Use the author–work association and beware of swapping authors of related literary sources.
xs: **Vishakhadatta** wrote **Mudrarakshasa** — option **(3)**.
It is a Sanskrit drama on the **overthrow of the Nandas** and **rise of Chandragupta** (**APPSC-G1 2002**).
**Hemachandra** wrote **Parishishtaparvan**; **Dandin** **Dashakumaracharita**; **Patanjali** **Mahabhashya**.
xa: **Kathasaritsagara** — **Somadeva**; **Brihatkathamanjari** — **Kshemendra**.
**Rajatarangini** — **Kalhana**.
The **Puranas** (esp. **Vishnu Purana**) give Mauryan king lists.

33.s: Mamulanar, belonging to the Sangam tradition, is associated with references to the Mauryas'
33.x: Mamulanar's Sangam reference concerns the southward push of the Mauryas.
33.tq: Identify the distinctive event linked with the named literary source.
xs: Sangam poet **Mamulanar** refers to the Mauryas' **southward push** — option **(3)**.
**Conversion to Jainism** is Chandragupta's story in the Jain **Parishishtaparvan**.
xa: Tamil Sangam poems thus record **southern expansion** of the Mauryas.
Mauryan **punch-marked coins** and **NBPW** are found as far as **Andhra** and **Karnataka**.
**Mudrarakshasa** (Vishakhadatta) covers the rise of **Chandragupta**.

33.s: Which Purana is usually cited as an important source for Mauryan king lists and genealogies?
33.x: The Puranas provide Mauryan king lists and genealogies, with the Vishnu Purana being the one usually cited.
33.tq: Match the historical use of the Puranas with the specifically cited Purana.
xs: The **Vishnu Purana** is the one usually cited for **Mauryan king lists** — option **(3)**.
The **Puranas** give **genealogies** of Mauryan kings.
xa: **Mudrarakshasa** (**Vishakhadatta**) — overthrow of the Nandas.
**Dipavamsa** and **Mahavamsa** — Ashoka and Buddhism in Lanka.
**Parishishtaparvan** (**Hemachandra**) — Chandragupta's conversion to Jainism.

33.s: Which one of the following works is a commentary on the Mahavamsa?
33.x: Vamsatthapakasini is identified as a commentary on the Mahavamsa.
33.tq: Discriminate between similarly listed literary works by identifying the work's specific function.
