**Mahadeva Bhikshu** (not Megasthenes) is tied to Amaravati; **"Andhapatha"** is in the **Vinayavatthu**, a text.
xa: He was the **first to mention forts in Andhra** — **30 walled towns** (G2 **2002**).
He was the ambassador of **Seleucus**.
The first mention of the Andhras at all is the **Aitareya Brahmana**.

40.s: According to Megasthenes, the Andhras possessed how many forts or walled towns?
40.x: Megasthenes stated that the Andhras possessed 30 forts, described as walled towns, and that they lived in towns.
40.tq: Use the distinctive quantitative detail attached to Megasthenes’ description.
xs: Megasthenes says the Andhras had **30 forts** (walled towns) — option **(2)**.
He was the **first to mention forts in Andhra** (G2 **2002**).
xa: He noted the **Andhras lived in towns**.
His **Indica** is the first foreign source to mention the Andhras.
He came as the ambassador of **Seleucus**.

40.s: Which early historic site in Krishna district shows continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times?
40.x: Gudiwada Dibba in Krishna district is an early historic mound showing continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times.
40.tq: Use the site–district–cultural sequence combination for archaeological identification.
xs: **Gudiwada Dibba** (Krishna district) shows continuous occupation from **Mauryan to Satavahana** times — option **(2)**.
**Adurru** was a Mahasanghika centre; **Rajula Mandagiri** has an Ashokan minor edict; **Nagarjunakonda** is ancient Sriparvata.
xa: The **Nagarjunasagar valley** digs give material proof of early Andhra settlement.
⚠ Some notes place **Siddharthaka chaitya** at Gudiwada; the key says **Guntupalli**.
Andhra was a distinct region **before the Satavahanas**.

40.s: Adurru, located in East Godavari district, was an important centre of the:
40.x: Adurru in East Godavari district was a Mahasanghika Buddhist centre.
40.tq: Match the archaeological site with its religious affiliation.
xs: **Adurru** (East Godavari) was a **Mahasanghika** Buddhist centre — option **(4)**.
The **Andhakas** were a separate Buddhist school (Kathavatthu, Third Council).
xa: **Gudiwada Dibba** shows Mauryan-to-Satavahana occupation.
**Nagarjunasagar valley** excavations prove early Andhra settlement.
The Mauryan phase made Buddhism **institutional** in Andhra.

40.s: What is the principal historical significance of excavations in the Nagarjunasagar valley?
o: They prove that Amaravati was a Mauryan capital.
They establish that the region was first settled only under the Satavahanas.
They provide material proof of an early Andhra settlement.
They reveal the earliest Greek settlement in Andhra.
40.x: Excavations in the Nagarjunasagar valley provide material evidence for an early Andhra settlement, supporting the antiquity of Andhra as a distinct region.
40.tq: Infer the historical significance from the archaeological evidence rather than the religious association of the site.
xs: **Nagarjunasagar valley** excavations give **material proof of early "Andhra" settlement** — option **(3)**.
They do not make Amaravati a Mauryan capital or date settlement only to the Satavahanas.
xa: **Sriparvata / Vijayapuri** = **Nagarjunakonda**.
**Gudiwada Dibba**: occupation from **Mauryan to Satavahana** times.
**Adurru**: a **Mahasanghika** centre.

40.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
40.x: Siddharthaka Chaitya is identified with Guntupalli in Eluru district. Sriparvata is Nagarjunakonda, Andhranagari is Amaravati-Dharanikota, and Andhapura is associated with the Telavaha crossing in the Serivanija Jataka.
40.tq: Start with the sure ancient-name–modern-site pair and eliminate the swapped identifications.
xs: **Siddharthaka chaitya** = **Guntupalli** (Eluru district) — option **(1)** (G2 **2008** key).
**Sriparvata** = **Nagarjunakonda**, not Amaravati; **Andhranagari** = **Amaravati-Dharanikota**, not Nagarjunakonda.
**Andhapura** was reached across the **Telavaha** (Serivanija Jataka), not Dharanikota.
xa: ⚠ Some notes put Siddharthaka at **Gudiwada** — go with the key.
Sriparvata is also called **Vijayapuri**.
**Guntupalli** chaitya is compared with the **Barabar caves**.

40.s: Andhranagari or Dhanyakataka is identified with:
40.x: Andhranagari, also called Dhanyakataka, is identified with Amaravati-Dharanikota on the Krishna River. The river identification is associated with P. C. Ray.
40.tq: Distinguish ancient place names by combining the modern site and river clues.
xs: **Andhranagari / Dhanyakataka** = **Amaravati-Dharanikota on the Krishna** — option **(1)**.
**P.C. Ray** identified the river there as the **Krishna**.
**Guntupalli** = Siddharthaka chaitya; **Bodhan** was Assaka's capital; **Nagarjunakonda** = Sriparvata.
xa: **Mahadeva Bhikshu** enshrined the Buddha's **bone relics** at Amaravati.
Amaravati has a fragment of an **Ashokan pillar edict**.
**Sriparvata / Vijayapuri** = Nagarjunakonda.

40.s: The ancient place name Andhapura or Andhakapura, mentioned in the Serivanija Jataka, refers to a city reached across the river:
40.x: The Serivanija Jataka refers to Andhapura or Andhakapura, a city reached by crossing the river Telavaha.
40.tq: Use the distinctive river-name clue to distinguish similar ancient place identifications.
xs: **Andhapura / Andhakapura** was reached across the river **Telavaha** — option **(1)**.
Merchants traded there in the **Serivanija Jataka**.
xa: **Andhranagari** = **Amaravati-Dharanikota** on the **Krishna**.
**Assaka** lay on the **Godavari**.
Andhra guilds used **Kalingapatnam**, later **Masulipatnam**.

40.s: Which Jataka refers to merchants trading to Andhapura?
40.x: The Serivanija Jataka refers to merchants trading to Andhapura.
40.tq: Associate the narrative subject—merchant trade—with the correct Jataka.
xs: The **Serivanija Jataka** has merchants trading to **Andhapura** — option **(4)**.
**Chulla-Kalinga Jataka** is about Asmaka's **Satakarni** defeating **Kharavela**; **Bhimasena Jataka** demarcates the Andhra region.
xa: Andhapura was reached across the river **Telavaha**.
Andhra lay on the **Dakshinapatha** trade route.
"**Andhapatha**" is in the **Vinayavatthu**.

40.s:
Assertion (A): Andhra had a distinct regional identity before the rise of the Satavahanas.
Reason (R): Early literary, epigraphic and archaeological evidence refers to Andhra as a region or people before the Satavahana period.

Select the correct answer:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
40.x: Both A and R are true and R explains A. Andhra appears as a people or region in the Aitareya Brahmana, Buddhist and Jataka texts, Megasthenes' Indica and Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict, and in sites such as Gudiwada Dibba and the Nagarjunasagar valley, all before the Satavahanas.
40.tq: Test whether the evidence stated in the Reason directly explains the historical conclusion in the Assertion.
xs: Both A and R are true and **R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**: Andhra was a **distinct region before the Satavahanas**.
Literary: **Aitareya Brahmana**, **Vinayavatthu**, Jatakas, Megasthenes' **Indica**, the **13th Major Rock Edict**.
Archaeological: **Gudiwada Dibba** and the **Nagarjunasagar valley** digs.
xa: The **Mauryan phase** made Buddhism **institutional**.
Megasthenes counted **30 forts** of the Andhras.
Ashokan edicts in Andhra: **Erragudi**, **Rajula Mandagiri**, **Amaravati**.

40.s: Which of the following current-affairs developments is correctly matched?
o: Devnimori — Buddhist relics discovered in Andhra and sent to Ujjain
Vaishya Tekri — Kshatrapa-period site in Gujarat
Vaishya Tekri — proposed renewed excavation of a possible large Mauryan stupa near Ujjain
40.x: The Madhya Pradesh government is to resume digging at Vaishya Tekri near Ujjain, where a possible Mauryan stupa larger than Sanchi has been identified.
40.tq: Separate current archaeological developments by site, region and cultural period.
xs: **Vaishya Tekri** — MP is to **resume digging** near **Ujjain** at a possible **Mauryan stupa larger than Sanchi** — option **(4)** (**23 Aug 2026**).
**Devnimori** is a **Kshatrapa**-period site in **Gujarat**, not Andhra or Amaravati.
xa: Devnimori's **Buddha relics** were sent to **Colombo** for exhibition (**Jun 2026**).
Vaishya Tekri is in **Madhya Pradesh**, not Gujarat.
In Andhra, **Gudiwada Dibba** shows Mauryan-to-Satavahana occupation.

40.s: Devnimori is associated with which of the following?
o: A Mauryan stupa near Ujjain larger than Sanchi
A Buddhist site in the Nagarjunasagar valley
A Mahasanghika centre in East Godavari
A Kshatrapa-period site in Gujarat whose Buddha relics were sent to Colombo for exhibition
40.x: Devnimori is a Kshatrapa-period site in Gujarat. Buddha relics from the site were sent to Colombo for exhibition.
40.tq: Use the site–region–period combination to distinguish two contemporary archaeological developments.
xs: **Devnimori** is a **Kshatrapa-period site in Gujarat** whose **Buddha relics were sent to Colombo** for exhibition — option **(4)** (**Jun 2026**).
The large possible Mauryan stupa is at **Vaishya Tekri** (Ujjain); the Mahasanghika centre is **Adurru**.
xa: MP to resume digging at Vaishya Tekri (**23 Aug 2026**).
**Nagarjunasagar valley** digs prove early Andhra settlement.
Andhra was a **distinct region** before the Satavahanas.

40.s: Which statement best describes the significance of the Mauryan phase for Buddhism in Andhra?
o: It made Buddhism institutional in the region
It led to the disappearance of Buddhism from Andhra
It replaced Buddhism with Jainism as the state religion
It introduced Vajrayana Buddhism for the first time
40.x: The Mauryan phase made Buddhism institutional in Andhra, which was already a distinct region before the Satavahanas.
40.tq: Ashoka's Mauryan era = Buddhism gets institutions in Andhra.
xs: The **Mauryan phase made Buddhism institutional** in Andhra — option **(1)**.
Buddhism did not disappear or yield to Jainism as a state religion.
xa: **Mahadeva Bhikshu**, sent by Ashoka, was the first Buddhist teacher in Andhra.
Buddhist ideas had reached the Godavari even **before** the Mauryas (**Bavari**).
Andhra was already a **distinct region** before the Satavahanas.

41.s: The Yavana advance on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura and Pataliputra is described in which source?
41.x: The Gargi Samhita records the Yavana advance on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura and Pataliputra.
41.tq: Match a source with its distinctive historical information.
xs: The **Gargi Samhita** (Yuga Purana) records the **Yavana advance on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura and Pataliputra** — option **(3)**.
The **Ayodhya inscription** records Pushyamitra's **two Ashvamedhas**; the **Divyavadana** calls him a persecutor; the **Harshacharita** tells of Brihadratha's killing.
xa: The Yavana invasion is recorded in **Gargi Samhita, Mahabhashya and Malavikagnimitram** (APPSC G1 **2022**).
⚠ It is NOT in Visakhadatta's **Mudrarakshasa**, which is about Chandragupta Maurya.
The **Mahabhashya** mentions the Yavana siege of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**.

41.s: Who wrote the Mahabhashya, which refers to the Yavana siege of Saketa and Madhyamika?
41.x: Patanjali authored the Mahabhashya, which contains references to the Yavana sieges of Saketa and Madhyamika.
41.tq: Use a source–author trap involving closely related literary and epigraphic evidence.
xs: **Patanjali** wrote the **Mahabhashya**, which mentions the Yavana siege of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika** — option **(1)**.
**Garga** is linked with the **Gargi Samhita**; **Taranatha** was a Tibetan monk; **Dhana** issued the Ayodhya inscription.
xa: The Mahabhashya comments on **Panini's Ashtadhyayi** through **Katyayana's Varttikas**.
Grammarian trio: **Panini-Katyayana-Patanjali**.
Patanjali is believed to have been the royal priest of **Pushyamitra**.

41.s:
Consider the following pairs of sources and what they record:
a. Malavikagnimitram — Vasumitra's victory over the Yavanas on the Sindhu
b. Harshacharita — Pushyamitra killing Brihadratha while showing him the army
c. Divyavadana — Pushyamitra as a generous patron of Buddhists
d. Ayodhya inscription of Dhana — Pushyamitra's two Ashvamedhas
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
41.x: Pairs a, b and d are correct. Pair c is wrong: the Divyavadana portrays Pushyamitra as a persecutor of Buddhists, not a patron. So 'a, b and d only'; 'a and b only' leaves out the Ayodhya inscription and the options with c accept the false pair.
41.tq: Divyavadana = persecutor story.
xs: Pair a is correct: **Malavikagnimitram** — **Vasumitra** beat the Yavanas on the **Sindhu**.
Pair b is correct: **Harshacharita** — Pushyamitra killed **Brihadratha** while showing him the army.
Pair c is wrong: the **Divyavadana** calls Pushyamitra a **persecutor** of Buddhists; pair d is correct — option **(2) a, b and d only**.
xa: The **Ayodhya inscription of Dhana(deva)** records **two Ashvamedhas** (UPSC).
The **Harshacharita** was written by **Banabhatta**.
**Taranatha** (16th c.) also portrays him as a persecutor.

41.s: Which one of the following works is associated with Kalidasa and describes Agnimitra as its hero?
41.x: Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram presents Agnimitra as its principal hero and also refers to the Vidarbha conflict and Vasumitra's victory.
41.tq: Identify the author–work relationship rather than the event alone.
xs: **Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram** has **Agnimitra** as its hero — option **(3)**.
It also records **Vasumitra**'s victory on the **Sindhu** and the war with **Vidarbha**.
xa: Agnimitra, Pushyamitra's son, was viceroy at **Vidisha** and fought **Yajnasena of Vidarbha**.
⚠ **Agnimitra** = son; **Vasumitra** = grandson.
**Mahabhashya** is by **Patanjali**; **Harshacharita** by **Banabhatta**.

41.s: Visakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa is not generally used as evidence for the Yavana invasion during Pushyamitra's reign because it deals primarily with:
o: The Satavahana conquest of the Deccan
41.x: Mudrarakshasa concerns Chandragupta Maurya and the establishment of Mauryan power, not the Yavana invasion during Pushyamitra's reign.
41.tq: Use the NOT-supported source distinction and reject a famous but contextually unsuitable work.
xs: **Mudrarakshasa** deals with **Chandragupta Maurya** — option **(2)** — so it is not a source for the Yavana invasion (APPSC G1 **2022** trap).
The Yavana invasion is in the **Gargi Samhita, Mahabhashya and Malavikagnimitram**.
xa: Mudrarakshasa is by **Visakhadatta**.
Gargi Samhita: Yavanas advanced on **Saketa, Panchala, Mathura, Pataliputra**.
Mahabhashya: Yavana siege of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**.

41.s:
Arrange the following dynasties in chronological order of their rule:
A. Kanva
B. Maurya
C. Kushana
D. Sunga
41.x: The sequence is Maurya, Sunga, Kanva and Kushana.
41.tq: Fix the first and last dynasties, then place the intervening Sunga and Kanva periods.
xs: The order is **Maurya → Sunga → Kanva → Kushana** — **B, D, A, C**, option **(1)** (BPSC **2025**).
Mauryas c. **321-187 BC**; Sungas **187-75 BC**; Kanvas c. **73-28 BC**.
xa: UPSC dates the Sungas **187-78 BC**; APHQ **185-73 BCE**.
The Kanvas had **4** kings.
The Puranas say the **Satavahanas** defeated the Sungas and Kanvas.

41.s: Which of the following correctly matches the dynasty with its founder?
41.x: Chandragupta founded the Mauryan dynasty. Pushyamitra founded the Sungas, Vasudeva founded the Kanvas, and the other pairings are incorrect.
41.tq: Apply the founder–dynasty trap by separating successive ruling houses.
xs: **Maurya — Chandragupta** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
The **Sungas** were founded by **Pushyamitra**, the **Kanvas** by **Vasudeva Kanva**; **Brihadratha** was the last Maurya.
xa: Brihadratha was killed by Pushyamitra.
The last Sunga, **Devabhuti**, was killed by his minister Vasudeva.
The last Kanva, **Susharman**, was overthrown by **Simuka (Srimukha)**.

41.s: Who killed Devabhuti, the last Sunga ruler?
41.x: Devabhuti was killed by his minister Vasudeva, who founded the Kanva dynasty.
41.tq: Use the minister–last ruler succession trap.
xs: **Devabhuti**, the last Sunga, was killed by **his minister Vasudeva** — option **(2)**.
Vasudeva then founded the **Kanva** dynasty.
**Susharman** was the last Kanva; **Simuka** overthrew him; **Bhagabhadra** was a Sunga king.
xa: Kanvas ruled c. **73-28 BC**, **4** kings.
Devabhuti is the last Sunga per UPSC.
Sunga dates: **187-75 BC**.

41.s: According to the Puranic tradition, which dynasties were defeated by the Satavahanas?
41.x: The Puranas state that the Satavahanas defeated the Sunga and Kanva dynasties.
41.tq: Identify the specific predecessor dynasties associated with a later dynastic conquest.
xs: The Puranas say the **Satavahanas defeated the Sungas and Kanvas** (Sunga and Kanva dynasties) — option **(3)**.
**Simuka (Srimukha)**, the Satavahana founder, overthrew the last Kanva **Susharman**.
xa: AP angle: **Satakarni I** is said to have defeated **Pushyamitra**.
The Sungas had already lost the **Deccan** to the Satavahanas.
Order: **Maurya → Sunga → Kanva → Kushana**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements about the Sungas:
1. They were Brahmins.
2. Their heartland was Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha and the Narmada valley.
3. They lost the north-west to the Satavahanas and the Deccan to the Yavanas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Sungas were Brahmins. Statement 2 is correct: their heartland was Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha and the Narmada valley. Statement 3 is wrong: it is reversed; the north-west went to the Yavanas and the Deccan to the Satavahanas. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Reverse-pairing trap: NW = Yavanas, Deccan = Satavahanas.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the Sungas were **Brahmins**.
Statement 2 is correct: their heartland was **Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha and the Narmada valley**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is reversed — the **north-west** went to the **Yavanas**, the **Deccan** to the **Satavahanas**. So option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: They broadly kept the **Mauryan administrative institutions**.
Feudatories **Bhojas, Maharathis, Rastrikas** rose.
Pushyamitra's dominions included **Pataliputra, Ayodhya and Vidisha**.

41.s:
With reference to the Sunga rulers, consider the following pairs:
1. Agnimitra — Viceroy at Vidisha
2. Vasumitra — Defeat of the Yavanas on the Sindhu
3. Bhagabhadra — Court visited by Heliodorus
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
41.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Agnimitra served as viceroy at Vidisha, Vasumitra defeated the Yavanas on the Sindhu, and Heliodorus came to Bhagabhadra’s court.
41.tq: Start from the sure ruler–event pairs and verify the remaining pair.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **Agnimitra** was viceroy at **Vidisha**.
Pair 2 is correct: **Vasumitra** defeated the Yavanas on the **Sindhu**.
Pair 3 is correct: **Heliodorus** came to **Bhagabhadra**'s court — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
xa: ⚠ **Agnimitra** = son; **Vasumitra** = grandson of Pushyamitra.
Agnimitra fought **Yajnasena of Vidarbha**.
Heliodorus set up the **Besnagar pillar** near Vidisha.

41.s: Agnimitra, a prominent Sunga ruler, is associated with which of the following developments?
o: Receiving the Besnagar pillar from Heliodorus
Defeating the Yavanas on the Sindhu
41.x: Agnimitra is noted for fighting Yajnasena of Vidarbha. The defeat of the Yavanas on the Sindhu is associated with Vasumitra, while the other alternatives refer to different historical contexts.
41.tq: Use the ruler–deed association and reject deeds belonging to neighbouring dynasties or rulers.
xs: **Agnimitra** fought **Yajnasena of Vidarbha** — option **(4)** (UPSC).
The **Sindhu** victory was **Vasumitra**'s; Heliodorus came to **Bhagabhadra**; the Kanvas were ended by **Simuka**.
xa: Agnimitra was Pushyamitra's son and viceroy at **Vidisha**.
He is the hero of Kalidasa's **Malavikagnimitram**.
The last Sunga was **Devabhuti**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements about Sunga rule:
1. The Sungas broadly kept the Mauryan administrative institutions.
2. Powerful feudatories such as the Bhojas, Maharathis and Rastrikas rose in this period.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Sungas broadly kept Mauryan administrative institutions. Statement 2 is correct: Bhojas, Maharathis and Rastrikas rose as powerful feudatories. So 'Both 1 and 2'; '1 only' and '2 only' each leave out a true statement and 'Neither' rejects both.
41.tq: Sunga: Mauryan administration kept; feudatories rose.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the Sungas **broadly kept Mauryan administrative institutions**.
Statement 2 is correct: powerful feudatories — **Bhojas, Maharathis, Rastrikas** — rose. So option **(3) Both 1 and 2**.
xa: Sunga heartland: **Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha, Narmada valley**.
The Sungas were **Brahmins**.
The north-west was lost to the **Yavanas**, the Deccan to the **Satavahanas**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements about Pushyamitra Sunga:
1. He came to power c. 187 BC after killing Brihadratha.
2. His dominions reached the Narmada and included Pataliputra, Ayodhya and Vidisha.
3. He defeated Menander after the Greeks challenged his sacrificial horse.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: he killed Brihadratha c. 187 BC. Statement 2 is correct: his dominions reached the Narmada with Pataliputra, Ayodhya and Vidisha. Statement 3 is wrong: the Bactrian Greek he defeated over the sacrificial horse was Demetrius. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Sacrificial horse challenge = Demetrius.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Pushyamitra killed **Brihadratha** in **187 BC** (APPSC GS **2023** key).
Statement 2 is correct: his dominions reached the **Narmada**, with **Pataliputra, Ayodhya and Vidisha** (UPSC).
Statement 3 is wrong: the Bactrian Greek he defeated over the **sacrificial horse** was **Demetrius**, not Menander — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: He was the Mauryan **commander-in-chief**.
He performed **two Ashvamedhas** (Ayodhya inscription of Dhana).
**Patanjali** is believed to have been his royal priest.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the debate on Pushyamitra's attitude towards Buddhism:
1. Divyavadana and Taranatha portray him as a persecutor of Buddhists.
2. Romila Thapar and Etienne Lamotte regard the persecution account as exaggerated and sectarian.
3. Buddhist artistic activity completely disappeared during his reign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Buddhist art continued to flourish at Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya, so statement 3 is false.
41.tq: Find the false absolute statement and separate literary tradition from modern historical interpretation.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Divyavadana** and **Taranatha** (16th c.) call him a persecutor — destroying stupas, a bounty on monks' heads.
Statement 2 is correct: **Romila Thapar and Etienne Lamotte** call this **exaggerated and sectarian**.
Statement 3 is wrong: Buddhist art **flourished** at **Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: Royal patronage fell, but **merchants and guilds** kept funding Buddhism.
Hostility was probably aimed at monasteries **allied with the Indo-Greeks**.
One tradition blames him for destroying the original **Bodhi Tree**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements offered against the theory that Pushyamitra persecuted Buddhists:
1. Merchants and guilds kept funding Buddhism even as royal patronage fell.
2. Any hostility was probably aimed at monasteries allied with the Indo-Greeks.
3. Buddhist art at Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya declined under his rule.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: merchants and guilds kept funding Buddhism. Statement 2 is correct: hostility was probably aimed at monasteries allied with the Indo-Greeks. Statement 3 is wrong: Buddhist art flourished at Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya, which is itself an argument against persecution. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Sanchi/Bharhut flourished = argument against persecution.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **merchants and guilds** kept funding Buddhism as royal patronage fell.
Statement 2 is correct: hostility was probably aimed at monasteries **allied with the Indo-Greeks**.
Statement 3 is wrong: Buddhist art **flourished** at **Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya** — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: Critics of the persecution story: **Romila Thapar** and **Etienne Lamotte**.
Bharhut inscriptions name **guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers** as donors.
The persecution charge comes from the **Divyavadana** and **Taranatha**.

41.s: The tradition concerning the destruction of the original Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya is associated with which two rulers?
o: Pushyamitra Sunga and Shashanka of Gauda
41.x: One tradition attributes destruction of the original Bodhi Tree to Pushyamitra and also records a similar act by Shashanka of Gauda in the seventh century CE.
41.tq: Discriminate between rulers associated with similar acts in different periods.
xs: One tradition blames **Pushyamitra Sunga** for destroying the original **Bodhi Tree**, and **Shashanka of Gauda** did the same in the **7th c.** — option **(4)**.
**Ashoka**, **Devabhuti**, **Vasudeva Kanva** and **Antialcidas** have no such tradition in the notes.
xa: This was in the news in **2026** with the listing of the **Ashtamahasthana** (**8** Buddhist sacred sites).
The persecution charge rests on the **Divyavadana** and **Taranatha**.
**Bodh Gaya** has an early stone railing of the Sunga period.

41.s: Heliodorus erected the Besnagar pillar while serving as ambassador of:
41.x: Heliodorus was the ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas at the court of the Sunga king Bhagabhadra.
41.tq: Use the ambassador–sending ruler–receiving court relationship precisely.
xs: **Heliodorus** was ambassador of the **Indo-Greek king Antialcidas** — option **(2)**.
He came to the court of the **Sunga king Bhagabhadra**, not Pushyamitra.
**Demetrius** was the Bactrian Greek Pushyamitra defeated.
xa: Heliodorus was a native of **Taxila**.
The pillar is at **Besnagar**, near **Vidisha (MP)**.
He called himself a **Bhagavata**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements about the Besnagar pillar:
1. Heliodorus, who erected it, was a native of Taxila.
2. It stands at Besnagar near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh.
3. Its inscription is in Sanskrit written in Kharoshthi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: Heliodorus was from Taxila. Statement 2 is correct: the pillar is at Besnagar near Vidisha (MP). Statement 3 is wrong: the inscription is Prakrit in Brahmi script. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Besnagar: Prakrit / Brahmi.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Heliodorus** was a native of **Taxila**.
Statement 2 is correct: the pillar is at **Besnagar near Vidisha (MP)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the inscription is **Prakrit** in **Brahmi** — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: It is a **Garuda-dhvaja** dedicated to **Vasudeva**.
It is the **earliest inscriptional proof of Bhagavatism**.
Heliodorus served the Indo-Greek king **Antialcidas**.

41.s: The Besnagar pillar is best described as a:
41.x: The Besnagar monument is a Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva, and Heliodorus describes himself as a Bhagavata.
41.tq: Distinguish religious symbols and dedications associated with different traditions.
xs: The Besnagar pillar is a **Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva** — option **(4)**.
Heliodorus calls himself a **Bhagavata**.
xa: It is the **earliest inscriptional proof of Bhagavatism** (early Vaishnavism).
It also shows the absorption of **foreigners** into Indian religion.
It was set up at the court of **Bhagabhadra**.

41.s: The major historical significance of the Besnagar pillar lies in its evidence for:
o: The earliest use of iron in the Ganga valley
The establishment of the Kanva dynasty
Early Bhagavatism and the absorption of a foreigner into an Indian religious tradition
41.x: The pillar is early inscriptional evidence of Bhagavatism, an early form of Vaishnavism, and shows the assimilation of a foreigner into an Indian religious tradition.
41.tq: Identify the broader significance rather than merely the monument's location.
xs: The pillar is the **earliest inscriptional proof of Bhagavatism** and shows the **absorption of a foreigner** into Indian religion — option **(3)**.
**Heliodorus**, a Greek from **Taxila**, calls himself a **Bhagavata**.
xa: It is a **Garuda-dhvaja** to **Vasudeva**.
Language/script: **Prakrit / Brahmi**.
Bhagavatism's rise is part of the Sunga period's significance.

41.s:
Consider the following statements about Patanjali and the Mahabhashya:
1. The Mahabhashya comments on Panini's Ashtadhyayi through Katyayana's Varttikas.
2. It gives evidence on 2nd-century-BCE society, geography, language and Yavana raids.
3. Patanjali is believed to have been the royal priest of Vasudeva Kanva.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: the grammarian trio is Panini-Katyayana-Patanjali. Statement 2 is correct: the Mahabhashya is evidence for 2nd-century-BCE society and the Yavana raids. Statement 3 is wrong: Patanjali was a contemporary and believed royal priest of Pushyamitra Sunga. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Patanjali = Pushyamitra's priest.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Mahabhashya** comments on **Panini's Ashtadhyayi** through **Katyayana's Varttikas**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is evidence on **2nd-century-BCE** society, geography, language and **Yavana raids**.
Statement 3 is wrong: Patanjali was the believed royal priest of **Pushyamitra**, not Vasudeva Kanva — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: Grammarian trio: **Panini-Katyayana-Patanjali**.
The Mahabhashya says "we perform sacrifices for **Pushyamitra**".
It mentions the Yavana siege of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**.

41.s: Which development is associated with the Sunga court?
o: Replacement of Sanskrit by Greek as the court language
Introduction of Persian as the official language
Revival of classical Sanskrit, while Ashoka had used Prakrit
41.x: The Sunga court encouraged a revival of classical Sanskrit, in contrast to Ashoka's prominent use of Prakrit.
41.tq: Use a court-language comparison and reject an absolute claim of linguistic replacement.
xs: The Sunga court led a **revival of classical Sanskrit**, while **Ashoka** had used **Prakrit** — option **(4)**.
Greek or Persian were not court languages, and Prakrit did not vanish — the **Besnagar** inscription itself is in Prakrit.
xa: **Patanjali**'s Mahabhashya belongs to this revival.
The **Manusmriti** took early shape in this period.
The Sunga period saw a **Brahmanical revival**.

41.s: The Manusmriti is said to have taken its early shape during the Sunga period and classified foreigners as:
41.x: The Manusmriti took early shape in this period and classified foreigners as Vratya Kshatriyas.
41.tq: Recall the exact technical social category instead of a broad caste label.
xs: The **Manusmriti**, taking shape in this period, classed foreigners as **"Vratya Kshatriyas"** — option **(4)**.
So foreigners were fitted into the varna order as Kshatriyas who had lapsed, not as Shudras or Brahmanas.
xa: Foreigners were also absorbed via **Bhagavatism** — e.g. **Heliodorus**.
The Sunga court revived **classical Sanskrit**.
The period is marked by a **Brahmanical revival**.

41.s: Which major artistic transition is associated with the Sunga period?
o: A transition from wood and ivory to stone
A transition from bronze to terracotta alone
A transition from stone to wood and ivory
A transition from mural painting to coin engraving
41.x: Sunga art marks a significant movement from earlier wood and ivory traditions towards stone architecture and sculpture.
41.tq: Test the direction of a cultural transition by reversing the true comparison in distractors.
xs: Sunga art marks a transition from **wood and ivory to stone** — option **(1)**.
Examples: Sanchi's brick stupa **encased in stone**, stone railings at **Bharhut** and **Bodh Gaya**.
xa: Bharhut inscriptions name guilds of **ivory workers** and **stone carvers**.
The **Mathura** style of sculpture began under the Sungas.
"The **Bharhut stupa** is a fine example of **Shunga** architecture" (RPSC **2023**).

41.s:
Consider the following statements about Sanchi:
1. Ashoka's brick stupa was encased in stone and given stone railings (vedika).
2. Its toranas carry Jataka tales and scenes from the Buddha's life.
3. Its south torana is linked to Pushyamitra through the inscription of Ananda.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct: the brick stupa was encased in stone with railings. Statement 2 is correct: the toranas show Jataka tales and the Buddha's life. Statement 3 is wrong: the inscription of Ananda links the south torana to Satakarni II, so the gateways are often dated to the Satavahana period. So '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: South torana = Satakarni II (Ananda inscription).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Ashoka's brick stupa was **encased in stone** with **stone railings (vedika)**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **toranas** carry **Jataka tales** and the Buddha's life.
Statement 3 is wrong: Ananda's inscription links the south torana to **Satakarni II**, not Pushyamitra — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: The gateways are therefore often dated to the **Satavahana** period.
**Bharhut** has railings and gateways of early **narrative art**.
**Bodh Gaya** has an early stone railing.

41.s: Which statement about Bharhut is correct?
o: Its inscriptions record only royal donations by the Mauryan emperors.
Its inscriptions name guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers who financed the monument.
It was situated near Taxila and was built by Indo-Greek rulers.
It contained no railings or gateways of narrative art.
41.x: Bharhut's inscriptions mention guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers who contributed to its construction and decoration.
41.tq: Use the patronage detail to distinguish Bharhut from royal-only monuments.
xs: **Bharhut** inscriptions name the **guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers** who paid for it — option **(2)**.
It has **railings and gateways** of early **narrative art**, in **MP**, not near Taxila.
xa: "The Bharhut stupa is a fine example of **Shunga** architecture" (RPSC **2023**).
Guild funding fits the view that **merchants and guilds** kept funding Buddhism.
The art shifted from **wood/ivory to stone**.

41.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Mathura — beginning of Gupta temple architecture under the Sungas
Bharhut — early narrative art in railings and gateways
41.x: Mathura sculpture began under the Sungas, but Gupta temple architecture did not begin there under the Sungas. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
41.tq: Find the one anachronistic or wrongly attributed cultural development.
xs: **Mathura** saw the **Mathura style of sculpture** begin under the Sungas — not Gupta temple architecture; so option **(3)** is NOT correctly matched.
**Bodh Gaya** (early stone railing), **Sanchi** (toranas with Jataka scenes), **Bharhut** (narrative railings, gateways) are correct.
xa: Sanchi's south torana is linked to **Satakarni II** (inscription of Ananda).
Bharhut was paid for by guilds of **ivory workers and stone carvers**.
Transition: **wood/ivory → stone**.

41.s: Which one of the following best describes the broader cultural significance of the Sunga period?
o: Complete disappearance of Brahmanical traditions and decline of Buddhist art
Exclusive promotion of Jainism and rejection of all forms of image-making
Brahmanical revival, rise of Bhagavatism and development of stone Buddhist art
Replacement of religious traditions by a purely secular imperial culture
41.x: The Sunga period is associated with Brahmanical revival, the rise of Bhagavatism and the development of stone Buddhist art.
41.tq: Choose the option that combines the three stated cultural developments without an absolute distortion.
xs: The Sunga period stands for **Brahmanical revival, the rise of Bhagavatism and stone Buddhist art** — option **(3)**.
Brahmanism grew (two **Ashvamedhas**), and Buddhist art flourished at **Sanchi** and **Bharhut**.
xa: Bhagavatism: the **Besnagar** Garuda-dhvaja of **Heliodorus**.
Debate: Pushyamitra as persecutor (**Divyavadana**) vs the archaeology of Sanchi and Bharhut.
The court revived **classical Sanskrit**.

41.s: According to the traditional account associated with Andhra history, which ruler is said to have defeated Pushyamitra Sunga?
41.x: Satakarni I is said to have defeated Pushyamitra Sunga. Simuka is associated with ending the Kanva dynasty, while Vasumitra is linked with the defeat of the Yavanas on the Sindhu.
41.tq: Distinguish closely related dynastic and military associations.
xs: AP angle: **Satakarni I** is said to have defeated **Pushyamitra** — option **(4)**.
**Simuka** ended the **Kanvas**; **Vasumitra** beat the Yavanas; **Yajnasena** of Vidarbha fought **Agnimitra**.
xa: The Puranas say the **Satavahanas** defeated the Sungas and Kanvas.
**Satakarni II** is linked to Sanchi's south torana.
The Sungas lost the **Deccan** to the Satavahanas.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly states the relationship between Simuka and the Kanvas?
o: Simuka defeated the Yavanas on the Sindhu during Kanva rule.
Simuka served as the viceroy of the Kanvas at Vidisha.
Simuka founded the Kanva dynasty after overthrowing the Sungas.
41.x: Simuka is said to have ended the Kanva dynasty. The other alternatives incorrectly transfer Sunga-period events or offices to Simuka.
41.tq: Use the dynasty-transition clue and reject swapped ruler–event associations.
xs: **Simuka (Srimukha)**, the Satavahana founder, **ended the Kanva dynasty** by overthrowing **Susharman** — option **(1)**.
The Kanvas were founded by **Vasudeva Kanva**; the Sindhu victory was **Vasumitra**'s; the Vidisha viceroy was **Agnimitra**.
xa: Kanvas ruled c. **73-28 BC** with **4** kings.
**Satakarni I** is said to have defeated Pushyamitra.
Order: **Maurya → Sunga → Kanva → Kushana**.

42.s:
Consider the following statements about the Bactrian Greeks:
1. Pressure from the Scythians (Sakas) pushed them south into India.
2. The weak successors of Ashoka helped their entry.
3. Diodotus I founded their independent kingdom by revolting against the Mauryas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: Statement 1 is correct: Scythian (Saka) pressure pushed them south. Statement 2 is correct: Ashoka's weak successors helped their entry. Statement 3 is wrong: Diodotus I revolted against the Seleucids, not the Mauryas. So '1 and 2 only'.
42.tq: Diodotus I revolted against the Seleucids.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: pressure from the **Scythians (Sakas)** pushed the Bactrian Greeks south.
Statement 2 is correct: the **weak successors of Ashoka** helped their entry.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Diodotus I** revolted against the **Seleucids**, not the Mauryas — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: The revolt came in the **3rd c. BCE** and created an independent Bactrian Greek kingdom (UPSC).
Their raids reached **Saketa, Madhyamika** and towards **Pataliputra**.
Successors in the north-west: **Sakas → Parthians (Pahlavas) → Kushanas**.

42.s: Bactria, where Greeks settled after Alexander, was located in which region?
42.x: Bactria was situated in north Afghanistan, where Greek settlers established themselves after Alexander’s campaigns.
42.tq: Use the geographical location to distinguish Bactria from the later areas of Indo-Greek expansion.
xs: **Bactria** lay in **north Afghanistan** — option **(1)**.
Greeks settled there **after Alexander**.
xa: **Diodotus I** revolted against the **Seleucids** to found an independent kingdom.
Pushed by the **Scythians (Sakas)**, they moved south into India.
**Demetrius** was the first Bactrian Greek to invade India (c. **180 BC**).

42.s:
According to the Mahabhashya-related account, the raids of the Bactrian Greeks reached which of the following places?
1. Saketa
2. Madhyamika
3. The region towards Pataliputra
Which of the statements given above are correct?
42.x: The raids are described as reaching Saketa and Madhyamika and extending towards Pataliputra.
42.tq: Retain all three geographical limits and avoid the partial-list distractors.
xs: The raids reached **Saketa** and **Madhyamika** and went **towards Pataliputra** — all three, option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (UPSC; **Mahabhashya**).
Patanjali's **Mahabhashya** is the source for the sieges of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**.
xa: The Mahabhashya is by **Patanjali**.
Their entry was helped by the **weak successors of Ashoka**.
They were pressed south by the **Scythians (Sakas)**.

42.s: Who was the first Bactrian Greek ruler to invade India around 180 BCE?
42.x: Demetrius was the first Bactrian Greek ruler credited with invading India around 180 BCE.
42.tq: Use the ruler–achievement association and distinguish the invading ruler from later Indo-Greek kings.
xs: **Demetrius** was the **first Bactrian Greek to invade India** (c. **180 BC**) — option **(2)**.
**Antialcidas** sent Heliodorus; **Menander I** was the greatest; **Eucratides** led a rival dynasty.
xa: Demetrius was defeated by **Pushyamitra**, and by **Kharavela** per the **Hathigumpha**.
⚠ FIRST = **Demetrius**; greatest = **Menander**; LAST = **Hermaius**.
**Eucratides** issued the largest known ancient gold coin (**20 staters**).

42.s:
With reference to Demetrius, consider the following statements:
1. He was defeated by Pushyamitra.
2. The Hathigumpha inscription associates his defeat with Kharavela.
3. He founded the independent Bactrian Greek kingdom after revolting against the Seleucids.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
42.x: Demetrius is associated with defeats by Pushyamitra and, according to the Hathigumpha account, by Kharavela. The independent Bactrian Greek kingdom was founded by Diodotus I, not Demetrius.
42.tq: Identify the swapped-founder trap in statement 3 while retaining the two facts linked with Demetrius.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Demetrius** was defeated by **Pushyamitra**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **Hathigumpha** credits **Kharavela** with defeating him.
Statement 3 is wrong: the independent kingdom was founded by **Diodotus I** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: Demetrius was the **first** Bactrian Greek to invade India (c. **180 BC**).
**Eucratides** founded a rival dynasty to Demetrius.
The Hathigumpha is **Kharavela**'s inscription.

42.s: Which Indo-Greek ruler is regarded as the greatest among the Indo-Greek rulers and is associated with the spread of Hellenistic culture in India?
42.x: Menander I, also known as Milinda, is regarded as the greatest Indo-Greek ruler and is associated with the spread of Hellenistic culture.
42.tq: Match the ruler with the distinctive contribution rather than with a coinage detail.
xs: **Menander I (Milinda)** was the **greatest** Indo-Greek and spread **Hellenistic culture** — option **(1)**.
**Strato** was his son; **Agathocles** issued Vasudeva-Sankarshana coins; **Hermaius** was the last ruler.
xa: Reign **165-145 BCE**; capital **Sakala** (modern **Sialkot**).
He issued coins with **Indian symbols** (APPSC key), including the **Buddhist wheel**.
He debated **Nagasena** in the **Milindapanho**.

42.s: Which ruler sent Heliodorus as an envoy to the court of the Sunga ruler at Vidisha?
42.x: Antialcidas sent Heliodorus to the Sunga court at Vidisha.
42.tq: Apply the envoy–ruler association and avoid confusing Antialcidas with Menander.
xs: **Antialcidas** sent **Heliodorus** to the Sunga court at **Vidisha** — option **(2)**.
The Sunga king there was **Bhagabhadra**.
xa: Heliodorus, from **Taxila**, set up the Besnagar **Garuda pillar** honouring **Vasudeva**.
He called himself a **Bhagavata**.
Other envoys: **Megasthenes** (Seleucus I), **Daimachos** (Antiochus I, to Bindusara).

42.s: The defeat of which ruler marked the end of Greek rule in the north-west, according to the succession of Indo-Greek powers?
42.x: Hermaius was the last ruler of the line, and his defeat ended Greek supremacy south of the Hindu Kush.
42.tq: Use the LAST-ruler clue to identify the terminal point of Indo-Greek rule.
xs: **Hermaius** was the **last** ruler of the line; his defeat ended Greek supremacy **south of the Hindu Kush** — option **(2)**.
UPSC says he was defeated by the **Parthians**.
xa: ⚠ FIRST = **Demetrius**; greatest = **Menander**; LAST = **Hermaius**.
**Strato** (Menander's son) ruled after the regency of **Agathocleia**.
Successors: **Sakas → Parthians → Kushanas**.

42.s:
Arrange the powers that successively replaced the Indo-Greeks in the north-west in the correct order:
A. Kushanas
B. Sakas
C. Parthians
Which of the following is correct?
42.x: The Sakas replaced the Indo-Greeks first, followed by the Parthians or Pahlavas, and finally the Kushanas.
42.tq: Fix the first successor and then place the later successor powers in sequence.
xs: The order is **Sakas → Parthians (Pahlavas) → Kushanas** — **B, C, A**, option **(2)** (UPSC).
The **Kushanas** came last, so options putting them first or second are wrong.
xa: The last Greek ruler, **Hermaius**, fell to the **Parthians** (UPSC).
The Kushanas issued gold on a **large scale** (**Vima Kadphises**).
**Gandhara** art flourished under the **Kushanas**.

42.s: Coins depicting Sankarshana (Balarama) and Vasudeva (Krishna) were issued by the Indo-Greek ruler
42.x: Agathocles issued coins showing Sankarshana and Vasudeva (UPPSC 2017 key). Menander's coins carry the Buddhist wheel, Eucratides issued the largest ancient gold coin, and Strato was Menander's son.
42.tq: Sankarshana + Vasudeva on coins = Agathocles, not Kushana or Gupta rulers.
xs: **Agathocles** issued coins showing **Sankarshana (Balarama) and Vasudeva (Krishna)** — option **(2)** (UPPSC **2017** key).
**Menander**'s coins carry the **Buddhist wheel**; **Eucratides** issued the largest ancient gold coin; **Strato** was Menander's son.
xa: Exam angle: "Sankarshana + Vasudeva on coins" = Agathocles, not Kushana or Gupta rulers.
Greek deities on coins: **Zeus, Athena, Heracles**.
Coins carried **bilingual legends** — Greek and **Kharoshthi**.

42.s: Menander I ruled approximately during which period?
42.x: Menander I, or Milinda, is assigned a reign of approximately 165–145 BCE.
42.tq: Distinguish the close BCE ranges by placing the reign in the correct chronological interval.
xs: **Menander I** reigned **165-145 BCE** — option **(1)**.
His capital was **Sakala** (modern **Sialkot**) (UPSC).
xa: He is the **greatest** Indo-Greek.
A **Kharoshthi** inscription records his reign (UPSC).
**16 coins** of Menander were found at **Bairat** (RPSC **2018**).

42.s:
Consider the following statements about Menander and the Milindapanho:
1. Menander's capital Sakala is identified with modern Sialkot.
2. The Milindapanho is a dialogue between Menander and the monk Nagasena.
3. The Milindapanho was written in Sanskrit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sakala is modern Sialkot. Statement 2 is correct: the Milindapanho is Menander's dialogue with Nagasena. Statement 3 is wrong: it was written in Pali. So '1 and 2 only'.
42.tq: Milindapanho = Pali.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Sakala** = modern **Sialkot**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **Milindapanho** is Menander's dialogue with the monk **Nagasena**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is in **Pali**, not Sanskrit (UKPSC **2024**; UPPSC **2023**) — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: Menander **converted to Buddhism**.
"Milindapanho" means **"Questions of Milinda"**.
His coins carry the **Buddhist wheel**.

42.s: Sixteen coins of Menander were discovered at which site?
42.x: Sixteen coins of Menander were found at Bairat.
42.tq: Associate the specific archaeological find with its site rather than with Menander’s capital.
xs: **16 coins of Menander** were found at **Bairat** — option **(2)** (RPSC **2018**).
**Junagadh** is Rudradaman I's inscription; **Besnagar** has Heliodorus' pillar; **Sakala** was Menander's capital.
xa: A **Kharoshthi** inscription records Menander's reign.
His coins bore **Indian symbols**.

42.s:
Arrange the following associations in the correct order from the matching tradition:
A. Gandhara art
B. Junagadh rock inscription
C. Milindapanho
D. Taxila copper plate
1. Rudradaman I
2. Menander
3. Patika
4. Kushanas
Which of the following is correct?
42.x: Gandhara art is associated with the Kushanas, the Junagadh rock inscription with Rudradaman I, Milindapanho with Menander, and the Taxila copper plate with Patika.
42.tq: Start from the sure pairs and eliminate codes that swap the ruler, art form or inscription.
xs: **Gandhara art – Kushanas**, **Junagadh rock inscription – Rudradaman I**, **Milindapanho – Menander**, **Taxila copper plate – Patika**: **A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3** — option **(1)** (UPPSC **2017**).
The other codes mix up Gandhara art and the Junagadh inscription.
xa: Gandhara grew from **Hellenistic art**, later under the Kushanas.
The Milindapanho is in **Pali**.
Menander's capital: **Sakala (Sialkot)**.

42.s:
Which statement correctly describes the coinage of the Indo-Greeks?
1. Their coins are among the first in India that can be definitely attributed to particular kings.
2. They were the first rulers in India to issue gold coins.
3. Their coinage consisted exclusively of gold.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
42.x: The Indo-Greeks were among the first rulers to issue definitively attributable royal coins and the first to issue gold coins in India. Their coins were mainly silver and copper, so statement 3 is false.
42.tq: Reject the extreme word ‘exclusively’ while retaining the two established FIRST claims.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Indo-Greek coins are the first in India definitely **attributed to kings**.
Statement 2 is correct: they were the **first to issue gold coins** in India.
Statement 3 is wrong: coins were mainly **silver and copper**; gold was **rare** — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: ⚠ First **large-scale** gold = **Kushanas (Vima Kadphises)**.
Coins bore **realistic royal portraits** with helmets and diadems.
They are the main source for the list of more than **30** Indo-Greek kings.

42.s: In a typical bilingual Indo-Greek coin, which combination correctly identifies the scripts on the two sides?
o: Greek on the front and Sanskrit on the back
Brahmi on the front and Greek on the back
Greek on the front and Kharoshthi on the back
Kharoshthi on the front and Brahmi on the back
42.x: Indo-Greek coins commonly carried Greek legends on the front and Kharoshthi, representing Prakrit, on the back.
42.tq: Discriminate between the two scripts and their positions rather than merely recalling bilingualism.
xs: Bilingual legends: **Greek on the front** and **Kharoshthi (Prakrit) on the back** — option **(3)**.
The back legend is not **Sanskrit** or **Brahmi**, and Greek stays on the front.
xa: Coins showed **realistic royal portraits** (helmets, diadems).
Metals: mainly **silver and copper**.
A **Kharoshthi** inscription also records **Menander**'s reign.

42.s: Which feature of Indo-Greek coins most directly indicates realistic royal representation?
o: Use of only abstract geometric symbols
Portraits showing rulers with helmets or diadems
Exclusive depiction of animals without legends
Absence of any human figure on the coins
42.x: Indo-Greek coins are noted for realistic royal portraits, often showing rulers wearing helmets or diadems.
42.tq: Connect the visual description with the characteristic portraiture of Indo-Greek coinage.
xs: Indo-Greek coins carry **realistic royal portraits**, with **helmets and diadems** — option **(2)**.
They were not symbol-only like earlier issues; they named kings with **bilingual legends**.
xa: Comparison: Indo-Greek = **portrait + bilingual legend**; Kushana = **large-scale gold + many deities**.
They were the first coins definitely **attributed to kings**.
Greek deities shown: **Zeus, Athena, Heracles**.

42.s:
Consider the following statements about deities and symbols on Indo-Greek coins:
1. Greek deities such as Zeus, Athena and Heracles appear.
2. Agathocles' coins show Vasudeva and Sankarshana.
3. Menander's coins carry the Garuda standard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: Statement 1 is correct: Zeus, Athena and Heracles appear. Statement 2 is correct: Agathocles' coins show Vasudeva and Sankarshana. Statement 3 is wrong: Menander's coins carry the Buddhist wheel. So '1 and 2 only'.
42.tq: Sankarshana + Vasudeva = Agathocles; wheel = Menander.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Zeus, Athena, Heracles** appear on the coins.
Statement 2 is correct: **Agathocles**' coins show **Vasudeva and Sankarshana**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Menander**'s coins carry the **Buddhist wheel** — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: ⚠ The **Garuda** standard belongs to **Heliodorus**' Besnagar pillar.
Agathocles' coin was the UPPSC **2017** key.
Legends: Greek front, **Kharoshthi** back.

42.s: Why are Indo-Greek coins particularly important for reconstructing Indo-Greek political history?
o: They contain no names or royal portraits.
They provide the main source for establishing the list of more than 30 Indo-Greek kings.
They record only the agricultural production of the period.
They were issued by a single ruler throughout the region.
42.x: Indo-Greek coins are the principal source used to reconstruct the list of more than 30 Indo-Greek kings.
42.tq: Apply the historical significance of coin evidence to the reconstruction of dynastic succession.
xs: The coins are the **main source for the list of more than 30 Indo-Greek kings** — option **(2)**.
They carry royal **names and portraits**, so they identify individual rulers.
xa: They were the first coins definitely **attributed to kings** in India.
They were the **first gold coins** in India.
Metals: mainly **silver and copper**.

42.s: The military governors of the Indo-Greek administration were known as:
42.x: Indo-Greek military governors were called strategos.
42.tq: Distinguish the exact administrative title from religious and Indian administrative terms.
xs: Indo-Greek military governors were called **Strategos** — option **(4)**.
**Bhagavatas** were devotees of Vasudeva; **Mahamatras** were Mauryan officials.
xa: The system is called **military governorship**.
**Yavanika** = theatre stage curtain.
**Hora** = Greek astronomy/astrology term (horoscope).

42.s: The Gandhara school of art developed from Hellenistic artistic influence and flourished later under which dynasty?
42.x: Hellenistic art contributed to the development of the Gandhara school, which flourished later under the Kushanas.
42.tq: Separate the origin of an influence from the dynasty under which the art form later flourished.
xs: **Hellenistic art** led to the **Gandhara** school, which flourished later under the **Kushanas** — option **(1)**.
It came **after** the Indo-Greeks, not under the Mauryas, Sungas or Satavahanas.
xa: UPPSC **2017** match: **Gandhara art – Kushanas**.
The Indo-Greek period produced a Greek-Indian synthesis in **art, religion and philosophy**.
The Kushanas also issued **large-scale gold** coins.

42.s:
Which pair is correctly matched?
1. Hora — Horoscope
2. Romaka Siddhanta — Greek influence in astronomy
3. Yavanika — Military governorship
Select the correct answer using the code below.
42.x: Hora refers to a horoscope and Romaka Siddhanta reflects Greek influence in astronomy. Yavanika means stage curtain, not military governorship.
42.tq: Use elimination through the swapped-meaning trap in statement 3.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **Hora** is the Greek term behind the **horoscope**.
Pair 2 is correct: **Romaka Siddhanta** reflects Greek influence on astronomy.
Pair 3 is wrong: **Yavanika** is the **theatre stage curtain**; military governors were **Strategos** — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: The Smritis call the absorbed Greeks **"Vratya Kshatriyas"**.
**Hellenistic art** → the **Gandhara** school.

42.s: In the Smritis, the Greeks absorbed into Indian society were described as:
42.x: The Smritis describe the Greeks absorbed into Indian society as Vratya Kshatriyas.
42.tq: Recall the exact social classification and distinguish it from religious and political labels.
xs: The Smritis describe the absorbed Greeks as **"Vratya Kshatriyas"** — option **(4)**.
**Bhagavatas** were Vasudeva devotees — Heliodorus called himself one, but that is a religious, not a social, label.
xa: **Heliodorus** shows the religious absorption of Greeks.
Greek words entered Indian use: **Yavanika** (stage curtain), **Hora** (horoscope).
Greek governors were **Strategos**.

42.s:
Consider the following statements about Heliodorus:
1. He was a native of Taxila.
2. His Besnagar Garuda pillar honours Vasudeva, and he calls himself a Bhagavata.
3. He was the envoy of Menander to the Sunga court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: Statement 1 is correct: Heliodorus was from Taxila. Statement 2 is correct: the pillar honours Vasudeva and he calls himself a Bhagavata. Statement 3 is wrong: he was the envoy of Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra. So '1 and 2 only'.
42.tq: Heliodorus = envoy of Antialcidas.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Heliodorus** was from **Taxila**.
Statement 2 is correct: his Besnagar **Garuda pillar** honours **Vasudeva**, and he calls himself a **Bhagavata**.
Statement 3 is wrong: he was the envoy of **Antialcidas** (not Menander) to **Bhagabhadra** — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
xa: The pillar stands at **Besnagar**, near **Vidisha**.
Other envoys: **Megasthenes** (Seleucus I), **Daimachos** (Antiochus I to Bindusara).
Heliodorus represents the **religious** side of Greek-Indian synthesis.

42.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Megasthenes — Seleucus I
2. Daimachos — Antiochus I to Bindusara
3. Heliodorus — Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra
Select the correct answer using the code below.
42.x: Megasthenes was associated with Seleucus I, Daimachos with Antiochus I’s mission to Bindusara, and Heliodorus with Antialcidas’s mission to Bhagabhadra.
42.tq: Start with the sure envoy pairs and verify that all three diplomatic relationships align.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **Megasthenes** was sent by **Seleucus I**.
Pair 2 is correct: **Daimachos** was sent by **Antiochus I** to **Bindusara**.
Pair 3 is correct: **Heliodorus** was sent by **Antialcidas** to **Bhagabhadra** — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
xa: Heliodorus' **Garuda pillar** at Besnagar honours **Vasudeva**.
Earlier Greek-Mauryan contacts include the Hellenistic kings of **Rock Edict XIII**.
Heliodorus was a native of **Taxila**.

42.s: The Hellenistic kings mentioned in Rock Edict XIII provide evidence of:
o: The establishment of the Gupta Empire
The origin of the Sunga dynasty
42.x: Rock Edict XIII refers to Hellenistic kings and is evidence of earlier Greek–Mauryan contacts.
42.tq: Associate the edict with the diplomatic context rather than with a dynastic foundation.
xs: The Hellenistic kings in **Rock Edict XIII** show **earlier Greek-Mauryan contacts** — option **(4)**.
It has nothing to do with the Kushanas, Guptas or Sunga origins.
xa: Other Greek-Mauryan contacts: **Megasthenes** (Seleucus I), **Daimachos** (Antiochus I to Bindusara).
Later, **Heliodorus** went from **Antialcidas** to the Sunga **Bhagabhadra**.
Bactrian Greeks settled in **north Afghanistan** after **Alexander**.

42.s:
Which statement best explains the historical significance of the Indo-Greek period?
1. It contributed to a Greek–Indian synthesis in Gandhara art.
2. It contributed to religious interaction represented by Heliodorus.
3. It contributed to philosophical exchange represented by Milindapanho.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
42.x: The Indo-Greek period is associated with Greek–Indian synthesis in Gandhara art, religious interaction through Heliodorus, and philosophical exchange through Milindapanho.
42.tq: Recognise the three-dimensional synthesis across art, religion and philosophy.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Greek-Indian synthesis in **art** — **Gandhara**.
Statement 2 is correct: in **religion** — **Heliodorus**.
Statement 3 is correct: in **philosophy** — the **Milindapanho** — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
xa: The Indo-Greeks also gave India its **first gold coins** and dated royal coinage.
The Milindapanho is Menander's dialogue with **Nagasena**, in **Pali**.
Heliodorus called himself a **Bhagavata**.

42.s: Which comparison between Indo-Greek and Kushana coinage is correct?
o: Indo-Greek coins are noted for portraits and bilingual legends, whereas Kushana coins are associated with large-scale gold coinage and many deities.
Indo-Greek coins used only gold, whereas Kushana coins used only copper.
Kushana coins preceded Indo-Greek coins in the use of royal portraits.
Both coinages were characterised exclusively by Kharoshthi legends and identical deities.
42.x: Indo-Greek coinage is especially noted for royal portraits and bilingual legends, while Kushana coinage is associated with large-scale gold and numerous deities.
42.tq: Compare the defining features on both sides instead of treating the two coinages as identical.
xs: **Indo-Greek** coins = **portraits and bilingual legends**; **Kushana** coins = **large-scale gold and many deities** — option **(1)**.
Indo-Greek coins were mainly **silver and copper**, not only gold, and they came **before** the Kushanas.
xa: First gold coins in India = **Indo-Greeks**; first **large-scale** gold = **Kushanas (Vima Kadphises)**.
Indo-Greek legends: Greek front, **Kharoshthi** back.
Agathocles' coins show **Vasudeva and Sankarshana**.

42.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kushanas — Large-scale issue of gold coins
Indo-Greeks — First large-scale issue of gold dinaras
Guptas — Coins made only of potin
Punch-marked coins — Coins bearing portraits of rulers
42.x: The Kushanas issued gold coins on a large scale; Vima Kadphises was the first to do so. B is wrong because the Indo-Greeks issued India's first gold coins but only rarely, not on a large scale. Punch-marked coins carry symbols, not royal portraits, which begin with the Indo-Greeks.
42.tq: Start with the sure coin-series association and eliminate swapped features.
xs: The **Kushanas** issued **gold coins on a large scale** — first by **Vima Kadphises** — option **(1)**.
The **Indo-Greeks** issued India's **first gold coins**, but gold was **rare**, not large-scale.
Royal **portraits** began with the **Indo-Greeks**, not punch-marked coins.
xa: Indo-Greek coins: mainly **silver and copper**, with realistic portraits.
Kushana coins carry **many deities**.
Indo-Greek coins were the first definitely **attributed to kings**.

43.s:
Arrange the following foreign groups in chronological order of their major appearance in ancient India:
A. Kushanas
B. Indo-Greeks
C. Parthians
D. Sakas
43.x: The sequence is Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Parthians and Kushanas.
43.tq: Fix the earliest and latest groups first, then place the middle two.
xs: The order is **Indo-Greeks → Sakas → Parthians → Kushanas** (B, D, C, A) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Indo-Greeks** came in the **2nd c. BC**, the **Sakas** in the **1st c. BC**, and the **Parthians** and **Kushanas** in the **1st c. CE**.
Options (2), (3) and (4) misplace the **Sakas** or reverse the sequence; the **Kushanas** come last.
xa: The first Saka king was **Maues/Moga**, c. **80 BC**.
**Gondophares** was the **greatest ruler** of the Parthians (Pahlavas).
Shared Saka–Kushana traits: **trousers, long coats, helmets, boots** and a **better cavalry**.
The **Saka era** (**78 CE**) is credited to **Kanishka** (UPSC).

43.s: The first prominent Saka king in the Indian context is generally identified as:
43.x: Maues, also known as Moga, is regarded as the first prominent Saka king, around 80 BC.
43.tq: Distinguish the earliest ruler from later regional Saka rulers.
xs: The first Saka king is **Maues or Moga**, c. **80 BC** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Chashtana** and **Rudradaman** were later **Kardamaka** rulers of **Ujjain**.
**Gondophares** was the greatest ruler of the **Parthians**, not a Saka.
xa: Foreign sequence: **Indo-Greeks** (2nd c. BC) → **Sakas** (1st c. BC) → **Parthians** → **Kushanas** (1st c. CE).
Centres of Saka rule: **Mathura, Ujjain, Girnar**.
North-west Saka rulers at **Taxila**: **Liaka Kusulaka** and **Patika** (Taxila copper plate).

43.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the two branches of the Western Kshatrapas?
o: Kshaharatas—Western Deccan; Kardamakas—Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar
Kshaharatas—Ujjain and Malwa; Kardamakas—Nasik and Junnar
43.x: The Kshaharatas were associated with the Western Deccan, whereas the Kardamakas ruled around Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar.
43.tq: Compare the branches by territory rather than by ruler alone.
xs: **Kshaharatas** ruled the **Western Deccan** (Nasik); **Kardamakas** ruled **Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar** — option **(3)** is correct.
Kshaharata rulers: **Bhumaka** and **Nahapana** (Nasik, Junnar, Karle).
Kardamaka rulers: **Chashtana** and **Rudradaman I** (Kathiawar-Malwa, Ujjain).
**Mathura** (Rajuvula, Sodasa) and **Taxila** (Liaka Kusulaka, Patika) were separate Saka branches.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Kardamaka = Ujjain**; **Kshaharata = Nasik** — options (1) and (4) swap them.
**Gautamiputra Satakarni** defeated the Kshaharata **Nahapana** and **restruck his silver coins**.
Kardamaka silver coins carry **Saka-era dates**.

43.s: Which of the following rulers belonged to the Kardamaka branch?
43.x: Chashtana belonged to the Kardamaka branch. Bhumaka and Nahapana belonged to the Kshaharata branch.
43.tq: Use ruler–branch discrimination among closely related names.
xs: **Chashtana** belonged to the **Kardamaka** branch of **Ujjain** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Bhumaka** and **Nahapana** were **Kshaharata** rulers of **Nasik** and the Western Deccan.
**Ayama** was Nahapana's **minister (amatya)**, issuer of the **Junnar** inscription.
xa: **Rudradaman I** was the other great Kardamaka ruler (c. **130-150 CE**).
**Chashtana** fought **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** — a clash recorded by **Ptolemy**.
**Ushavadatta**, Nahapana's son-in-law, issued the **Nasik** and **Karle** records.

43.s: The clash between Chashtana and Vasishthiputra Pulumavi is referred to by which ancient writer?
43.x: Ptolemy records the clash between Chashtana and the Satavahana ruler Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
43.tq: Match the historical event with the relevant classical source.
xs: The clash between **Chashtana** and **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** is recorded by **Ptolemy** — option **(4)** is correct.
Chashtana was a **Kardamaka** ruler of **Ujjain**; Pulumavi was a **Satavahana**.
xa: The **Sakas** were often at war with the **Satavahanas** (UPSC).
**Rudradaman I** twice defeated **Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha**, but spared him as a close relative.
After Rudradaman's defeat of Pulumavi, the Satavahana centre shifted to **Amaravati**.

43.s: Which statement regarding the coinage of the Western Kshatrapas is correct?
o: Their principal coins were exclusively gold.
Their silver coins were numerous in western India, and Kardamaka coins carried Saka-era dates.
Their coins were issued only in copper and bore Gupta-era dates.
Their silver coins were confined to the eastern Deccan.
43.x: Numerous silver coins have been found in western India, and Kardamaka silver coins carried dates in the Saka era.
43.tq: Avoid absolute wording and combine metal, region and dating evidence.
xs: Western Kshatrapa coinage: **numerous silver coins** in **western India**, and **Kardamaka** coins carried **Saka-era dates** — option **(2)** is correct.
The coins were mainly **silver**, so "exclusively gold" (1) and "only copper with Gupta-era dates" (3) are wrong.
They came from **western India**, not the eastern Deccan (4).
xa: **Gautamiputra Satakarni** restruck **Nahapana's** silver coins — found in the **Jogalthembi hoard**.
Nasik record ratio: **1 suvarna = 35 karshapanas** (gold-silver **1 : 35**).
The **Saka era** starts in **78 CE**: **CE = Saka + 78**.

43.s: The Sakas are described in the sources as ruling through which titles?
43.x: The Sakas ruled through the titles Satrapa and Mahasatrapa.
43.tq: Identify the characteristic administrative titles of a ruling group.
xs: The Sakas ruled under the titles **Satrapas and Mahasatrapas** — option **(4)** is correct.
Their administration is called the **Satrap system** (UPSC).
xa: The Sakas were absorbed into society as **Vratya Kshatriyas**.
Branches: **Kardamaka** (Ujjain) and **Kshaharata** (Nasik), plus **Mathura** and **Taxila**.
Centres of Saka rule: **Mathura, Ujjain, Girnar**.

43.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
43.x: Rajuvula and Sodasa belonged to the Mathura branch. The Upper Deccan branch was associated with the Kshaharatas Bhumaka and Nahapana.
43.tq: Find the swapped ruler–region pair.
xs: **Upper Deccan — Rajuvula and Sodasa** is wrongly matched — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Rajuvula** and **Sodasa** ruled the **Mathura** branch; the **Upper Deccan (Kshaharata)** rulers were **Bhumaka** and **Nahapana**.
Pairs (1), (2), (3) are correct: Western India — **Chashtana, Rudradaman**; North-west — **Liaka Kusulaka, Patika**; Mathura — **Rajuvula, Sodasa**.
xa: North-west rulers are known from the **Taxila copper plate**.
⚠ **Kardamaka** = Ujjain; **Kshaharata** = Nasik.
Kshaharata sites: **Nasik, Junnar, Karle**.

43.s: Which of the following was a centre of Saka rule?
43.x: Mathura, Ujjain and Girnar were important centres of Saka rule.
43.tq: Identify a regional centre from a restricted historical list.
xs: **Mathura** was a centre of Saka rule — option **(2)** is correct.
The centres of Saka rule were **Mathura, Ujjain and Girnar** (UPSC).
xa: Mathura Saka rulers: **Rajuvula** and **Sodasa**.
**Girnar** holds **Rudradaman's** Junagadh rock record — the **first long inscription in Sanskrit**.
**Ujjain** was the capital of the **Kardamakas** (Chashtana, Rudradaman I).

43.s: The Sakas were frequently engaged in conflict with which ruling power in the Deccan?
43.x: The Sakas were often at war with the Satavahanas, especially in western and upper Deccan regions.
43.tq: Test the major political rivalry of the period.
xs: The Sakas were often at war with the **Satavahanas** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Gautamiputra Satakarni** defeated **Nahapana**; **Rudradaman I** twice defeated **Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha**.
xa: **Chashtana** fought **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** (recorded by **Ptolemy**).
The **Nasik Prashasti** of **Gautami Balashri** calls Gautamiputra destroyer of the **Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas**.
Marriage alliance: **Rudradamanika**, Rudradaman's daughter, married **Vasishthiputra Satakarni**.

43.s: Which inscription records the deposit of 2,000 karshapanas by Ushavadatta in a weavers’ guild at Govardhana?
43.x: The Nasik cave inscription records Ushavadatta’s deposit of 2,000 karshapanas in the weavers’ guild at Govardhana.
43.tq: Identify the inscription by its distinctive content.
xs: The **Nasik cave inscription** records **Ushavadatta's** deposit of **2,000 karshapanas** in the **weavers' guild at Govardhana** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Karle** record (also Ushavadatta) is a gift of a village to the Karle chaitya monks.
The **Junnar (Manmodi)** record is **Ayama's** gift of a cave or mandapa; **Junagadh** is **Rudradaman's** Sanskrit record.
xa: The deposit earned **12%** a year; **Kolika** = weavers.
APPSC G2 **2017** asked it twice (as **Rishabhadatta** and as **Ushavadatta**) — answer **Nasik** both times.
Ushavadatta (**Rishabhadatta**) was **Nahapana's son-in-law**.

43.s:
With reference to the Kshaharata records, consider the following statements:
1. Ushavadatta was the son-in-law of Nahapana.
2. Ushavadatta deposited money in a weavers' guild at Govardhana at 12% a year.
3. The term 'Kolika' denotes a guild of potters.
4. The Nasik record equates 1 suvarna with 35 karshapanas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
43.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct: Ushavadatta was Nahapana's son-in-law, his Nasik record deposits 2,000 karshapanas with the weavers' guild at Govardhana at 12% a year, and it gives 1 suvarna = 35 karshapanas. Statement 3 is wrong: Kolika means weavers, not potters. So option A; B, C and D all include the false statement 3.
43.tq: Kolika = weavers (same as the Govardhana guild); 1 : 35 is the gold-silver ratio.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Ushavadatta** was **Nahapana's son-in-law**.
Statement 2 correct: he deposited **2,000 karshapanas** in the **weavers' guild at Govardhana** at **12%** a year.
Statement 3 wrong: **Kolika** means **weavers**, not potters.
Statement 4 correct: **1 suvarna = 35 karshapanas** (gold-silver ratio **1 : 35**).
xa: Interest on guild deposits was generally **12%**.
Ushavadatta also issued the **Karle** record — gift of a village to the Karle chaitya monks.
The gold-silver ratio was asked in **UKPSC 2021**.

43.s: The Junnar Manmodi inscription, dated to year 46, records which of the following?
o: A gift of a cave or mandapa
A deposit in a guild at Govardhana
43.x: The Junnar Manmodi inscription records Ayama’s gift of a cave or mandapa and is dated to year 46.
43.tq: Distinguish closely related inscriptions by their recorded donation.
xs: The **Junnar Manmodi** record, dated **year 46**, records a **gift of a cave or mandapa** — option **(1)** is correct.
Its issuer was **Ayama**, Nahapana's **minister (amatya)**.
The **Govardhana guild deposit** is in the **Nasik** record; the **Sudarshana lake** repair is in **Rudradaman's** Junagadh record, which also names the **Yaudheyas**.
xa: APPSC G2 **2017** keyed **Ayama** as the Junnar issuer.
⚠ Ushavadatta's records are at **Nasik** and **Karle**, not Junnar.
**Karle**: Ushavadatta's gift of a village to the monks of the Karle chaitya.

43.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
43.x: The Nasik inscription was issued by Ushavadatta. Ayama is associated with the Junnar inscription, while Ushavadatta is also associated with Karle.
43.tq: Separate similar inscription–issuer pairs before selecting the correct match.
xs: **Nasik inscription — Ushavadatta** is correctly matched — option **(4)** is correct.
**Junagadh** was issued by **Rudradaman**, not Nahapana.
**Junnar** was issued by **Ayama**, and **Karle** by **Ushavadatta** — options (2) and (3) swap them.
xa: Ushavadatta (**Rishabhadatta**) was **Nahapana's son-in-law**.
Nasik record: **2,000 karshapanas** deposited in the weavers' guild at **Govardhana** at **12%**.
⚠ The AP History PYQ book wrongly names Ushavadatta for Junnar; the epigraphic record names **Ayama**.

43.s: The Jogalthembi hoard is particularly associated with which of the following?
o: Restruck silver coins of Nahapana by Gautamiputra Satakarni
43.x: The Jogalthembi hoard contains silver coins of Nahapana restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni.
43.tq: Link an archaeological hoard with its distinctive coin evidence.
xs: The **Jogalthembi hoard** holds **Nahapana's** silver coins **restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is the proof of Gautamiputra's **reconquest** after defeating **Nahapana** (APHQ **2000**).
xa: The **Nasik Prashasti** of **Gautami Balashri** calls him destroyer of the **Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas**.
Western Kshatrapas issued **numerous silver coins** in western India.
Satavahana capitals: **Pratishthana (Paithan)** and **Amaravati**.

43.s: The Junnar (Manmodi) cave inscription of the Kshaharata period was issued by
43.x: The Junnar record, a gift of a cave or mandapa dated year 46, was issued by Ayama, Nahapana's amatya (APPSC G2 2017 key). Ushavadatta's records are at Nasik and Karle, Gautami Balashri issued the Nasik Prashasti, and Chashtana was a Kardamaka ruler.
43.tq: Junnar = Ayama; Nasik and Karle = Ushavadatta.
xs: The **Junnar (Manmodi)** inscription was issued by **Ayama, minister of Nahapana** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Ushavadatta's** records are at **Nasik** and **Karle**.
**Gautami Balashri** issued the **Nasik Prashasti**; **Chashtana** was a **Kardamaka** ruler of Ujjain.
xa: Content: gift of a **cave or mandapa**, dated **year 46**.
⚠ APPSC G2 **2017** keyed **Ayama**; the AP History PYQ book says Ushavadatta — the epigraphic record names **Ayama**.

43.s: The Nasik Prashasti, which calls Gautamiputra Satakarni the destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, was issued by
43.x: The Nasik Prashasti was issued by Gautami Balashri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni. Naganika is linked with the Nanaghat inscription, Ushavadatta with Nahapana's Nasik and Karle records, and Rudradamanika was Rudradaman's daughter.
43.tq: Nasik Prashasti = Gautami Balashri praising Gautamiputra.
xs: The **Nasik Prashasti** was issued by **Gautami Balashri**, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni — option **(3)** is correct.
**Ushavadatta** issued the **Nasik** cave and **Karle** records of the Kshaharatas.
**Rudradamanika** was **Rudradaman's daughter**, who married **Vasishthiputra Satakarni**.
xa: The Prashasti calls Gautamiputra destroyer of the **Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas**.
He defeated **Nahapana** and restruck his coins — proof in the **Jogalthembi hoard**.
Satavahana capitals: **Pratishthana (Paithan)** and **Amaravati**.

43.s:
Consider the following statements about Rudradaman I:
1. He ruled c. 130-150 CE from Ujjain.
2. His Junagadh inscription is dated Saka 72, which corresponds to 72 CE.
3. He conquered the Yaudheyas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
43.x: Statement 1 is correct: Rudradaman ruled c. 130-150 CE from Ujjain. Statement 2 is wrong: Saka 72 = 72 + 78 = 150 CE, not 72 CE. Statement 3 is correct: the Yaudheyas were among his conquests. So B; A omits 3, C and D include the false statement 2.
43.tq: Saka year + 78 = CE; Junagadh = Saka 72 = 150 CE.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Rudradaman I** ruled c. **130-150 CE** from **Ujjain**.
Statement 2 wrong: **Saka 72 = 150 CE** (72 + 78), not 72 CE.
Statement 3 correct: the **Yaudheyas** were among his conquests.
xa: He **twice defeated Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha**, but spared him as a close relative.
He repaired **Sudarshana lake** through his Pahlava minister **Suvishakha**.
His **Junagadh** record is the **first long inscription in Sanskrit**.

43.s: The Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman I is significant because it is:
o: The first copper-plate charter of the Guptas
The earliest inscription entirely in Tamil
The first long inscription in Sanskrit
43.x: The Junagadh or Girnar record is regarded as the first long inscription in Sanskrit; earlier long records were generally in Prakrit.
43.tq: Identify historical significance through a distinctive superlative.
xs: **Rudradaman's Junagadh (Girnar)** record is the **first long inscription in Sanskrit** — option **(4)** is correct.
Earlier inscriptions were in **Prakrit** (UPSC).
It is dated **Saka 72 = 150 CE**.
xa: It records the repair of **Sudarshana lake** by **Suvishakha** (BPSC **2022**).
The lake was built by **Pushyagupta Vaishya**, governor of **Chandragupta Maurya**.
Rudradaman ruled c. **130-150 CE** from **Ujjain**.

43.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.
List-I
(a) Pushyagupta
(b) Tushaspha
(c) Rudradaman I
(d) Chakrapalita
List-II
(i) Repaired Sudarshana lake during the Gupta period
(ii) Built Sudarshana lake
