⚠ Don't confuse with **Kumaragupta I** coins: **Kartikeya** + king feeding a **peacock**.
xa: Chandragupta II issued **lion-slayer** coins; his father the **tiger-slayer** type.
Later Gupta gold coins had **less gold, more alloy** — debasement.
**No Gupta coins or inscriptions** appear in western Malwa and Saurashtra after Skandagupta.

62.s: Which institutional change is associated with Skandagupta’s reign?
o: Governors became hereditary feudatories as central control weakened.
The Gupta Empire became a federation of independent republics immediately.
Provincial offices were transferred exclusively to Buddhist monasteries.
Governors were abolished and all provinces were directly administered from Pataliputra.
62.x: Central control weakened under Skandagupta, and governors increasingly became hereditary feudatories.
62.tq: Infer administrative decentralisation from the change in provincial offices.
xs: Under Skandagupta **central control weakened** and **governors became hereditary feudatories** — option **(1)**.
This fed the feudatory cause of decline: land grants + **hereditary governors** created feudatories.
xa: **Feudatories broke away**: Yashodharman; Bihar, Bengal, MP, **Valabhi**, Gujarat, western Malwa.
Gupta administration rested on feudatories, unlike the **centralised Mauryas**.
**Weak successors** after Skandagupta led to the last ruler **Vishnugupta** (**c. 540–550 CE**).

62.s: The Bhitari pillar inscription in Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) records the victories of which Gupta ruler over the Pushyamitras and the Hunas?
62.x: The Bhitari pillar records Skandagupta's victories over the Pushyamitras and the Hunas; he is the Gupta ruler who defeated the Hunas (UPPSC 2015). The first Huna attack came late in Kumaragupta I's reign, but it was Prince Skandagupta who repulsed it; Chandragupta II defeated the Sakas; Toramana's advance came under Budhagupta and later rulers.
62.tq: Bhitari = Skandagupta vs Hunas.
xs: The **Bhitari pillar** (Ghazipur, UP) records **Skandagupta's** victories over the **Pushyamitras** and **Hunas** — option **(2)**.
The first Huna attack came late in **Kumaragupta I's** reign but was repulsed by **prince Skandagupta**.
**Chandragupta II** beat the **Sakas**; **Toramana** advanced under **Budhagupta** and after.
xa: UPPSC **2014**: Bhitari pillar = Skandagupta's victory over the Hunas.
He repulsed the Hunas **twice** and took the title **Vikramaditya**.
The **Eran boar** records **Toramana's** first regnal year; the **Mandasor pillars** record Yashodharman's defeat of **Mihirakula**.

62.s: Who repelled the first Huna attack on the Gupta Empire?
62.x: Prince Skandagupta repelled the first Huna attack, which took place during the reign of Kumaragupta I.
62.tq: Discriminate between the attacked ruler and the military defender.
xs: **Prince Skandagupta** repelled the **first Huna attack**, late in **Kumaragupta I's** reign — option **(2)**.
**Yashodharman** and **Narasimhagupta Baladitya** defeated the later leader **Mihirakula**.
**Rudrasimha III** was the **Saka** ruler defeated by Chandragupta II.
xa: The Hunas were **Hephthalites / White Huns** from Central Asia via the **Oxus** valley.
They occupied **Gandhara** in the mid-5th century.
Exam angle (UPPSC **2016**): Kumaragupta I = first attack; Skandagupta = repulsed; Yashodharman = defeated Mihirakula.

62.s: The Hunas who entered India in the mid-fifth century were also known as:
62.x: The Hunas were Hephthalites, also called White Huns. They came from Central Asia through the Oxus valley.
62.tq: Distinguish closely associated Central Asian peoples by their alternative names.
xs: The Hunas were the **Hephthalites / White Huns** — option **(4)**.
They came from **Central Asia** via the **Oxus** valley and occupied **Gandhara** in the mid-5th century.
xa: First attack: late **Kumaragupta I**, repulsed by prince **Skandagupta**.
Leaders: **Toramana** and his son **Mihirakula**.
**By 485 CE** Hunas held Punjab, Rajasthan, Kashmir, eastern Malwa, central India.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about Skandagupta’s Huna campaigns:
1. He repulsed the Hunas twice.
2. He assumed the title Vikramaditya after his victories.
3. His campaigns belonged to the reign of Kumaragupta I alone.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: Skandagupta repulsed the Hunas twice and took the title Vikramaditya. The later Huna waves occurred during his own reign, so statement 3 is false.
62.tq: Detect the statement that improperly confines a continuing invasion to one reign.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Skandagupta **repulsed the Hunas twice**.
Statement 2 is correct: he took the title **Vikramaditya**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **later waves** came in **Skandagupta's own reign** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Only the **first attack** fell in late **Kumaragupta I's** reign.
The **Bhitari pillar** records his victories over the Hunas (UPPSC **2014**).
⚠ "Vikramaditya" is shared with **Chandragupta II** — questions usually want Chandragupta II (APPSC-G2 **2008**).

62.s: Which sequence correctly represents the Huna leaders and the Indian rulers associated with their defeat?
o: Toramana—no defeat stated; Mihirakula—Yashodharman and Narasimhagupta Baladitya
62.x: C is correct: Toramana occupied Malwa and central India (up to Eran) but no Indian ruler is recorded as defeating him, while Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa and Narasimhagupta Baladitya. Skandagupta fought the earlier Huna waves, and Rudrasimha III, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I and Samudragupta are not linked to defeating these two leaders.
62.tq: Separate the territorial advance of Toramana from the recorded defeat of Mihirakula.
xs: **Toramana** has no recorded defeat; **Mihirakula** was defeated by **Yashodharman and Narasimhagupta Baladitya** — option **(3)**.
**Skandagupta** fought the earlier Huna waves, not Mihirakula.
**Rudrasimha III** was a **Saka** ruler; Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I and Samudragupta are not linked to these leaders.
xa: **Toramana** conquered western India up to **Eran** (near Bhopal).
**Mihirakula** (**c. 515 CE**), Toramana's son, **persecuted Buddhists**; the **Maukharis** also fought him.
Yashodharman's **victory pillars** at **Mandasor (Sondani)** date to **c. 532 CE**.

62.s: Which statement about Mihirakula is correct?
o: He was defeated by Rudrasimha III in western Malwa.
He was the father of Toramana and patronised Buddhism.
He led the first Huna attack during Kumaragupta I’s reign.
He was the son of Toramana and persecuted Buddhists.
62.x: Mihirakula was the son of Toramana. He was described as a tyrant and iconoclast who persecuted Buddhists.
62.tq: Use the father–son relationship and religious policy as distinguishing clues.
xs: **Mihirakula** was the **son of Toramana** and **persecuted Buddhists** — option **(4)**.
He was a **tyrant and iconoclast**, not a patron of Buddhism.
The **first Huna attack** came under **Kumaragupta I**, before Mihirakula; **Rudrasimha III** was a Saka.
xa: He was defeated by **Yashodharman of Malwa**, **Narasimhagupta Baladitya** and the **Maukharis**.
Mihirakula is dated **c. 515 CE**.
Yashodharman's **Mandasor pillars** record his defeat of Mihirakula.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
A. First Huna attack
B. Later Huna waves
C. Toramana
D. Mihirakula

List-II
1. Narasimhagupta’s reign
2. Late Kumaragupta I’s reign
3. Skandagupta’s reign
4. Budhagupta and after

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The first attack occurred during late Kumaragupta I; later waves during Skandagupta; Toramana advanced under Budhagupta and after; Mihirakula is associated with Narasimhagupta’s reign.
62.tq: Start with the fixed first-attack and later-wave pairs.
xs: Correct match: **A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1** — option **(1)**.
**First Huna attack** → late **Kumaragupta I**; **later waves** → **Skandagupta's** reign.
**Toramana** → **Budhagupta** and after; **Mihirakula** → **Narasimhagupta's** reign.
xa: The first attack was repulsed by **prince Skandagupta**.
**By 485 CE** the Hunas held eastern Malwa and central India.
**Mihirakula** was defeated by **Yashodharman** of Malwa.

62.s:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order:
A. First Huna attack during the reign of Kumaragupta I
B. Saka conquest by Chandragupta II
C. Later Huna waves during the reign of Skandagupta
D. Advance of Toramana into western and central India

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The Saka conquest of Chandragupta II preceded the first Huna attack in late Kumaragupta I’s reign; later Huna waves occurred under Skandagupta, followed by Toramana’s advance under the weaker successors.
62.tq: Use the Gupta succession as the first framework, then place the invasions.
xs: The order is **B, A, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Saka conquest** by **Chandragupta II** (**c. 380–413 CE**) came first.
Then the **first Huna attack** (late **Kumaragupta I**) and **later waves** under **Skandagupta** (**455–467**).
**Toramana's** advance came under weak successors (**late 5th century**).
xa: **By 485 CE** the Hunas held Punjab, Rajasthan, Kashmir, eastern Malwa, central India.
**Mihirakula** (**c. 515 CE**) followed; Yashodharman's pillars date to **c. 532 CE**.
Toramana conquered up to **Eran** (near Bhopal).

62.s: Yashodharman, who rose in Malwa, was originally a:
62.x: Yashodharman was a Gupta feudatory in Malwa. His subsequent rise and victory over Mihirakula further undermined Gupta authority.
62.tq: Use the political relationship between a regional ruler and the Gupta centre as the discriminator.
xs: **Yashodharman** was a **Gupta feudatory in Malwa** — option **(4)**.
He belonged to the **Aulikaras** of **Mandsaur (Dashapura)**, not the Maitrakas, Vakatakas or Pushyabhutis.
xa: He defeated **Mihirakula**; victory pillars at **Mandasor (Sondani)**, **c. 532 CE**.
His rise **undermined Gupta authority**.
**Maitrakas** ruled Gujarat/western Malwa (capital **Valabhi**); **Pushyabhutis** ruled **Thanesar**.

62.s: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani near Mandasor are generally dated to approximately:
62.x: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani are dated to approximately 532 CE. They commemorate his victory over Mihirakula.
62.tq: Separate the date of Yashodharman's victory from the earlier Bilsad, silk-weaver and Eran dates.
xs: Yashodharman's victory pillars at **Mandasor (Sondani)** date to **c. 532 CE** — option **(4)**.
**415 CE** is Kumaragupta I's **Bilsad** inscription; **473** is the silk weavers' migration; **510 CE** is the **Eran** sati record.
⚠ Trap: some notes misread this as "**532 victory pillars**".
xa: The pillars commemorate his defeat of **Mihirakula**.
He was a Gupta **feudatory in Malwa**, of the **Aulikaras** of Mandsaur.
His victory **did not revive** the Gupta Empire.

62.s: Which inference most accurately follows from Yashodharman's victory over Mihirakula?
o: It brought Malwa permanently under direct Gupta administration.
It demonstrated the rise of a regional power and further weakened Gupta authority.
It ended the process of regionalisation in northern India.
It immediately restored the Gupta Empire to its former extent.
62.x: Yashodharman's victory did not revive the Gupta Empire; his own rise as a regional power undermined Gupta authority and reflected the wider process of political fragmentation.
62.tq: Distinguish the immediate military success from its broader political consequence.
xs: Yashodharman's victory showed the **rise of a regional power** and **further weakened Gupta authority** — option **(2)**.
The notes say his victory over the Hunas **did not revive the empire**.
xa: **Feudatories broke away**: Yashodharman; Bihar, Bengal, MP, Valabhi, Gujarat, western Malwa.
Rise of **Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas, Pushyabhutis** followed.
The break-up marks the move from a **single empire → regional kingdoms** + feudal order.

62.s: The Eran boar inscription is significant because it records:
o: Huna rule over Eran in the first regnal year of Toramana
The victory of Yashodharman over Mihirakula
The migration of silk weavers from Gujarat to Malwa
The foundation of Nalanda by Kumaragupta I
62.x: The Eran boar inscription was built in Toramana's first regnal year and records Huna rule over Eran.
62.tq: Link a monument with the exact Huna ruler and political circumstance named in the record.
xs: The **Eran boar (Varaha)** inscription records **Huna rule over Eran** in **Toramana's first regnal year** — option **(1)**.
Yashodharman's victory is on the **Mandasor pillars**; the **silk weavers'** guild is in the **Mandsaur prashasti**.
xa: Toramana conquered western India up to **Eran** (near Bhopal).
⚠ A separate **Eran** inscription (**510 CE**) of Goparaja is the **earliest sati** record.
The **Bhitari pillar** records **Skandagupta's** victory over the Hunas.

62.s: Which literary work, apart from inscriptions, mentions the Hunas?
62.x: Banabhatta's Harshacharita also mentions the Hunas. The other works are not identified here as the relevant literary reference.
62.tq: Match the historical group with the literary source that mentions it.
xs: **Banabhatta's Harshacharita** mentions the **Hunas** — option **(2)**.
**Vishakhadatta** in this topic is cited for **Devichandraguptam** (the Ramagupta episode).
xa: Inscriptions on the Hunas: **Bhitari pillar** (Skandagupta), **Eran boar** (Toramana), **Mandasor pillars** (Yashodharman).
The Hunas were **Hephthalites / White Huns** from the **Oxus** valley.
The **Pushyabhutis** of **Thanesar** were a successor power.

62.s: The Eran inscription of 510 CE, which records Goparaja, the general of Bhanugupta, is significant because it is
o: the earliest inscriptional record of sati
the record of Yashodharman's victory over Mihirakula
the record of Huna rule in Toramana's first regnal year
the record of the first Huna attack under Kumaragupta I
62.x: The Eran inscription of Bhanugupta's general Goparaja (510 CE) is the earliest record of sati. Yashodharman's victory is on the Mandasor pillars; Toramana's first regnal year is on the Eran boar; the first Huna attack is not linked to this record.
62.tq: Eran 510 CE (Goparaja) = first sati record.
xs: The **Eran inscription (510 CE)** of **Goparaja**, Bhanugupta's general, is the **earliest record of sati** — option **(1)**.
Yashodharman's defeat of Mihirakula is on the **Mandasor pillars**.
Huna rule in **Toramana's first regnal year** is on the **Eran boar**.
xa: Toramana reached **Eran** (near Bhopal).
The **Bhitari pillar** (Ghazipur) records Skandagupta's Huna victory.
**Bilsad** (Gupta year **96 = 415 CE**) is Kumaragupta I's earliest inscription.

62.s: Which of the following was an external factor contributing to the decline of the Gupta Empire?
o: Migration of silk weavers to Malwa
62.x: Repeated Huna invasions were an external cause of Gupta decline. The other factors represent economic or feudatory-related explanations.
62.tq: Classify the cause by distinguishing external pressure from internal administrative and economic causes.
xs: **Repeated Huna invasions** were the **external** factor in Gupta decline — option **(2)**.
They **drained the treasury and army**; the **Pushyamitra** attack was another external blow.
Silk weavers' migration and loss of a **professional army** are **economic**; hereditary governors are **feudatory** causes.
xa: ⚠ The **Arab invasion** was **not** a cause (UKPSC **2012**).
Later Guptas' **leaning to Buddhism** is listed as a cause in some questions.
Later gold coins had **less gold, more alloy**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of Gupta decline:
1. Land grants encouraged the growth of feudatories.
2. Hereditary governors strengthened the centralised control of the emperor.
3. The rise of Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas and Pushyabhutis weakened Gupta authority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because hereditary governors contributed to the growth of autonomous feudatories rather than strengthening centralised imperial control.
62.tq: Spot the reversed effect in the statement about hereditary governors.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **land grants** + hereditary governors **created feudatories**.
Statement 2 is wrong: hereditary governors **weakened** central control, as under Skandagupta.
Statement 3 is correct: the rise of **Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas, Pushyabhutis** weakened the Guptas — **1 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Gupta administration rested on feudatories, unlike the **centralised Mauryas**.
UPSC **2021**: **Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj, Maitrakas of Valabhi**.
⚠ Not the **Paramaras** of Malwa or **Yadavas** of Devagiri (both later).

62.s:
Assertion (A): The Gupta state found it difficult to maintain a professional army in the later period.
Reason (R): Land grants reduced the revenue available to the state.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
62.x: Both statements are true, and the reduction of state revenue through land grants directly weakened the state's ability to maintain a professional army.
62.tq: Test a direct cause-and-effect relationship between declining revenue and military weakness.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Land grants cut revenue**; with falling trade revenue, **no professional army** could be kept.
xa: **Loss of western India** cost trade income and the **Roman silk trade**.
Silk weavers migrated from Gujarat to Malwa (**AD 473**) and left their craft.
Coins gradually vanished post-Gupta → **payments shifted to land**; towns decayed.

62.s: Which one of the following best explains the economic impact of the loss of western India on the Gupta Empire?
o: It brought the western feudatories under tighter imperial control.
It enabled the state to maintain a larger professional army.
It increased the inflow of gold from western ports.
It reduced trade income, including income connected with Roman silk trade.
62.x: The loss of western India reduced trade income and contributed to the loss of revenue from the Roman silk trade. This aggravated the financial and military weakness of the empire.
62.tq: Apply the economic-cause chain from territorial loss to declining state revenue.
xs: The **loss of western India** reduced **trade income**, including the **Roman silk trade** — option **(4)**.
With **land grants** also cutting revenue, the state could keep **no professional army** — so option (2) is the reverse.
Western feudatories **broke away** (Valabhi, Gujarat, western Malwa), not tighter control.
xa: Silk weavers migrated from **Gujarat to Malwa** (**AD 473**) and left their craft.
**No Gupta coins or inscriptions** appear in western Malwa and Saurashtra after **Skandagupta**.
The **Maitrakas** of **Valabhi** ruled Gujarat / western Malwa after the Guptas.

62.s: Which one of the following was NOT identified as a cause of the decline of the Gupta Empire in the explanations listed?
62.x: The Arab invasion was not a cause of Gupta decline in this context. Huna invasions, the growth of feudatories and the loss of western trade revenue were identified causes.
62.tq: Use the explicit exception and separate a later invasion from the relevant Gupta-period causes.
xs: The **Arab invasion** was **not** a cause of Gupta decline (UKPSC **2012**) — option **(4)**.
**Huna invasions** drained the treasury and army — an external cause.
**Feudatories** grew from land grants and hereditary governors; **loss of western India** cut trade revenue.
xa: **Weak successors** after Skandagupta; last ruler **Vishnugupta** (**c. 540–550 CE**).
Later Guptas' **leaning to Buddhism** is listed as a cause in some questions.
Later gold coins show **less gold, more alloy**.

62.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the later Gupta period is correct?
o: The empire was strengthened by a succession of powerful rulers after Skandagupta.
The weakness of successors after Skandagupta contributed to imperial decline.
The loss of western India increased Gupta trade revenue.
The Gupta administration became more centralised than that of the Mauryas.
62.x: Weak successors after Skandagupta contributed to the decline of Gupta authority. The other statements reverse the recorded political and economic trends.
62.tq: Reject reversed comparisons and identify the correct succession-based explanation.
xs: **Weak successors after Skandagupta** contributed to decline — option **(2)**.
The loss of western India **cut** trade revenue, not raised it.
Gupta administration rested on **feudatories**, unlike the **centralised Mauryas**.
xa: **Skandagupta** was the **last great Gupta ruler**.
The main line ended with **Vishnugupta** (**c. 540–550 CE**).
Under Skandagupta, governors became **hereditary feudatories**.

62.s: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions in western Malwa and Saurashtra after the reign of Skandagupta indicates:
o: The complete end of trade in eastern India
Expansion of Gupta control into western India
Loss of Gupta control over those territories
62.x: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions after Skandagupta in western Malwa and Saurashtra is evidence that these areas were no longer under effective Gupta control.
62.tq: Infer territorial change from the geographic distribution of material evidence.
xs: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions there shows **loss of Gupta control** over those territories — option **(3)**.
Notes: **No Gupta coins or inscriptions** in **western Malwa and Saurashtra** after **Skandagupta**.
xa: **Loss of western India** cost trade income and the **Roman silk trade**.
Those areas passed to powers like the **Maitrakas** (capital **Valabhi**).
⚠ **Nalanda** was founded by **Kumaragupta I** — unrelated to this evidence.

62.s: Which feature of later Gupta gold coins is cited as evidence of the empire's economic decline?
o: They contained less gold and more alloy
They were struck in larger numbers than ever before
They were replaced by Roman gold coins
They carried the portraits of Huna rulers
62.x: Later Gupta gold coins were debased, with less gold and more alloy, and coins gradually disappeared as payments shifted to land. There is no record of more coins being struck, of Roman coins replacing them, or of Huna portraits on Gupta coins.
62.tq: Decline evidence: debased coins (less gold, more alloy).
xs: Later Gupta gold coins had **less gold and more alloy** — debasement, option **(1)**.
The notes record no larger issues, Roman replacement or **Huna** portraits on Gupta coins.
xa: Coins **gradually vanish** post-Gupta → payments shifted to **land**.
Earlier, **Skandagupta's** gold coins showed **bow and arrow, Garuda standard, Lakshmi**.
Towns **decayed** as trade revenue fell.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Power)
 a. Later Guptas
 b. Maitrakas
 c. Pushyabhutis
 d. Aulikaras

List-II (Centre or region)
 i. Mandsaur
 ii. Magadha
 iii. Valabhi
 iv. Thanesar and later Kannauj

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
62.x: The Later Guptas were associated with Magadha, the Maitrakas with Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and later Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur.
62.tq: Start with the sure pair of a dynasty and its principal centre, then complete the code.
xs: Correct match: **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Later Guptas** → **Magadha**; **Maitrakas** → **Valabhi** (Gujarat / western Malwa).
**Pushyabhutis** → **Thanesar**, later **Kannauj**; **Aulikaras** → **Mandsaur (Dashapura)**, Malwa.
xa: **Maukharis** ruled Bihar and UP (**Kannauj**); **Gaudas** ruled Bengal under **Shashanka**.
The Aulikara **Yashodharman** defeated **Mihirakula**.
UPSC **2021**: Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj, Maitrakas of Valabhi.

62.s: Which one of the following was NOT a power included among the major successor powers of the Guptas in the north and west?
62.x: The Paramaras of Malwa were a later power and were not included among the successor powers listed in this context. The Maukharis, Maitrakas and Pushyabhutis were included.
62.tq: Find the later dynasty that does not belong to the contemporary successor group.
xs: The **Paramaras of Malwa** were a **later** power, not a Gupta successor — option **(2)**.
**Maukharis** (Kannauj), **Maitrakas** (Valabhi) and **Pushyabhutis** (Thanesar) were successor powers.
xa: ⚠ The **Yadavas of Devagiri** are the other "later" trap (UPSC **2021**).
Other successors: **Later Guptas** (Magadha), **Aulikaras** (Mandsaur), **Gaudas** (Bengal).
The Pushyabhutis later moved to **Kannauj**.

62.s: The Mandsaur prashasti of the silk weavers' guild and the Mandsaur pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman are associated with which regional power?
62.x: Both groups of inscriptions come from the Aulikara area centred on Mandsaur in Malwa. They represent different aspects of the political and social history of that region.
62.tq: Link two inscriptional references through their common regional setting.
xs: Both records belong to the **Aulikaras** — the area of **Mandsaur (Dashapura), Malwa** — option **(1)**.
The **Mandsaur prashasti** of the **silk weavers' guild** names **Kumaragupta I + Bandhuvarman**.
Yashodharman's **Mandsaur pillars** record his defeat of **Mihirakula**.
xa: The pillars at **Mandasor (Sondani)** date to **c. 532 CE**.
Silk weavers migrated from Gujarat to Malwa in **AD 473**.
**Maitrakas** = Valabhi; **Pushyabhutis** = Thanesar; **Later Guptas** = Magadha.

62.s:
Which one of the following combinations is correct regarding the regional powers mentioned in the post-Gupta period?
1. Guptas — Magadha
2. Pushyabhutis — Thanesar
3. Maukharis — Kannauj
4. Maitrakas — Valabhi
62.x: All four combinations are correct. The Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj and Maitrakas of Valabhi formed important regional powers after Gupta authority weakened.
62.tq: Test a compact set of dynasty–centre associations, including the easily confused centres of Thanesar and Kannauj.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)** (UPSC **2021** answer).
**Guptas of Magadha**, **Pushyabhutis of Thanesar**, **Maukharis of Kannauj**, **Maitrakas of Valabhi**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: not the **Paramaras of Malwa** or **Yadavas of Devagiri** (both later).
**Aulikaras** held **Mandsaur**; **Gaudas** held Bengal under **Shashanka**.
The Maitrakas ruled **Gujarat / western Malwa**.

62.s: Which regional dynasty is correctly matched with its political and cultural profile?
o: Maitrakas — Banavasi; Rudrasena II patronised Ajanta
Vishnukundins — Gujarat; Madhava Varma II ruled Valabhi
Vakatakas — Vidarbha and northern Maharashtra; Harishena patronised Ajanta
62.x: The Vakatakas were associated with northern Maharashtra and Vidarbha, and Harishena patronised Ajanta. The other options incorrectly combine dynasties, regions and personalities.
62.tq: Use the dynasty–region–patron combination and detect swapped rulers or centres.
xs: **Vakatakas — Vidarbha and northern Maharashtra; Harishena patronised Ajanta** — option **(4)**.
**Banavasi** belongs to the **Kadambas**; **Mayurasharma** founded the Kadambas, not Nalanda (**Kumaragupta I**).
**Vishnukundins** were in **Andhra**; **Valabhi** was the Maitraka capital; **Rudrasena II** married Prabhavati Gupta.
xa: The Vakatakas were **Brahmins**, successors of the **Satavahanas**, contemporaries of the Guptas.
**Madhava Varma II** (**440–495 CE**) was the greatest **Vishnukundin**.
Vakataka **Rudrasena II** married **Prabhavati Gupta**, daughter of Chandragupta II.

62.s: The Kadambas of Banavasi were founded by:
62.x: Mayurasharma founded the Kadamba dynasty of Banavasi in Karnataka.
62.tq: Test the founder–dynasty association directly, a common historical trap.
xs: The **Kadambas** of **Banavasi** (Karnataka) were founded by **Mayurasharma** — option **(3)**.
**Madhava Varma II** was a **Vishnukundin**; **Rudrasena II** and **Harishena** were **Vakatakas**.
xa: Vakataka **Harishena** patronised **Ajanta**.
Madhava Varma II (**440–495 CE**) performed **11 Ashvamedhas**.
The Vakatakas ruled northern Maharashtra and **Vidarbha**.

62.s:
Which of the following statements about Madhava Varma II is correct?
1. He was a ruler of the Vishnukundins.
2. He ruled approximately from 440 to 495 CE.
3. He won over 100 battles.
4. He performed 11 Ashvamedhas.
62.x: All four statements are correct. Madhava Varma II was the greatest Vishnukundin ruler, ruled around 440–495 CE, won over 100 battles and performed 11 Ashvamedhas.
62.tq: Combine ruler, dates, military achievement and ritual achievement in one coded question.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: he was the **greatest Vishnukundin** ruler.
Statement 2 is correct: he ruled **440–495 CE**.
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: he **won over 100 battles** and performed **11 Ashvamedhas** — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
xa: **Indrabhattaraka Varma** (Vishnukundin) was defeated by the Maukhari **Ishanavarma** (**Jaunpur** inscription).
The Vishnukundins ruled **Andhra**.
This clash **links Andhra to North Indian politics**.

62.s: Which inscription records the defeat of Indrabhattaraka Varma by the Maukhari ruler Ishanavarma?
62.x: The Jaunpur inscription of Uttar Pradesh records the defeat of Indrabhattaraka Varma by the Maukhari ruler Ishanavarma.
62.tq: Match the political event with the specific inscription and location.
xs: The **Jaunpur inscription** (UP) records **Ishanavarma's** defeat of **Indrabhattaraka Varma** — option **(2)**.
**Mandsaur pillars** = Yashodharman over **Mihirakula**; **Bilsad** = Kumaragupta I; **Bhitari** = Skandagupta over the **Hunas**.
xa: Indrabhattaraka Varma was a **Vishnukundin** of Andhra.
The **Maukharis** ruled Bihar and UP (**Kannauj**).
The greatest Vishnukundin was **Madhava Varma II** (**440–495 CE**).

62.s: The clash between the Vishnukundins and the Maukharis is significant for Andhra history because it:
o: Links Andhra political developments with North Indian regional politics.
Proves that the Maukharis ruled the whole of coastal Andhra.
Marks the beginning of the Satavahana period.
Shows that the Vishnukundins founded the Gupta Empire.
62.x: The Vishnukundin–Maukhari conflict links Andhra history with the political struggles among northern Indian regional powers in the post-Gupta period.
62.tq: Apply a regional-history fact to its wider political significance.
xs: The Vishnukundin–Maukhari clash **links Andhra to North Indian politics** — option **(1)**.
It was the Maukhari **Ishanavarma's** defeat of **Indrabhattaraka Varma** (Jaunpur inscription).
The Vakatakas, not this clash, were **successors of the Satavahanas**.
xa: **Madhava Varma II** (**440–495 CE**) won over **100** battles and performed **11 Ashvamedhas**.
The Maukharis are tied to **Kannauj**.
Other Deccan powers: **Vakatakas** (Vidarbha) and **Kadambas** (Banavasi).

62.s: Which statement best expresses the historical significance of the Gupta decline?
o: It marked the transition from a single empire towards regional kingdoms and a feudal order.
It ended the emergence of all regional dynasties in northern India.
It converted all land grants into direct imperial taxation.
It resulted in the permanent restoration of Mauryan centralisation.
62.x: The break-up of Gupta authority marked a movement from a single empire to regional kingdoms and a more feudal political order.
62.tq: Identify the broad historical consequence without being misled by absolute alternatives.
xs: Gupta decline marked the move from a **single empire → regional kingdoms + feudal order** — option **(1)**.
Regional dynasties **rose**, not ended: **Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas, Pushyabhutis**.
**Land grants** cut revenue; administration rested on feudatories, unlike the **centralised Mauryas**.
xa: **Chandragupta II** took the empire to its **zenith**; **Skandagupta** was the last great Gupta ruler.
Feudatories broke away: **Yashodharman**; Bihar, Bengal, MP, **Valabhi**, Gujarat, western Malwa.
Coins vanished post-Gupta → **payments shifted to land**.

62.s: The title 'Vikramaditya' was used by which pair of Gupta rulers?
62.x: The title Vikramaditya was used by both Chandragupta II and Skandagupta. When a question asks for the principal Gupta ruler associated with Vikramaditya, it commonly refers to Chandragupta II, but both rulers used the title.
62.tq: Separate a shared title from the ruler most commonly associated with it.
xs: **Vikramaditya** was used by both **Chandragupta II and Skandagupta** — option **(4)**.
⚠ When one ruler is asked, the question usually wants **Chandragupta II** (APPSC-G2 **2008**).
**Kumaragupta I's** titles were **Shakraditya** and **Mahendraditya**.
xa: Chandragupta II's other title: **Simhavikrama**; other names **Devagupta / Devaraja**.
Skandagupta took the title after **repulsing the Hunas**.
Founder **Sri Gupta** bore the title **"Maharaja"**.

62.s: Which comparison is correctly stated regarding the decline of the Guptas and the Kushans?
o: The Guptas and Kushans both retained uninterrupted imperial control after regional powers rose.
The Kushans expanded after the Sasanians defeated them.
Only the Guptas faced external pressure; the Kushans declined solely because of trade.
Both faced external pressure along with the rise of an Indian power.
62.x: The Kushans declined under pressure from the Sasanians together with the rise of an Indian power, while the Guptas similarly faced external invasions and the rise of regional powers.
62.tq: Compare the common structural pattern rather than matching only one dynasty-specific event.
xs: Both faced **external pressure** plus the **rise of an Indian power** — option **(4)**.
The **Kushans** fell to a squeeze from the **Sasanians** + a rising Indian power.
The Guptas faced **Huna invasions** and the rise of feudatories like **Yashodharman**.
xa: Gupta decline led to **regional kingdoms + feudal order**.
Repeated Huna invasions **drained treasury and army**.
The Hunas came via the **Oxus** valley and took **Gandhara**.

63.s: Which of the following statements regarding Gupta kingship is correct?
o: The title Maharajadhiraja was used exclusively by village headmen
Gupta kings used titles such as Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka
Gupta kings rejected all divine associations
Gupta rulers claimed that kingship was elective
63.x: Gupta rulers used the exalted titles Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka and made divine claims about kingship.
63.tq: Recognise the cluster of royal titles rather than the absolute distractors.
xs: Gupta kings used **Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja, Paramabhattaraka** — option **(2)**.
They made **divine claims**: Gupta kings were likened to **Vishnu**, so "rejected all divine associations" is wrong.
Kingship was **hereditary**, not elective.
xa: **Samudragupta** was equated with **Kubera (Dhanada), Varuna, Indra and Yama (Antaka)**.
**Primogeniture was not firm** in Gupta succession.
Large areas were held by **feudatories (samantas)**.

63.s: Samudragupta was equated with which of the following deities or divine figures?
63.x: Samudragupta was equated with Kubera or Dhanada, Varuna, Indra and Yama or Antaka.
63.tq: Recall the complete set of divine comparisons associated with the ruler.
xs: **Samudragupta** was equated with **Kubera, Varuna, Indra and Yama** — option **(4)**.
Kubera is also called **Dhanada**, and Yama **Antaka**.
xa: Gupta kings in general were likened to **Vishnu**.
Royal titles: **Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja, Paramabhattaraka**.
Samudragupta **reinstated some feudatories**.

63.s: Which statement best describes succession and administration under the Gupta kings?
o: Kingship was hereditary, but primogeniture was not firmly established
Primogeniture was an inviolable constitutional rule
Kingship was transferred only through the feudatories
Kingship was elective and succession was determined by village councils
63.x: Gupta kingship was hereditary, but there was no firm rule of primogeniture. Several offices were also hereditary, and salaries were often paid in land or kind.
63.tq: Distinguish hereditary succession from the stronger and unsupported claim of fixed primogeniture.
xs: Kingship was **hereditary**, but **primogeniture was not firmly established** — option **(1)**.
It was not elective, and feudatories (**samantas**) did not transfer the crown.
xa: Many offices were also **hereditary** (e.g. **Harisena** inherited his post).
Salaries were often paid **in land or kind**.
⚠ **Mauryas** = centralised; **Guptas** = **decentralised**.

63.s:
With reference to the Gupta Empire, consider the following statements:
1. It was less centralised than the Mauryan Empire.
2. Feudatories and land grantees administered substantial parts of the empire.
3. Some offices were hereditary.
4. Samudragupta reinstated some feudatories.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All four statements are correct. Gupta administration relied substantially on feudatories and grantees, and it was considerably less centralised than Mauryan administration.
63.tq: Test the decentralisation pattern through several connected administrative features.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Guptas were **decentralised**, unlike the centralised **Mauryas**.
Statement 2 is correct: **feudatories (samantas)** and **grantees** ran much of the empire.
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: many offices were **hereditary**, and **Samudragupta reinstated** some feudatories — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
xa: **Harisena** inherited his post.
Salaries were often **in land or kind**.
Royal titles: **Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja, Paramabhattaraka**.

63.s: Which official was the Gupta minister of peace and war?
63.x: The Sandhivigrahika was the minister responsible for peace and war.
63.tq: Match the official with the specialised function.
xs: The **Sandhivigrahika** was the minister of **peace and war** — option **(4)**.
**Kumaramatya** = high-cadre officer; **Dandapashika** = district police; **Pustapala** = land records.
xa: **Harishena** held **kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika and mahadandanayaka** together.
**Mahadandanayaka** = chief judicial / military officer.
**Dutakas** were spies and messengers.

63.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Pustapala — Minister of peace and war
Dutaka — Chief artisan of the town
63.x: The Dandapashika was the district police officer. The Mahadandanayaka was a chief judicial or military officer, the Pustapala kept land-transfer records, and the Dutaka acted as a spy or messenger.
63.tq: Use function-based elimination among officials with similar administrative roles.
xs: **Dandapashika — district police officer** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Mahadandanayaka** = chief judicial officer / general, not record keeper.
**Pustapala** = land-transfer records; **Dutaka** = spy / messenger; peace and war = **Sandhivigrahika**.
xa: ⚠ **Dandapashika** = police, **not a judge**.
**Akshapataladhikrita** kept **royal records**.
The chief artisan on the town board was the **Prathama kulika**.

63.s: The Kumaramatyas in the Gupta administration were best described as
o: foreign ambassadors appointed only during wartime
guild representatives responsible for town sanitation
village accountants with no access to higher offices
high-cadre officers from whom ministers and commanders could be selected
63.x: Kumaramatyas were senior or high-cadre officers, ranked with princes; ministers and commanders were chosen from them. They had their own office and were often paid in cash.
63.tq: Identify the broader cadre role instead of a narrow functional description.
xs: **Kumaramatyas** were **high-cadre officers** from whom **ministers and commanders** were chosen — option **(4)**.
They ranked with **princes**, had their own office (**adhikarana**) and were often **paid in cash**.
xa: **Harishena** was kumaramatya, **sandhivigrahika** and **mahadandanayaka** at once.
Other salaries were often paid **in land or kind**.
Town representation was by **Nagarashreshthi, Sarthavaha, Prathama kulika, Prathama kayastha**.

63.s: Which official was responsible for keeping royal records, while the Pustapala maintained land-transfer records?
63.x: The Akshapataladhikrita kept royal records, whereas the Pustapala was the keeper of land-transfer records.
63.tq: Separate the two record-keeping offices by the type of record maintained.
xs: The **Akshapataladhikrita** kept **royal records** — option **(1)**.
⚠ **Pustapala** = **land records**; **Dandapashika** = police; **Mahadandanayaka** = judicial / military; **Dutaka** = messenger.
xa: **Village headman's consent** was needed for land transactions.
Land measures included **Kulyavapa** and **Dronavapa**.
**Sandhivigrahika** = minister of peace and war.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial system of the Gupta period:
1. Civil and criminal law were more clearly separated than in earlier periods.
2. Theft and adultery were treated as criminal offences.
3. Disputes relating to property were treated as civil matters.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All three statements are correct. The period witnessed a clearer distinction between civil and criminal law; theft and adultery were criminal matters, while property disputes were civil matters.
63.tq: Test each statement independently before selecting the combination containing all the correct statements.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **civil and criminal law** were **clearly separated**, more than earlier.
Statement 2 is correct: **theft and adultery** were **criminal**.
Statement 3 is correct: **property disputes** were **civil** — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Laws followed the **varna hierarchy**.
**Mahadandanayaka** was the chief judicial officer.
⚠ **Dandapashika** = district police, not a judge.

63.s:
Assertion (A): The law books of the Gupta period did not treat all persons uniformly before law.
Reason (R): The laws followed a hierarchy based on varna.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
63.x: Both statements are true, and the varna-based hierarchy explains why legal treatment was not uniform for all persons.
63.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the unequal legal treatment described in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Gupta laws followed the **varna hierarchy**, so people were not treated uniformly.
xa: The system was **more developed** than earlier: **civil and criminal law clearly separated**.
Criminal: **theft, adultery**; civil: **property disputes**.
**Mahadandanayaka** = chief judicial officer.

63.s: Which Gupta official is known to have held the titles of kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika and mahadandanayaka together?
63.x: Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, held all three top titles: kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika and mahadandanayaka. His post was also inherited. Virasena was a minister of Chandragupta II, Vishakhadatta was a dramatist, and Parnadatta was a governor under Skandagupta.
63.tq: Harishena = Prayag prashasti author + three titles
xs: **Harishena** held all three top titles — **kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika, mahadandanayaka** — option **(2)**.
He also illustrates **hereditary offices**: **Harisena inherited his post**.
xa: **Sandhivigrahika** = minister of **peace and war**.
**Mahadandanayaka** = chief judicial officer / general.
Ministers and commanders were chosen from the **kumaramatyas**.

63.s:
Arrange the following Gupta administrative units from the largest to the smallest:
A. Grama
B. Vithi
C. Bhukti
D. Vishaya
63.x: The correct descending order is Bhukti, Vishaya, Vithi and Grama.
63.tq: Use the administrative hierarchy from province to village.
xs: Largest to smallest: **Bhukti → Vishaya → Vithi → Grama** (C, D, B, A) — option **(1)** (UPPSC **2023** key).
**Bhukti** = province; **Vishaya** = district; **Vithi** = group of villages; **Grama** = village.
xa: ⚠ **Uparika** = province (bhukti); **Vishayapati** = district (vishaya).
The Vithi is found in **eastern India**, with **Ayuktaka** and others.
Village officer: **Gramika / gramadhyaksha**, with **kutumbis** and **mahattaras**.

63.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
63.x: The Vithi, particularly in eastern India, was associated with the Ayuktaka and other officials. A Bhukti was headed by an Uparika, a Vishaya by a Vishayapati, and a village by a Gramika or Gramadhyaksha.
63.tq: Start with the sure officer–unit pair and eliminate the swapped administrative levels.
xs: **Vithi — Ayuktaka** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Bhukti** was under the **Uparika**, not the Vishayapati.
**Vishaya** was under the **Vishayapati**; **Grama** under the **Gramika**, not the Sandhivigrahika.
xa: The Uparika was **appointed by the king**, sometimes called **"Maharaja"**.
Other names: bhukti = **desha / rashtra**; vishaya = **pradesha**.
Order: **Bhukti → Vishaya → Vithi → Grama** (UPPSC **2023**).

63.s: Which administrative practice indicates the participation of village authorities in land transactions during the Gupta period?
o: Consent of the village headman was required
Approval of the Sandhivigrahika was required
The town board alone authorised village transfers
Only the king could validate every transaction
63.x: The village headman’s consent was required for land transactions, indicating a role for local village authority.
63.tq: Apply the institutional fact to the land-transfer situation.
xs: **Consent of the village headman** was needed for land transactions — option **(1)**.
The **Sandhivigrahika** was minister of peace and war, not a land-transfer authority.
xa: Village officer: **Gramika / gramadhyaksha**, with **kutumbis and mahattaras**.
**Pustapala** kept land-transfer records.
The **Damodarpur copper plates** describe a **district council** assisting the officer.

63.s: Who represented the chief artisan community on the Gupta town board?
63.x: The Prathama kulika represented the chief artisans or craft guilds on the town board.
63.tq: Match the occupational representative with the social group represented.
xs: The **Prathama kulika** represented the **chief artisans** (craft guilds) — option **(1)**.
**Prathama kayastha** = chief **scribe**; **Nagarashreshthi** = chief banker / merchant; **Sarthavaha** = chief caravan trader.
xa: The Nagarashreshthi was **chairman** of the town council.
The town board was called the **adhikarana**.
"**Kayastha**" = scribes (APPSC G2 **2012**).

63.s: Which member of the Gupta town board served as its chairman?
63.x: The Nagarashreshthi, the chief banker or merchant, served as chairman of the town council or adhikarana.
63.tq: Distinguish the presiding member from the other professional representatives.
xs: The **Nagarashreshthi**, chief **banker / merchant**, chaired the town board — option **(1)**.
**Sarthavaha** = caravan traders; **Prathama kayastha** = scribes; **Prathama kulika** = artisans.
xa: The town board = **adhikarana**.
The **Damodarpur copper plates** describe a **district council**.
"**Kayastha**" = scribes (APPSC G2 **2012**).

63.s: The Damodarpur copper plates are associated with which aspect of Gupta administration?
o: Description of a district council assisting an officer
Appointment of the Mauryan provincial governors
63.x: The Damodarpur copper plates describe a district council that assisted the concerned officer.
63.tq: Link the epigraphic source with the administrative institution it records.
xs: The **Damodarpur copper plates** describe a **district council** assisting the officer — option **(2)**.
The district (**vishaya**) was headed by the **Vishayapati**.
xa: Town board (**adhikarana**) members: **Nagarashreshthi, Sarthavaha, Prathama kulika, Prathama kayastha**.
Province (**bhukti**) was under the **Uparika**.
The **Vithi** (eastern India) had **Ayuktaka** and others.

63.s: In Gupta administrative terminology, the term ‘Kayastha’ primarily referred to
63.x: Kayasthas were associated with scribal and official work; the Prathama kayastha represented the chief scribes on the town board.
63.tq: Discriminate the exact occupational meaning of a familiar administrative term.
xs: "**Kayastha**" meant **scribes** — option **(4)** (APPSC G2 **2012**).
The **Prathama kayastha** was the **chief scribe** on the town board.
Caravan traders were represented by the **Sarthavaha**.
xa: The chief artisan was the **Prathama kulika**.
The **Nagarashreshthi** chaired the town council.
The town board was called the **adhikarana**.

63.s: Which of the following correctly describes ‘bhoga’ in the Gupta-period revenue system?
o: A tax on the sale and purchase of land
Periodic supplies such as fruits, firewood and flowers to the king
63.x: Bhoga consisted of periodic supplies in kind, including fruits, firewood and flowers, made to the king.
63.tq: Separate periodic in-kind supplies from cash and land-related taxes.
xs: **Bhoga** = **periodic supplies in kind** (fruits, firewood, flowers) to the king — option **(4)**.
Land sale tax = **Klipta / Upaklipta**; cash tax = **Hiranya**; plough tax = **Halivakara**.
xa: ⚠ **Bhaga** = share of produce; **Bhoga** = supplies in kind.
Bhaga was the main land revenue — **one-sixth**.
**Sulka / Shulka** = customs duty / tolls.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Udranga was an additional or new tax.
2. Uparikara was probably imposed on temporary tenants.
3. Udakabhaga denoted a water tax.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Udranga and uparikara were additional or new taxes, with uparikara probably associated with temporary tenants. Udakabhaga referred to a water tax.
63.tq: Combine closely related tax terms and eliminate the code containing a reversed meaning.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Udranga** was an **additional / new tax**, possibly water or police tax.
Statement 2 is correct: **Uparikara** was probably on **temporary tenants**.
Statement 3 is correct: **Udakabhaga** = **water tax** — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: **Kara** = periodic tax; **Hiranya** = tax in cash.
**Bali**: at first voluntary, later **compulsory**.
**Trend**: land taxes rose, trade taxes fell.

63.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sulka — forced labour for the army
Bali — initially voluntary and later compulsory
63.x: Sulka was a customs duty or toll. Forced labour for the army and officials was called vishti; hiranya was a cash tax, bali changed from voluntary to compulsory, and kara was a periodic tax.
63.tq: Identify the deliberately swapped meaning among neighbouring revenue terms.
xs: **Sulka — forced labour** is wrong — option **(1)**; **Sulka / Shulka** = **customs duty / tolls**.
Forced labour was **Vishti** (Telugu **vetti**).
**Kara** = periodic tax; **Bali** = voluntary then compulsory; **Hiranya** = cash — all correct.
xa: **Halivakara** = plough tax.
**Udakabhaga** = water tax.
**Klipta / Upaklipta** = taxes on land sale and purchase.

63.s: The term ‘halivakara’ denoted:
63.x: Halivakara was the tax imposed on the plough.
63.tq: Use the occupational clue in the term while separating it from other tax categories.
xs: **Halivakara** = **plough tax** — option **(4)**.
Customs = **Sulka**; water tax = **Udakabhaga**; tax on temporary tenants = **Uparikara**.
xa: ⚠ **Bhaga** = produce share; **Bhoga** = supplies in kind; **Hiranya** = cash.
**Vishti** = unpaid forced labour.
Trend: **land taxes rose, trade taxes fell**.

63.s: Which of the following trends in taxation is associated with the period under consideration?
o: Land taxes rose while trade taxes fell
Land taxes fell while trade taxes rose
Both land taxes and trade taxes disappeared
Both land taxes and trade taxes rose at the same rate
63.x: The broad trend was an increase in land taxes accompanied by a decline in trade taxes.
63.tq: Read the direction of both trends together and reject the reversed comparison.
xs: **Land taxes rose while trade taxes fell** — option **(1)**.
Notes list many new land levies: **Udranga, Uparikara, Halivakara**.
xa: **Bhaga** (one-sixth) was the main land revenue.
Feudalism evidence: **7th-century** fall in long-distance trade and **gold coinage**.
**Bali**: voluntary at first, later **compulsory**.

63.s: In the Gupta revenue system, 'bhaga', the main land revenue, was the king's share of the produce. What share did the law books prescribe?
63.x: Bhaga was the king's share of produce and the main land revenue; the law books prescribed one-sixth. Actual rates in the sources vary (1/4 to 1/6, about 1/7), but one-half, one-third and one-tenth are not the prescribed share.
63.tq: Bhaga = 1/6 (shadbhaga)
xs: The law books prescribed **one-sixth** as **bhaga** — option **(3)**.
Rates in the notes vary: **1/6**, **1/4–1/6**, about **1/7** — never one-half, one-third or one-tenth.
xa: ⚠ **Bhaga** = share of produce; **Bhoga** = supplies in kind (fruits, firewood, flowers).
**Hiranya** = tax in cash; **Kara** = periodic tax.
Trend: **land taxes rose**, trade taxes fell.

63.s: Kuliyavapa and dronavapa were used as terms for:
63.x: Kuliyavapa and dronavapa denoted measures of land.
63.tq: Test the paired terms together so that a tax term is not confused with a measurement term.
xs: **Kuliyavapa** and **dronavapa** were **measures of land** — option **(4)** (UPSC **2020**).
They meant the area sown with one **kulya** / one **drona** of seed.
xa: **Pataka** ≈ **60–80 acres**; **Nivartana** ≈ **1.5 acres**.
Forced labour = **Vishti**.
**Kshetra** = cultivated land; **Khila** = untilled waste.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Land term)
a. Kshetra
b. Khila
c. Vastu
 d. Aprahata

List-II (Meaning)
i. Habitable house-site land
ii. Cultivated or fertile land
iii. Untilled waste land
iv. Uncultivated forest land

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: Kshetra means cultivated or fertile land, Khila means untilled waste land, Vastu means habitable house-site land, and Aprahata denotes uncultivated forest land in this classification.
63.tq: Start with the sure pair and eliminate codes that reverse the land categories.
xs: Correct match: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Kshetra** = cultivated land; **Khila** = untilled waste; **Vastu** = house-site; **Aprahata** = uncultivated forest land.
xa: ⚠ **Aprahata** is glossed as cultivable wasteland in one glossary; the **BPSC 2016** key takes it as forest land.
**Kulyavapa, Dronavapa** = land measures (UPSC **2020**).
**Bhumichchhidranyaya**: first reclaimer of waste owns it, tax-free.

63.s: In the classification of land types, Aprahata was generally understood as:
63.x: Aprahata is generally taken as uncultivated forest or jungle land in the standard classification used for this period.
63.tq: Discriminate between similar land categories by matching the term with its precise description.
xs: **Aprahata** = **uncultivated forest (jungle) land** — option **(1)** (BPSC **2016**).
**Vastu** = house-site land; **Kshetra** = cultivated land.
xa: ⚠ One glossary calls it cultivable wasteland; the BPSC key takes it as forest.
**Khila** = untilled waste land.
Grants in **forest areas** brought **virgin land under cultivation**.

63.s: Pataka and Nivartana were measures of land. Which of the following correctly represents their approximate extent?
63.x: A Pataka was approximately 60–80 acres, while a Nivartana was approximately 1.5 acres.
63.tq: Keep the two measures separate and watch for the reversed-value trap.
xs: **Pataka ≈ 60–80 acres**; **Nivartana ≈ 1.5 acres** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) reverses them.
xa: **Satavahanas** gave **100 nivartanas** to Buddhist monks.
**Kulyavapa, Dronavapa** = land measured by seed sown.
Satavahanas made the **earliest land grants** in India.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Grant)
a. Brahmadeya
b. Agrahara
c. Devagrahara

d. Secular grant

List-II (Grantee)
i. Officials or feudatories
 ii. Temples and monasteries
 iii. Brahmanas, individually or collectively
 iv. Brahmanas as religious functionaries

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
63.x: Brahmadeya was granted to Brahmanas singly or collectively, agrahara was tax-free land or a village given to Brahmanas, devagrahara was assigned to temples and monasteries, and secular grants went to officials or feudatories in lieu of salary.
63.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped grantee.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Brahmadeya** → Brahmanas singly or jointly; **Agrahara** → Brahmanas as religious functionaries (tax-free).
**Devagrahara / Devadana** → **temples and monasteries**; **secular grants** → officials, feudatories.
xa: ⚠ One set of notes reverses Agrahara / Brahmadeya; MPPSC **2014**: tax-free land went to **Brahmins**.
Secular grants gave revenue **in lieu of salary**.
Agraharas were **hereditary**, often with administrative rights.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding land grants in tribal and forest regions:
1. They brought virgin land under cultivation.
2. They contributed to the absorption of tribal groups into the caste order.
3. The absorbed tribal groups could emerge as new sub-castes.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Land grants in tribal and forest frontiers brought virgin land under cultivation and integrated tribal communities into the caste order, where they could appear as new sub-castes.
63.tq: Test the full chain of cause, social effect and resulting classification.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: grants in tribal and forest areas brought **virgin land under cultivation**.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: tribes were **absorbed into the caste order** as **new sub-castes** — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2023**).
xa: **B.D. Chattopadhyaya's** integrative model: grants spread state society into **new areas**.
Grantees got **revenue + administrative, judicial and police rights**.
Peasants sank to **semi-servile status**.

63.s: The earliest land grants in India are associated with which dynasty?
63.x: The Satavahanas are associated with the earliest land grants in India.
63.tq: Direct dynasty–institution recall with nearby-period distractors.
xs: The **Satavahanas** made the **earliest land grants** in India — option **(2)**.
They gave **100 nivartanas** to **Buddhist monks** plus agrahara-type grants to Brahmanas.
xa: 1 nivartana ≈ **1.5 acres**.
**Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya** grants barred royal officials.
The **Vakatakas** succeeded the Satavahanas.

63.s:
Match the following tenures with their descriptions:

a. Nivi dharma
b. Nivi dharma akshayana
c. Aprada dharma
d. Bhumichchhidranyaya

i. Enjoyment of income without the right of alienation
 ii. Perpetual endowment
 iii. Trust
 iv. Ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
63.x: Nivi dharma meant a trust, nivi dharma akshayana a perpetual endowment, aprada dharma enjoyment of income without alienation, and bhumichchhidranyaya ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land.
63.tq: Match each technical tenure with its distinctive legal consequence.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Nivi dharma** = trust; **Nivi dharma akshayana** = perpetual endowment.
**Aprada dharma** = enjoy income, cannot alienate; **Bhumichchhidranyaya** = first reclaimer of waste owns it, tax-free.
xa: **Brahmadeya** carried tax exemption + administrative rights.
**Devagrahara / Devadana** gave revenue for worship to **temples and monasteries**.
**Khila** = untilled waste land.

63.s: Which of the following statements about granted villages is NOT correct?
o: Royal officials were often barred from entering the granted area.
The grantees could receive the revenue from the land.
The grant necessarily abolished all forms of local authority and produced direct royal administration.
Administrative, judicial and police rights could accompany the grant.
63.x: Grants tended to remove or restrict direct royal intervention rather than produce direct royal administration. The grantees could receive revenue and administrative, judicial and police rights, while royal officials were often barred from entry.
63.tq: Find the statement that reverses the effect of delegated rights.
xs: Option **(3)** is NOT correct: grants did **not** produce **direct royal administration** — royal officials were **barred**.
Grantees got **revenue plus administrative, judicial and police rights** and collected taxes from peasants.
Barring officials led to **sub-infeudation**.
xa: **Village headman's consent** was needed for land transactions.
**Satavahana and Ikshvaku** brahmadeya grants also barred royal officials.
Peasants: **tenants-at-will**, sharecropping, forced labour (**vishti**).

63.s: Vishti in the Gupta-period agrarian context meant:
o: Unpaid forced labour rendered to the state or the donee
A system of military land grants to feudatories
A tax collected on forest produce
A voluntary religious donation by peasants
63.x: Vishti was unpaid forced labour performed for the state or for the recipient of a land grant; in Telugu usage it is associated with vetti.
63.tq: Use the functional meaning of the term and reject related but different revenue and grant concepts.
xs: **Vishti** = **unpaid forced labour** for the state or donee — option **(1)**.
It served the **army and officials** too; Telugu **vetti**.
xa: **R.S. Sharma** cites vishti as a feature of **Indian feudalism**.
Peasants sank to **semi-servile status**.
**Halivakara** = plough tax; **Bali** = later compulsory.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the condition of peasants:
1. Peasants increasingly became semi-servile.
2. Tenant farming and sharecropping were among the forms of agrarian dependence.
3. Tenants-at-will and multiple taxes added to their vulnerability.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All three statements are correct. Peasant dependence was reflected in semi-servile status, tenant farming, sharecropping, tenancy at will and the burden of many taxes.
63.tq: Treat each description of peasant dependence as a separate factual test.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: peasants sank to **semi-servile status**.
Statement 2 is correct: **tenant farming and sharecropping** spread.
Statement 3 is correct: **tenants-at-will**, forced labour and **many taxes** — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: ⚠ **Harbans Mukhia** argues the reverse: **no serfdom**, a largely free peasantry.
**Vishti** = unpaid forced labour (Telugu **vetti**).
Grantees could **collect taxes** from peasants.

63.s: Which historian associated Indian feudalism with land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay?
63.x: R.S. Sharma argued that Indian feudalism crystallised through land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay.
63.tq: Use the historian–argument association directly.
xs: **R.S. Sharma** linked Indian feudalism to **land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade, urban decay** — option **(2)**.
**D.C. Sircar** and **Harbans Mukhia** were **critics**; **B.D. Chattopadhyaya** gave an **integrative** model.
xa: Sharma also cited **fewer gold coins**.
Sircar: grants transferred **revenue rights, not ownership**.
Mukhia: **no serfdom**, free peasantry.

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: D.C. Sircar — Grants transferred revenue rights rather than ownership
Harbans Mukhia — Existence of widespread serfdom in India
B.D. Chattopadhyaya — Integrative and processual model
R.S. Sharma — Land grants and urban decay as elements of Indian feudalism
63.x: Harbans Mukhia argued that there was no serfdom and that Indian peasants were largely free and retained autonomy.
63.tq: Find the swapped or opposite interpretation in a historian–position pair.
xs: **Harbans Mukhia — widespread serfdom** is wrong — option **(2)**; he argued **no serfdom** and a **largely free peasantry**.
**Sircar** (revenue rights, not ownership), **Chattopadhyaya** (integrative / processual) and **Sharma** (land grants, urban decay) are correct.
xa: Mukhia asked "**Was there feudalism in Indian history?**"
⚠ **Sharma** = proponent; **Sircar, Mukhia** = critics.
Sircar: **no feudalism in the European sense**.

63.s: Which of the following was cited as evidence for the emergence of Indian feudalism in the seventh century?
o: Expansion of long-distance trade and rapid urbanisation
Decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage
Opening of villages to unrestricted external trade
Increase in the circulation of gold coins
63.x: The evidence cited included the seventh-century decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage, shrinking towns and a closed village economy.
63.tq: Identify the option that preserves the stated historical trend rather than reversing it.
xs: Evidence cited: **7th-century decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage** — option **(2)**.
Also **shrinking towns** and a **closed village economy** — the reverse of options 1, 3, 4.
xa: **R.S. Sharma** stressed **urban decay** and fewer gold coins.
Trend: **land taxes rose, trade taxes fell**.
**Chattopadhyaya** rejects decay as the full story.

63.s: In the context of feudalism, which combination represents its essential elements?
o: Control and possession of land, lord–vassal relationship and weak central authority
Strong central authority, salaried bureaucracy and absence of land control
Popular sovereignty, elected local bodies and monetised taxation
Maritime trade, urban guilds and direct imperial administration
63.x: The essential elements are power based on control of land, lord–vassal ties and weak central authority. A strong centre with weak local authority is not a feudal feature.
63.tq: Separate the essential features from the deliberately reversed strong-centre description.
xs: Essentials: **control and possession of land**, **lord–vassal** relationship, **weak central authority** — option **(1)** (UPSC **2015**).
⚠ A **strong centre** with weak local authority is **not** feudal.
xa: Feudalism = land grant by an overlord **with financial, administrative and judicial rights**.
Gupta grants carried **judicial and police rights** too.
Barring royal officials led to **sub-infeudation**.

63.s: Which of the following best represents the central issue in the debate on Indian feudalism?
o: Whether the Mauryas introduced village self-government
Whether Buddhist monks controlled all agricultural land
Whether Gupta rulers used gold coins for all payments
Whether land grants contributed to a feudal structure, as argued by R. S. Sharma, or whether the absence of serfdom limits that interpretation
63.x: The debate centres on R. S. Sharma’s land-grant thesis and the criticism that the absence of serfdom makes the European model of feudalism unsuitable or limited for India.
63.tq: Compare the two opposing interpretations rather than selecting a related agrarian fact.
xs: The debate: **R.S. Sharma's land-grant thesis** vs critics who see **no serfdom** — option **(4)**.
**Gupta land grants** anchor the "Indian feudalism" debate.
xa: **Harbans Mukhia**: no serfdom; **D.C. Sircar**: revenue rights, not ownership.
**B.D. Chattopadhyaya**: **integrative / processual** model.
Sharma's evidence: **sub-infeudation, vishti, urban decay**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about Mauryan and Gupta administration:
1. The Mauryan state was centrally regulated.
2. Gupta administration relied to a greater extent on feudatories and grantees.
3. Both systems were identical in their degree of central control.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Mauryan state was centrally regulated, whereas Gupta administration relied more on feudatories and grantees; therefore, statement 3 is false.
63.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap in the statement claiming that two administrative systems were identical.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Mauryan** state was **centrally regulated**.
Statement 2 is correct: Gupta rule relied on **feudatories and grantees**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the two were not equally centralised — **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Gupta feudatories were **samantas**; Samudragupta reinstated some.
Many Gupta offices were **hereditary**.
Salaries were often in **land or kind**.

63.s: A Satavahana grant to Buddhist monks records 100 nivartanas of land. The approximate area of this grant would be:
63.x: Since one nivartana was approximately 1.5 acres, 100 nivartanas amounted to about 150 acres.
63.tq: Convert the historical land measure by multiplying the unit value by the stated number.
xs: **100 nivartanas × about 1.5 acres = about 150 acres** — option **(4)**.
**1 nivartana ≈ 1.5 acres** per the notes.
xa: This Satavahana grant to **Buddhist monks** is among the **earliest land grants** in India.
**Pataka** ≈ **60–80 acres**.
**Satavahana and Ikshvaku** brahmadeya grants barred royal officials.

63.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes a feature of Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya grants?
o: They were grants made exclusively to Buddhist monks.
They barred royal officials from interfering in the granted areas.
They abolished the jurisdiction of all local territorial divisions.
They expressly permitted all royal officials to interfere in grant administration.
63.x: Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya grants barred royal officials from interfering in the granted areas. The grants were not exclusively Buddhist, nor did they abolish all territorial divisions.
63.tq: Identify the specific administrative privilege attached to the grant and reject absolute alternatives.
xs: **Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya** grants **barred royal officials** — option **(2)**.
Brahmadeya grants went to **Brahmanas**, not exclusively Buddhist monks.
**Andhra vishayas continued** under later dynasties — divisions were not abolished.
xa: Satavahanas gave **100 nivartanas** to Buddhist monks.
Barring officials later fed **sub-infeudation**.
Brahmadeya = **tax exemption + administrative rights**.

64.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Fa-Hien’s journey to and from India?
o: He followed a wholly maritime route in both directions.
He came by sea through Sri Lanka and returned overland through Central Asia.
He came through the Deccan and returned through the north-western passes.
He came overland through Central Asia and Gandhara and returned by sea via Sri Lanka.
64.x: Fa-Hien travelled overland through Central Asia and Gandhara and returned by sea through Sri Lanka, including the port of Tamralipti on his return route.
64.tq: Separate the inward overland route from the outward maritime route.
xs: Fa-Hien came **overland via Central Asia and Gandhara** and **returned by sea via Sri Lanka** — option **(4)**.
His sea return passed through **Tamralipti** and Sri Lanka, so options 1 and 2 are wrong.
xa: He came in the reign of **Chandragupta II**, **c. 399–414 CE**, but never named the king.
His account: **Fo-kwo-ki** ("Record of Buddhist Kingdoms").
**Tamralipti** (Tamluk, Bengal) was the chief eastern port.

64.s: Fa-Hien’s Indian travels are generally dated to approximately:
64.x: Fa-Hien travelled in India approximately from 399 to 414 CE, during the reign of Chandragupta II.
64.tq: Use the date range linked with the traveller rather than the broader Gupta chronology.
xs: Fa-Hien's travels are dated **c. 399–414 CE** — option **(4)**.
This falls in **Chandragupta II's** reign (UPSC **2025** key).
xa: He never named the king — he was interested in **Buddhism**.
He saw **20 viharas at Mathura** and **free hospitals** at **Pataliputra**.
He noted **no death penalty** — fines instead.

64.s:
Which of the following statements about Fa-Hien’s account is correct?
1. He was a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim.
2. He recorded the name of the Gupta king in detail.
3. His work is known as the Fo-kwo-ki.
4. His main interest was Buddhism.
64.x: Fa-Hien was a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim interested in Buddhism, and his account is called the Fo-kwo-ki or Record of Buddhist Kingdoms. He did not record the king’s name.
64.tq: Reject the false statement created by reversing what the traveller recorded and what he omitted.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Fa-Hien was a **Chinese Buddhist pilgrim**.
Statement 2 is wrong: he **never named the king**.
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: his work is the **Fo-kwo-ki**, and his interest was **Buddhism** — **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: Fo-kwo-ki = "**Record of Buddhist Kingdoms**".
He came in **Chandragupta II's** reign, **c. 399–414 CE**.
He noted decay at **Kapilavastu, Gaya, Kushinagar**.

64.s: Fa-Hien observed that the government was generally mild and that:
o: taxation was heavy and compulsory military service was universal
there were few taxes and no death penalty
capital punishment was the normal penalty for serious crimes
all offences were punished by imprisonment
64.x: Fa-Hien described light taxation and the absence of the death penalty; fines were generally imposed for offences.
64.tq: Pair the two related administrative observations instead of selecting an extreme punishment claim.
xs: Government was **mild**, with **few taxes** and **no death penalty** — option **(2)**.
Offences drew **fines**; persistent rebellion meant **cutting off the right hand**.
xa: People were **peaceful and prosperous**.
**Cowrie shells** were used in daily exchange.
**Hindus and Buddhists** lived in harmony.

64.s:
Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched with Fa-Hien’s observations?
1. Mathura — 20 viharas
2. Pataliputra — free hospitals
3. Highways — rest houses
4. Kapilavastu, Gaya and Kushinagar — signs of decay
64.x: All four associations are correct. Fa-Hien noted 20 viharas at Mathura, free hospitals at Pataliputra, rest houses on highways and decay at the three listed sacred places.
64.tq: Match each place or facility with the observation specifically associated with it.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**20 viharas at Mathura**; **free hospitals at Pataliputra** funded by leading families.
**Rest houses** on highways; **decay** at **Kapilavastu, Gaya, Kushinagar**.
xa: He came in **Chandragupta II's** reign, **c. 399–414 CE**.
People avoided **meat, onion, garlic, liquor** — except **chandalas**.
He returned by sea via **Tamralipti and Sri Lanka**.

64.s: The Chandalas, according to Fa-Hien, were required to:
o: wear gold ornaments and avoid all manual work
live outside settlements and strike a piece of wood when approaching others
serve as officials in the Gupta administration
live within the royal quarter and carry official seals
64.x: Fa-Hien states that the Chandalas lived outside towns or settlements and struck a piece of wood to warn others of their approach.
64.tq: Combine the location and identifying practice to distinguish the Chandalas from other groups.
xs: Chandalas **lived outside villages/towns** and **struck a piece of wood** to announce their approach — option **(2)**.
They were **outside the four varnas**; **untouchability intensified**.
xa: Chandalas were the exception to the **food restrictions** (meat, onion, garlic, liquor).
⚠ **Shudras** improved but **Chandalas** sank.
The **Narada Smriti** lists **15 types of slaves**.

64.s:
Which of the following statements about society as described by Fa-Hien is correct?
1. Cowrie shells were used in daily exchange.
2. Hindus and Buddhists lived in harmony.
3. The people were generally described as peaceful and prosperous.
4. Chandalas followed exactly the same food restrictions as the general population.
64.x: Cowries were used in daily exchange, Hindus and Buddhists lived in harmony, and the people were described as peaceful and prosperous. The Chandalas were an exception to the general food restrictions, so statement 4 is false.
64.tq: Identify the exception hidden in an otherwise correct description of society.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: **cowrie shells** in daily exchange; **Hindus and Buddhists** in harmony; people **peaceful and prosperous**.
Statement 4 is wrong: people avoided meat, onion, garlic, liquor **except chandalas** — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Government was **mild** with **few taxes**.
**No death penalty**; fines instead.
**Free hospitals** at Pataliputra; **rest houses** on highways.

64.s: The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of which Gupta ruler?
64.x: Fa-Hien was in India c. 399-414 CE, in the reign of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), though he never named the king. Samudragupta ruled before this; Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta ruled after it.
64.tq: Fa-Hien = Chandragupta II; Hiuen Tsang = Harsha
xs: Fa-Hien visited during the reign of **Chandragupta II** — option **(2)** (UPSC **2025** key).
He was in India **c. 399–414 CE** but **never named the king**.
xa: His interest was **Buddhism**; account = **Fo-kwo-ki**.
He came **overland via Central Asia + Gandhara**.
He saw **20 viharas** at **Mathura**.

64.s: The assertion of the Varna order during the Gupta period is associated with which concept?
64.x: The asserted social order of the period was expressed through the concept of Varnashram Dharma.
64.tq: Discriminate between the exact technical term and terms referring to grants, labour or trade.
xs: The varna order was asserted as **Varnashram Dharma** — option **(1)**.
**Brahmadeya** = land grants to Brahmanas; **vishti** = forced labour; **Sarthavaha** = caravan trader — not social-order concepts.
xa: **Brahmanas** gained through **brahmadeya** grants.
Gupta rulers were originally **Vaishyas**, later regarded as **Kshatriyas**.
Castes **multiplied into jatis** by absorbing **foreigners and tribes**.

64.s:
Assertion (A): Castes multiplied into numerous sub-castes during the Gupta period.
Reason (R): Foreigners and tribes were absorbed into the caste structure, particularly through land grants.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
64.x: Both statements are true, and the absorption of foreigners and tribes through land-grant processes explains the multiplication of jatis.
64.tq: Test whether the social process stated in the Reason directly explains the demographic change in the Assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Castes **multiplied into sub-castes (jatis)** by absorbing **foreigners** and **tribes** via land grants.
xa: **Kayasthas** rose as a new caste group from the land-grant bureaucracy.
**Untouchability intensified** for Chandalas.
The **Shudras'** status improved.

64.s: The Kayasthas emerged primarily from which occupational and administrative background?
o: Scribes and record-keepers connected with land grants
64.x: Kayasthas emerged as scribes and record-keepers of land grants and became a new caste or class.
64.tq: Match the social group with its distinctive occupational origin.
xs: **Kayasthas** were **scribes and record-keepers of land grants** — option **(3)**.
They rose as a new caste group from the **land-grant bureaucracy**.
xa: They sat in town councils as the **prathama kayastha**.
The **Damodarpur** plates list the town council: nagarashreshthi, sarthavaha, prathama kulika, prathama kayastha.
**Bronze Buddha images** were a craft of the period, unrelated to Kayasthas.
