Zamindars moved to cities like **Calcutta** and left collection to agents.

175.s: Under the Sunset Law associated with the Permanent Settlement, an estate could be auctioned when:
o: the annual revenue was not paid by sunset on the due date
the tenant refused to accept a patta
the zamindar failed to improve the land within ten years
175.x: If the required revenue was not paid by sunset of the due date, the estate could be auctioned.
175.tq: Focus on the precise trigger for an estate sale and reject broader consequences.
xs: Under the **Sunset Law**, an estate was auctioned if revenue was **not paid by sunset of the due date** — option **(1)**.
It did not deal with pattas, land improvement or prices.
xa: Permanent vs Ryotwari default: estate **forfeited (Sunset Law)** vs **land auctioned**.
Many old zamindars lost estates to **urban merchants and moneylenders** at auction.
**Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** let zamindars seize tenants' property.

175.s: The sale of many old zamindari estates under the Permanent Settlement contributed to the emergence of:
o: a new body of village karanams
a class of hereditary ryot proprietors in Madras
a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders
a class of Palegar intermediaries in Rayalaseema
175.x: Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.
175.tq: Trace the ownership change caused by arrears and auction sales.
xs: Estate sales created **a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders** — option **(3)**.
Many old zamindars lost estates for **arrears** under the Sunset Law.
xa: Zamindari areas → **merchant-landlords**; ryotwari and mahalwari areas → **moneylender-landlords**.
**Karanams** were village officers under the Collector in Ryotwari — not a new class.
**Palegars** were suppressed by **Munro**, not created.

175.s: Which regulations empowered zamindars to seize the property of tenants under the Permanent Settlement?
175.x: The regulations of 1799, known as Haftam, and 1812, known as Panjam, enabled zamindars to seize tenants' property.
175.tq: Pair the two regulations with their coercive effect rather than with settlement dates.
xs: The **Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** regulations let zamindars seize tenants' property — option **(3)**.
**1822** and **1833** are Mahalwari regulations; **1793** made the settlement permanent.
xa: The result was **endless litigation** between zamindars and tenants.
Peasants were reduced to **tenants-at-will**.

175.s:
Which of the following developments was associated with the Permanent Settlement?
1. Absentee landlordism
2. Sub-infeudation
3. Rack-renting
4. Reduction of peasants to tenants-at-will
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
175.x: All four were effects of the Permanent Settlement. The system strengthened landlordism, encouraged layers of subordinate interests and exposed peasants to insecure tenancy and high rents.
175.tq: Recognise a complete cluster of social and agrarian consequences.
xs: All four were effects of the Permanent Settlement — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Absentee landlordism**: zamindars moved to **Calcutta**, leaving agents to collect.
**Sub-infeudation** and **rack-renting** spread; peasants became **tenants-at-will**.
xa: Andhra effects: absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation, **no investment in land**, loss of estates for arrears.
Land became a **saleable commodity** concentrated in few hands.

175.s: The decennial settlement under the Permanent Settlement was made permanent in:
175.x: The ten-year, or decennial, settlement was made permanent in 1793.
175.tq: Separate the year of permanent confirmation from the years of later coercive regulations.
xs: The decennial settlement was **made permanent in 1793** — option **(3)**.
**1765** is the **Diwani**/Northern Circars period; **1792** is Baramahal; **1812** is the **Panjam** regulation.
xa: It was introduced by **Lord Cornwallis**, planned with **John Shore**.
⚠ Not **1795** (APPSC-G2 **2025**); in Andhra it applied from **1802**.

175.s: According to the commonly cited distribution of rent under the Permanent Settlement, what share was retained by the zamindar?
175.x: The commonly cited distribution gave the state 10/11 of the rent collected and the zamindar 1/11. Some accounts mention a 9/10 and 1/10 division, but the cited assessment here uses 1/11.
175.tq: Distinguish the zamindar's retained share from the much larger state share.
xs: The zamindar kept **1/11** of the rent — option **(2)**; the state took **10/11**.
Some notes give **9/10** to government and **1/10** to the zamindar in Andhra — the commonly cited split is 10/11 : 1/11.
xa: The demand was fixed at a **very high level** — no share of later growth for the state.
Ryotwari revenue was also high, often **50%+** of produce.

175.s: Which of the following was NOT a rationale advanced for making the Permanent Settlement revenue demand fixed?
o: Ensuring that the Company would receive every future increase in agricultural prices
Reducing the cost of revenue collection
Securing an assured income for the Company
175.x: The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land. A fixed demand actually prevented the Company from receiving additional revenue from later price increases.
175.tq: Find the option that contradicts the economic consequence of revenue fixity.
xs: Getting **every future increase in agricultural prices** was NOT a rationale — option **(2)**; a **fixed** demand gave the Company nothing extra.
Real rationales: **fixed, assured income**, **low collection cost** and a **loyal landlord class**.
xa: Another rationale: the hope that **zamindars would improve land**.
APPSC-GS **2022**: gains from agriculture went to the **zamindars**, not the Company.

175.s: The first experimental introduction of the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency took place in which area?
175.x: The first experiment was conducted in Baramahal, comprising areas such as Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai.
175.tq: Distinguish the first experimental area from the later area of wider implementation.
xs: Ryotwari was first introduced experimentally in **Baramahal** — option **(1)** (APHQ **2008** key).
It was done by **Captain Alexander Read**, assisted by **Thomas Munro**, in **1792**.
The **Ceded Districts** came later (**1802**) — that is the first in **Andhra**.
xa: Exam angle: "first in Andhra" = **Rayalaseema**; "in the Madras Presidency" = **Baramahal**.
Munro was **Collector of South Canara** in **1799**.

175.s: Baramahal came under the control of the East India Company as a consequence of which event?
175.x: Baramahal came to the Company after the Third Mysore War in 1792.
175.tq: Link a territorial acquisition with the correct war rather than with a similar treaty or conflict.
xs: Baramahal came to the Company after the **Third Mysore War (1792)** — option **(1)**.
Baramahal = **Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri, Tiruvannamalai**.
xa: **Read** ran the first Ryotwari experiment there with **Munro** as assistant (**1792-99**).
Munro had served in the **Mysore wars** from **1780** to **1792**.

175.s: In the Ceded Districts, the Ryotwari system was extended by Thomas Munro in 1802 after he had:
175.x: Munro introduced Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts in 1802 after suppressing the Palegars.
175.tq: Connect an administrative reform with the immediate regional political development.
xs: Munro brought Ryotwari to the Ceded Districts in **1802** after he **suppressed the Palegars** — option **(2)**.
He suppressed them with military officer **Campbell**; about **80** palegars resisted, suppression took **18** months.
xa: Munro also **abolished the auction system** there.
Rayalaseema was chosen because it had **no strong zamindars**.
The **Sunset Law** belongs to the Permanent Settlement, not to Munro.

175.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the geographical distribution of revenue systems in the Madras Presidency is correct?
o: Haveli lands were permanently settled with zamindars before British control.
The Northern Circars were entirely under Ryotwari from the beginning.
The Northern Circars were mainly under zamindari settlement, while Haveli lands later came under Ryotwari.
The Ceded Districts were mainly governed through the Mahalwari system.
175.x: The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari areas, whereas Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.
175.tq: Compare neighbouring regional arrangements and identify the qualified statement.
xs: The **Northern Circars** were mainly **zamindari**, while **Haveli** lands later came under **Ryotwari** — option **(3)**.
Haveli lands were under **direct Company control**, not settled with zamindars.
The **Ceded Districts** were the Ryotwari heartland, not Mahalwari.
xa: Haveli lands were grouped into **mootahs** and auctioned to **mootahdars**; many fell into arrears.
The Northern Circars were obtained in **1765-66** (Mughal farman + Nizam treaty).

175.s: Under the Ryotwari system, which of the following rights was available to the ryot so long as the assessment was paid?
o: Only the right to cultivate, without transfer rights
The right to sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land
The right to remit all land revenue permanently
The right to collect revenue from other cultivators
175.x: The ryot held proprietary rights and could sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land as long as the assessment was paid.
175.tq: Identify the legal incidents of ryot ownership rather than confusing them with revenue-collection powers.
xs: The ryot could **sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land** as long as the assessment was paid — option **(2)**.
These were **proprietary rights**; he was not evicted while revenue was paid.
xa: Assessment was fixed on **land, not crop**.
On default the **land was auctioned**.
Problems: **over-assessment**, no proper records, corrupt subordinates → peasants to **moneylenders**.

175.s: In the Ryotwari system, the amount of revenue could rise or fall primarily with changes in:
o: the number of zamindars in the district
the market value of urban property
175.x: Ryotwari revenue was linked to the actual area cultivated, so the amount could rise or fall accordingly.
175.tq: Distinguish the determining factor in Ryotwari from unrelated administrative and market factors.
xs: Ryotwari revenue rose or fell with **the actual area cultivated** — option **(3)**.
Assessment was fixed on **land, not crop**, and **revised periodically** (usually **20-30** years).
xa: Settlement was made **ryot by ryot**.
**Karanams** and village officers worked under the **Collector**.
Ryotwari had **no famine remission**, unlike the Mughal **zabt**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari settlement:
1. Settlement was made ryot by ryot.
2. Revenue was fixed on the land rather than directly on the crop produced.
3. The assessment was ordinarily revised about every thirty years.
4. Karanams and village officers worked under the Collector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: All four statements describe features of the Ryotwari arrangement: individual settlement, land-based assessment, periodic revision and supervision through village officers under the Collector.
175.tq: Test a cluster of features while checking whether the option preserves the full set.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Settlement was **ryot by ryot**; assessment fixed on **land, not crop**.
Revised about **every 30 years**; **karanams** and village officers worked under the **Collector**.
xa: APPSC-GS **2018** asked these Ryotwari features.
Ryots had **proprietary rights** — sell, mortgage, gift, lease.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **destroyed the village system** and isolated farmers.

175.s: Which of the following regions were included in the Baramahal ryotwari experiment?
175.x: The Baramahal experiment covered areas identified with Salem, Krishnagiri and Dharmapuri.
175.tq: Test the regional composition of an early experiment rather than its general label.
xs: Baramahal covered **Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri** (and Tiruvannamalai) — option **(4)**.
**Kurnool**, **Gooty** and **Pattikonda** are Rayalaseema places linked to Munro's death and burial.
xa: Baramahal came after the **Third Mysore War (1792)**.
First Ryotwari experiment there by **Read** and **Munro** (APHQ **2008** key).

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari system:
1. In the Andhra region it was first introduced in the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) by Thomas Munro in 1802.
2. It was adopted generally across the Madras Presidency in 1820, when Munro was Governor.
3. It was first introduced in the Andhra region in the Northern Circars.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Statement 1 is correct: Munro brought Ryotwari to Rayalaseema in 1802. Statement 2 is correct: general adoption in the Madras Presidency came in 1820 under Munro as Governor. Statement 3 is wrong: the Northern Circars were mainly zamindari, only Haveli lands came under Ryotwari later. So options with statement 3 are wrong.
175.tq: First in Andhra = Rayalaseema 1802; first in Madras Presidency = Baramahal 1792; general = 1820.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: Ryotwari first came to Andhra in **Rayalaseema** by **Munro** in **1802**.
Statement 2 correct: general Madras adoption in **1820** under Munro as **Governor**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Northern Circars** were mainly **zamindari**.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
From **1808** village-lease settlements replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts until restored around **1820**.

175.s: Thomas Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was located at:
175.x: Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was at Anantapur.
175.tq: Separate an official headquarters from the place of death and the wider regional headquarters.
xs: Munro's HQ as first **Collector of the Ceded Districts (1800)** was **Anantapur** — option **(2)**.
**Pattikonda** (Kurnool) is where he died of cholera in **1827**.
xa: He was **Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts** from **1800-07** (some notes say 1802 for the start).
He was buried at **Gooty**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

175.s:
Consider the following pairs regarding Thomas Munro's career:
1. Military service in the Mysore wars — 1780–1792
2. Assistant to Alexander Read in the Baramahal — 1792–1799
3. Collector of South Canara — 1799
4. President of the Judicial Commission — 1800–1807
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
175.x: Munro served in the Mysore wars from 1780 to 1792, assisted Read in the Baramahal from 1792 to 1799, and became Collector of South Canara in 1799. The period 1800–1807 belonged to his tenure as Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, not President of the Judicial Commission.
175.tq: Check each date-post pair separately, especially where neighbouring tenures are swapped.
xs: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**1780-92** Mysore wars; **1792-99** assistant to Read; **1799** Collector of **South Canara**.
Pair 4 wrong: **1800-07** was **Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts**; the Judicial Commission was **1814-18**.
xa: He arrived in Madras in **1780** as a military cadet (born **27 May 1761**, Glasgow).
**Governor of Madras**: **1820-27** (UPSC notes say 1819-26).

175.s:
Arrange the following stages of Thomas Munro's career in chronological order:
A. Governor of Madras
B. Assistant to Alexander Read in the Baramahal
C. Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts
D. President of the Judicial Commission
175.x: Munro served as Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission, and finally Governor of Madras.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest posts first, then place the middle appointments.
xs: Order: Assistant to Read (**1792-99**) → Principal Collector, Ceded Districts (**1800-07**) → Judicial Commission (**1814-18**) → Governor of Madras (**1820-27**) — option **(1) B, C, D, A**.
In between he was **Collector of South Canara** (**1799**).
xa: He died at **Pattikonda** on **6 July 1827**, buried at **Gooty**.
As Governor he saw general Ryotwari adoption in Madras (**1820**).

175.s: Which of the following was a feature of Thomas Munro's field survey of 1802–1807?
o: Fields were numbered and their holders were registered.
All land was transferred to zamindars permanently.
Revenue collection was suspended throughout the Ceded Districts.
Village headmen alone were recognised as proprietors.
175.x: Munro's field survey numbered fields and registered their holders. This was part of his direct ryotwari-oriented administration.
175.tq: Identify the administrative measure directly associated with the stated survey.
xs: Munro's **field survey (1802-07)** **numbered fields and registered holders** — option **(1)**.
He settled **directly with the peasant**, not with zamindars or headmen.
xa: He gave ryots **advances for seed and implements**.
In the **1802** drought he repaired tanks without waiting for orders.

175.s: During the 1802 drought, Thomas Munro repaired tanks without waiting for orders and also—
o: abolished field surveys in the Ceded Districts
gave ryots advances for seed and agricultural implements
auctioned all village lands to merchants
introduced permanent revenue assessment in Rayalaseema
175.x: Munro gave cultivators advances for seed and implements and repaired tanks during the drought without awaiting orders.
175.tq: Link a crisis-response action with the officer's broader administrative philosophy.
xs: In the **1802** drought Munro also **gave ryots advances for seed and implements** — option **(2)**.
He repaired **tanks** without waiting for orders.
xa: His **field survey (1802-07)** numbered fields and registered holders.
He **abolished the auction system** in the Ceded Districts.
He spoke **Telugu** fluently and was fond of Rayalaseema.

175.s: Which of the following best represents Thomas Munro's administrative philosophy?
o: Exclusive reliance on village headmen and moneylenders
Direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries and communication in fluent Telugu
Permanent fixation of revenue irrespective of local conditions
Indirect rule through zamindars and complete absence of official contact with cultivators
175.x: Munro favoured direct contact with cultivators, avoided intermediaries and was fluent in Telugu. He was also particularly fond of Rayalaseema.
175.tq: Choose the option that combines the distinctive elements of a stated administrative philosophy.
xs: Munro stood for **direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries**, and spoke **fluent Telugu** — option **(2)**.
He **distrusted Palegars** and big intermediaries, so indirect rule through zamindars is the opposite.
xa: He worked **without interpreters**.
Rayalaseema was chosen because it had **no strong zamindars**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about Sir Thomas Munro:
1. He served as Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827.
2. He died of cholera at Pattikonda in Kurnool district in 1827.
3. He was buried at Anantapur, his headquarters as Collector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Munro was Governor of Madras 1820-27 and died of cholera at Pattikonda (Kurnool) on 6 July 1827. Statement 3 is wrong: Anantapur was his headquarters as Collector of the Ceded Districts, but he was buried at Gooty. So every option containing 3 is wrong.
175.tq: Munro: HQ Anantapur, died Pattikonda, buried Gooty.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Governor of Madras 1820-27**.
Statement 2 correct: died of cholera at **Pattikonda** (Kurnool), **6 July 1827**.
Statement 3 wrong: he was buried at **Gooty**; **Anantapur** was his Collector HQ.
xa: UPSC notes give his governorship as **1819-26**.
He was born **27 May 1761** in **Glasgow**.

175.s:
With reference to the Mahalwari System, consider the following statements:

1. Holt Mackenzie proposed the system in 1822.
2. It was revised under Lord William Bentinck in 1833.
3. R. M. Bird was associated with the revision.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Holt Mackenzie proposed the Mahalwari System in 1822. It was revised under Bentinck in 1833, with R. M. Bird associated with that revision.
175.tq: Keep the original proposal distinct from the later revision and its associated official.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Holt Mackenzie** proposed Mahalwari in **1822**.
It was revised under **Bentinck** in **1833**, by **R.M. Bird**.
xa: Mackenzie's law: **Regulation VII of 1822**; Bird's revision: **Regulation IX of 1833**.
**James Thomason** carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
⚠ Some notes credit **Bentinck (1833)** as originator — that is only the revision.

175.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists:

List-I (Official)
a. Holt Mackenzie
b. R.M. Bird
c. James Thomason

List-II (Role)
i. Carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP
ii. Devised the Mahalwari system
iii. Revised the system through a survey-based settlement

The correct matching is:
175.x: Holt Mackenzie devised the system, R.M. Bird revised it through survey-based settlement, and James Thomason carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
175.tq: Start from the sure official–role pair and eliminate codes that repeat the wrong function.
xs: **Mackenzie** devised it, **Bird** revised it, **Thomason** carried it on — option **(1) a–ii, b–iii, c–i**.
**Holt Mackenzie**: **Regulation VII of 1822**.
**R.M. Bird**: **Regulation IX of 1833**, survey-based settlement.
xa: Bird is called the **"father of land settlement in north India"**.
**Thomason** was Lt.-Governor of the NWP.

175.s: R.M. Bird is remembered in connection with the Mahalwari system mainly because he:
o: revised the system through a survey-based settlement under Regulation IX of 1833
created the zamindari system in Bengal
175.x: R.M. Bird revised the Mahalwari system through a survey-based settlement under Regulation IX of 1833 during Bentinck's period.
175.tq: Use the official's specific reform role to distinguish him from the original designer and later executor.
xs: **R.M. Bird** revised Mahalwari through a **survey-based settlement** under **Regulation IX of 1833** — option **(1)**.
The **Sunset Law** and Bengal zamindari belong to the Permanent Settlement; **Baramahal** Ryotwari to **Read**.
xa: The revision came under **Bentinck**.
**Holt Mackenzie** devised it by **Regulation VII of 1822**.

175.s: Approximately what proportion of British India was covered by the Mahalwari system?
175.x: The Mahalwari system covered approximately 30 percent of British India.
175.tq: Use the middle numerical option only after distinguishing the approximate share from exact-looking distractors.
xs: Mahalwari covered **about 30 percent** of British India — option **(1)**.
Areas: **NWP (Agra-Oudh region), Punjab, Central India**.
xa: Unit of settlement: the **mahal** (village or estate).
Joint ownership forms: **"Bhai Chara"** or **"Mahali"**.
Collection by the village headman (**lambardar**).

175.s:
Arrange the following developments associated with land revenue administration in chronological order:
A. Baramahal came under Company control after the Third Mysore War
B. Regulation VII of 1822 associated with Holt Mackenzie
C. Regulation IX of 1833 associated with R.M. Bird
D. Permanent Settlement made permanent
175.x: Baramahal came under Company control in 1792, the Permanent Settlement became permanent in 1793, Regulation VII was issued in 1822 and Regulation IX in 1833.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two nineteenth-century regulations.
xs: Order: Baramahal (**1792**) → Permanent Settlement made permanent (**1793**) → **Regulation VII of 1822** → **Regulation IX of 1833** — option **(1) A, D, B, C**.
Baramahal came after the **Third Mysore War**; 1822 is **Mackenzie**, 1833 is **Bird**.
xa: Ryotwari: Rayalaseema **1802**, general Madras **1820**.
**Haftam 1799**, **Panjam 1812**.

175.s: Which statement correctly describes the unit and method of assessment under the Mahalwari system?
o: The individual ryot was the sole unit; revenue was collected only by zamindars
The province was the unit; revenue was permanently fixed by the Company
The mahal was the unit; revenue was fixed for the village or estate and collected through the headman or village community
The profession was the unit; revenue was collected through urban merchants
175.x: Under Mahalwari, the mahal meant a village or estate. Revenue was fixed for it and collected by the headman or village community, with each cultivator liable for his share.
175.tq: Split the question into unit, assessment and collection authority.
xs: Under Mahalwari the **mahal** (village or estate) was the unit; revenue was fixed for it and collected by the **headman or village community** — option **(3)**.
Each cultivator was liable for his share; it was **periodically revised**.
xa: Individual ryots = **Ryotwari**; zamindars = **Permanent Settlement**.
Mahalwari broke village solidarity through **collective liability**.
On default the **village was collectively liable**.

175.s: The common ownership arrangements associated with the Mahalwari system were known as:
175.x: Common ownership arrangements under the Mahalwari framework were called Bhai Chara or Mahali.
175.tq: Discriminate between closely related revenue terms from different systems.
xs: Mahalwari joint-ownership forms were called **"Bhai Chara" or "Mahali"** — option **(2)**.
**Zabt** and **taccavi** were Mughal; **Peshkash** and **Haveli** are Andhra revenue terms.
xa: **Moturpha** was a tax on professions, trades and looms in Madras.
Mahalwari: **joint village ownership**, unit = **mahal**.

175.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the Mahalwari-type arrangement is specifically associated with which area or areas?
175.x: The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in Nellore and Chittoor in the relevant regional account; in some accounts, Nellore alone is specifically mentioned.
175.tq: Use regional identification while avoiding confusion with named Zamindari estates.
xs: In Andhra, the Mahalwari-type arrangement is linked to **Nellore and Chittoor** — option **(2)**.
Some notes give **Nellore** only; there **village headmen** collected and remitted the tax.
**Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram, Nuzvid** were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement.
xa: All three systems ran in Andhra: zamindari in the **Circars**, ryotwari in the **Ceded Districts**, mahalwari in **Nellore**.
Farmers depended on **village elders**.

175.s: The Mahalwari system of land revenue was introduced mainly in which of the following regions?
o: North-Western Provinces and parts of Punjab
175.x: Mahalwari covered the North-Western Provinces (Agra-Oudh) and parts of Punjab, plus Central India (APPSC 2018). Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and the Northern Circars were Permanent Settlement areas; Madras and Bombay were Ryotwari areas.
175.tq: Mahalwari = NWP + Punjab; Ryotwari = Madras + Bombay; Zamindari = Bengal.
xs: Mahalwari was mainly in the **North-Western Provinces and parts of Punjab** — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2018**).
**Bengal, Bihar**, **Odisha** and the **Northern Circars** were Permanent Settlement areas; **Madras and Bombay** were Ryotwari.
xa: Mahalwari also covered the Gangetic valley and **Central India** — about **30%** of British India.
Proposed by **Holt Mackenzie (1822)**.

175.s: The Ryotwari settlement was introduced in the Ceded Districts in 1802 after which development?
o: The Ceded Districts were transferred by the Nizam in 1800
The Northern Circars were obtained through a Mughal farman in 1765
Guntur was acquired by the Company in 1788
The Madras Estates Abolition Act was passed in 1948
175.x: The Ceded Districts were ceded by the Nizam in 1800, after which Munro became principal collector and introduced Ryotwari there in 1802.
175.tq: Use the immediate administrative cause rather than confusing it with later settlement dates.
xs: Ryotwari came after **the Ceded Districts were transferred by the Nizam in 1800** — option **(1)**.
Munro became the first Collector (**1800**) and introduced Ryotwari in **1802**.
**1765** (Circars), **1788** (Guntur) and **1948** (Estates Abolition) are other Andhra milestones.
xa: The name **Rayalaseema** was proposed by **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**.
APHQ **2025** order: **Guntur (1788)** → **Padmanabham (1794)** → **Ryotwari (1802)** → zamindari abolition (**1948**).

175.s: Who assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the Palegars in the Ceded Districts before the introduction of Ryotwari settlement?
175.x: Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer Campbell before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.
175.tq: Discriminate between persons associated with administration, resistance and nomenclature.
xs: Munro suppressed the Palegars with military officer **Campbell** — option **(2)**.
**Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** was a Kurnool Polygar who revolted in the **1840s**.
**Vijayarama Gajapati Raju** was the Vizianagaram zamindar defeated at **Padmanabham (1794)**.
**Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** proposed the name **Rayalaseema**.
xa: About **80** palegars resisted; suppression took **18** months.
Uyyalawada looted the treasury at **Kovela Kuntla**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the land arrangements in Coastal Andhra:
1. Coastal lands were divided into Haveli and Zamindari areas.
2. Haveli areas were under direct Company control.
3. Zamindars in Zamindari areas paid peshkash.
4. The auction system was never used in Haveli areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Haveli areas were directly controlled by the Company, while Zamindars paid peshkash. The auction system was initially used in Coastal Andhra, including Haveli lands, so statement 4 is false.
175.tq: Find the exception created by the absolute word 'never'.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Coastal lands were **Haveli** (direct Company control) and **Zamindari**; zamindars paid **peshkash**.
Statement 4 wrong: **Haveli** lands were **auctioned** — grouped into **mootahs** and sold to **mootahdars**.
xa: Old estates of **Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram** came under peshkash.
Mootahs were held like proprietary estates after **1802**; many fell into arrears.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** confirmed valid **inam** titles on a **quit-rent**.

175.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
175.x: Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were old estates brought under the Zamindari arrangement. Kovela Kuntla is associated with the treasury looted during Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt.
175.tq: Use the location-and-event mismatch to eliminate the wrong pair.
xs: **Kovela Kuntla — Zamindari estate** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
Kovela Kuntla is where **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** looted the treasury in his **1840s** revolt.
**Pithapuram, Vizianagaram and Bobbili** were zamindaris under the **Permanent Settlement**.
xa: Other Andhra zamindaris: **Peddapuram** and **Nuzvid**.
Old estates of **Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram** paid **peshkash**.
Uyyalawada was a **Kurnool Polygar**; Palegar resistance followed Munro's ryotwari.

175.s: The Permanent Settlement introduced by Cornwallis in 1793 was implemented in Andhra in 1802 with which immediate effect?
o: The auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed
The zamindars were replaced by village headmen
Land revenue was remitted during every crop failure
All Zamindari estates were immediately abolished
175.x: In Andhra, Cornwallis's 1793 Act was implemented in 1802; it abolished the auction system and fixed the tax. Zamindari abolition occurred much later in 1948.
175.tq: Apply the general settlement policy to its Andhra implementation.
xs: When Cornwallis's **1793** settlement was implemented in Andhra in **1802**, **the auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed** — option **(1)**.
Zamindars were not replaced or abolished; abolition came only in **1948**.
There was **no famine remission** under British revenue systems.
xa: Agreements ran for **10** years; farmers were reduced to **tenants**.
Andhra effects: absentee landlordism, **sub-infeudation**, no investment in land.
Some notes give the Andhra split as **9/10** to government, **1/10** to the zamindar.

175.s: Which legislation provided for the full conversion of Zamindari estates into Ryotwari holdings in the Madras Presidency?
o: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
175.x: The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 provided for the abolition of estates and their conversion into Ryotwari holdings.
175.tq: Match the exact statute with its administrative purpose.
xs: Full conversion came with the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — option **(3)**.
**1793** made the zamindari settlement permanent — it created, not abolished, zamindaris.
xa: Some notes date zamindari abolition to **1952** (First Plan).
APHQ **2025** order ends with zamindari abolition (**1948**) after **Guntur (1788)**, **Padmanabham (1794)**, **Ryotwari (1802)**.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** dealt with **inam** (rent-free) titles.

175.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Guntur was acquired by the Company
B. Battle of Padmanabham
C. Ceded Districts were obtained from the Nizam
D. Permanent Settlement was applied in the Circars and Ryotwari was introduced in Rayalaseema
175.x: The correct sequence is Guntur acquired in 1788, Battle of Padmanabham in 1794, Ceded Districts obtained in 1800, and the 1802 settlements.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest dates first, then place the middle events.
xs: Order: **Guntur (1788)** → **Padmanabham (1794)** → Ceded Districts from the Nizam (**1800**) → Permanent Settlement in Circars + Ryotwari in Rayalaseema (**1802**) — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
This follows the APHQ **2025** order.
xa: The **Northern Circars** came earlier, in **1765-66**.
**Uyyalawada**'s revolt came in the **1840s**; zamindari abolition in **1948**.

175.s: The Battle of Padmanabham of 1794 resulted in the defeat of:
o: Vijayarama Gajapati Raju, the Vizianagaram zamindar
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao, the proposer of the name Rayalaseema
Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy, the Kurnool Polygar
175.x: In the Battle of Padmanabham in 1794, Vijayarama Gajapati Raju, the Vizianagaram zamindar, was defeated.
175.tq: Use the person-event association rather than confusing a later rebel with an earlier zamindar.
xs: The **Battle of Padmanabham (1794)** defeated **Vijayarama Gajapati Raju**, the **Vizianagaram zamindar** — option **(2)**.
**Munro** was the Collector who brought Ryotwari; **Uyyalawada** revolted in the **1840s**.
xa: Padmanabham is **2nd** in the APHQ **2025** order, after **Guntur (1788)**.
Vizianagaram was one of the old estates under **peshkash**.

175.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt in the 1840s is associated with which incident?
o: Defeating the Vizianagaram zamindar at Padmanabham
Introducing the Mahalwari system in Nellore
Obtaining the Northern Circars through a Mughal farman
Looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla
175.x: During the Kurnool Polygar revolt in the 1840s, Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy looted the treasury at Kovela Kuntla.
175.tq: Link the rebel with the specific action and place.
xs: **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy**'s **1840s** revolt is linked to **looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla** — option **(4)**.
He was a **Kurnool Polygar**; Padmanabham (**1794**) was the Vizianagaram zamindar's defeat.
xa: Palegar resistance (**Uyyalawada**) followed **Munro**'s ryotwari in Rayalaseema.
Munro had suppressed about **80** palegars with **Campbell**.

175.s: The Northern Circars came under Company control in 1765–66 through which combination?
o: A settlement with zamindars and a grant from the Madras Council
A ryotwari agreement and a Permanent Settlement Regulation
A treaty with Tipu Sultan and a sanad from the Marathas
A Mughal farman and a treaty with the Nizam
175.x: The Company obtained the Northern Circars in 1765–66 through a Mughal farman and a treaty with the Nizam.
175.tq: Identify the correct pair of instruments and authorities.
xs: The **Northern Circars** came in **1765-66** through **a Mughal farman and a treaty with the Nizam** — option **(4)**.
They were mainly **zamindari**; **Haveli** lands came under ryotwari later.
xa: The Permanent Settlement was applied in the Circars in **1802**.
**Guntur** was acquired separately in **1788**.

175.s: The name 'Rayalaseema' was proposed by:
175.x: The name Rayalaseema for the Ceded Districts was proposed by Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao.
175.tq: Separate the person associated with regional nomenclature from administrators and rebels.
xs: The name **Rayalaseema** was proposed by **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** — option **(3)**.
**Munro** was the first Collector there; **Uyyalawada** a Kurnool Polygar; **Vijayarama Gajapati Raju** the Vizianagaram zamindar.
xa: Rayalaseema = the **Ceded Districts**, ceded by the **Nizam in 1800**.
Ryotwari came there first in Andhra, in **1802**.

175.s: Moturpha in the Madras Presidency was a tax imposed on:
175.x: Moturpha was a tax on professions, trades and looms, affecting weavers, artisans and merchants in the Madras Presidency.
175.tq: Distinguish an occupational tax from land revenue assessments.
xs: **Moturpha** was a tax on **professions, trades and looms** in Madras — option **(4)**.
It fell on **weavers, artisans, merchants**.
xa: **Peshkash** = fixed payment by **zamindars**.
**Inam** = rent-free title.
**Haveli** = government/direct Company land.

175.s: Haveli lands were grouped into mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars after 1802. The mootahdars generally held them as—
175.x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of proprietary estates. Many mootahdars later failed and fell into arrears.
175.tq: Identify the legal-economic character of the holding created by a settlement arrangement.
xs: **Mootahdars** held the auctioned mootahs as **proprietary estates** after **1802** — option **(2)**.
Many failed and **fell into arrears**.
xa: **Haveli** lands were under direct Company control (vs **Zamindari**).
Haveli lands used auction, village or ryotwari methods.

175.s: Which statement about village-lease settlements in the Ceded Districts is correct?
o: They replaced ryotwari after Munro left in 1808 and continued until ryotwari was restored around 1820.
They preceded the 1792 Baramahal experiment and ended in 1799.
They were introduced only in the Northern Circars and never in the Ceded Districts.
They permanently replaced all forms of direct settlement in Rayalaseema.
175.x: Village-lease settlements, in which village headmen acted as lessees, replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts after Munro's departure from 1808 onward and lasted until about 1820.
175.tq: Track the temporary replacement and subsequent restoration of a revenue system.
xs: **Village-lease settlements** replaced ryotwari after Munro left (**1808** onward) until ryotwari was **restored around 1820** — option **(1)**.
Village **headmen** acted as lessees.
They were in the **Ceded Districts**, not the Circars, and were not permanent.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the Andhra ryotwari date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
General Madras adoption came in **1820** under Munro as Governor.

175.s: In Nellore, the Mahalwari-type arrangement involved—
o: village headmen collecting and remitting the tax
zamindars fixing revenue permanently with the Government
individual ryots paying revenue only in kind
175.x: In Nellore, village headmen collected and remitted the tax under an arrangement resembling the Mahalwari system.
175.tq: Identify the operational role of the village headman in a regional variant.
xs: In **Nellore**, **village headmen collected and remitted the tax** — option **(1)**.
Farmers depended on **village elders**.
xa: Some notes add **Chittoor** to Nellore.
Andhra contrast: zamindari in the **Circars**, ryotwari in the **Ceded Districts**, mahalwari in **Nellore**.
Mahalwari unit: the **mahal**; collector: the **lambardar**.

175.s: The Madras Inam Commission was established in which year to investigate which matter?
175.x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.
175.tq: Pair the commission with both its year and its specific purpose.
xs: The **Madras Inam Commission** came in **1858** to investigate **inam (rent-free) titles** — option **(3)**.
**1793**, **1802** and **1822** belong to the Permanent Settlement, mootahs and Mahalwari.
xa: Valid titles were confirmed on payment of a **quit-rent**.
Full ryotwari conversion of estates came in **1948**.

175.s: What happened to valid inam titles after investigation by the Madras Inam Commission?
o: They were converted into permanent zamindaris without payment.
They were automatically cancelled without examination.
They were auctioned to merchants under the Sunset Law.
They were confirmed on payment of a quit-rent.
175.x: Valid rent-free inam titles were confirmed subject to payment of a quit-rent.
175.tq: Distinguish validation with a financial condition from outright confirmation or cancellation.
xs: Valid inam titles were **confirmed on payment of a quit-rent** — option **(4)**.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** examined them; there was no automatic cancellation.
xa: **Inam** = rent-free title.
The **Sunset Law** auctions applied to zamindari estates, not inams.

175.s: Why did rigid land revenue demands frequently push ryots towards moneylenders?
o: The government accepted revenue only in manufactured goods
Moneylenders alone were authorised to cultivate government land
Revenue had to be paid in cash even when crops failed
Ryots were prohibited from selling agricultural produce
175.x: The inflexible cash demand continued even during crop failures, forcing ryots to borrow from Mahajans and often mortgage or lose their land.
175.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from revenue rigidity to indebtedness.
xs: Revenue had to be **paid in cash even when crops failed** — option **(3)**.
This rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**, then mortgage and eviction.
xa: There was **no famine remission**, unlike the Mughal **zabt**.
Cash revenue forced **cash crops** (indigo, cotton, opium, jute).
Result: rural indebtedness and **land alienation**.

175.s: Which feature distinguished the rigid British revenue demand from the Mughal zabt system mentioned in the context of agrarian administration?
o: The Mughal system imposed no assessment on agricultural land
The Mughal system provided a one-third share arrangement and taccavi loans
The British system provided taccavi loans to every ryot
The British system routinely remitted revenue during famine
175.x: The Mughal zabt is described as involving a one-third share and taccavi loans, whereas the British demand was rigid and offered no famine remission.
175.tq: Contrast the two systems through their treatment of risk and relief.
xs: The Mughal **zabt** had a **one-third share** and **taccavi loans** — option **(2)**.
The British demand gave **no famine remission**.
xa: Mahalwari broke village solidarity through **collective liability**.
All three systems took revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

175.s: Which of the following correctly explains the economic effect of cash-based land revenue assessment?
o: It encouraged the cultivation of commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute
It transferred all agricultural profits directly to cultivators
It eliminated dependence on markets by encouraging subsistence crops alone
It prevented the sale and mortgage of agricultural land
175.x: The need to meet cash revenue demands encouraged cultivation of commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute.
175.tq: Infer the cropping response from the pressure to obtain cash.
xs: Cash revenue forced **commercial crops — indigo, cotton, opium, jute** — option **(1)**.
Profits did not go to cultivators; land became **saleable** and indebtedness grew.
xa: Ryotwari areas: the **American Civil War** cotton slump → defaults → land to moneylenders.
Low investment in agriculture; **overcrowding** as ruined artisans fell back on land.

175.s: In Ryotwari areas, the cotton slump associated with the American Civil War led to:
o: Defaults and transfer of land to moneylenders
A rise in the purchasing power of ryots
Permanent remission of all land revenue
175.x: The cotton slump caused defaults in Ryotwari areas, after which land often passed into the hands of moneylenders.
175.tq: Follow the chain from market shock to default and land alienation.
xs: The **American Civil War** cotton slump caused **defaults and transfer of land to moneylenders** — option **(1)**.
It did not raise ryots' purchasing power or end moneylending.
xa: Ryotwari and mahalwari areas produced **moneylender-landlords**.
Ryotwari problems: **over-assessment**, no land records, corrupt officials.

175.s: Which pairing of newly strengthened rural classes with the areas in which they emerged is correct?
o: Merchant-landlords — Zamindari areas; moneylender-landlords — Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas
Moneylender-landlords — Zamindari areas; merchant-landlords — Ryotwari areas only
Artisan-landlords — all areas; merchants — no rural areas
Village headmen — Zamindari areas; zamindars — Ryotwari areas only
175.x: Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.
175.tq: Match each rural class with the revenue system that enabled its rise.
xs: **Merchant-landlords** rose in **zamindari** areas; **moneylender-landlords** in **ryotwari and mahalwari** areas — option **(1)**.
Old zamindars lost estates to **urban merchants and moneylenders** at auction.
xa: The common result: **rural indebtedness + land alienation**.
Land became a **saleable commodity**, concentrated in few hands.

175.s: Which of the following statements about the wider economic consequences of colonial land revenue systems is correct?
o: Land became a saleable commodity, concentration of ownership increased, and ruined artisans added to overcrowding on the land
Land ceased to be transferable and agricultural ownership became widely dispersed
Agricultural investment rose uniformly because revenue demands were flexible
The decline of handicrafts reduced pressure on agricultural land
175.x: Land became saleable and concentrated in fewer hands. Low agricultural investment and the return of ruined artisans to the countryside increased overcrowding and rural pressure.
175.tq: Select the option that combines the linked economic consequences without reversing them.
xs: **Land became a saleable commodity**, ownership concentrated, and **ruined artisans** overcrowded the land — option **(1)**.
Land became more transferable, not less; investment stayed **low** because demands were rigid.
xa: Rigid cash demand → **moneylenders (Mahajans)**; mortgage and eviction.
Cash crops: **indigo, cotton, opium, jute**.

175.s: Which of the following was NOT identified as a major problem of the Ryotwari system?
o: Permanent fixing of revenue at a low and unchangeable rate
175.x: Ryotwari suffered from over-assessment, inadequate records and unclear boundaries. Its revenue was periodically revised and often heavy, not permanently fixed at a low rate.
175.tq: Find the option that contradicts the characteristic weaknesses of the system.
xs: **Permanent fixing at a low, unchangeable rate** was NOT a Ryotwari problem — option **(4)**; Ryotwari was **periodically revised** and high.
Real problems: **over-assessment**, **no proper land records**, **unclear boundaries**, corrupt subordinate officials.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
Revision came about **every 30 years**.
The **Permanent Settlement** was the one **fixed forever**.

175.s: What was a major consequence of over-assessment and defaults under the Ryotwari system?
o: Land could not be transferred or auctioned under any circumstances.
Peasants turned to moneylenders, and land was auctioned and alienated after defaults.
Moneylending disappeared because revenue was paid only after good harvests.
Peasants became permanent zamindars without further revenue obligations.
175.x: Heavy assessments pushed peasants towards moneylenders; defaults could lead to land auctions and alienation.
175.tq: Follow the chain from excessive assessment to indebtedness and loss of land.
xs: **Peasants turned to moneylenders**, and defaults led to **land auctions and alienation** — option **(2)**.
Ryotwari land was **transferable** — it could be sold, mortgaged, auctioned.
xa: Causes: **over-assessment**, no land records, unclear boundaries.
On default under Ryotwari, **land was seized/auctioned**.

175.s: Which combination correctly describes the impact of Zamindari on tenants and zamindars?
o: Rent-racking of tenants and growth of absentee landlords; old zamindars lost estates to merchants at auction.
Low rents, direct state contact and universal protection of old zamindars.
Abolition of auctions and replacement of merchants by village communities.
No change in tenancy relations because revenue was collected directly from ryots.
175.x: Zamindari was associated with rent-racking of tenants and absentee landlordism. Old zamindars could lose their estates at auction to merchants.
175.tq: Combine two linked consequences while guarding against reversal of the landlord-tenant relationship.
xs: Zamindari brought **rent-racking** of tenants, **absentee landlords**, and old zamindars **lost estates to merchants at auction** — option **(1)**.
Rents were high, not low, and old zamindars were not protected.
xa: Zamindars moved to cities like **Calcutta**; tenants became **tenants-at-will**.
**Sub-infeudation** and endless litigation followed.
**Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** let zamindars seize tenants' property.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly describes revenue fixation under the three principal land revenue systems?
o: Permanent Settlement—periodically revised; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—fixed forever
Permanent Settlement—fixed forever; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—no revenue assessment
Permanent Settlement—fixed forever; Ryotwari—periodically revised; Mahalwari—periodically revised
Permanent Settlement—annually revised; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—annually revised
175.x: Revenue was fixed permanently under the Permanent Settlement, whereas assessments under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems were periodically revised.
175.tq: Compare the rate-setting column across all three systems and watch for reversed descriptions.
xs: Permanent Settlement **fixed forever**; Ryotwari and Mahalwari **periodically revised** — option **(3)**.
None of the systems was revised annually.
xa: Settlement with: **zamindars** / **individual ryots** / **village community (mahal)**.
Ownership: zamindar as proprietor / cultivator as owner / village jointly.

175.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

a. Permanent Settlement — Zamindar
b. Ryotwari System — Individual farmer
c. Mahalwari System — Lambardar

d. Mahalwari System — Individual ryot
175.x: The zamindar was the collector under the Permanent Settlement, the individual farmer under the Ryotwari System, and the village headman or lambardar under the Mahalwari System. The individual ryot was not the collector under Mahalwari.
175.tq: Separate the person with whom settlement was made from the person responsible for collection.
xs: Pairs a, b and c are correct — option **(2) a, b and c only**.
Collection: **Zamindar** (Permanent), **individual farmer** (Ryotwari), village headman **lambardar** (Mahalwari).
Pair d wrong: Mahalwari settled with the **village community**, not the individual ryot.
xa: Intermediaries: present / absent / limited.
Mahalwari joint ownership: **Bhai Chara** or **Mahali**.

175.s:
Which of the following correctly indicates the presence of intermediaries in the three systems?

1. Permanent Settlement — intermediaries present
2. Ryotwari System — intermediaries absent
3. Mahalwari System — intermediaries limited

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
175.x: Intermediaries were present under the Permanent Settlement, absent under the Ryotwari System and limited under the Mahalwari System.
175.tq: Read the comparison vertically and test the intermediary column without confusing it with ownership.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Intermediaries: **present** in Permanent Settlement, **absent** in Ryotwari, **limited** in Mahalwari.
xa: On default: zamindari **confiscated/auctioned**; ryotwari **land seized**; mahalwari **village collectively liable**.
Munro's ryotwari philosophy: settle **directly with the peasant**.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly states the consequence of default under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems respectively?
o: Revenue permanently remitted; village ownership abolished
175.x: Under the Ryotwari System, the cultivator's land could be seized on default. Under the Mahalwari System, the village was collectively liable for the revenue.
175.tq: Compare default consequences in sequence and avoid transferring the zamindari penalty to other systems.
xs: On default: Ryotwari — **land seized**; Mahalwari — **village collectively liable** — option **(3)**.
Zamindari confiscation or auction belongs to the **Permanent Settlement**.
xa: Zamindari defaults fell under the **Sunset Law**.
Mahalwari's **collective liability** broke village solidarity.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly compares revenue assessment under Permanent Settlement and Ryotwari?
o: Permanent Settlement was based on a share of produce, whereas Ryotwari was fixed permanently.
Permanent Settlement was fixed permanently, whereas Ryotwari was revised periodically and was often 50 per cent or more of the produce.
Both were revised annually and neither involved a high demand.
Both systems fixed the demand permanently at the same rate.
175.x: Permanent Settlement fixed the revenue demand permanently. Ryotwari assessments were periodically revised and were often very high, at 50 per cent or more of the produce.
175.tq: Compare the systems through the assessment rule and its quantitative feature.
xs: Permanent Settlement was **fixed permanently**; Ryotwari was **revised periodically** and often **50%+** of produce — option **(2)**.
Neither was revised annually, and the zamindari demand was set at a **very high level**.
xa: Permanent: introduced by **Cornwallis, 1793**; Ryotwari by **Read and Munro** (**1792** experiment, **1820** general).
Agreement with: **zamindar** vs **individual ryot**.

175.s: What was the stated consequence of default under the two systems?
o: Under Zamindari the land was auctioned only to cultivators, while under Ryotwari no penalty applied.
Under both systems the land was automatically restored after one harvest.
Under Zamindari the estate could be forfeited, while under Ryotwari the land could be auctioned.
Under Zamindari the ryot was imprisoned, while under Ryotwari the zamindar received compensation.
175.x: Default under Zamindari could result in forfeiture of the estate under the Sunset Law, while default under Ryotwari could lead to auction of the land.
175.tq: Compare consequences of default instead of merely recalling the names of the systems.
xs: Under Zamindari the **estate was forfeited** (Sunset Law); under Ryotwari the **land was auctioned** — option **(3)**.
The Sunset Law: revenue due **by sunset of the due date**.
xa: Ownership: **zamindar as proprietor** vs **cultivator as owner**.
Mahalwari default: **village collectively liable**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the three major land-revenue settlements:
1. They made land a transferable commodity.
2. They contributed to the formation of a loyal landlord class.
3. They were associated with rural indebtedness and peasant revolts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: The three settlements made land transferable, helped create a loyal landlord class and contributed to rural indebtedness, which in turn fed peasant revolts.
175.tq: Test the common long-term significance of several systems through cumulative statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The settlements made **land a transferable commodity** and produced a **loyal landlord class**.
They led to **rural indebtedness** and **peasant revolts**.
xa: They shaped agrarian class structure that land reforms after **1947** tried to undo.
All three were **extractive**, with revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

175.s: Alice Thorner criticised the Ryotwari system on the ground that it—
o: abolished all direct contact between the state and zamindars
created a permanent landlord class in the Northern Circars
made the village community the sole unit of settlement
destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government
175.x: Alice Thorner argued that Ryotwari destroyed the village system and isolated individual farmers from the government.
175.tq: Associate a named critic with the precise argument attributed to her.
xs: **Alice Thorner** said ryotwari **destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government** — option **(4)**.
Making the village the unit is **Mahalwari**; a landlord class in the Circars is **zamindari**.
xa: Another criticism: the state became the **"ultimate landlord"**.
Ryotwari revenue was **as heavy as Zamindari rent**.

175.s: The statement that the state became the “ultimate landlord” was particularly connected with which criticism?
o: Permanent Settlement transferred all ownership to individual cultivators.
Inam grants were confirmed without any quit-rent.
Mahalwari abolished the role of village communities.
Ryotwari revenue was as heavy as Zamindari rent despite direct settlement with ryots.
175.x: The criticism held that the state became the ultimate landlord and that Ryotwari revenue could be as burdensome as Zamindari rent.
175.tq: Separate the formal ownership arrangement from the practical burden of revenue demand.
xs: The state as **"ultimate landlord"** goes with the criticism that **Ryotwari revenue was as heavy as Zamindari rent** — option **(4)**.
This held despite **direct settlement with ryots**.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **isolated farmers** from the government.

175.s: Which of the following correctly expresses the principal Andhra contrast in land-revenue systems?
o: All three systems operated only in Rayalaseema
Mahalwari in the Circars, Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in Nellore
Ryotwari in the Circars, Mahalwari in Rayalaseema and Zamindari in Nellore
Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
175.x: The Andhra pattern was Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and a Mahalwari-type arrangement in Nellore.
175.tq: Use a three-region comparison to distinguish closely related settlement systems.
xs: **Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts, Mahalwari in Nellore** — option **(4)**.
This contrast — **Munro**'s Rayalaseema ryotwari vs zamindari **Circars** — is a core APPSC point.
xa: Circar zamindaris: **Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Peddapuram, Pithapuram, Nuzvid**.
Ryotwari came to Rayalaseema in **1802**.
Some notes add **Chittoor** to Nellore for Mahalwari.

175.s: Why is Thomas Munro particularly remembered in relation to Rayalaseema?
o: He replaced all ryotwari settlements with village leases permanently.
He was the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and established the direct ryot–state relationship there.
He introduced permanent Zamindari in the Northern Circars.
He served as the first head of the Madras Inam Commission.
175.x: Munro is remembered as the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and for establishing its direct relationship between the ryot and the state through ryotwari administration.
175.tq: Connect an official designation with its lasting regional legacy.
xs: Munro was the **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema** and set up the **direct ryot-state relationship** there — option **(2)** (PYQ **2025**).
He did not bring zamindari to the Circars; village leases replaced his ryotwari only after he left (**1808**).
xa: HQ: **Anantapur**; died at **Pattikonda**, buried at **Gooty** (**1827**).
He spoke **Telugu** fluently and worked without interpreters.

175.s: Which of the following best describes the broader post-1947 significance of the three land settlements?
o: They made rural indebtedness irrelevant to agrarian policy.
They shaped agrarian class structures that later land reforms attempted to undo.
They prevented the transferability of land after 1947.
They ended all landlordism before Independence.
175.x: The three settlements shaped agrarian class relations and structures, which post-1947 land reforms sought to dismantle or modify.
175.tq: Distinguish a historical legacy from an immediate administrative feature.
xs: The settlements **shaped agrarian class structures that later land reforms tried to undo** — option **(2)**.
These reforms came after **1947**.
xa: Andhra zamindari was abolished by the **Madras Estates Abolition Act (1948)**.
AP current relevance: **201 families** in **Pulladigunta** (**Guntur**) got ownership of **'Thopu Poramboke'** land after nearly a century.

176.s: Which stage of colonialism was characterised by Company trade monopoly, direct plunder and the use of Bengal revenue to buy export goods?
176.x: The mercantilist stage from 1757 to 1813 was marked by the Company's trade monopoly, direct plunder and the use of Bengal revenue for purchasing export goods.
176.tq: Match the defining economic features with the correct colonial stage and period.
xs: The **Mercantilist stage, 1757-1813** had **Company trade monopoly**, **direct plunder** and **Bengal revenue** buying export goods — option **(3)**.
The **free-trade stage (1813-1858)** made India a market for British goods; the **finance-capital** stage began in **1858**.
xa: The stages were proposed by **R.P. Dutt** (**India Today**), drawing on **Karl Marx**.
The **Charter Act 1813** ended the Company's monopoly, opening the free-trade stage.
The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.

176.s: During the free-trade or industrial-capital stage of colonialism, India primarily became:
o: A protected market for Indian manufactured goods
A market for British goods and a source of raw materials
A centre of British financial capital alone
An exporter of finished machinery to Britain
176.x: From 1813 to 1858, India became a market for British goods and a source of raw materials.
176.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap by distinguishing India's role as market and raw-material supplier.
xs: In the **free-trade / industrial-capital stage (1813-1858)** India became **a market for British goods and a source of raw materials** — option **(2)**.
India was not a protected market: **one-way free trade** let British goods in at low duty.
xa: British capital in railways, plantations and banks marks the **finance-capital** stage (from **1858**).
By **1850** India imported **one-fourth** of all British cotton exports.
Indian manufactures faced **heavy duties** in Britain.

176.s: The finance-capital stage of colonialism in India began in 1858 and was marked by British capital entering:
176.x: From 1858 onwards, the finance-capital stage involved British capital in railways, plantations and banks.
176.tq: Identify the characteristic investment sectors instead of confusing finance capital with direct Company trade.
xs: The **finance-capital** stage (from **1858**) saw British capital enter **railways, plantations and banks** — option **(4)**.
**Railways** carried a **guaranteed 5%** interest to British investors.
xa: Before **1914** about **97%** of British capital went to government projects, plantations and finance houses.
The scheme of stages comes from **R.P. Dutt**'s **India Today**.

176.s: The interpretation of colonialism in terms of mercantile, industrial-capital and finance-capital stages was proposed by:
o: Dadabhai Naoroji in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
Richard Strachey in the Famine Code
Arthur Cotton in an irrigation report
176.x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three-stage interpretation in India Today, drawing on Karl Marx.
176.tq: Match the analytical framework with its author and work, not with other economic critics.
xs: The three-stage interpretation was proposed by **R.P. Dutt** in **India Today** — option **(1)**, drawing on **Karl Marx**.
**Naoroji**'s **Poverty and Un-British Rule** is the drain-theory text; **Strachey** is linked to the Famine Code; **Arthur Cotton** to the Godavari anicut.
xa: R.P. Dutt was a **later Marxist writer**, not an original drain theorist.
⚠ Do not confuse **R.P. Dutt** (India Today) with **R.C. Dutt** (**Economic History of India**).

176.s: Who popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory in colonial India?
176.x: Dadabhai Naoroji popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.
176.tq: Direct identification of the proponent associated with a theory.
xs: The Drain of Wealth theory was popularised by **Dadabhai Naoroji** — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**R.C. Dutt**, **Ranade** and **Digby** developed or expanded it but did not popularise it.
xa: Naoroji's book: **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"** (**1901**).
He first stated it in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)** and coined **"moral drain"**.
He is called the **"Grand Old Man"** and **"father of Indian Nationalism"**.

176.s: Dadabhai Naoroji first stated the idea of India's economic drain in which work?
176.x: Naoroji first stated the drain argument in England's Debt to India in 1867.
176.tq: Match the thinker with his earliest contribution.
xs: Naoroji first stated the drain idea in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)** — option **(4)**.
**Economic History of India** is **R.C. Dutt**'s; **Essays on Indian Economics** is **Ranade**'s; **'Prosperous' British India** is **Digby**'s.
xa: His main drain text: **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (1901)**.
He coined the term **"moral drain"**.

176.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: R.C. Dutt — Economic History of India
William Digby — Essays on Indian Economics
G. Subramania Iyer — Economic History of India
176.x: R.C. Dutt wrote Economic History of India in two volumes. Prosperous British India was written by William Digby, while Essays on Indian Economics was associated with M.G. Ranade.
176.tq: Use the author–work pair and reject swapped authors.
xs: **R.C. Dutt — Economic History of India** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**'Prosperous' British India** was by **William Digby**, not Ranade.
**Essays on Indian Economics** was by **M.G. Ranade**, not Digby.
xa: R.C. Dutt's work ran to **2 vols, 1901-03**; he critiqued the drain with Naoroji and **Dinshaw Wacha**.
⚠ **Naoroji** = Poverty and Un-British Rule; **R.C. Dutt** = Economic History; **Digby** = 'Prosperous' British India.

176.s: The term 'moral drain' in the context of colonial economic exploitation was coined by:
176.x: Dadabhai Naoroji coined the expression 'moral drain' while explaining the economic consequences of colonial rule.
176.tq: Direct recall of a distinctive metaphor associated with a thinker.
xs: **Dadabhai Naoroji** coined **"moral drain"** — option **(4)**.
**Ranade** expanded the theory; **R.C. Dutt** wrote Economic History of India; **R.P. Dutt** wrote India Today.
xa: Naoroji first stated the drain in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)**.
Per Naoroji (APPSC-GS **2024**), the reason for drain was **profits taken by British capitalists**.

176.s: Which of the following best describes the Drain of Wealth from India?
o: Transfer of Indian wealth to England without an adequate economic or material return
Movement of Indian capital from agriculture to indigenous industries
Exchange of Indian primary goods for British capital goods on equal terms
Import of British gold and silver into Indian markets
176.x: The Drain represented the transfer of India's wealth to England without a corresponding economic or material return.
176.tq: Apply the definition rather than selecting an associated but incorrect trade feature.
xs: The drain was **Indian wealth sent to England with no economic or material return** — option **(1)**.
India's **export surplus** brought **no gold or silver**; it paid British office and war expenses.
xa: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Components: **Home Charges**, interest, salaries and pensions, railway returns, military spending, profits.
**Unequal trade** was also a component.

176.s: The Drain of Wealth from India is considered to have begun with the:
176.x: The drain is traced to the grant of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, after which Indian resources were transferred to England without economic return.
176.tq: Chronological discrimination among closely related colonial milestones.
xs: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)** — option **(1)**.
**1757** opens the mercantilist stage; **1793** is the Permanent Settlement; the **Suez Canal (1869)** tightened British control later.
xa: In the mercantilist stage, **Bengal revenue** bought export goods.
Naoroji's first statement of the drain: **1867**.

176.s: Which of the following was NOT among the demands raised by the Moderates in response to the economic effects of colonial rule?
176.x: The Moderates demanded cuts in military spending, not its expansion. They also demanded lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and protective tariffs.
176.tq: Find the reversed policy demand in a list of related measures.
xs: **Expansion of military expenditure** was NOT a Moderate demand — option **(2)**; they wanted **cuts in military spending**.
The Moderates demanded **lower land revenue**, abolition of the **salt tax** and **protective tariffs**.
xa: Drain theory = the Moderates' **greatest contribution** and the base of **Swadeshi**.
The drain **shattered the myth of British benevolence**.

176.s: Which one of the following was an effect of the Drain of Wealth on the Indian economy?
o: Growth of India's share in world income
Stifling of capital formation and industrialisation
Rapid expansion of indigenous capital formation
Replacement of primary exports by machinery exports
176.x: The drain reduced the resources available for domestic investment, thereby stifling capital formation and industrialisation.
176.tq: Link the economic cause with its stated structural consequence.
xs: The drain **stifled capital formation and industrialisation** — option **(2)**.
India's world income share fell from **27% (1700) to 3% (1950)** (Maddison) — it did not grow.
xa: It also **shattered the myth of British benevolence**.
India went from leading exporter of manufactures to **supplier of raw materials**.

176.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the purpose of the funds paid under Home Charges?
o: Costs of the Secretary of State's India Office in London, paid from Indian revenue
Capital grants for Indian-owned cotton mills
Subsidies paid by Britain to Indian peasants
Compensation paid by India for imported gold and silver
176.x: Home Charges included the costs of the Secretary of State's India Office in London, which were paid from Indian revenues.
176.tq: Identify the authority, location and source of payment in a colonial finance item.
xs: **Home Charges** were the **Secretary of State's India Office costs in London, paid from Indian revenue** — option **(1)**.
They were a drain component — not grants to Indian mills or payment for gold and silver.
xa: Other components: **interest** on public debt raised in Britain, **salaries and pensions**, **guaranteed railway returns**.
**Military expenditure** was the largest single budget head.

176.s: Interest included in the colonial drain primarily referred to interest on:
o: capital invested by Indian merchants in villages
private savings deposited in Indian banks
loans raised exclusively from Indian peasants
176.x: A component of the drain was interest on public debt raised in Britain and paid out of Indian resources.
176.tq: Distinguish the source of the debt from unrelated domestic financial activities.
xs: The interest component was on **public debt raised in Britain** — option **(3)**.
It was part of the drain alongside **Home Charges** and **salaries and pensions**.
xa: Railway investors got **guaranteed 5%** returns whether lines earned or not.
**Profits** of British capitalists, merchants and banks were also sent home.

176.s: Which of the following formed part of the drain through salaries and pensions?
o: Dividends paid to Indian cooperative societies
Payments to British civil and military officials remitted to Britain
Pensions paid only to retired Indian artisans
Wages paid to Indian agricultural labourers
176.x: Salaries and pensions of British civil and military officials were remitted home and therefore formed part of the drain.
176.tq: Identify the beneficiary and destination of the payment.
xs: Salaries and pensions of **British civil and military officials**, **remitted to Britain**, were a drain — option **(2)**.
Their savings went home too.
xa: **Home Charges** paid the India Office in London from Indian revenue.
**Military expenditure** covered the British Indian Army and imperial wars (**Afghanistan, Burma**).

176.s: Guaranteed railway returns in colonial India assured British railway investors an interest rate of:
176.x: British railway investors were guaranteed a 5 percent return, whether or not the railway lines earned sufficient revenue.
176.tq: Recall the guaranteed return and reject nearby percentage distractors.
xs: British railway investors were assured **5%** interest — option **(2)**.
They got this **whether lines earned or not**, making it part of the drain.
xa: Andhra's first railway: **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.
Railways carried raw materials out and British goods inland — a cause of **deindustrialisation**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements regarding military expenditure under British rule:
1. India paid for the British Indian Army.
2. Indian revenues contributed to imperial wars in Afghanistan and Burma.
3. Military expenditure was the smallest among the major drain components.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Military expenditure was the largest, not the smallest, single budget head among the listed components.
176.tq: Spot the reversed comparison in the third statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: India paid for the **British Indian Army**.
Statement 2 correct: Indian revenue funded imperial wars in **Afghanistan** and **Burma**.
Statement 3 wrong: military spending was the **largest single budget head**.
xa: The Moderates demanded **cuts in military spending**.
India's export surplus paid for British **war expenses**.

176.s: Which of the following was identified as a reason for the Drain of Wealth in the context of British colonial rule?
o: Excess imports of gold into India
Rapid growth of Indian-owned heavy industries
Profits taken by British capitalists from India
High domestic savings by Indian peasants
176.x: Profits taken by British capitalists from India were a recognised reason for the drain. An excess of imports was not the stated explanation.
176.tq: Choose the precise drain cause instead of the reversed trade claim.
xs: Per Naoroji, the drain came from **profits taken by British capitalists from India** — option **(3)** (APPSC-GS **2024**).
⚠ Trap: the drain was NOT an **excess of imports**; India's export surplus brought **no gold or silver**.
xa: Naoroji popularised the theory (APPSC-GS **2025**).
Drain effects: stifled **capital formation** and **industrialisation**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about India's export surplus under colonial rule:
1. It did not generally result in corresponding imports of gold or silver.
2. It helped meet British office and war expenses.
3. It represented a complete economic return to India for its exports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The export surplus financed British expenses and invisible imports rather than providing India with a complete economic return.
176.tq: Separate the true components of export surplus from the reversed conclusion.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **export surplus** brought **no gold or silver**.
Statement 2 correct: it paid British **office and war expenses** and invisible imports.
Statement 3 wrong: the drain is exactly wealth sent **with no economic or material return**.
xa: APPSC **2023** key: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
Colonial legacy: **deindustrialisation** + drain of wealth.

176.s: The book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), a key text of the drain theory, was written by:
176.x: Dadabhai Naoroji wrote 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901). R.C. Dutt wrote 'Economic History of India', William Digby wrote ''Prosperous' British India' and M.G. Ranade wrote 'Essays on Indian Economics'.
176.tq: Naoroji = Poverty and Un-British Rule; Digby = Prosperous British India.
xs: **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (1901)** was written by **Dadabhai Naoroji** — option **(3)**.
**R.C. Dutt** wrote **Economic History of India**; **Digby** wrote **'Prosperous' British India** (**1901**); **Ranade** wrote **Essays on Indian Economics**.
xa: ⚠ Both Naoroji's and Digby's books date to **1901**.
Naoroji first stated the drain in **1867**.

176.s: Which legislative measure ended the monopoly of the East India Company and enabled the entry of British machine-made goods into India?
176.x: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly, after which British machine-made goods entered India at low duty.
176.tq: Link the Act with its specific economic consequence.
xs: The **Charter Act of 1813** ended the Company's monopoly and let British machine goods in — option **(4)**.
This began **one-way free trade**: British goods entered **almost duty-free**.
xa: The **1813-1858** free-trade stage followed.
Lancashire cloth had been first offered in Bengal in **1786**.

176.s: The term “one-way free trade” in the context of Indian deindustrialisation refers to
o: Free export of Indian manufactures and prohibition of British imports
Low-duty entry of British goods into India while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain
Exclusive trade between Indian princely states
Equal tariff treatment for Indian and British manufactures
176.x: British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.
176.tq: Discriminate between equal free trade and an unequal tariff arrangement.
