xs: **One-way free trade**: British goods entered India at **low duty** while Indian goods faced **heavy duties in Britain** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **Charter Act 1813**.
xa: By **1793** Indian calicoes and muslins were displaced.
Comparative note: IMF-World Bank **Structural Adjustment Programmes** caused deindustrialisation by the same logic.

176.s:
Which of the following was NOT identified as a cause of the decline of Indian handicrafts?

1. Loss of princely patrons
2. Export of raw materials
3. Special privileges for British traders
4. Expansion of royal patronage to Indian artisans
176.x: The decline was associated with the loss, not the expansion, of royal patronage. Export of raw materials and special privileges for British traders were recognised causes.
176.tq: Spot the reversed cause among closely related economic factors.
xs: **Expansion of royal patronage** was NOT a cause — option **(3) 4 only**; artisans actually **lost** princely patrons.
**Loss of patrons**, **export of raw materials** and **special privileges for British traders** were real causes (B.D. Basu's list).
xa: Other causes: internal **transit and customs duties**, **railways**, artisans forced to divulge trade secrets.
Town handicrafts suffered a **"sudden and complete collapse"**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of deindustrialisation:
1. Railways carried British goods into the interior.
2. Artisans were forced to reveal trade secrets.
3. Internal transit duties and customs duties affected indigenous trade.
4. British traders were denied special privileges.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. British traders received special privileges, so statement 4 is false.
176.tq: Test a cluster of causes while reversing one key relationship.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Railways** carried British goods inland; artisans were forced to **divulge trade secrets**; **transit and customs duties** hurt trade.
Statement 4 wrong: British traders got **special privileges**.
xa: Causes are from **B.D. Basu**'s list.
Weavers were coerced by Company agents (**Bolt, 1772**).

176.s: What was the principal effect of the collapse of town handicrafts on the rural economy?

Artisans moved to plantations and reduced agricultural pressure

Marx: Britain "inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons".

176.s: Karl Marx characterised British imports into India by stating that Britain had

ended the production of cotton in Britain
inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons
converted India into the leading exporter of machinery

xs: Marx said Britain had "**inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons**" — option **(3)**.

xa: By **1850** India imported **one-fourth** of all British cotton exports.
Marx's ideas underpin **R.P. Dutt**'s stages of colonialism.

176.s: The cotton excise duty imposed during 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was intended to
o: promote the export of Indian handlooms to China
abolish all duties on Indian textiles
offset the import duty on British goods

xs: The **cotton excise duty (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth was meant to **offset the import duty** on British goods — option **(3)**.
It is the classic example of colonial **tariff policy**.
xa: The Moderates demanded **protective tariffs** for Indian industry.
**Cotton mills** in Maharashtra and Gujarat were **Indian-owned**; jute mills were foreign-owned.

176.s: By 1850, India imported approximately what proportion of all British cotton exports?

xs: By **1850** India imported **one-fourth** of all British cotton exports — option **(1)**.

xa: India went from leading exporter of manufactures to **supplier of raw materials**.

176.s: During the British period in Andhra, which sector provided the second-largest employment after agriculture?

xs: **Textiles** were Andhra's **second-largest employment after agriculture** in the British period — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**Machilipatnam** was the most famous handloom and textile port of the **16th-17th centuries**.
xa: Andhra products: **Srikakulam** muslin, **Uppada** jamdani silk, **Ponduru** khadi.
**Nellore** was the world leader in **manganese** (**1892-1929**).

176.s: Machilipatnam was particularly famous during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries as a centre of

Its products: **chintz** (painted cloth), dyed fabrics, muslins.

High Company duties shrank the trade to small boats carrying salt and groceries.

176.s: Which one of the following was associated with Machilipatnam textiles?

176.s: Why did peasants increasingly cultivate cash crops under colonial rule?
o: Because food crops were legally prohibited throughout India
To obtain free land from the Company
To ensure food security during famines

176.s: Who fed the famine-stricken people during the 1866 Kurnool famine and later received a gold medal from Queen Victoria?

xs: The **Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co. (1854)** is linked to **Cowasji Nanabhai Davar** (C.N. Davar) — option **(3)**.
**Purshottamdas Thakurdas** argued for a **1s 4d** rupee; **Arthur Cotton** built anicuts.
xa: ⚠ First cotton mill = **Bombay 1854**; first jute mill = **Rishra 1855**.
Cotton mills were **Indian-owned** in **Maharashtra** and **Gujarat**.

176.s: Rishra in Bengal is associated with the establishment of India's first:
176.x: The first jute mill was established at Rishra in Bengal in 1855.
176.tq: Identify the industry from the specific location rather than from the year alone.
xs: **Rishra (Bengal), 1855** was India's first **jute mill** — option **(2)**.
First cotton mill: **Bombay, 1854**; first tea company: **Assam Company, 1839**; iron and steel: **TISCO, 1907**.
xa: Jute mills in Bengal were **foreign-owned**.
Andhra jute mills: **Chittivalasa and Nellimarla** (**1920s**).

176.s: TISCO was incorporated in 1907 at:
176.x: TISCO, the Tata Iron and Steel Company, was incorporated in 1907 at Jamshedpur.
176.tq: Combine the institution, year and location instead of relying on the year in isolation.
xs: **TISCO** was incorporated in **1907** at **Jamshedpur** — option **(2)**.
**Rishra** = first jute mill; **Bombay** = first cotton mill; **Rajahmundry** = Andhra paper mill.
xa: Iron and steel grew from the early **20th** century.
Even so, India had **no capital-goods base** — capital goods were only **one-fourth** of output.

176.s: The first railway in the Andhra region mentioned in the context of colonial industrial development was opened between:
176.x: The first railway was the Puttur-Renigunta line, opened in 1862.
176.tq: Use the exact terminal-pair distinction to avoid confusing railways with industrial centres.
xs: Andhra's first railway ran between **Puttur and Renigunta (1862)** — option **(3)**.
**Chittivalasa and Nellimarla** were jute mills, not a rail line.
xa: Railways guaranteed **5%** interest to British investors.
Railways carried raw materials out and British goods inland.

176.s: Which one of the following statements about early industrialisation in Andhra Pradesh is NOT correctly matched?
176.x: Ponduru was associated with Andhra textiles, not an iron and steel plant. Chittivalasa and Nellimarla had jute mills, while Rajahmundry had a paper mill.
176.tq: Find the industry–location mismatch among otherwise familiar Andhra associations.
xs: **Ponduru — iron and steel plant** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**; Ponduru is known for fine hand-spun **khadi**.
**Rajahmundry** = paper mill; **Chittivalasa** and **Nellimarla** = jute mills (**1920s**).
xa: Cotton ginning was at **Anantapur, Guntur, East Godavari, Kurnool**.
The first iron and steel unit was **TISCO (1907)** at **Jamshedpur**.

176.s: During 1892-1929, which district of the Andhra region was a world leader in the production of manganese?
176.x: Nellore district was the world leader in manganese during 1892-1929 (APHQ 2019 key; some sources credit Vizag). Kurnool, Anantapur and Guntur are associated with cotton ginning, not world-leading manganese output.
176.tq: Nellore = manganese (APHQ 2019) and mica.
xs: **Nellore** district was the world leader in **manganese** in **1892-1929** — option **(3)** (APHQ **2019** key).
Some notes say **Vizag** district (world No.1 till **1929**).
xa: Nellore was also known for **mica**.
Nellore manganese + Andhra textiles = Andhra's examinable pair.

176.s: India's first tea company, the Assam Company, was set up in:
176.x: The Assam Company, the first tea company, dates from 1839. 1854 is the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company (first cotton mill), 1855 the Rishra jute mill and 1907 the incorporation of TISCO.
176.tq: Tea 1839, cotton mill 1854, jute 1855, TISCO 1907.
xs: The **Assam Company**, India's first tea company, was set up in **1839** — option **(1)**.
**1854** = first cotton mill; **1855** = first jute mill; **1907** = TISCO.
xa: Tea's main region: **Assam**.
Chinese **tea** was part of the opium triangular trade.

176.s: The Hilton Young Commission was formally known as the:
o: Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance
Royal Commission on Indian Agriculture and Land
176.x: The Hilton Young Commission was the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, appointed in 1926.
176.tq: Distinguish the official name of a commission from the subject-specific names of other commissions.
xs: The **Hilton Young Commission (1926)** was the **Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance** — option **(2)**.
It fixed the rupee at **1s 6d** (**18** pence).
xa: It recommended a **central bank** → **RBI (1935)**.
Indian business (**Purshottamdas Thakurdas**) wanted **1s 4d**.

176.s: The Hilton Young Commission recommended fixing the rupee at:
176.x: The commission fixed the rupee at 1 shilling 6 pence, or 18 pence. Indian business interests, including Purshottamdas Thakurdas, preferred 1 shilling 4 pence.
176.tq: Separate the officially fixed ratio from the alternative ratio demanded by Indian business.
xs: Hilton Young fixed the rupee at **1 shilling 6 pence** (**18** pence) — option **(1)**.
**1s 4d** was what Indian business (**Purshottamdas Thakurdas**) wanted.
xa: ⚠ Hilton Young = **1s 6d**; Indian business = **1s 4d**.
The higher ratio made British imports cheaper and hurt Indian exporters.

176.s: Which institution emerged in 1935 following the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission?
176.x: The commission's recommendation for a central bank led to the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India in 1935.
176.tq: Trace the commission–recommendation–institution chain.
xs: The **Reserve Bank of India (1935)** came from Hilton Young's call for a **central bank** — option **(1)**.
The Commission sat in **1926** as the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance.
xa: It fixed the rupee at **1s 6d**.
Indian business (**Purshottamdas Thakurdas**) wanted **1s 4d**.

176.s:
Assertion (A): The higher rupee-sterling ratio hurt Indian exporters.
Reason (R): The higher ratio made British imports cheaper in India.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
176.x: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A higher rupee-sterling ratio (1s 6d rather than the 1s 4d Indian business wanted) made Indian goods dearer abroad, and that is what hurt exporters. Cheaper British imports were a separate effect that hurt Indian producers in the home market.
176.tq: Test whether the economic consequence in the Reason explains the currency-policy criticism in the Assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
The notes list both as separate effects of the higher ratio: it **made British imports cheaper** and it **hurt Indian exporters**.
Cheaper British imports is a parallel effect, not the reason exporters suffered.
xa: Hilton Young (**1926**) fixed **1s 6d**; Indian business wanted **1s 4d**.
The Commission also led to the **RBI (1935)**.

176.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between agriculture and GDP in India on the eve of independence?
o: Over 75% of the workforce was in agriculture, which contributed about 50% of GDP.
Agriculture employed less than 25% of the workforce but contributed about 50% of GDP.
About 50% of the workforce was in agriculture, which contributed over 75% of GDP.
Agriculture employed over 75% of the workforce and contributed over 75% of GDP.
176.x: More than 75 percent of the workforce depended on agriculture, but the sector contributed only about 50 percent of GDP, indicating low productivity and disguised unemployment.
176.tq: Match the workforce share with the corresponding GDP share.
xs: In **1947**, **over 75%** of the workforce was in agriculture, which gave only about **50% of GDP** — option **(1)**.
This meant **disguised unemployment** and low productivity.
xa: Per-capita income: **Rs 265** a year (~**$60**).
Life expectancy **32 years**; literacy **under 16%** (female under **9%**).

176.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
176.x: Indian-owned cotton mills were concentrated in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Foreign-owned jute mills were concentrated in Bengal.
176.tq: Use ownership and regional concentration to eliminate swapped industry locations.
xs: **Cotton mills — Maharashtra and Gujarat** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Jute mills** were in **Bengal**, not Maharashtra, Gujarat, Mysore or Madras.
xa: ⚠ **Cotton mills** = Indian-owned; **jute mills** = foreign-owned.
First jute mill: **Rishra, 1855**.

176.s: Which of the following was a major weakness of Indian industry on the eve of independence?
o: Complete dependence on indigenous heavy machinery
176.x: India had no adequate capital-goods base. The public sector was also limited mainly to railways, power, communications and ports.
176.tq: Identify the structural deficiency rather than a broad but inaccurate industrial claim.
xs: A major weakness was the **absence of a capital-goods base** — option **(2)**.
Basic/capital goods were only about **one-fourth** of industrial output.
The public sector was **limited** to railways, power, communications, ports — not excessive.
xa: India imported finished consumer and **capital goods**.
Iron and steel only from the early **20th** century (**TISCO, 1907**).

176.s: Which one of the following was NOT a primary product exported by India during colonial rule?
176.x: India exported primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute. Finished consumer and capital goods were imported.
176.tq: Separate the export list from the imported manufactured-goods list.
xs: **Finished consumer machinery** was NOT a primary export — option **(1)**; finished goods were **imported**.
India exported primary products: **raw silk**, cotton, wool, sugar, **indigo**, **jute**.
xa: The **Suez Canal (1869)** tightened British control over trade.
India went from exporter of manufactures to **supplier of raw materials**.

176.s:
Which of the following statements correctly describes deindustrialisation in colonial India?
1. British policy contributed to the decline of Indian industry.
2. Indian industry lost markets.
3. Agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: All three statements are correct. British policy contributed to deindustrialisation, industry declined through loss of markets and agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
176.tq: Test the linked features of deindustrialisation and agrarian stagnation together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (APPSC **2023** keys).
**Deindustrialisation** came by British policy; industry declined from **loss of markets**.
Agriculture stayed **stagnant with low productivity**.
xa: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
The economy was **agrarian**.

176.s: On the eve of independence, which one of the following combinations is correct regarding India’s socio-economic conditions?
o: Per capita income about Rs 1,000, life expectancy 50 years and literacy above 30%
Per capita income about Rs 265, life expectancy 50 years and literacy above 25%
Per capita income about Rs 500, life expectancy 32 years and literacy above 30%
Per capita income about Rs 265, life expectancy 32 years and literacy below 16%
176.x: Per capita income was approximately Rs 265, life expectancy was 32 years and literacy was below 16% on the eve of independence.
176.tq: Test the complete data combination rather than an isolated indicator.
xs: In **1947**: per-capita income about **Rs 265**, life expectancy **32 years**, literacy **below 16%** — option **(4)**.
Life expectancy was not **50**, and literacy was not above **25%** or **30%**.
xa: Female literacy was under **9%**.
Per-capita income ~**$60** a year.

176.s: Which of the following best explains the colonial ‘drain of wealth’ mentioned in relation to India?
o: India’s export earnings were invested mainly in Indian capital goods.
British trade policy eliminated all Indian exports.
India’s imports were financed entirely through domestic taxation.
India’s export surplus was spent on Britain’s office and war expenses.
176.x: The export surplus generated by India was used for Britain’s office expenses and war expenses, contributing to the drain of wealth.
176.tq: Identify the mechanism of the drain rather than a general consequence of colonialism.
xs: India's **export surplus** was spent on **Britain's office and war expenses** — option **(4)**.
It brought **no gold or silver** — the **drain of wealth**.
xa: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Colonial legacy: **deindustrialisation** + drain.

176.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Basic and capital goods — approximately one-fourth of industrial output
Suez Canal — tightened British control over trade
Public sector before independence — steel, automobiles and aviation as its principal areas
176.x: Before independence, the public sector was limited mainly to railways, power, communications and ports. It did not principally cover all the industries listed in option d.
176.tq: Find the option that extends a limited colonial public sector beyond its stated scope.
xs: **Public sector — steel, automobiles and aviation** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The public sector was **limited to railways, power, communications, ports**.
Capital goods ~**one-fourth** of output, **TISCO 1907** and the **Suez Canal (1869)** are correct.
xa: Before **1914** about **97%** of British capital went to government projects, plantations and finance houses.
⚠ **Cotton mills** = Indian-owned; **jute mills** = foreign-owned.

176.s: Which of the following received top priority in the First Plan in response to the immediate economic challenges after independence?
o: Heavy engineering, automobiles and export subsidies
176.x: Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power. Post-partition stabilisation was another immediate challenge.
176.tq: Link the policy priority with the immediate food and inflation problem.
xs: The **First Plan** gave top priority to **agriculture, irrigation, power** — option **(4)**.
This answered **large foodgrain imports and inflation**.
xa: Other challenge: **post-partition stabilisation**.
Agriculture had **over 75%** of the workforce but only about **50%** of GDP.

176.s: According to Angus Maddison, India's share of world income changed from about ______ in 1700 to about ______ in 1950.
176.x: Maddison's estimate (APPSC-GS 2024 key) is that India's share of world income fell from about 27% in 1700 to about 3% in 1950, reflecting deindustrialisation and drain. The reversed pair (3% to 27%) is wrong, and 50%/10% and 15%/7% are not the cited figures.
176.tq: Maddison PYQ pair: 27% (1700) -> 3% (1950).
xs: Maddison: India's world income share fell from **27 per cent** (**1700**) to **3 per cent** (**1950**) — option **(1)** (APPSC-GS **2024** key).
Option 2 reverses the pair; learn the PYQ pair for MCQs.
xa: Some notes give world GDP share **22.6% (1700) to 3.8% (1952)**.
The **1700** figure was almost Europe's **23.3%**.

176.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Andhra cultural-industrial context?
o: Textiles — Machilipatnam, Srikakulam, Uppada and Ponduru
Jute — Nellore, Kurnool, Guntur and Anantapur only
176.x: Machilipatnam, Srikakulam, Uppada and Ponduru are associated with Andhra textiles. The other options incorrectly assign industries or locations.
176.tq: Start from the complete textiles–places pair and eliminate cross-sector substitutions.
xs: **Textiles — Machilipatnam, Srikakulam, Uppada and Ponduru** is correct — option **(1)**.
Jute mills were at **Chittivalasa** and **Nellimarla**; paper at **Rajahmundry**; manganese at **Nellore**.
xa: Textiles + **Nellore manganese** = Andhra's examinable pair.
**Uppada** = jamdani silk; **Ponduru** = khadi.

176.s: Which statement best expresses the economic transformation of India under colonial rule?
o: India retained its position as an autonomous industrial exporter throughout colonial rule.
India changed from a raw-material supplier into the leading exporter of manufactures.
India changed from a leading exporter of manufactures into a supplier of raw materials.
India became exclusively a financial centre without agricultural exports.
176.x: Colonial economic change involved the decline of India's manufacturing export position and its transformation into a supplier of raw materials.
176.tq: Test the direction of structural change; reversed comparisons are the principal distractor.
xs: India changed **from a leading exporter of manufactures into a supplier of raw materials** — option **(3)**.
Option 2 reverses the direction.
xa: APPSC **2023** key: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
Maddison: world income share **27% (1700) to 3% (1950)**.

176.s: The economic critique of colonialism made by the Moderates became an important base for:
o: The Swadeshi movement and early nationalism
The expansion of Company trade monopoly
176.x: The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.
176.tq: Trace the political consequence of an economic critique rather than selecting an administrative reform.
xs: The Moderates' economic critique was a base for **Swadeshi** and **early nationalism** — option **(1)**.
Drain theory = the Moderates' **greatest contribution**.
xa: **Naoroji** popularised it; **R.C. Dutt** and **Ranade** expanded it.
The **Famine Code (1883)** came from the Strachey report, not from the Moderates.

176.s:
Assertion (A): Colonial railways and ports had a dual economic character.
Reason (R): They served military mobility and raw-material extraction, while also integrating the Indian economy.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
176.x: Both statements are true. The infrastructure served colonial military and extractive purposes but also produced the unintended effect of integrating the economy.
176.tq: Recognise a balanced historical assessment instead of treating the infrastructure as wholly beneficial or wholly destructive.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
Railways and ports were built for **military mobility** and **raw-material extraction**, yet **integrated the economy**.
xa: Railways gave a **guaranteed 5%** to British investors.
Andhra's first railway: **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.

176.s: According to the comparative economic argument concerning structural adjustment programmes, sudden tariff removal in the Global South caused deindustrialisation by applying:
o: A ban on international trade and capital movement
A one-way free-trade logic comparable to that imposed on colonial India
A system of equal tariffs for all domestic producers
A policy of permanent protection for local industries
176.x: The comparison holds that IMF–World Bank structural adjustment programmes caused deindustrialisation through sudden tariff removal, reflecting a one-way free-trade logic comparable to colonial India.
176.tq: Identify the causal policy mechanism—sudden tariff removal—rather than the institution alone.
xs: **Structural Adjustment Programmes** caused deindustrialisation through **one-way free-trade logic** like colonial India's — option **(2)**.
It came from **sudden tariff removal** in the Global South (**14 May 2026**).
xa: Colonial one-way free trade followed the **Charter Act 1813**.
British goods entered India **almost duty-free**; Indian goods faced **heavy duties** in Britain.

177.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Orissa Famine — West and central India, 1899–1900
177.x: The Chalisa famine of 1783-84 struck North India (Delhi, Awadh, Punjab). The other pairs are wrong: Doji Bara was 1791-92 in the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars (Bengal 1770 is the Great Bengal Famine); the 1943 Bengal famine is not the 'Great Famine' (that name belongs to 1876-78 and 1896-97); and the Orissa famine was 1865-66 (1899-1900 hit west and central India).
177.tq: Use the year-region pair to eliminate swapped famine locations.
xs: **Chalisa Famine — North India, 1783-84** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Doji Bara** was **1791-92** in the Deccan, Hyderabad and Northern Circars, not Bengal 1770.
The **1943** famine was the **Bengal Famine**; the Great Famine was **1876-78**; the **1899-1900** famine (West and central India) was not the Orissa famine.
xa: Chalisa hit **Delhi, Awadh, Punjab**; it is named after **Vikram Samvat 1840**.
⚠ **Chalisa** = North India (**1783-84**); **Doji Bara** = skull famine (**1791-92**).
The **Orissa** famine was **1865-66**.

177.s:
Consider the following statements about the Doji Bara famine:
1. It is also known as the skull famine.
2. It affected the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars.
3. It occurred in 1791–92.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
177.x: The Doji Bara famine, also called the skull famine, occurred in 1791–92 and affected the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars.
177.tq: Combine the epithet, region and year before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Doji Bara** is the **"skull famine"** of **1791-92**.
It hit the **Deccan, Hyderabad and Northern Circars**.
xa: CDX notes date the Northern Circars famine as **1790-92**.
**Chalisa** (**1783-84**) hit North India.

177.s: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the appointment of which commission?
177.x: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the Campbell Commission.
177.tq: Link a famine directly with the commission appointed after it.
xs: The **Orissa and Ganjam famine (1865-66)** led to the **Campbell Commission** — option **(1)**.
Campbell (**1866**) was under Viceroy **John Lawrence** — the **first famine commission**.
xa: **MacDonnell** (**1901**, Curzon) followed the **1899-1900** famine.
**Lyall** followed the **1896-97** famine (**Elgin II**).
Last colonial commission: **Woodhead (1944)**.

177.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Great Famine of 1876–78 is correct?
o: It was confined to the Northern Circars under Cartier.
It occurred in West and Central India under Curzon.
It affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay under Lytton.
It affected only Bengal and Bihar under Elgin II.
177.x: The Great Famine of 1876–78 affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay and occurred during Lytton’s tenure. It also devastated Rayalaseema and coastal Andhra.
177.tq: Discriminate a famine by combining its year, affected regions and contemporary Viceroy.
xs: The **Great Famine of 1876-78** hit **Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay** under **Lytton** — option **(3)**.
**Cartier** was the **1770** Bengal famine; **Curzon** the **1899-1900** famine; **Elgin II** the **1896-97** famine.
xa: It devastated **Rayalaseema** and coastal Andhra.
The **Strachey Commission (1880)** followed, leading to the **Famine Code, 1883**.
**Sir Richard Temple** fixed the **Temple wage** in the **1877 Madras famine**.

177.s:
Arrange the following famines in chronological order:
A. Great Bengal Famine
B. Doji Bara Famine
C. Orissa and Ganjam Famine
D. Great Famine of 1876–78
177.x: The correct sequence is Great Bengal Famine (1770), Doji Bara (1791–92), Orissa and Ganjam (1865–66), and Great Famine (1876–78).
177.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the middle famines by year.
xs: Order: **Great Bengal (1770)** → **Doji Bara (1791-92)** → **Orissa and Ganjam (1865-66)** → **Great Famine (1876-78)** — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
The **1770** famine came under **Cartier**; the **1876-78** famine under **Lytton**.
xa: **Chalisa** (**1783-84**) falls between the first two.
**Guntur** (**1832-33**) falls between Doji Bara and Orissa.

177.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bengal Famine of 1943 — Bengal — Linlithgow and Wavell years
Great Famine of 1896–97 — Many parts of India — Elgin II
Great Bengal Famine of 1770 — Bengal — Lytton
Famine of 1899–1900 — West and Central India — Curzon
177.x: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred under Cartier, not Lytton. The other pairs are correctly matched.
177.tq: Find the swapped administrator in an otherwise familiar famine association.
xs: **Great Bengal Famine of 1770 — Lytton** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**; it was under **Cartier**.
**Lytton** belongs to the **1876-78** Great Famine.
**1943**–Linlithgow and Wavell, **1896-97**–Elgin II and **1899-1900**–Curzon are correct.
xa: In **1770** about **two million** died; the Company **kept collecting revenue**.
**Woodhead (1944)** under **Wavell** followed the **Bengal Famine 1943**.

177.s: Approximately how many people died in the Bengal Famine of 1943 according to the standard estimate?
177.x: The standard estimate given for the Bengal Famine of 1943 is about 30 lakh deaths.
177.tq: Distinguish the standard estimate from the approximate figure used in an earlier examination question.
xs: The standard estimate for the **Bengal Famine of 1943** is **30 lakh** — option **(3)**.
⚠ APPSC-GS **2018** asked the "nearest figure" and keyed **about 20 lakh** (the largest option offered then).
xa: It came in the **Linlithgow and Wavell** years.
It led to the **Woodhead Commission (1944)** — the last colonial famine commission.

177.s: Which of the following statements about famines in Andhra during the nineteenth century is correct?
o: Andhra experienced only two famines in the late nineteenth century.
Andhra experienced 11 famines in the late nineteenth century.
All the famines occurred exclusively in coastal districts.
The record begins only with the famine of 1945.
177.x: Andhra had 11 famines in the late nineteenth century. The other statements wrongly restrict their number, location or period.
177.tq: Reject extreme qualifiers such as ‘only’ and ‘exclusively’ when testing a numerical fact.
xs: Andhra had **11 famines** in the late **19th** century — option **(2)**.
Famines were not only coastal: **1823** hit **Kadapa, Kurnool, Chittoor**, Guntur, Vizag and Nellore.
xa: The worst in the south: **Guntur (1832-33)**, Dokkala Karuvu.

177.s: The Great Famine of 1876–78 mainly devastated:
o: Rayalaseema and parts of coastal Andhra
The Bombay Presidency and Punjab alone
177.x: The Great Famine of 1876–78 devastated Rayalaseema and parts of coastal Andhra. Relief was marked by a laissez-faire approach.
177.tq: Match the famine with its regional impact and distinguish it from famine locations elsewhere.
xs: The **Great Famine of 1876-78** devastated **Rayalaseema and coastal Andhra** — option **(1)**.
It hit **Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad, Bombay** under **Lytton**.
xa: The **Temple wage** (about **1 lb** of grain a day) was fixed in the **1877** Madras famine.
The **Strachey Commission (1880)** followed.

177.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Commission)
(a) Campbell
(b) Strachey
(c) Lyall
(d) MacDonnell

List-II (Viceroy)
(i) Curzon
(ii) Elgin II
(iii) John Lawrence
(iv) Lytton

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
177.x: Campbell was associated with John Lawrence, Strachey with Lytton, Lyall with Elgin II and MacDonnell with Curzon.
177.tq: Start from the sure commission–Viceroy pair and complete the code.
xs: **Campbell–John Lawrence, Strachey–Lytton, Lyall–Elgin II, MacDonnell–Curzon** — option **(1) a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i**.
Campbell (**1866**) for Orissa; Strachey (**1880**) after the **1876-78** Great Famine.
Lyall after **1896-97**; MacDonnell (**1901**) after **1899-1900**.
xa: **Woodhead (1944)** came under **Wavell**.
The **Famine Code (1883)** was framed on Strachey's recommendations.

177.s: Which commission assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures against future famines?
177.x: The Lyall Commission assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures to prevent or mitigate future famines.
177.tq: Distinguish the commission’s function from its associated famine year.
xs: The **Lyall Commission** assessed the **causes** and recommended measures against **future famines** — option **(3)**.
It followed the **1896-97** famine under **Elgin II**.
**MacDonnell** stressed **early relief + more irrigation**; **Campbell** was the first (Orissa); **Woodhead** the last (Bengal **1943**).
xa: MacDonnell: **1901**, Curzon.
The **Famine Code (1883)** was framed on the **Strachey** Commission's recommendations.

177.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Woodhead Commission — 1897 — Elgin II — famine of 1896–97
177.x: The MacDonnell Commission was appointed in 1901 during Curzon’s tenure in relation to the famine of 1899–1900. The other options interchange commission years, Viceroys or famine triggers.
177.tq: Check all three elements—commission, year and Viceroy—before accepting a match.
xs: **MacDonnell Commission — 1901 — Curzon — famine of 1899-1900** is correct — option **(2)**.
**1944**/**Wavell**/Bengal belongs to **Woodhead**, not Lyall.
**1897**/**Elgin II** belongs to **Lyall**, not Woodhead; **1880**/**Lytton** to **Strachey**, not Campbell.
xa: MacDonnell stressed **early relief + more irrigation**.
Campbell: **1866**, **John Lawrence**, Orissa famine.

177.s: What was the principal emphasis of the MacDonnell Commission?
177.x: The MacDonnell Commission stressed early relief and greater irrigation as measures against famine.
177.tq: Identify the policy recommendation rather than the commission’s name or date.
xs: The **MacDonnell Commission** stressed **early relief and more irrigation** — option **(1)**.
It came in **1901** under **Curzon**.
xa: R.C. Dutt wrote **"Open Letters to Lord Curzon"** (**1900**).
**Lyall** assessed causes and measures against future famines.

177.s: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed primarily on the recommendations of which commission?
177.x: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed on the recommendations of the Strachey Commission of 1880.
177.tq: Link a policy code to the commission whose recommendations formed its basis.
xs: The **Famine Code, 1883** was framed on the **Strachey Commission (1880)** recommendations — option **(1)**.
**Campbell** (**1866**) came earlier; **Lyall** and **Woodhead** came later.
xa: Provisions: stages of scarcity and famine, **relief works**, **gratuitous relief**, revenue suspension or remission.
A **Famine Relief and Insurance Fund** was also set up.

177.s:
Consider the following provisions of the Famine Code:
1. Classification of stages of scarcity and famine
2. Relief works for the able-bodied
3. Gratuitous relief for the old and infirm
4. Suspension or remission of revenue
Which of the above were provisions of the Code?
177.x: The Famine Code provided for stages of scarcity and famine, relief works for able-bodied persons, gratuitous relief for the old and infirm, and suspension or remission of revenue.
177.tq: Recognise a complete set of administrative provisions rather than one isolated relief measure.
xs: All four were provisions — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Stages of scarcity and famine**; **relief works** for the able-bodied.
**Gratuitous relief** for the old and infirm; **suspension or remission of revenue**.
xa: ⚠ **Relief works** = able-bodied; **gratuitous relief** = old and infirm.
It also created a **Famine Relief and Insurance Fund**.
The Code dates to **1883**, on the **Strachey** report.

177.s: Which of the following was included in the Famine Code as a financial safeguard?
o: A Famine Relief and Insurance Fund
177.x: The Famine Code provided for a Famine Relief and Insurance Fund.
177.tq: Identify the exact official fund from among similarly worded administrative alternatives.
xs: The Code created a **Famine Relief and Insurance Fund** — option **(2)**.
It was part of the **Famine Code, 1883**.
xa: Other provisions: **relief works**, **gratuitous relief**, revenue suspension or remission.
In the Company period the government **never adopted a famine code**.

177.s: Which statement regarding famine policy during the Company period is correct?
o: The government adopted a comprehensive famine code and provided extensive relief.
The government never adopted a famine code and gave minimal relief.
The government suspended revenue in every famine without exception.
The government transferred all famine relief to village councils.
177.x: During the Company period, the government never adopted a famine code and provided only minimal relief.
177.tq: Watch for absolute claims about uniform revenue suspension or comprehensive relief.
xs: In the Company period the government **never adopted a famine code** and gave **minimal relief** — option **(2)**.
In the **1770** Bengal famine the Company **kept collecting revenue**.
xa: The first Famine Code came only in **1883**.
Nationalists blamed **rigid revenue collection in drought** for famines.

177.s: The Temple wage during the Madras famine of 1877 consisted approximately of which ration?
o: About 1 pound of grain a day on relief works
About 5 pounds of grain a day on relief works
One rupee a day without grain
A weekly ration of ten pounds of rice
177.x: The Temple wage provided about 1 pound of grain per day on relief works and was criticised as a starvation wage.
177.tq: Distinguish the exact quantitative ration from plausible but exaggerated alternatives.
xs: The **Temple wage** was **about 1 pound (1 lb) of grain a day** on relief works — option **(1)**.
**Sir Richard Temple** fixed it in the **1877 Madras famine**.
xa: It was criticised as a **starvation wage**.
Relief works gave employment on **roads and canals**.

177.s: Public works undertaken as famine relief commonly provided employment on which of the following?
177.x: Famine relief public works included employment on roads and canals.
177.tq: Identify the practical form of relief employment from the work categories given.
xs: Public-works relief gave employment on **roads and canals** — option **(4)**.
The idea goes back to **Kautilya**'s famine duties.
xa: The **Famine Code (1883)** made **relief works** the remedy for the able-bodied.
The **Temple wage** paid about **1 lb** of grain a day on relief works.

177.s: Which of the following famine duties associated with Kautilya included measures such as seeds, food, tax exemption and public works?
o: Famine relief responsibilities of the state
177.x: Kautilya’s famine duties included supplying seeds and food, granting tax exemption and undertaking public works.
177.tq: Infer the broader administrative purpose from a cluster of related measures.
xs: Kautilya's famine duties were the state's **famine relief responsibilities** — **seeds, food, tax exemption, public works** — option **(2)**.
They are the ancient root of **public works as relief**.
xa: Colonial relief works offered employment on **roads and canals**.
The **Famine Code (1883)** included **suspension or remission of revenue**.

177.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of famines under colonial rule:
1. Rigid revenue collection aggravated the impact of drought.
2. Export of food grains contributed to famine conditions.
3. Famines were caused exclusively by failure of the monsoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
177.x: Rigid revenue collection and export of food grains were identified as important causes of famines. The nationalist critique rejected the view that famines resulted exclusively from monsoon failure.
177.tq: Identify the statement using the extreme word ‘exclusively’ and separate structural causes from a single natural cause.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **rigid revenue collection in drought** aggravated famines.
Statement 2 correct: the **export of food grains** contributed.
Statement 3 wrong: famines were **not just monsoon failure**.
xa: Aggravators: **commercialisation** (cotton in **Ganjam**) + **laissez-faire** relief.
**Naoroji & R.C. Dutt** linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain**.

177.s: Who among the following linked Indian famines with high land revenue and the drain of wealth?
o: Dadabhai Naoroji and Sir Arthur Cotton
177.x: Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt connected famines with the burden of high land revenue and the drain of wealth.
177.tq: Use the thinker–argument association and reject combinations that mix a critic with an administrator or engineer.
xs: **Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt** linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain** — option **(2)**.
**Arthur Cotton** was an irrigation engineer; **Curzon** was the Viceroy R.C. Dutt wrote to.
xa: R.C. Dutt wrote **"Open Letters to Lord Curzon"** (**1900**).
Nationalists blamed **export of food grains** too.

177.s: With reference to R.C. Dutt, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: He wrote Open Letters to Lord Curzon in 1900.
He chaired the Woodhead Commission in 1944.
He led the construction of the Godavari anicut in 1833.
He introduced the IPC food-insecurity scale in 2025.
177.x: R.C. Dutt’s work titled Open Letters to Lord Curzon was associated with the year 1900. The other options incorrectly associate him with a famine commission, a modern food-security scale or an irrigation project.
177.tq: Match the historical personality with the precise work and year; the wrong options swap roles across different subjects.
xs: **R.C. Dutt** wrote **"Open Letters to Lord Curzon"** in **1900** — option **(1)**.
He did not chair **Woodhead (1944)**, build the Godavari anicut (that was **Cotton**), or devise the **IPC** scale.
xa: With **Naoroji** he linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain**.
The **MacDonnell Commission (1901)** came under **Curzon**.

177.s: The commercialisation of agriculture and the policy of laissez-faire relief had what effect on famine conditions?
o: They made food grains unavailable only in Europe.
They ended the drain of wealth.
They eliminated the impact of drought.
177.x: Commercialisation, illustrated by cotton cultivation in Ganjam, and laissez-faire relief deepened the disasters caused by famine.
177.tq: Apply the cause–effect relationship rather than selecting an option that reverses the stated impact.
xs: **Commercialisation** and **laissez-faire** relief **deepened the disasters** — option **(1)**.
Example: **cotton in Ganjam** during the American Civil War.
xa: Real causes per nationalists: **rigid revenue collection** + **export of food grains**.
The **1876-78** Great Famine saw **laissez-faire relief**.

177.s: The Guntur famine convinced the Company of the need for which long-term response?
177.x: The Guntur famine convinced the Company that irrigation was necessary, contributing to later irrigation initiatives associated with Arthur Cotton.
177.tq: Connect a crisis to the institutional policy response it produced.
xs: The **Guntur famine** convinced the Company that **irrigation** was needed — option **(1)**.
The response was **Arthur Cotton's** Godavari anicut at **Dowleswaram**.
xa: Arthur Cotton was born **15 May 1803**.
Guntur (**1833**) → Cotton's anicut is a favourite AP angle.
The anicut cost only **Rs 1,50,000**.

177.s: Which one of the following correctly presents the sequence of the Godavari anicut project at Dowleswaram?
o: Report in 1844, sanction in 1846, work begun in 1847, main structure finished in April 1852
Report in 1846, sanction in 1847, work begun in 1852, main structure finished in 1855
Report in 1847, sanction in 1852, work begun in 1844, main structure finished in 1860
Report in 1852, sanction in 1844, work begun in 1846, main structure finished in 1872
177.x: Arthur Cotton’s Godavari anicut project was reported in 1844, sanctioned in 1846, begun in 1847 and had its main structure completed in April 1852.
177.tq: Arrange the project milestones in sequence, keeping the report before sanction and construction.
xs: **Report 1844 → sanction 1846 → work began 1847 → main structure finished April 1852** — option **(1)**.
⚠ **APPSC-G2 2012** keyed **1855** for the Dhavaleswaram Dam — in APPSC MCQs choose **1855**; the notes say built **1847-52**.
xa: Cost only **Rs 1,50,000**.
Revenue rose from **Rs 20.38 lakh (1853-54)** to **Rs 55.18 lakh (1894-95)**.
**Veenam Veeranna** helped Cotton build it.

177.s: Which of the following correctly describes the initial irrigation impact of the Godavari anicut?
o: Three main canals served about 6.62 lakh acres.
Three canals served exactly 10 lakh acres from the outset.
Two canals served about 2 lakh acres.
177.x: The Godavari anicut had three main canals serving about 6.62 lakh acres initially; the area later rose to 10 lakh acres for two crops.
177.tq: Separate the initial acreage and canal count from the later expanded irrigation figure.
xs: The Godavari anicut's **3 main canals** served about **6.62 lakh acres** — option **(1)**.
**10 lakh** acres for two crops came **later**, not at the outset.
xa: The old anicut was later replaced by the **Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage**.

177.s: Which of the following pairs relating to irrigation works is correctly matched?
o: Krishna anicut — Bezwada — proposed by Henry Atlock Lake
Godavari anicut — Bezwada — supervised by Charles Orr
177.x: The Krishna anicut at Bezwada was proposed by Colonel Henry Atlock Lake. The Penna anicut was at Nellore, while the K.C. Canal began from Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra.
177.tq: Use location and responsible engineer together to reject swapped irrigation projects.
xs: **Krishna anicut — Bezwada — proposed by Henry Atlock Lake** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Penna** anicut is at **Nellore** (**1860**); **K.C. Canal** is from **Sunkesula** (**1872**).
The **Godavari** anicut is at **Dowleswaram**; **Charles Orr** supervised the **Krishna** anicut.
xa: Krishna anicut: begun **1853**, finished by end-**1854**.
⚠ **Godavari** = Dowleswaram; **Krishna** = Bezwada; **Penna** = Nellore.

177.s: Who supervised the construction of the Krishna anicut at Bezwada?
177.x: The Krishna anicut at Bezwada was proposed by Colonel Henry Atlock Lake and supervised by Charles Orr.
177.tq: Distinguish the proposer from the person who supervised construction.
xs: **Charles Orr** supervised the **Krishna anicut** at **Bezwada** — option **(3)**.
**Col. Henry Atlock Lake** only **proposed** it.
**John Clough** ran famine canal relief; **Sir Richard Temple** fixed the Temple wage.
xa: Krishna anicut: begun **1853**, finished by end-**1854** (some notes date it 1853).
⚠ **Godavari** = Dowleswaram; **Krishna** = Bezwada; **Penna** = Nellore.

177.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: K.C. Canal — Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra — 1872
177.x: The Godavari anicut was at Dowleswaram, not Nellore. The Penna anicut was at Nellore in 1860, and the K.C. Canal dates from 1872 at Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra.
177.tq: Find the wrong location in a list of otherwise correctly matched irrigation projects.
xs: **Godavari anicut — Nellore — 1860** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
The Godavari anicut is at **Dowleswaram**, built **1847-52**; **Nellore 1860** is the **Penna** anicut.
**K.C. Canal** (Sunkesula, **1872**) and **Krishna** anicut (Bezwada, **1853**-54) are correct.
xa: Penna anicut was built on **Cotton's plan**.
⚠ **Godavari** = Dowleswaram; **Krishna** = Bezwada; **Penna** = Nellore.

177.s: The Penna anicut at Nellore was constructed according to whose plan?
177.x: The Penna anicut at Nellore, dating from 1860, was constructed according to Arthur Cotton’s plan.
177.tq: Match the irrigation project with the engineer whose plan it followed.
xs: The **Penna anicut** at **Nellore** (**1860**) was built on **Arthur Cotton**'s plan — option **(2)**.
**Lake** proposed and **Orr** supervised the **Krishna** anicut; **K.S. Gupta** formed a Famine Relief Committee in the Northern Coastal Famine.
xa: Cotton's main work: the **Godavari anicut** at **Dowleswaram**.
The **K.C. Canal** (**1872**) starts from **Sunkesula** on the Tungabhadra.

177.s: The old anicut associated with Arthur Cotton was later replaced by which structure?
177.x: The old anicut was later replaced by the Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage.
177.tq: Identify the later structure that replaced the original colonial-era anicut.
xs: The old anicut was later replaced by the **Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage** — option **(2)**.
The original was the **Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram** (**1847-52**).
xa: It reached **6.62 lakh acres** at first, later **10 lakh** acres for two crops.
**Veenam Veeranna** helped Cotton build it (APPSC-G2 **2019** key).

177.s: Which Andhra official assisted Sir Arthur Cotton in building the Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram?
177.x: Veenam Veeranna was the Andhra official who helped Cotton build the Godavari dam (APPSC-G2 2019 key). Charles Orr supervised the Krishna anicut at Bezwada, Budda Vengalareddy fed people in the 1866 Kurnool famine and K.S. Gupta formed a relief committee in the 1945 famine.
177.tq: Cotton's Godavari helper = Veenam Veeranna.
xs: **Veenam Veeranna** helped Cotton build the Godavari dam — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2019** key).
**Charles Orr** supervised the **Krishna** anicut; **Budda Vengalareddy** fed people in the Kurnool famine; **K.S. Gupta** led **1945** relief.
xa: Cotton was born **15 May 1803**.
The Guntur famine convinced the Company irrigation was needed.

177.s: The IPC food-insecurity scale places the following phases in which correct order from least severe to most severe?
177.x: The five phases progress from Phase 1 Minimal through Phase 2 Stressed, Phase 3 Crisis and Phase 4 Emergency to Phase 5 Catastrophe/Famine.
177.tq: Arrange the stages by increasing severity, beginning with the least severe and ending with famine.
xs: The IPC scale runs **Phase 1 Minimal, 2 Stressed, 3 Crisis, 4 Emergency, 5 Catastrophe/Famine** — option **(1)**.
It is a current-relevance point (**Jun 2025**).
xa: Modern food security = **availability, accessibility and affordability** through the **PDS**.
⚠ **IPC** here is the food-insecurity scale, not the Indian Penal Code.

177.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kurnool famine — 1833; impetus to Cotton’s Godavari anicut
Guntur famine — 1833; impetus to Cotton’s Godavari anicut
Ganjam famine — 1833; impetus to Cotton’s Godavari anicut
Guntur famine — 1944; impetus to Cotton’s Godavari anicut
177.x: The Guntur famine of 1833 led to the construction of Cotton’s Godavari anicut. The other options assign the event to the wrong famine or year.
177.tq: Discriminate between the closely associated Andhra famine names and their years.
xs: **Guntur famine — 1833; impetus to Cotton's Godavari anicut** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Kurnool** was **1866**, **Ganjam** **1865-66**; **1944** is the **Woodhead** Commission.
xa: Guntur famine = **Dokkala Karuvu** (**1832-33**), worst in the south.
Ganjam (**1865-66**) and Kurnool (**1866**) are favourite Andhra famine MCQs.

177.s: Modern food security, as reflected through the Public Distribution System, rests on which of the following three elements?
177.x: Modern food security through the PDS is based on availability, accessibility and affordability of food.
177.tq: Recall the three-part framework and distinguish positive food-security conditions from policy instruments or problems.
xs: Modern food security rests on **availability, accessibility and affordability** through the **PDS** — option **(4)**.
Scarcity, export and revenue collection describe colonial famine conditions, not modern food security.
xa: The IPC scale ends at **Phase 5 Catastrophe/Famine**.
Colonial famines were made worse by the **export of food grains** and **rigid revenue collection**.

177.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the first and the last famine commissions of the colonial period mentioned in the context of British India?
o: Campbell Commission in 1866 and Woodhead Commission in 1944
Woodhead Commission in 1866 and Campbell Commission in 1944
Lyall Commission in 1866 and Hunter Commission in 1944
Campbell Commission in 1833 and Woodhead Commission in 1865–66
177.x: The Campbell Commission of 1866 was the first famine commission, while the Woodhead Commission of 1944 was the last colonial famine commission.
177.tq: Use the first–last comparison and verify both the commission names and their years.
xs: First famine commission = **Campbell (1866)**; last colonial one = **Woodhead (1944)** — option **(1)**.
Campbell followed the **Orissa** famine; Woodhead followed the **Bengal Famine 1943**.
xa: Campbell: Viceroy **John Lawrence**; Woodhead: **Wavell**.
In between: **Strachey (1880)**, **Lyall**, **MacDonnell (1901)**.

178.s: Which was the first educational institution set up by the East India Company in India?
178.x: Calcutta Madrasa, established in 1781, was the first educational institution set up by the Company in India.
178.tq: Use the institutional sequence and identify the earliest establishment.
xs: The first educational institution set up by the Company was the **Calcutta Madrasa** (**1781**, **Warren Hastings**) — option **(4)**.
**Sanskrit College, Benares** came in **1791**, **Fort William College** in **1800**, **Hindu College** in **1817**.
xa: The **Asiatic Society of Bengal** (**1784**) was founded by **William Jones**.
First three universities: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.
Exam angle: "first educational institution in British India" = **Calcutta Madrasa**.

178.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Asiatic Society of Bengal — William Jones
2. Sanskrit College, Benares — Jonathan Duncan
3. Hindu College, Calcutta — David Hare with leading Calcutta citizens
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
178.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Asiatic Society was founded in 1784, the Sanskrit College in 1791, and Hindu College in 1817.
178.tq: Start from the sure institution-founder pairs and test all three matches.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** — **William Jones**; **Sanskrit College, Benares (1791)** — **Jonathan Duncan** (Resident).
**Hindu College (1817)** — **David Hare** with **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** and leading Calcutta citizens.
xa: ⚠ Trap: Sanskrit College Benares is NOT William Jones.
Hindu College is now **Presidency University**.
**Ram Mohan Roy** also set up the **Vedanta College** (**1825**).

178.s: Fort William College at Calcutta was established in 1800 by:
178.x: Lord Richard Wellesley established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train Company civil servants.
178.tq: Use the precise first name to avoid the Wellesley-name trap.
xs: **Fort William College (1800)** was founded by **Lord Richard Wellesley** — option **(3)**.
⚠ Trap: it was **Richard**, not **Arthur**, Wellesley.
**Dalhousie** is linked to the **1853** Minute and Wood's Despatch; **Bentinck** to the **1835** English Education Act.
xa: It trained **Company civil servants**.
It was replaced by the East India College, **Haileybury** (England), by **1806**.

178.s: Hindu College at Calcutta was established in:
178.x: Hindu College, Calcutta, was established in 1817 by David Hare with leading citizens of Calcutta.
178.tq: Arrange the institutional years mentally and select the corresponding date.
xs: **Hindu College**, Calcutta, was set up in **1817** — option **(4)**.
**1781** = Calcutta Madrasa; **1791** = Sanskrit College, Benares; **1800** = Fort William College.
xa: Founded by **David Hare** with **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** and leading Calcutta citizens.
It is now **Presidency University**.

178.s: The principal purpose for establishing Fort William College was to:
o: Train civil servants of the East India Company
Provide primary education to Indian children
178.x: Fort William College was established to train Company civil servants.
178.tq: Identify the institution from its stated administrative purpose.
xs: **Fort William College** was set up to **train Company civil servants** — option **(2)**.
It was founded in **1800** by **Lord (Richard) Wellesley**.
xa: It was replaced by **Haileybury** (England) by **1806**.
The Company's first educational institution was the **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)**.

178.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
178.x: Jonathan Duncan founded the Sanskrit College at Benaras in 1791. It was not founded by William Jones.
178.tq: Use the explicit founder distinction in a same-period institutional matching question.
xs: **Sanskrit College, Benaras — Jonathan Duncan** is correct — option **(2)**.
⚠ Trap: Sanskrit College is NOT **William Jones**, who founded the **Asiatic Society of Bengal**.
**Fort William College** = **Wellesley**; **Vedanta College** = **Ram Mohan Roy**; **David Hare** = **Hindu College**.
xa: Sanskrit College was founded in **1791**; Duncan was the **Resident**.
**Hindu College (1817)** = **David Hare** with **Ram Mohan Roy**.

178.s:
Arrange the following institutions in chronological order of their foundation:
A. Calcutta Madrasa
B. Asiatic Society of Bengal
C. Sanskrit College, Benaras
D. Fort William College
178.x: The institutions were founded in the order Calcutta Madrasa (1781), Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784), Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791), and Fort William College (1800).
178.tq: Arrange institutions by their foundation years and verify the first and last entries.
xs: Order: **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)** → **Asiatic Society (1784)** → **Sanskrit College, Benares (1791)** → **Fort William College (1800)** — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
The Calcutta Madrasa was the **first educational institution** set up by the Company.
xa: After these: **Hindu College (1817)** and **Vedanta College (1825)**.
Founders: **Warren Hastings**, **William Jones**, **Jonathan Duncan**, **Richard Wellesley**.

178.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Charter Act
B. General Committee of Public Instruction
C. English Education Act
D. Wood's Despatch
178.x: The Charter Act was passed in 1813, the General Committee was established in 1823, the English Education Act followed in 1835, and Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854.
178.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intermediate measures.
xs: Order: **Charter Act (1813)** → **General Committee of Public Instruction (1823)** → **English Education Act (1835)** → **Wood's Despatch (1854)** — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
The Committee managed the **1813** grant; the **1835** Act settled its Orientalist-Anglicist split in favour of English.
xa: **Dalhousie's Minute (1853)** came just before Wood's Despatch.
⚠ English Education Act **1835** = **Bentinck + Macaulay**; Wood's Despatch **1854** = **Charles Wood + Dalhousie**.

178.s:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It earmarked Rs 1 lakh a year for the revival of Indian literature and the promotion of science.
2. The earmarked sum was released immediately from 1813 onwards.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
178.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Act provided Rs 1 lakh a year for literature and science. Statement 2 is wrong: the money was actually released only in the 1830s. So '1 only'; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are therefore wrong.
178.tq: 1813 = Rs 1 lakh promised, paid only in the 1830s.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **1813** Act gave **Rs 1 lakh** a year for **revival of Indian literature** and **promotion of science**.
Statement 2 wrong: the money was **actually released only in the 1830s**.
xa: The same Act ended the Company's **trade monopoly** (except **tea and China** trade).
It also **admitted missionaries**.
The grant was managed by the **General Committee of Public Instruction (1823)**.

178.s: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the Charter Act of 1813 mentioned in the context of education and colonial policy?
o: Establishing the General Committee of Public Instruction
Ending the Company's trade monopoly except over tea and China trade
Earmarking Rs 1 lakh for literature and science
178.x: The General Committee of Public Instruction was set up in 1823, not by the Charter Act of 1813. The Act admitted missionaries, ended most of the Company's trade monopoly, and earmarked Rs 1 lakh.
178.tq: Separate the Charter Act provisions from the later institutional measure of 1823.
xs: **Establishing the General Committee of Public Instruction** was NOT a **1813** provision — option **(1)**; the Committee came in **1823**.
The **1813** Act did end the trade monopoly (except **tea and China**), earmark **Rs 1 lakh**, and admit **missionaries**.
xa: The Committee **split into Orientalist vs Anglicist camps**.
The **1813** grant was released only in the **1830s**.

178.s:
Consider the following statements about the General Committee of Public Instruction:
1. It managed the education grant.
2. It split into Orientalist and Anglicist camps.
3. It was created by the Charter Act of 1813.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
178.x: Statement 1 is correct: the GCPI (1823) managed the education grant. Statement 2 is correct: it split into Orientalist and Anglicist camps. Statement 3 is wrong: it was set up in 1823, ten years after the Charter Act of 1813. Hence '1 and 2 only'; the other options either miss 2 or include 3.
178.tq: GCPI = 1823, not 1813; it was the arena of the Orientalist-Anglicist debate.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: it **managed the education grant**.
Statement 2 correct: it **split into Orientalist and Anglicist camps**.
Statement 3 wrong: it came in **1823**, not by the **1813** Act.
xa: The debate ended with the **English Education Act 1835** (Bentinck, on **Macaulay's Minute**).
English became the medium of **higher education**.

178.s:
Consider the following statements about the English Education Act of 1835:
1. It made English the medium of higher education.
2. It was passed under Lord Dalhousie on the basis of Wood's recommendations.
3. It dealt a fatal blow to the district and tahsildari vernacular schools of Madras.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
178.x: Statement 1 is correct: English became the medium of higher education. Statement 2 is wrong: the Act was passed under Bentinck on the basis of Macaulay's Minute; Dalhousie and Wood belong to 1853-54. Statement 3 is correct: the 1835 resolution was a fatal blow to Madras district/tahsildari vernacular schools. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
178.tq: 1835 = Bentinck + Macaulay; 1854 = Dalhousie + Wood.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: it made **English the medium of higher education**.
Statement 2 wrong: it was passed under **Bentinck**, on **Macaulay's Minute** — not Dalhousie or Wood.
Statement 3 correct: it dealt a **fatal blow** to Madras **district/tahsildari vernacular schools**.
xa: **Dalhousie's Minute (1853)** later backed vernacular education.
Critics say its **downward filtration** neglected mass literacy.

178.s: Which statement correctly describes the sequence involving Dalhousie's Minute and Wood's Despatch?
o: Wood's Despatch supported vernacular education and was followed by Dalhousie's Minute.
Dalhousie's Minute supported vernacular education and was followed by Wood's Despatch.
Both documents rejected vernacular education in favour of Persian.
Dalhousie's Minute preceded the Charter Act of 1813.
178.x: Dalhousie's Minute of 1853 backed vernacular education, and Wood's Despatch followed in 1854.
178.tq: Use both sequence and policy direction to distinguish two closely related documents.
xs: **Dalhousie's Minute (1853)** backed **vernacular education** and was followed by **Wood's Despatch (1854)** — option **(2)**.
Option 1 reverses the order; neither document favoured **Persian**.
xa: Wood's Despatch was drafted by **Sir Charles Wood**, President of the **Board of Control**.
It called for **vernacular primary schools** at the base.

178.s:
Consider the following statements about Wood's Despatch of 1854:
1. It was drafted by Sir Charles Wood as President of the Board of Control.
2. It was issued under Governor-General Lord William Bentinck.
3. It proposed universities in the presidency towns on the model of London University.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
178.x: Statement 1 is correct: Wood drafted it as President of the Board of Control. Statement 2 is wrong: it was issued under Dalhousie, not Bentinck. Statement 3 is correct: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities (1857) followed the London University model. So '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses 3, and the options with 2 are wrong.
178.tq: Wood's Despatch = Wood (Board of Control) + Dalhousie + London model; Bentinck belongs to 1835.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: drafted by **Sir Charles Wood**, President of the **Board of Control**.
Statement 2 wrong: it came under **Dalhousie**, not **Bentinck**.
Statement 3 correct: universities in presidency towns on the **London University** model.
xa: The universities: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.
Epithet: **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"**.

178.s: Which of the following represents the graded educational hierarchy envisaged by Wood's Despatch?
o: Universities → affiliated colleges → Anglo-vernacular schools → vernacular primary schools
Vernacular primary schools → Anglo-vernacular high schools → affiliated colleges → universities
Anglo-vernacular schools → universities → primary schools → affiliated colleges
Affiliated colleges → vernacular primary schools → universities → high schools
178.x: The Despatch proposed a hierarchy beginning with vernacular primary schools and progressing through Anglo-vernacular high schools and affiliated colleges to universities.
178.tq: Read the educational structure from its base upward.
xs: **Vernacular primary schools → Anglo-vernacular high schools → affiliated colleges → universities** — option **(2)**.
Primary schools were at the **base** of Wood's graded hierarchy.
xa: It also brought **grants-in-aid** for private (largely missionary) enterprise.
English for **higher**, vernacular for **lower** education.

178.s: Which one of the following was a provision of Wood's Despatch of 1854?
o: Replacement of English by Persian in higher education
Exclusive state control over every school
Introduction of grants-in-aid to encourage private educational enterprise
Abolition of all vernacular primary schools
178.x: Wood's Despatch introduced a grants-in-aid system to encourage private, largely missionary, educational enterprise.
178.tq: Identify the positive institutional provision among reversed policy statements.
xs: Wood's Despatch introduced **grants-in-aid** to encourage **private educational enterprise** — option **(3)**.
Much of that enterprise was **missionary**.
It did not replace English with Persian or abolish vernacular schools — it kept them at the base.
xa: Result-based grants-in-aid to primary schools came from **1877-78** in Andhra.
It also called for **training of teachers**.

178.s:
With reference to Wood's Despatch, consider the following statements:
1. It recommended government supervision of vernacular education.
2. It provided for the training of teachers.
3. It prescribed English for higher education and vernacular languages for lower education.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
178.x: Wood's Despatch recommended supervision of vernacular education, teacher training, and a differentiated language policy using English at higher levels and vernacular languages at lower levels.
178.tq: Test the provisions together and watch for the language-level distinction.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Wood's Despatch provided **government supervision of vernacular education** and **training of teachers**.
It prescribed **English for higher** and **vernacular for lower** education.
xa: It set up universities on the **London University** model: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.
It is the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"**.

178.s: Which document is called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'?
178.x: Wood's Despatch (1854), drafted by Sir Charles Wood under Dalhousie, is called the Magna Carta of English Education in India. Macaulay's Minute (1835) led to the English Education Act, the Hunter Commission (1882) dealt with primary and secondary education, and the Charter Act (1813) sanctioned Rs 1 lakh for education.
178.tq: Magna Carta of English education = Wood's Despatch 1854.
xs: **Wood's Despatch, 1854** is called the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"** — option **(2)**.
**Macaulay's Minute** led to the **1835** English Education Act; the **Hunter** Commission came in **1882**.
xa: It was drafted by **Sir Charles Wood** under **Dalhousie**.
**Madras University** followed on **5 September 1857**.

178.s: The principal area of concern of the Hunter Commission was:
o: Only technical education in presidency towns
178.x: The Hunter Commission focused primarily on primary and secondary education.
178.tq: Identify the commission from its educational level of focus.
xs: The **Hunter Commission (1882)** focused on **primary and secondary education** — option **(1)**.
University education was the field of the **Universities Commission (1902)** and **Sadler (1917-19)**.
xa: It handed schools to **local boards and municipalities**.
It was under **Ripon**; recommendations took effect in **1883-84**.
It also stressed backward classes (esp. **Muslims**) and **women**.

178.s:
Consider the following statements about the Hunter Commission:
1. It recommended that schools be handed over to local boards and municipalities.
2. It gave attention to the education of backward classes, especially Muslims, and of women.
3. It was appointed in 1882 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Curzon.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
178.x: Statement 1 is correct: Hunter recommended handing schools to local boards and municipalities. Statement 2 is correct: it stressed education of backward classes (esp. Muslims) and women. Statement 3 is wrong: the 1882 Hunter Commission was under Ripon; Curzon is linked with the 1902 Universities Commission. Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' leaves out 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
178.tq: Hunter 1882 = Ripon; Curzon = 1902 Universities Commission.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: schools went to **local boards and municipalities**.
Statement 2 correct: it stressed **backward classes (esp. Muslims) and women**.
Statement 3 wrong: Hunter (**1882**) was under **Ripon**, not Curzon.
xa: ⚠ **Hunter 1882** = Ripon; **Universities Commission 1902** = Curzon.
It also wanted **qualified Indians** in the education department.

178.s: The Indian Universities Commission of 1902 led to the:
178.x: The 1902 Indian Universities Commission led to the Indian Universities Act of 1904, which increased government control over universities.
178.tq: Link the commission to its immediate legislative outcome.
xs: The **Indian Universities Commission (1902)** led to the **Indian Universities Act 1904** — option **(4)**.
The Act brought **tighter government control of universities**.
xa: It was under **Curzon**.
The **1913** Resolution came next, under **Hardinge II**.

178.s: The Resolution on Education Policy of 1913 was issued during the Viceroyalty of:
178.x: The 1913 Resolution on Education Policy was issued during the Viceroyalty of Lord Hardinge II.
178.tq: Match the policy resolution with its Viceroy and year.
xs: The **1913** Resolution on Education Policy came under **Hardinge II** — option **(4)**.
**Chelmsford** = Sadler (**1917-19**); **Curzon** = Universities Commission (**1902**); **Irwin** = Hartog (**1929**).
xa: It answered **Gokhale's** demand for compulsory primary education.
It provided funding for **primary education**.

178.s: Which educational sequence was recommended by the Sadler Commission?
o: Twelve-year school course followed directly by a four-year degree
Twelve-year school course, an intermediate stage and a three-year degree
Ten-year school course followed directly by a two-year degree
Eight-year school course followed by a five-year degree
178.x: The Sadler Commission recommended a 12-year school course, an intermediate stage, and a three-year degree.
178.tq: Compare the duration and intermediate stage instead of relying only on the commission name.
xs: Sadler recommended a **12-year school course**, an **intermediate stage**, then a **3-year degree** — option **(2)**.
It dealt with **university education** (**Calcutta University**).
xa: Sadler sat in **1917-19** under **Chelmsford**.
**Hartog (1929)** returned to primary-education **wastage and stagnation**.

178.s: The Hartog Committee of 1929 concentrated on:
178.x: The Hartog Committee examined wastage and stagnation in primary education and continued to support vernacular education.
178.tq: Identify the committee from its distinctive technical terms.
xs: The **Hartog Committee (1929)** studied **primary education wastage and stagnation** — option **(4)**.
It kept priority on **vernacular education**.
xa: It was under **Irwin**.
Criticism: **downward filtration** neglected mass literacy; **Hunter** and **Hartog** kept returning to primary education.

178.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
178.x: The Hartog Committee of 1929 was associated with Lord Irwin, not Lord Wavell. Wavell was the Viceroy associated with the Sargent Plan of 1944.
178.tq: Locate the swapped Viceroy in a multi-column factual match.
xs: **Hartog Committee — 1929 — Wavell** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**; Hartog was under **Irwin**.
**Wavell** goes with the **Sargent Plan (1944)**.
Sadler–**Chelmsford**, Hunter–**Ripon** and Universities Commission–**Curzon** are correct.
xa: The **1913** Resolution came under **Hardinge II**.
⚠ **Hunter 1882** = Ripon; **Universities Commission 1902** = Curzon.

178.s: The Sargent Plan was formulated in:
178.x: The Sargent Plan was formulated in 1944 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Wavell.
178.tq: Use the sequence of later education plans to identify the final chronological entry.
xs: The **Sargent Plan** came in **1944** — option **(3)**.
**1913** = Resolution on Education Policy; **1929** = Hartog Committee.
xa: It sought universal free compulsory education for **6-14** years.
It came under **Wavell**.

178.s: The Sargent Plan envisaged universal free and compulsory education for children in the age group:
178.x: The Sargent Plan proposed universal, free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years.
178.tq: Recall the exact age range and reject shifted lower or upper limits.
xs: The Sargent Plan proposed universal free compulsory education for **6-14 years** — option **(4)**.
It was framed in **1944** under **Wavell**.
xa: The **1913** Resolution had responded to **Gokhale's** call for compulsory primary education.
The **Hartog (1929)** report found primary **wastage and stagnation**.

178.s: The Resolution on Education Policy of 1913 was primarily a response to the demand of:
o: Gopal Krishna Gokhale for compulsory primary education
178.x: The 1913 Resolution on Education Policy responded to Gopal Krishna Gokhale's demand for compulsory primary education.
178.tq: Identify the demand that triggered a specific policy resolution.
xs: The **1913** Resolution responded to **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**'s demand for **compulsory primary education** — option **(2)**.
**Macaulay** pushed English higher education (**1835**); **Curzon** tightened university control (**1904**); **Hunter** handed schools to local boards.
xa: It was issued under **Hardinge II**.
It provided funding for **primary education**.

178.s: The Sadler Commission of 1917–19 dealt chiefly with:
o: Primary education wastage in all provinces
Calcutta University and the transition from school to university
178.x: The Sadler Commission examined Calcutta University and the transition from school education to university education.
178.tq: Distinguish commissions by their subject and institutional focus.
xs: The **Sadler (Calcutta University) Commission (1917-19)** dealt with **Calcutta University** and the **school-to-university** transition — option **(4)**.
It recommended a **12-year** school course and an **intermediate stage** before a **3-year** degree.
Primary-education wastage was the **Hartog** Committee's subject.
xa: Sadler came under **Chelmsford**.
The earlier **Universities Commission (1902)** led to the **Indian Universities Act 1904**.

178.s: The result-based grants-in-aid to primary schools in Andhra were introduced from:
178.x: In Andhra, result-based grants-in-aid to primary schools began from 1877-78.
178.tq: Distinguish the Andhra follow-up date from the dates of the main education policies.
xs: Result-based **grants-in-aid** to primary schools came from **1877-78** — option **(2)**.
It was a **Wood's Despatch** follow-up.
**1883-84** is when **Hunter**'s recommendations took effect.
xa: Wood's Despatch (**1854**) began grants-in-aid for private, largely **missionary**, enterprise.
**Hindu College, Visakhapatnam** was set up in **1878**.

178.s: Which missionary organisation was the first missionary body to spread Western education in Andhra?
178.x: The London Missionary Society was the first missionary body associated with the spread of Western education in Andhra. It began its work in 1805.
178.tq: Directly identify the earliest organisation from a group of closely related missionary bodies.
xs: The **London Missionary Society** was the first missionary body (**1805**) — option **(4)**.
**Kadapa** became its centre in **1824**.
xa: **North German Society**: Rajahmundry and Eluru (**1843**).
**Church Missionary Society**: **Machilipatnam** (**Rev. Robert Noble**).
**American Baptists**: Rayalaseema, **Ongole** and **Nellore**.

178.s: The institution at Machilipatnam founded by Reverend Robert Noble is presently known as
178.x: The Machilipatnam institution founded by Reverend Robert Noble and upgraded in 1864 is now known as Noble College.
178.tq: Discriminate among similarly named colleges by linking the institution to its founder and location.
xs: Rev. Robert Noble's Machilipatnam institution is today **Noble College** — option **(1)**.
He founded the school in **1843** for the **Church Missionary Society**; it became a college in **1864**.
**Mrs A.V.N. College** is the old Hindu College, Visakhapatnam; **Khallikota College** is in **Berhampur**.
