xa: Some notes say **1813** or **1841**, or credit the **LMS**.
⚠ **Noble** = Machilipatnam (**1843**); **G.N. Taylor** = Narsapur (**1852**).

178.s: The Central Collegiate Institute at Madras, established in 1841, was the forerunner of which institution?
178.x: The Central Collegiate Institute, Madras, established in 1841, was the forerunner of Presidency College.
178.tq: Match the predecessor institution with the later college it developed into.
xs: The **Central Collegiate Institute, Madras (1841)** was the forerunner of **Presidency College** — option **(1)**.
**Noble College** is at Machilipatnam; **Hindu College** at Visakhapatnam (**1878**); **Khallikota** at Berhampur (**1879**).
xa: **Madras University** came on **5 September 1857**.
**1841** is also when the **CMS** began work in Krishna-Godavari.

178.s:
Arrange the following developments in Rajahmundry in chronological order:
A. Establishment of the Government second-grade college
B. Elphinstone's scheme
C. Establishment of the regional school
D. Conversion into a degree college
178.x: Elphinstone's scheme dates to 1839, the regional school to 1854, the second-grade college to 1873 and the degree college to 1877.
178.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intervening institutional stages by year.
xs: Order: **Elphinstone's scheme (1839)** → regional school (**1854**) → second-grade college (**1873**) → degree college (**1877**) — option **(1) B, C, A, D**.
Elphinstone's scheme produced **only one** regional school, at **Rajahmundry**.
xa: Rajahmundry was the base of **Veeresalingam**'s reform journalism.
AP angle: **Noble (1843)**, **G.N. Taylor (Narsapur 1852)** and **Rajahmundry (1854/1873)**.

178.s: Who was G.N. Taylor in the context of education in the Godavari region?
o: The Sub-Collector of Godavari who promoted an Anglo-Vernacular School at Narsapur
The principal of Hindu College at Visakhapatnam
The founder of Noble College at Machilipatnam
The head of the North German Society at Rajahmundry
178.x: G.N. Taylor, or George Noble Taylor, was the Sub-Collector of Godavari who established the Anglo-Vernacular School at Narsapur in 1852.
178.tq: Use the official position and educational initiative to identify the correct individual.
xs: **G.N. Taylor** was **Sub-Collector of Godavari** who set up the **Anglo-Vernacular School, Narsapur** — option **(1)**.
He was based at **Narsapur** (Rajahmundry sub-division); the school dates to **1852**.
**Noble College** was founded by **Rev. Robert Noble**; the **North German Society** worked at Rajahmundry.
xa: He drafted the **1854 Godavari District Education Scheme**.
The school had branches at **Palakollu, Penugonda, Achanta**.

178.s:
The Anglo-Vernacular School established at Narsapur in 1852 had branches at which of the following places?
1. Palakollu
2. Penugonda
3. Achanta
4. Eluru
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
178.x: The Narsapur Anglo-Vernacular School had branches at Palakollu, Penugonda and Achanta. Eluru was associated with the North German Society, not listed as a branch of this school.
178.tq: Separate the places directly linked with one institution from a nearby missionary centre.
xs: The Narsapur school had branches at **Palakollu, Penugonda, Achanta** — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Eluru** was a **North German Society** centre, not a branch.
xa: The school was set up in **1852** by **G.N. Taylor**.
Taylor drafted the **1854 Godavari District Education Scheme**.

178.s: Who drafted the 1854 Godavari District Education Scheme?
178.x: G.N. Taylor drafted the Godavari District Education Scheme in 1854 while serving as Sub-Collector of Godavari.
178.tq: Avoid the founder-substitution trap by associating the scheme with the official who prepared it.
xs: **G.N. Taylor** drafted the **1854 Godavari District Education Scheme** — option **(3)**.
**Rev. Robert Noble** founded the Machilipatnam school; **Father Heyer** led Lutherans in **Guntur**; **Elphinstone**'s scheme (**1839**) gave Rajahmundry its school.
xa: Taylor was **Sub-Collector** of Godavari.
He founded the **Anglo-Vernacular School, Narsapur (1852)**.

178.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Mrs A.V.N. College — former Hindu College, Visakhapatnam
178.x: Noble College is located at Machilipatnam, not Rajahmundry. Hindu College was established at Visakhapatnam and is now known as Mrs A.V.N. College, while Khallikota College is at Berhampur.
178.tq: Find the wrong location by checking each institution-place pairing.
xs: **Noble College — Rajahmundry** is wrongly matched — option **(2)**; Noble College is at **Machilipatnam**.
**Mrs A.V.N. College** = former **Hindu College, Visakhapatnam** (**1878**); **Khallikota College** = **Berhampur** (**1879**).
xa: Noble's school (**1843**) became a college in **1864**.
Rajahmundry got a government second-grade college in **1873**.

178.s:
Match List-I (Mission) with List-II (Area of work in Andhra):
List-I
a. North German Society
b. Lutherans under Father Heyer
c. American Baptists
d. London Missionary Society
List-II
i. Guntur
ii. Rajahmundry and Eluru
iii. Rayalaseema, Ongole and Nellore
iv. Kadapa
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
178.x: Correct: North German Society - Rajahmundry and Eluru (1843); Lutherans under Father Heyer - Guntur; American Baptists - Rayalaseema, Ongole and Nellore; London Missionary Society - Kadapa (centre in 1824). Option B swaps the German Society and the Lutherans; option C swaps the Lutherans and the Baptists; option D swaps the German Society and the LMS.
178.tq: Father Heyer = Guntur; Baptists = Ongole/Nellore; Germans = Rajahmundry/Eluru.
xs: **North German–Rajahmundry and Eluru; Lutherans (Heyer)–Guntur; American Baptists–Rayalaseema, Ongole, Nellore; LMS–Kadapa** — option **(1) a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv**.
The North German Society came to Rajahmundry and Eluru in **1843**.
xa: The **LMS** was the first missionary body (**1805**); Kadapa centre in **1824**.
The **Church Missionary Society** worked at **Machilipatnam**.
Mission schools admitted **Sudras and Panchamas**.

178.s: The Machilipatnam National College became notable as a centre of Home Rule protests in:
178.x: The Machilipatnam National College was a centre of Home Rule protests in 1917.
178.tq: Discriminate among close years associated with a political institution.
xs: The **Machilipatnam National College** was a centre of **Home Rule** protests in **1917** — option **(3)**.
It grew from Rev. **Robert Noble**'s **1843** school.
xa: Noble's school became a college in **1864**.
Noble worked for the **Church Missionary Society**.

178.s: Madras University was established on 5 September 1857 under the:
178.x: Madras University was established on 5 September 1857 under Wood’s Despatch.
178.tq: Match the institution with the education policy that shaped its establishment.
xs: **Madras University** (**5 September 1857**) was set up under **Wood's Despatch** — option **(3)**.
The Despatch called for universities in presidency towns on the **London University** model.
xa: The first three universities: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.
Its forerunner college: the **Central Collegiate Institute (1841)** → **Presidency College**.

178.s: Rajahmundry was an important base for the reform journalism of:
178.x: Rajahmundry served as the base of Kandukuri Veeresalingam’s reform journalism.
178.tq: Identify the reformer associated with the place and activity.
xs: Rajahmundry was the base of **Kandukuri Veeresalingam**'s reform journalism — option **(2)**.
English education created the **reformist middle class** of coastal Andhra, e.g. Veeresalingam.
xa: Rajahmundry: regional school **1854**, second-grade college **1873**, degree college **1877**.
The **North German Society** worked in Rajahmundry and Eluru (**1843**).

178.s: Which of the following sequences is in the correct chronological order?
o: Madras University — Central Collegiate Institute — Noble School — grants-in-aid system
Central Collegiate Institute — Noble School — Madras University — grants-in-aid system
Noble School — Central Collegiate Institute — grants-in-aid system — Madras University
Central Collegiate Institute — Madras University — Noble School — grants-in-aid system
178.x: The correct order is Central Collegiate Institute (1841), Noble School (1843), Madras University (1857), and the grants-in-aid system linked to results (1877–78).
178.tq: Place the earliest and latest items first, then resolve the middle dates.
xs: Order: **Central Collegiate Institute (1841)** → **Noble School (1843)** → **Madras University (1857)** → **grants-in-aid (1877-78)** — option **(2)**.
The result-based **grants-in-aid system** was a **Wood's Despatch** follow-up, hence after the university.
xa: Noble's school became a college in **1864**.
**Hindu College, Visakhapatnam** followed in **1878**.

178.s: Who contributed most to the early spread of Western education in Andhra?
178.x: Western education in Andhra was first spread by Christian missionaries (APPSC key), beginning with the London Missionary Society in 1805 and followed by the CMS, North German, Lutheran and American Baptist missions. Zamindars, the Mahajana Sabha and karanams were not the pioneers.
178.tq: Western education in Andhra = missionaries first (LMS 1805).
xs: Western education in Andhra was first spread by **Christian missionaries** — option **(2)** (APPSC key for "who contributed most").
The **London Missionary Society (1805)** was the first missionary body.
xa: Mission schools admitted **Sudras and Panchamas**.
Wood's **grants-in-aid** encouraged largely **missionary** enterprise.

178.s: Which of the following correctly describes a significance of English education in coastal Andhra?
o: It eliminated the need for primary education among the masses
It prevented the emergence of a pan-Indian educated elite
It remained confined entirely to missionary personnel
It created a reformist middle class, including figures such as Kandukuri Veeresalingam
178.x: English education contributed to the emergence of a reformist middle class in coastal Andhra, represented by Kandukuri Veeresalingam, and also helped create a pan-Indian educated elite.
178.tq: Select the option that captures both the regional and wider social consequence without an extreme claim.
xs: English education **created a reformist middle class** in coastal Andhra, e.g. **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** — option **(4)**.
It also produced a **pan-Indian educated elite**, so option 2 is the reverse.
It did not remove the need for primary education — **downward filtration** neglected mass literacy.
xa: **Hunter** and **Hartog** kept returning to primary education.
First three universities: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.

178.s: Which educational policy approach was criticised for neglecting mass literacy?
178.x: The downward filtration approach was criticised because it prioritised educating a limited section and neglected mass literacy.
178.tq: Match the criticism with the exact policy term rather than a general education objective.
xs: **Downward filtration** was criticised for **neglecting mass literacy** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It educated a small upper section in **English**, expecting knowledge to filter down to the masses, which left **primary education** weak.
**Compulsory primary education** was in fact a later demand: **Gokhale's** demand drew the **1913 Resolution on Education Policy**.
xa: **Hunter (1882)** and **Hartog (1929)** kept returning to **primary education** to correct this neglect.
**Sargent Plan (1944)** proposed **universal free compulsory education** for **6-14** years.
English education still created the **reformist middle class** of coastal Andhra, e.g. **Kandukuri Veeresalingam**.
⚠ **English Education Act 1835** (Bentinck + Macaulay) made **English** the medium of higher education.

178.s: Which commissions repeatedly returned attention to primary education in their discussions?
178.x: The Hunter and Hartog Commissions repeatedly emphasised the importance of primary education, especially against the limitations of downward filtration.

179.s: The Press Act of 1835 is popularly associated with which description?
179.x: Charles Metcalfe’s Press Act of 1835 repealed the 1823 restrictions and earned him the description ‘liberator of the Indian press’.
179.tq: Distinguish the positive label of Metcalfe’s measure from the negative label of the Vernacular Press Act.
xs: **Metcalfe's Press Act (1835)** earned him the title **"liberator of the Indian press"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It **repealed the 1823 Licensing Regulations**.
**"Gagging Act"** = Lytton's **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**; the anti-Extremist law was the **Newspapers Act 1908**.
xa: Pattern: freedom after **1835** → gag of **1878** → repeal **1882** → repression in **1908** and **1910**.
⚠ **1835** is also the year of **Macaulay's Minute** and the English Education Act.

179.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Registration Act was enacted in 1867.
2. It dealt with the registration of printers and presses.
3. It was associated with John Lawrence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
179.x: All three statements are correct. The 1867 Registration Act, formally linked with the Press and Registration of Books framework, concerned registration of printers and presses under John Lawrence.
179.tq: Test year, authority and provision together.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
The **Registration Act (1867)**, under **John Lawrence**, covered **registration of printers and presses** (Press and Registration of Books Act).
xa: It was replaced by the **Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023**, w.e.f. **1 March 2024**.
The RNI is now the **Press Registrar General of India**.
John Lawrence also opened telegraph links with **Europe (1864-69)**.

179.s: Under Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code, which act was treated as an offence from 1870?
o: Printing a newspaper without depositing security
Publishing without registering a printing press
Refusing to submit proofs to a censor
179.x: Sedition under Section 124A IPC made ‘exciting disaffection’ an offence in 1870 during the tenure of Lord Mayo.
179.tq: Recall the exact statutory expression associated with the provision.
xs: **Section 124A IPC (1870)** made **"exciting disaffection"** against the Government an offence (sedition) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It came under **Mayo**.
Security deposits belong to the **VPA 1878** and **Indian Press Act 1910**; registration of presses to the **1867** Act; censor proofs to the VPA.
xa: Before it: **Registration Act (1867)**, **John Lawrence**.
After it: **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, **Lytton**.
Mayo also introduced **state railways**.

179.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act, 1908 — Minto II
179.x: The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act of 1908 was associated with Minto II and enabled magistrates to seize presses of papers inciting violence.
179.tq: Use the year–Governor-General pair to catch swapped authorities.
xs: **Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act, 1908 — Minto II** is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Section 124A (1870)** = **Mayo**, not Ripon; **Registration Act (1867)** = **John Lawrence**, not Lytton.
**Licensing Regulations (1823)** = **John Adams**; Metcalfe repealed them in **1835**.
xa: The 1908 Act let magistrates **seize presses** of papers inciting violence (anti-Extremist).
**Indian Press Act 1910** (also Minto II) imposed heavy **security deposits**.

179.s: The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act of 1908 empowered magistrates to:
o: Seize the presses of newspapers inciting violence
Appoint a press commissioner in every province
Repeal all licensing requirements for newspapers
179.x: The 1908 Act empowered magistrates to seize presses of newspapers that incited violence and was directed against extremist activities.
179.tq: Ask who exercised the power and what action the law authorised.
xs: The **1908 Act** let magistrates **seize the presses** of papers **inciting violence** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was an **anti-Extremist** measure under **Minto II**.
A **press commissioner** was appointed after the VPA repeal in **1882**, not in 1908.
xa: **Indian Press Act 1910** revived **VPA** features: heavy **security deposits**, confiscation.
Both followed the **Swadeshi movement**, ending about **25 years** of relative press freedom.

179.s: What was the principal feature of the Indian Press Act of 1910?
o: Abolition of all press registration requirements
Revival of Vernacular Press Act features with heavy security deposits
Transfer of press control to local self-government bodies
179.x: The Indian Press Act of 1910 revived features of the Vernacular Press Act and imposed heavy security deposits.
179.tq: Identify the later law that revived an earlier restrictive pattern.
xs: The **Indian Press Act 1910** **revived Vernacular Press Act features** with heavy **security deposits** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It also allowed **confiscation**; it came under **Minto II**.
xa: **Annie Besant's** Commonweal and New India deposited **Rs 2,000**, then **Rs 10,000**, under the Press Act.
VPA was repealed in **1882** by **Ripon**.

179.s: Which sequence correctly represents the broad development of press policy in colonial India?
o: Freedom after Metcalfe — gag of 1878 — repeal in 1882 — repression in 1908 and 1910
Gag of 1878 — freedom after Metcalfe — repeal in 1882 — repression in 1908 and 1910
Repression in 1908 — repeal in 1882 — gag of 1878 — freedom after Metcalfe
Repeal in 1882 — gag of 1878 — freedom after Metcalfe — repression in 1910
179.x: Metcalfe’s 1835 measure brought relative freedom, the 1878 Act imposed restrictions, it was repealed in 1882, and repression returned through the 1908 and 1910 measures.
179.tq: Trace the policy trend rather than merely ordering isolated dates.
xs: Sequence: **freedom after Metcalfe (1835)** → **gag of 1878** → **repeal in 1882** → **repression in 1908 and 1910** — so option **(1)** is correct.
After the **1882** repeal came about **25 years** of relative freedom, until the post-**Swadeshi** laws.
xa: **Metcalfe** = "liberator of the Indian press".
**Lytton's** VPA = "**Gagging Act**"; **Ripon** repealed it.
**1908** = Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act; **1910** = Indian Press Act.

179.s: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was introduced in the background of:
o: The Swadeshi movement and the First Factory Act
The famine of 1876–77 and the lavish Delhi Durbar of 1877
The Revolt of 1857 and the Ilbert Bill controversy
The Permanent Settlement and the Regulating Act
179.x: The Act was passed by Lord Lytton amid public anger over the 1876–77 famine and the lavish Delhi Durbar held in 1877.
179.tq: Connect a law with its immediate political and economic context.
xs: The VPA came amid anger over the **1876-77 famine** and the lavish **Delhi Durbar (1877)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was passed by **Lord Lytton**.
xa: It was nicknamed the **"Gagging Act"**.
It applied only to **Indian-language** papers, not English ones.
Repealed in **1882** by **Ripon**.

179.s:
Consider the following statements about the Vernacular Press Act, 1878:
1. District magistrates could make printers and publishers of vernacular papers sign bonds not to publish seditious matter.
2. A paper could obtain exemption by submitting proofs to a government censor before publication.
3. An appeal against the magistrate's action lay to the High Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
179.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: magistrates could demand bonds, and exemption was available by submitting proofs to a government censor. Statement 3 is wrong: there was no appeal to a court of law. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
179.tq: VPA: bonds, deposits, seizure, NO appeal; exemption only via pre-censorship.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **district magistrates** could make printers/publishers sign **bonds** not to publish seditious matter.
Statement 2 correct: exemption only by **submitting proofs to a government censor**.
Statement 3 wrong: there was **no appeal to a court of law**.
xa: Magistrates could also demand forfeitable **security deposits** and **seize presses** for repeat offences.
Targets: **Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash, Samachar**.

179.s: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the Vernacular Press Act, 1878?
o: Security deposits could be demanded and forfeited
There was no appeal to a court of law
Presses could be seized for repeated offences
English-language newspapers were subjected to the same restrictions
179.x: The Act was discriminatory: it applied to Indian-language papers and not to English-language newspapers. The other three were provisions of the Act.
179.tq: Find the exception by testing the discriminatory scope of the law.
xs: The VPA did **not** cover **English-language newspapers** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
It was **discriminatory**: it applied only to **Indian-language** papers.
**Security deposits**, **no appeal** and **seizure of presses** were all real provisions.
xa: **Amrita Bazar Patrika** turned **English** overnight to escape it.
Passed by **Lytton** (**1878**); repealed by **Ripon** (**1882**).

179.s: Which of the following newspapers was among those targeted by the Vernacular Press Act?
179.x: Som Prakash was one of the newspapers targeted by the Vernacular Press Act, along with Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.
179.tq: Recognise a target newspaper from the specified list.
xs: **Som Prakash** was a target of the **Vernacular Press Act** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**The Hindu** was English (outside the Act); **Commonweal** was **Annie Besant's** paper of the **1916-17** period.
xa: Other targets: **Bharat Mihir**, **Dacca Prakash**, **Samachar**.
Amrita Bazar Patrika escaped by becoming **English** in **1878**.

179.s: The Vernacular Press Act was repealed in 1882, and the pre-censorship clause was dropped. Which additional measure followed the repeal?
o: Transfer of press powers to district magistrates
Compulsory English publication by all newspapers
179.x: After the repeal in 1882, the pre-censorship clause was dropped and a press commissioner was appointed.
179.tq: Test the consequence of repeal rather than the identity of the repealing Viceroy.
xs: After the **1882** repeal, a **press commissioner** was appointed — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **pre-censorship clause** was dropped at the same time.
xa: The repeal was by **Lord Ripon**.
**1882** under Ripon also saw the **Resolution on Local Self-Government** and the **Hunter Commission**.
Ripon's other years: **First Factory Act (1881)**, **Famine Code** and **Ilbert Bill (1883)**.

179.s: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, nicknamed the 'Gagging Act', was repealed in 1882 by:
179.x: Lord Ripon repealed the 'Gagging Act' in 1882. Lytton passed it in 1878, Mayo is linked with Section 124A (1870), and Minto II with the press laws of 1908 and 1910.
179.tq: Lytton gagged (1878), Ripon freed (1882).
xs: **Lord Ripon** repealed the "**Gagging Act**" in **1882** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lytton** passed it in **1878**; **Mayo** is linked with **Section 124A (1870)**; **Minto II** with the **1908** and **1910** laws.
xa: The repeal dropped the **pre-censorship clause** and appointed a **press commissioner**.
Ripon also appointed the **Hunter Commission (1882)**.
**Famine Code 1883** (APPSC-G1 2022) also came under Ripon.

179.s: To escape the Vernacular Press Act, which newspaper converted itself overnight into an English-language paper in 1878?
179.x: Amrita Bazar Patrika became an English paper overnight because the VPA applied only to Indian-language papers. Som Prakash was a target of the Act. The Hindu was already in English, and Kesari was a Marathi paper.
179.tq: ABP dodged the VPA by switching to English.
xs: **Amrita Bazar Patrika** became an **English** paper overnight in **1878** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The VPA applied only to **Indian-language** papers. **Som Prakash** was a target; **The Hindu** was already English; **Kesari** was Marathi.
xa: Amrita Bazar Patrika was run by **Sisir Kumar and Motilal Ghosh**, Calcutta.
Other VPA targets: **Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash, Samachar**.

179.s: Who was the leader of the Anglicist group in the education debate?
179.x: T.B. Macaulay was the leader of the Anglicist group.
179.tq: Match the debate camp with its principal protagonist.
xs: **T.B. Macaulay** led the **Anglicists** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**H.T. Colebrooke** and **H.H. Wilson** were **Orientalists**; **Thomas Munro** backed pathashalas and vernacular schooling in Madras.
xa: Anglicists favoured **Western science + English literature**; Orientalists **Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian** learning.
Macaulay's Minute: **2 February 1835**, approved by **Bentinck**.
Famous remark: "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia".

179.s: Which of the following was associated with the Orientalist group?
179.x: H.T. Colebrooke was an Orientalist. H.H. Wilson was another prominent Orientalist, whereas Macaulay, Bentinck and Trevelyan were associated with the Anglicist side.
179.tq: Identify the camp affiliation of a named protagonist.
xs: **H.T. Colebrooke** was an **Orientalist** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Macaulay** (leader), **Bentinck** and **Charles Trevelyan** were **Anglicists**.
xa: **H.H. Wilson** was another Orientalist; in Madras **Thomas Munro** backed vernacular schooling.
**Munro's Survey (1826)** found a wide network of vernacular village schools.
**Bentinck** = "Father of Modern Western Education in India".

179.s: Thomas Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education in 1826 found:
o: No organised system of village education in Madras
A complete absence of pathashalas in rural areas
Only English-medium colleges in the presidency towns
A wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency
179.x: Munro's 1826 survey found a wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency.
179.tq: Use the survey's empirical finding to reject absolute claims about indigenous education.
xs: **Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education (1826)** found a **wide network of vernacular village schools** in the **Madras Presidency** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So options claiming no system or no pathashalas are wrong; Munro himself **backed pathashalas and vernacular schooling**.
xa: Munro is counted on the **Orientalist** side, in Madras.
Munro's collectorate and tahsildari schools (**2** in Kadapa, **1** Nellore, **2** Vizag by **1830**) were closed in **1836**.
The **1835 Resolution** banned regional-language instruction in Madras district schools.

179.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Thomas Munro — English-only education in Madras
179.x: Thomas Munro supported pathashalas and vernacular schooling, not English-only education in Madras. Colebrooke and Wilson were Orientalists, while Trevelyan was an Anglicist.
179.tq: Find the reversed position of a regional education-policy protagonist.
xs: **Thomas Munro — English-only education** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is the answer.
Munro **backed pathashalas and vernacular schooling** in Madras.
The rest are right: **H.H. Wilson** and **H.T. Colebrooke** = **Orientalists**; **Charles Trevelyan** = **Anglicist**.
xa: Anglicist leader: **T.B. Macaulay**, with **Bentinck**.
**Munro's Survey (1826)** found a wide network of vernacular village schools.
Orientalists favoured **Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian**; Anglicists **Western science + English literature**.

179.s: Macaulay's Minute on education was approved by:
179.x: Macaulay's Minute of 1835 was approved by Lord William Bentinck, who is associated with modern Western education in India.
179.tq: Match the policy document with the Governor-General who approved it.
xs: **Lord William Bentinck** approved **Macaulay's Minute (1835)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Dalhousie** is linked with **Wood's Despatch (1854)**; **Ripon** with the **Hunter Commission (1882)**.
xa: Bentinck is called the **"Father of Modern Western Education in India"**.
The Minute is dated **2 February 1835**.
It made **English** the medium of higher education.

179.s: T.B. Macaulay wrote the Minute on Education while serving as:
o: Resident at Benares and Director of Public Instruction
Law Member and President of the General Committee of Public Instruction
Education Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council
President of the Board of Control and Governor-General
179.x: Macaulay was the Law Member and President of the General Committee of Public Instruction when he wrote the Minute.
179.tq: Combine the person with his specific institutional positions.
xs: Macaulay was **Law Member** and **President of the General Committee of Public Instruction** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **President of the Board of Control** behind Wood's Despatch was **Sir Charles Wood**, not Macaulay.
xa: He led the **Anglicists**; the Minute is dated **2 February 1835**.
The **General Committee of Public Instruction (1823)** managed education funds.
The Minute was approved by **Bentinck**.

179.s: The principal recommendation of Macaulay's Minute regarding the use of education funds was to spend them:
o: Equally on Persian, Arabic and English education
Exclusively on English-medium teaching of Western science and literature
Exclusively on Sanskrit and Arabic learning
179.x: Macaulay recommended that education funds be used exclusively for English-medium teaching of Western science and literature.
179.tq: Test the exact policy preference rather than the broader objective of education.
xs: Macaulay wanted education funds spent **exclusively on English-medium teaching of Western science and literature** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**British higher education** was prioritised over **mass primary schooling**.
Sanskrit and Arabic learning was what the **Orientalists** wanted, not Macaulay.
xa: Famous remark: "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia" (**APPSC-G2 2025**).
It led to the **Downward Filtration Theory**.
Approved by **Bentinck**, **1835**.

179.s: Which of the following best describes the Downward Filtration Theory?
o: A small upper class should first be educated so that learning would filter down to the masses
Education should begin with village schools and move upward to universities
Traditional learning should filter into English institutions through translation
Primary education should be universal before higher education is introduced
179.x: The theory proposed educating a small upper class first, expecting knowledge to descend or filter down to the wider population.
179.tq: Translate the policy theory into its practical educational sequence.
xs: **Downward Filtration**: educate a **few upper-class Indians** so knowledge **filters down to the masses** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Starting from village schools upward is the reverse — that was the ladder of **Wood's Despatch**, which **rejected** downward filtration.
xa: The theory relates to **education** (**APPSC-G2 2024**).
Wood's Despatch asked the Company to take up **mass instruction**.
It grew from **Macaulay's Minute (1835)**.

179.s: Macaulay's proposed educated class was intended to be:
o: Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect
Indian in language and tradition, but European in administration only
English in blood and colour, but Indian in taste and intellect
Indian in blood, colour, taste, opinions, morals and intellect
179.x: Macaulay sought a class Indian in blood and colour but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect, to act as interpreters between rulers and ruled.
179.tq: Use the precise wording of the famous formulation to reject reversed descriptions.
xs: Macaulay wanted a class **"Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect"** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This class was to serve as **interpreters between rulers and ruled**.
xa: This underlies the **Downward Filtration Theory**.
His remark: a single shelf of a good **European library** was worth the whole native literature of **India and Arabia**.
Funds were to go **exclusively** to **English-medium** teaching.

179.s: Which statement correctly reflects Macaulay's view expressed in the Minute?
o: European literature should be excluded from Indian education.
A single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia.
Arabic and Sanskrit literature alone should receive public funds.
The whole native literature of India and Arabia was superior to European literature.
179.x: Macaulay made the well-known comparison that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia.
179.tq: Recognise the exact author–remark association and avoid reversing the comparison.
xs: Macaulay wrote that **"a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He wanted funds **exclusively** for English-medium Western learning, the opposite of options 1, 3 and 4.
xa: The remark was asked in **APPSC-G2 2025**.
Macaulay led the **Anglicists**; **H.T. Colebrooke** and **H.H. Wilson** were Orientalists.
The Minute was approved by **Bentinck** in **1835**.

179.s:
Consider the following statements about Wood's Despatch:
1. It recommended grants-in-aid.
2. It asked the Company to take up mass instruction.
3. It supported the downward filtration of education from a few upper-class Indians.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
179.x: Wood's Despatch recommended grants-in-aid and mass instruction. It rejected, rather than supported, the downward filtration approach.
179.tq: Spot the reversed policy position in the statement about downward filtration.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: Wood's Despatch recommended **grants-in-aid**.
Statement 2 correct: it asked the Company to take up **mass instruction**.
Statement 3 wrong: it **rejected downward filtration**.
xa: Called the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"**; dated **1854**, under **Dalhousie**.
Ladder: **vernacular primary** → **Anglo-vernacular high school** → **university**.
Universities of **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** followed in **1857**.

179.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Anglicists from the Orientalists?
o: Anglicists favoured Persian learning, whereas Orientalists favoured English literature
Anglicists favoured Western science and English literature, whereas Orientalists favoured classical Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning
Both groups rejected Western science and English education
Both groups demanded only vernacular primary education
179.x: Anglicists supported Western science and English literature, while Orientalists supported Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning.
179.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap to distinguish two rival educational positions.
xs: **Anglicists** favoured **Western science and English literature**; **Orientalists** favoured **Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian** learning — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option 1 reverses the two camps.
xa: Orientalists: **H.T. Colebrooke**, **H.H. Wilson**; in Madras **Thomas Munro**.
Anglicists: **T.B. Macaulay** (leader), **Bentinck**, **Charles Trevelyan**.
Macaulay's Minute (**1835**) settled the debate for English.

179.s: Which of the following statements about the 1835 educational resolution is correct?
o: It transferred Madras schools to municipalities
It introduced regional-language instruction in all Madras district schools
It established the first universities in India
It banned regional-language instruction in Madras district schools
179.x: The 1835 resolution banned regional-language instruction in Madras district schools.
179.tq: Test the exact policy direction and avoid replacing a ban with an introduction.
xs: The **1835 Resolution** **banned regional-language instruction** in **Madras district schools** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The first universities came later, in **1857**, after **Wood's Despatch**.
xa: Munro's collectorate and tahsildari schools were closed in **1836**.
By **1830** these schools were **2** in Kadapa, **1** in Nellore, **2** in Vizag.
The resolution followed **Macaulay's Minute**, approved by **Bentinck**.

179.s: Which policy position was rejected by Wood's Despatch of 1854?
179.x: Wood's Despatch rejected the downward filtration theory and asked the Company to take up mass education.
179.tq: Identify the rejected policy among the provisions actually recommended.
xs: **Wood's Despatch** rejected the **downward filtration theory** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It asked the Company to take up **mass instruction**.
**Grants-in-aid**, **government supervision of vernacular education** and **teacher training** were its own provisions.
xa: Called the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"** (**1854**).
Ladder: vernacular primary → Anglo-vernacular high school → university.
Universities: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857)**.

179.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Charter Act of 1813 provided not less than Rs 1 lakh a year for literature and science.
2. The money under the 1813 Act was released only in the 1830s.
3. The General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) was set up mainly to train teachers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
179.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 1813 Act set aside at least Rs 1 lakh a year, but the money was released only in the 1830s. Statement 3 is wrong: the GCPI managed education funds; it was not a teacher-training body. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
179.tq: GCPI = manager of the education fund.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the **Charter Act 1813** set aside not less than **Rs 1 lakh** a year for literature and science.
Statement 2 correct: the money was released only in the **1830s**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **General Committee of Public Instruction (1823)** **managed education funds**.
xa: The 1813 Act also **allowed missionaries**.
**Macaulay** was later President of the General Committee of Public Instruction.

179.s: Wood's Despatch of 1854 is popularly known as the:
o: Magna Carta of English Education in India
179.x: Wood's Despatch of 1854 is known as the Magna Carta of English Education in India.
179.tq: Identify the exact epithet attached to a major policy document.
xs: **Wood's Despatch (1854)** is the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was issued under **Dalhousie**.
xa: It recommended **grants-in-aid** and a ladder from **vernacular primary** to **university**.
Universities of **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** came in **1857**.
It **rejected downward filtration** and asked for **mass instruction**.

179.s: Following Wood's Despatch, universities were set up in 1857 at:
179.x: Wood's Despatch (1854) planned a ladder from vernacular primary school to Anglo-vernacular high school to university, and universities were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857. Allahabad, Lahore, Benares, Mysore and Hyderabad were not among the 1857 universities.
179.tq: 1857: three presidency universities - Calcutta, Bombay, Madras.
xs: Universities were set up in **1857** at **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other places listed were not among the **1857** universities.
xa: They followed **Wood's Despatch (1854)**.
AP angle: **Madras University (1857)** is a favourite Andhra education fact.
⚠ **1854** = Wood's Despatch; **1857** = three universities; **1882** = Hunter Commission.

179.s: The Hunter Commission on education is usually dated to:
179.x: The Hunter Commission is usually dated 1882; some sources say it was appointed in 1880. 1813 was the Charter Act grant of Rs 1 lakh, 1854 Wood's Despatch, and 1857 the founding of the three universities.
179.tq: Hunter Commission = 1882 (Ripon).
xs: The **Hunter Commission** is usually dated **1882** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Some notes say it was appointed in **1880**.
**1813** = Charter Act grant; **1854** = Wood's Despatch; **1857** = three universities.
xa: It came under **Ripon**, the same year as the **VPA repeal** and the **Resolution on Local Self-Government**.
Ripon: **First Factory Act 1881**; **Famine Code** and **Ilbert Bill 1883**.

179.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Act or policy)
A. Wood’s Despatch
B. First Factory Act
C. Famine Code
D. Resolution on Local Self-Government

List-II (Year)
1. 1854
2. 1881
3. 1882
4. 1883

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
179.x: Wood’s Despatch was issued in 1854, the First Factory Act in 1881, the Famine Code in 1883, and the Resolution on Local Self-Government in 1882.
179.tq: Start with the distinctive 1854 and 1883 dates, then resolve the remaining pair.
xs: Correct pairs: **A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Wood's Despatch 1854**; **First Factory Act 1881**; **Famine Code 1883**; **Resolution on Local Self-Government 1882**.
xa: Wood's Despatch = **Dalhousie**; the other three = **Ripon**.
Famine Code **1883** was asked in **APPSC-G1 2022**.
⚠ Some notes give **1882** for the First Factory Act; the APPSC key is **1881**.

179.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The First Factory Act dealt with child labour.
2. It is dated 1881 in the APPSC-aligned chronology.

The **First Factory Act** dealt with **child labour**, is dated **1881** (APPSC key), under **Ripon**.

Ripon's **1882**: VPA repeal, **Resolution on Local Self-Government**, **Hunter Commission**.

179.s:

179.s: Which of the following combinations best expresses the significance of English education, the press, railways and the telegraph in colonial India?
o: They restricted communication to European officials alone.
They created an educated middle class and helped form an all-India public sphere for nationalism.
They eliminated regional languages from public life immediately.
They confined political mobilisation to individual princely states.
179.x: English education, the press, railways and the telegraph helped create an educated middle class and an all-India public sphere in which nationalism developed.
179.tq: Apply the combined cause-and-effect relationship to a broader historical outcome.
xs: They created an **educated middle class** and an **all-India public sphere** for nationalism — so option **(2)** is correct.
Railways, post and telegraph also gave a **national market** and faster **pan-Indian mobilisation**.
xa: Railways brought **shared public travel across castes**.
English education created the **reformist middle class** that led the national movement.
Vernacular press built the public sphere; Lytton's **VPA (1878)** tried to curb it.

179.s: Which of the following statements about early education and journalism in Andhra is correct?
o: Telugu journalism began in Andhra only after 1900.
Madras University was established before the Central Collegiate Institute, Madras.

xa: AP angle: **Andhra Prakasika**, **Krishna Patrika**, **Andhra Patrika**; **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.
**Madras University** dates to **1857**.
**Hitavadi** came from **Masulipatnam (1848)**.

179.s:

xs: All four are correct — so option **(1) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.

180.s: Which one of the following best describes the principal features associated with Lord Cornwallis's civil service reforms in India?
o: A military service based on hereditary succession and private trade
A merit-based covenanted service, prohibition of private trade and gifts, and promotion by seniority
A wholly Indian civil service recruited through provincial elections
A service recruited exclusively through examinations conducted in India
180.x: Cornwallis established a merit-based covenanted civil service, prohibited private trade and acceptance of gifts, and introduced promotion substantially based on seniority.
180.tq: Use the cluster of reforms associated with the correct administrator rather than relying on a single keyword.
xs: Cornwallis built a **merit-based covenanted** service, **banned private trade and gifts**, and gave **seniority promotions** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His service was **dominated by Europeans**, so a "wholly Indian" service is wrong; exams in India came only from **1922**.
xa: Cornwallis is the **"Father of Civil Services in India"**.
He also **separated revenue from justice**.
⚠ **Sardar Patel** called the ICS the **"Steel Frame"**.
**Wellesley** set up the **College of Fort William (1800)** to train recruits.

180.s: The College of Fort William was established at Calcutta in 1800 primarily for which of the following purposes?
o: Administering the Provincial Public Service Commission
Conducting the first simultaneous ICS examination
Training only Indian judges in customary law
Training recruits of the Company's civil service
180.x: Wellesley established the College of Fort William at Calcutta in 1800 to train recruits of the Company's civil service.
180.tq: Match the institution with its specific administrative function and founder.
xs: **Wellesley** founded the **College of Fort William**, Calcutta (**1800**) for **training recruits** of the Company's civil service — so option **(4)** is correct.
Simultaneous ICS exams in India began only in **1922**; PSCs came under the **GoI Act 1935**.
xa: It was replaced by the **East India College, Haileybury** (England) by **1806**.
Haileybury taught **law, political economy** and **Indian languages**.
**Cornwallis** = "Father of Civil Services in India".

180.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Macaulay Committee report:

2. It favoured preference for graduates of Oxford and Cambridge.
3. It recommended continuation of appointments solely through the patronage of Company Directors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
180.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Macaulay recommendations were associated with competitive examination, not continuation of the Company's patronage system.

xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the **Macaulay Committee** wanted exams **in London**.
Statement 2 correct: it preferred **Oxford/Cambridge graduates**.
Statement 3 wrong: patronage had ended with the **Charter Act 1853**, which brought **open competitive examination**.

**Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** backed the open competitive examination.
Patronage of the Company's **Directors** lasted **till 1853** (APPSC **2018**).

180.s: The Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 provided for which of the following?
o: Replacement of the ICS by the IAS
Abolition of all civil service examinations in London
Immediate parity between Indians and Europeans in all covenanted posts
Limited Indian entry, mainly into uncovenanted posts, subject to conditions including residence and language examination
180.x: The Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 allowed limited Indian entry, mainly into uncovenanted posts, with conditions including seven years' residence and an examination in the local language.
180.tq: Separate limited statutory entry from the later policy of Indianisation and post-1947 changes.
xs: The **Indian Civil Services Act 1861** allowed **limited Indian entry**, mainly to **uncovenanted** posts — so option **(4)** is correct.
Conditions: **7+ years' residence** and a **local language exam**.
The ICS became the **IAS** only in **1947**; **50:50** parity was the **Lee Commission's** idea.
xa: Next step: **Statutory Civil Service** (**1878-79**, **Lytton**) — **1/6** of covenanted posts to Indians of "high families".
**Aitchison Commission (1886)** dropped covenanted/uncovenanted terms.
First Indian in the ICS: **Satyendranath Tagore (1864)**.

180.s: The reduction of the maximum age for the civil service examination to 19 years in 1878 was associated with the tenure of:
180.x: The maximum age was reduced to 19 in 1878 during the tenure of Lord Lytton, and this became an important Indian grievance.
180.tq: Link the numerical change to the Viceroy in office when it occurred.
xs: The maximum age was cut to **19** in **1878** under **Lord Lytton** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Dufferin** appointed the **Aitchison Commission (1886)**, which raised the limit to **23**; **Hardinge II** = **Islington**; **Reading** = **Lee**.
xa: It was a key **Indian grievance**; the INC demanded to **raise the age limit** from **1885**.
Lytton also set up the **Statutory Civil Service** (**1878-79**).

180.s: Which of the following statements correctly explains the statutory civil service scheme introduced under Lord Lytton in 1878–79?
o: One-half of the ICS posts were reserved for Indians under the Lee Commission.
All covenanted posts were opened equally to Indians and Europeans through local examinations.
One-sixth of the covenanted posts were set aside for Indians of high families, and the scheme was later abolished.

180.tq: Separate the limited statutory concession under Lytton from the later Lee Commission parity proposal.
xs: Lytton's **Statutory Civil Service** gave **one-sixth** (**1/6**) of covenanted posts to Indians of **"high families"**, and was **later abolished** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**50:50** parity came from the **Lee Commission (1923-24)**, not Lytton.
xa: Lytton also cut the maximum age to **19** (**1878**).
The **Aitchison Commission (1886)** followed, with **Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate** services.
Earlier, the **1861 Act** opened mainly **uncovenanted** posts.

180.s: The patronage of the Company's Directors over civil service appointments was abolished, and open competitive examination introduced, by the:

Patronage of the Company's **Directors** lasted **till 1853**; the **1861 Act** opened mainly **uncovenanted** posts to Indians.
xa: **Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** backed the open exam.
**Macaulay Committee (1854)**: exams in **London**, preference for Oxford/Cambridge graduates.
Patronage till **1853** was asked in **APPSC 2018**.

180.s: Who was the first Indian to enter the Indian Civil Service?
180.x: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian in the ICS in 1864 (many texts say 1863). Ram Mohan Roy, in 1832, was the first to demand Indians in higher posts. Surendranath Banerjea and Dadabhai Naoroji are not the 'first Indian ICS' answer.

180.s: The demand for raising the age limit and holding the civil service examination simultaneously in India and England was taken up by the Indian National Congress from:
180.x: The INC began pressing these demands from its first session in 1885.

xs: The INC took up these demands from its **first session (1885)** — so option **(1)** is correct.

xa: The **GoI Act 1919 / Montford reforms** provided a separate ICS exam in India.
Exams were held in India from **1922** (Allahabad, later Delhi) alongside London.
Lytton had cut the maximum age to **19** in **1878**.

180.s:
Consider the following statements about the Aitchison (Public Service) Commission:

3. It recommended 50:50 Indian-European parity in the ICS within 15 years.

180.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Aitchison (1886, Dufferin) replaced covenanted/uncovenanted with Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate services. Statement 3 is wrong: 50:50 parity was the Lee Commission's (1923-24) proposal. Hence '1 and 2 only'.

xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.

Statement 2 correct: it replaced covenanted/uncovenanted with **Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate** services.
Statement 3 wrong: **50:50** parity within **15** years was the **Lee Commission's** proposal.
xa: The three-tier plan was implemented under **Lansdowne**; the age limit was raised to **23**.
**Islington (1912-15)** = Indianisation of higher posts.

180.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Islington Commission (1912-15) dealt with Indianisation of higher posts.
2. The Lee Commission proposed 50:50 Indian-European parity in the ICS within 15 years.

180.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: Islington = Indianisation of higher posts; Lee = 50:50 parity; the PSC came on 1 October 1926. Statement 4 is wrong: the Lee Commission (1923-24) was under Reading; Hardinge II was the Viceroy for Islington. Hence '1, 2 and 3 only'.

xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Islington (1912-15)** = **Indianisation** of higher posts; **Lee** = **50:50** parity in **15** years; a **PSC** came on **1 October 1926**.
Statement 4 wrong: the **Lee Commission (1923-24)** was under **Reading**; **Hardinge II** was Viceroy for Islington.
xa: **GoI Act 1935** created the **Federal PSC** + provincial PSCs.
**UPSC** replaced the Federal PSC from **1950**.
⚠ **Aitchison** = three-tier services (**1886**).

180.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relevant civil service provisions of the Government of India Act, 1919?
o: It established the Federal Public Service Commission in place of all provincial services.
It abolished the ICS and created the IAS with immediate effect.
It provided for a separate ICS examination in India, enabling simultaneous examinations with England from 1922.

xs: The **GoI Act 1919** provided a **separate ICS examination in India**, held from **1922** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Federal PSC** came with the **GoI Act 1935**; the ICS became the **IAS** in **1947**.
xa: Exams were held at **Allahabad, later Delhi**, alongside London.
This was an INC demand from its first session (**1885**).
UPPSC **2021** keyed both such statements correct.

180.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: 1950 — UPSC replaced the Federal Public Service Commission
Government of India Act, 1919 — UPSC replaced the Federal Public Service Commission
Government of India Act, 1935 — Federal Public Service Commission and Provincial Public Service Commissions
180.x: The Government of India Act, 1919, dealt with the provision for a separate ICS examination in India. The Federal and Provincial Public Service Commissions were provided for by the 1935 Act, and UPSC replaced the Federal PSC in 1950.

xs: **GoI Act 1919 — UPSC replaced the Federal PSC** is wrong — so option **(3)** is the answer.
The **1919 Act** gave a separate ICS exam in India; the **Federal PSC** came under the **GoI Act 1935**, and **UPSC** replaced it from **1950**.
The other pairs are right: ICS → **IAS** in **1947**.
xa: The **Lee Commission** led to a **Public Service Commission** on **1 October 1926**.
Lee proposed **50:50** Indian-European parity in the ICS.

180.s: Who described the Indian Civil Service as the 'Steel Frame' of India?
180.x: Sardar Patel described the Indian Civil Service as the 'Steel Frame' of India.

**Cornwallis** is the "Father of Civil Services"; **Ram Mohan Roy** first demanded Indians in higher posts (**1832**).
xa: Cornwallis, Wellesley and Macaulay built the "steel frame"; UPSC traces its roots to British-era bodies.
The ICS became the **IAS** in **1947**.

180.s: Who established the district Diwani and Faujdari Adalats in 1772?
180.x: Warren Hastings established the district Diwani Adalats for civil cases and Faujdari Adalats for criminal cases in 1772.
180.tq: Directly identify the Governor-General associated with a judicial reform.
xs: **Warren Hastings** set up district **diwani** (civil) and **faujdari** (criminal) adalats in **1772** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The civil adalat was **under the Collector**.
xa: He also set up the **Sadar Diwani** and **Sadar Nizamat Adalat** at Calcutta.
⚠ **Hastings** = Collector gets civil adalat; **Cornwallis** = Collector **loses judicial powers**.
**Regulating Act 1773** set up the **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)**.

180.s: Which one of the following was a feature of the Cornwallis Code of 1793?
o: Separation of commercial, judicial and revenue branches
Establishment of High Courts at the presidency towns
Abolition of all provincial courts of appeal
Replacement of Persian by vernacular languages in courts
180.x: The Cornwallis Code of 1793 separated the commercial, judicial and revenue branches. The other reforms belonged to later administrative developments.
180.tq: Use the reform directly associated with the named code and period.
xs: The **Cornwallis Code 1793** separated the **commercial, judicial and revenue branches** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**High Courts** came under the **1861** Act; **Bentinck** abolished the provincial courts of appeal and replaced **Persian** in courts.
xa: The Collector was **deprived of judicial powers**; the post of **District Judge** was created.
Provincial courts of appeal: **Calcutta, Dacca, Murshidabad, Patna**.
Cornwallis also divided districts into **thanas** under **darogas**.

With reference to Cornwallis's judicial administration, consider the following statements:

180.x: Under Cornwallis, the Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats at Calcutta were presided over by the Governor-General in Council.

xs: Under **Cornwallis**, the **Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats** at Calcutta were presided over by the **Governor-General in Council** — so option **(2)** is correct.

180.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly associated with Bentinck's judicial reforms?
o: Abolition of Cornwallis's provincial courts of appeal
Creation of provincial courts of appeal at Dacca and Patna
Transfer of circuit courts' work to Commissioners
Establishment of separate Sadar courts at Allahabad

180.tq: Find the reform belonging to another Governor-General.
xs: **Creating provincial courts of appeal at Dacca and Patna** was **Cornwallis's**, not Bentinck's — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Bentinck** **abolished** those courts and circuit courts, gave their work to **Commissioners**, and set up separate Sadar courts at **Allahabad**.
xa: Bentinck also replaced **Persian** with vernacular/English in courts.
⚠ **Hastings** = Collector gets civil adalat; **Cornwallis** = Collector loses judicial powers; **Bentinck** = abolishes provincial courts.

180.s: Which language change was introduced in the courts during Bentinck's administration?
o: English and vernacular languages replaced Persian
Persian replaced English and vernacular languages
Sanskrit replaced Persian in all courts
Only English was permitted in every court

xs: Under **Bentinck**, **vernacular and English replaced Persian** in the courts — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Persian** was dropped, not restored; no Sanskrit-only or English-only rule was made.
xa: Bentinck abolished Cornwallis's **provincial courts of appeal and circuit**.
He set up separate **Sadar courts at Allahabad**.
The circuit courts' work went to **Commissioners**.

**C.P. Ilbert** was the Law Member behind the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**; **Macaulay** headed the **Law Commission** (Charter Act **1833**).

The Ilbert Bill (**1883**) row was the **"White Mutiny"**.

180.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Madras — Presidency governing Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema
180.x: Munro is associated with the Madras judicial and police models. Ripon is associated with local self-government, not the Madras judicial model.
180.tq: Find the swapped personality–reform association.
xs: **Ripon — Madras judicial model** is wrong — so option **(1)** is the answer.
The **Madras judicial/police model** is **Munro's**; Ripon is linked with **local self-government**.
**Madras** was the presidency governing **Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema**.
xa: Munro headed the **Judicial Commission (1814-18)**.
He wanted police supervision **under the Collector**, and village officers to try minor crimes.

180.s:
With reference to the administrative legacy of British rule in India, consider the following statements:
1. Cornwallis, Wellesley and Macaulay contributed to building the administrative ‘steel frame’.
2. The UPSC, CAG and Election Commission can trace their institutional roots to British-era bodies.
3. The administrative legacy was confined exclusively to the police and did not extend to constitutional institutions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
180.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the legacy also extended to institutions whose successors include the UPSC, CAG and Election Commission.
180.tq: Reject the extreme word ‘exclusively’ when the institutional legacy spans several branches of administration.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cornwallis, Wellesley and Macaulay** built the "steel frame"; **UPSC, CAG and Election Commission** trace roots to British-era bodies.
Statement 3 wrong: the legacy spread well beyond the police.
xa: ICS, codified laws, the **1861** police model and Ripon's local bodies are direct ancestors of today's systems.
**Sardar Patel** called the ICS the **"Steel Frame"**.

180.s: In July 2026, which action was taken in relation to the Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC)?
o: The KPSC was dissolved by the Supreme Court after a constitutional amendment.
The KPSC Chairperson resigned after the Governor transferred the Commission to Andhra Pradesh.
The KPSC was placed under the direct control of the Union Public Service Commission.
The KPSC Chairperson was suspended by the Karnataka Governor pending inquiry, and a reference was sought from the Supreme Court under Article 317(1).
180.x: The Karnataka Governor suspended the KPSC Chairperson pending inquiry and sought a Supreme Court reference under Article 317(1). This was described as a first for the KPSC.
180.tq: Match the constitutional authority with the action and the relevant Article.
xs: The **Karnataka Governor suspended the KPSC Chairperson** pending inquiry and sought a Supreme Court reference under **Art. 317(1)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was **a first for KPSC** (**14 Jul 2026**).
xa: PSCs trace back to the **Lee Commission** (PSC set up **1 October 1926**) and the **GoI Act 1935** (provincial PSCs).
**UPSC** replaced the Federal PSC from **1950**.

181.s: Which one of the following was NOT a condition of the Subsidiary Alliance devised by Lord Wellesley?
o: The ruler had to maintain a British subsidiary force at his own cost
The ruler had to accept a British Resident
The ruler had to exclude other Europeans from his service
The ruler could freely conduct an independent foreign policy
181.x: A subsidiary ally had to surrender independent foreign-policy control. The other conditions were part of the system devised by Wellesley.
181.tq: Spot the option that reverses the central consequence of the alliance.
xs: A subsidiary ally could **not** run an **independent foreign policy** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Real terms: keep a **British subsidiary force** at his cost, accept a **British Resident**, no other **Europeans** in service.
xa: The ruler also had to **disband his own army**; unpaid subsidy → **ceding territory**.
Devised by **Lord Wellesley, 1798**.
First to accept: **Nizam of Hyderabad** (**September 1798**).

181.s: If a ruler under the Subsidiary Alliance failed to pay the prescribed subsidy, the British could require him to
o: cede territory in lieu of payment
181.x: Unpaid subsidy could result in the cession of territory to the British.
181.tq: Apply the financial condition of the alliance to the consequence of default.
xs: An unpaid subsidy meant **ceding territory** — so option **(3)** is correct.
E.g. the Nizam's **1800** treaty ceded the Rayalaseema districts = **"Ceded Districts"**.
xa: The ally had to keep a **British subsidiary force** at his own cost.
Princes lost **sovereignty** and **foreign-policy independence**.

181.s:
Arrange the following Subsidiary Alliance acceptances in chronological order:
A. Bhonsle of Berar
B. Awadh
C. Scindia
D. Peshwa
181.x: Awadh accepted the alliance in November 1801, the Peshwa in December 1802 (Treaty of Bassein), Bhonsle of Berar in December 1803 and Scindia in February 1804.
181.tq: Place Awadh (1801) and the Peshwa (1802) first, then distinguish the 1803 and 1804 agreements.
xs: Order **B, D, A, C** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Awadh (November 1801)** → **Peshwa (December 1802**, Treaty of Bassein) → **Bhonsle of Berar (December 1803)** → **Scindia (February 1804)**.
xa: Earlier: **Hyderabad (September 1798)**, **Mysore (1799)**, **Tanjore (October 1799)**.
Last Maratha to sign: **Holkar (1818)**.

181.s: The 1800 treaty involving the Nizam resulted in the cession of the Rayalaseema districts, which came to be known as the
181.x: The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts in 1800 to meet the cost of the subsidiary force; these became known as the Ceded Districts.
181.tq: Link the treaty, territorial transfer and historical regional name.
xs: The Rayalaseema districts ceded in **1800** became the **"Ceded Districts"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They paid for the **subsidiary force** kept for the Nizam.
xa: The Nizam was the **first** subsidiary ally (**September 1798**), again **1800**.
AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.

181.s: The British pressure that led the Nizam of Hyderabad to accept the Subsidiary Alliance was connected with his raising of French battalions under
181.x: The Nizam raised French battalions under Raymond. Resident Kirkpatrick reported this to Wellesley, who then forced the alliance.
181.tq: Separate the officer who commanded the French battalions from the Resident who reported them.
xs: The Nizam raised **French battalions under Raymond** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He was angry at **Sir John Shore's neutrality** in the **1795** Maratha war; **Wellesley** devised the alliance.
xa: The Nizam accepted it first, **September 1798**.
Subsidiary allies had to keep **no other Europeans** in service.

181.s: The first Indian ruler to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (September 1798) was the:
181.x: The Nizam of Hyderabad was first, in September 1798 (and again in 1800). Mysore followed in 1799, Awadh in November 1801, and the Peshwa signed through the Treaty of Bassein.
181.tq: First subsidiary ally = Nizam, 1798.
xs: The **Nizam of Hyderabad** was first, in **September 1798** (again **1800**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Mysore** followed in **1799**, **Awadh** in **November 1801**, the **Peshwa** in **December 1802** (Treaty of Bassein).
xa: AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.
The **1800** treaty created the **"Ceded Districts"** (Rayalaseema).

181.s: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, when the ruler of a dependent state died without a natural heir, the state:
o: lapsed to the East India Company
became an independent monarchy under the adopted heir
was placed under the direct rule of the Governor-General without annexation
was transferred automatically to the Mughal emperor
181.x: A dependent state without a natural heir lapsed to the East India Company under the Doctrine of Lapse.
181.tq: Apply the definition to the legal consequence of the ruler's death.
xs: Such a state **lapsed to the East India Company** — so option **(1)** is correct.
An adopted son **could not inherit the throne**; adoption counted only for **private property**.
xa: Policy of **Lord Dalhousie (1848-56)**.
First lapse annexation: **Satara (1848)**.
⚠ **Awadh** (**1856**) was annexed for **misgovernment**, not lapse.

181.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Doctrine of Lapse:
1. It was associated with Lord Dalhousie.
2. An adopted son could inherit the ruler's private property.
3. An adopted son could automatically inherit the throne of the dependent state.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
181.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Under the policy, an adopted son could inherit private property but not the throne.
181.tq: Separate private-property succession from succession to political sovereignty.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: it was **Dalhousie's** policy.
Statement 2 correct: adoption was allowed only for **private property**.
Statement 3 wrong: an adopted son **could not inherit the throne**.
xa: Withdrawn by **Queen Victoria's Proclamation** (**1 November 1858**), which **recognised adoption**.
**APPSC-GS 2018** called it "the policy of annexation devised by the EIC".

181.s: Lord Dalhousie announced the Doctrine of Lapse in
181.x: Lord Dalhousie formulated and applied the Doctrine of Lapse from 1848.
181.tq: Use the earliest date in the sequence of Dalhousie’s annexations and policies.
xs: Dalhousie applied the **Doctrine of Lapse** from **1848** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1853** = **Jhansi** lapsed; **1856** = **Awadh** annexed for misgovernment.
xa: First lapse annexation: **Satara (1848)**.
Dalhousie's term: **1848-56**.

181.s: The policy of annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse was formally abandoned after the Revolt of 1857 through
181.x: Queen Victoria’s Proclamation, read by Canning at the Allahabad Durbar on 1 November 1858, abolished the policy and recognised adoption.
181.tq: Connect the policy change with the correct proclamation, date and official occasion.
xs: **Queen Victoria's Proclamation** (**1 November 1858**) abandoned annexation — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was read by **Canning** at the **Allahabad Durbar**; the Treaty of Bassein was the Peshwa's subsidiary alliance.
xa: It **recognised adoption**.
Canning called the princes **"breakwaters to the storm"**.
After **1858** the Crown guaranteed princely states in return for **paramountcy**.

181.s: Which of the following grievances was associated with Nana Saheb?
o: Denial of the pension of his adoptive father, Baji Rao II
Refusal to recognise his adopted son as ruler of Jhansi
Removal from the Red Fort and loss of the imperial title
181.x: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied the pension of his adoptive father.
181.tq: Match the leader with his personal political grievance, avoiding swapped revolutionary leaders.
xs: **Nana Saheb** was denied the pension of his adoptive father **Baji Rao II** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jhansi** throne = **Rani Lakshmibai**; **Jagdishpur** estates = **Kunwar Singh**; Red Fort/title = **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
xa: Baji Rao II was the **last Peshwa**.
Nana Saheb led the revolt at **Kanpur**.

181.s: Dalhousie announced that the successors of Bahadur Shah would have to leave the
o: Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli
Qutub at Mehrauli and move to Calcutta
Agra Fort and move to Delhi
Allahabad Fort and move to Lucknow
181.x: Dalhousie declared that Bahadur Shah’s successors would have to leave the Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli.
181.tq: Use the place pair—Red Fort and Qutub, Mehrauli—to avoid confusing Mughal centres.
xs: **Dalhousie** said Bahadur Shah's successors must **leave the Red Fort** and move to the **Qutub, Mehrauli** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The move was from the **Red Fort** to the **Qutub**, not the reverse; Calcutta, Agra and Allahabad play no part.
xa: ⚠ **Dalhousie** = leave the **Red Fort**; **Canning (1856)** = lose the **imperial title**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's grievance: loss of **title and Red Fort** for his successors.

181.s: What did Canning announce in 1856 regarding the successors of Bahadur Shah Zafar?
o: They would receive pensions equal to those of the Peshwas
They would lose the imperial title and become mere princes
They would be recognised as governors of Awadh
They would inherit the imperial title and the Red Fort
181.x: Canning announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar, his successors would lose the imperial title and would be treated merely as princes.
181.tq: Distinguish Canning’s announcement about imperial status from Dalhousie’s order about residence.
xs: **Canning (1856)** announced the successors would **lose the imperial title** and be **mere princes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This would apply after **Bahadur Shah Zafar**; they would not inherit the title or the Red Fort.
xa: ⚠ **Dalhousie** had said they must **leave the Red Fort** for the **Qutub, Mehrauli**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar led the revolt at **Delhi**.

181.s: Which of the following titles were abolished in 1855?
o: The titles of the Nizam and the Peshwa
The titles of the Raja of Satara and the ruler of Jhansi
The titles of the Mughal emperor and the Nawab of Awadh
The titles of the Carnatic Nawab and the Tanjore Raja
181.x: The titles of the Carnatic Nawab and the Tanjore Raja were abolished in 1855.
181.tq: Match the year with the two specific titles rather than with rulers affected by the Doctrine of Lapse.
xs: In **1855** the titles of the **Carnatic Nawab** and the **Tanjore Raja** were abolished — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Mughal** title was only threatened for Bahadur Shah's successors (Canning, **1856**), and **Awadh** was annexed in **1856** for misgovernment.
xa: **Nana Saheb** was denied his father's pension.
**Pindaris and irregular troops** were disbanded, adding to unemployment.
Mughal successors were to lose the **Red Fort** (Dalhousie) and the **imperial title** (Canning).

181.s: Which of the following developments added to the number of unemployed persons before the Revolt of 1857?
o: Disbanding of Pindaris and irregular troops
181.x: The disbanding of Pindaris and irregular troops increased unemployment and contributed to discontent.
181.tq: Identify the administrative action that produced the stated economic consequence.
xs: **Disbanding Pindaris and irregular troops** created more unemployed — so option **(1)** is correct.
Adopted heirs were **not** recognised before **1858**, and the **Carnatic** title was abolished in **1855**, not restored.
xa: Awadh's annexation also threw the Nawab's **lords, officials, retainers and soldiers** out of work.
Subsidiary allies had to **disband their own armies**.

181.s: The annexation of Awadh in 1856 was justified by the British on the ground of
o: Absence of a natural male heir
181.x: Awadh was annexed by Lord Dalhousie in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment, not under the Doctrine of Lapse.
181.tq: Distinguish the stated ground of annexation from the commonly associated Doctrine of Lapse.
xs: **Awadh (1856)** was annexed on the ground of **misgovernment** (maladministration) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was **not** a lapse case: no natural male heir was the test for **lapse**.
xa: Annexed by **Dalhousie**, **February 1856**.
Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was deposed and exiled to **Calcutta**.
⚠ **Lapse** = **1848** (Satara first); **Awadh** = misgovernment (**1856**).

181.s: Who among the following was deposed and exiled to Calcutta after the annexation of Awadh?
181.x: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was deposed after Awadh was annexed and was exiled to Calcutta.
181.tq: Use the ruler–territory association to avoid swapping rulers of different annexed states.
xs: Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was deposed and exiled to **Calcutta** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Birjis Qadr** was **Begum Hazrat Mahal's** son, proclaimed ruler in **1857**; **Bahadur Shah Zafar** was at Delhi.
xa: Awadh was annexed in **1856** for **"misgovernment"**.
The **Summary Revenue Settlement (1856)** dispossessed the **taluqdars**.

181.s:
With reference to the Summary Revenue Settlement introduced in Awadh in 1856, consider the following statements:
1. The settlement was made directly with village proprietors.
2. Taluqdars were dispossessed of their estates.
3. Taluqdars were allowed to retain their arms and forts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
181.x: The settlement was made directly with village proprietors, while taluqdars lost their estates, were disarmed and had their forts demolished. Statement 3 is false.
181.tq: Find the false statement by checking the reversal of a specific administrative consequence.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: settlement was made **directly with village proprietors**.
Statement 2 correct: **taluqdars were dispossessed** of their estates.
Statement 3 wrong: taluqdars were **disarmed** and their **forts demolished** (UPSC **2026** key).
xa: It "deeply alienated the **sepoys** and the **landed aristocracy**".
The Bengal Army drew heavily from **Awadh**.

181.s: The annexation of Awadh particularly alienated the Bengal Army sepoys because
o: most Bengal Army sepoys were recruited from Punjab alone
their families in Awadh were affected by the new revenue burden
their own regiments were immediately disbanded
they were denied promotion to the rank of Resident
181.x: The Bengal Army drew heavily from Awadh, and the new revenue burden directly affected the families of its sepoys.
181.tq: Link the social base of recruitment with the direct effect of annexation on soldiers’ families.
xs: The **Bengal Army** drew heavily from **Awadh**, and sepoys' **families bore the new revenue burden** — so option **(2)** is correct.
So the sepoys were **hurt directly** by the annexation; Awadh, not Punjab, was the recruiting ground.
xa: The Nawab's **lords, officials, retainers and soldiers** were thrown out of work.
Awadh became a **centre of unrest**.
Settlement: **Summary Revenue Settlement (1856)**.

181.s: Begum Hazrat Mahal’s political grievance during the Revolt of 1857 was primarily connected with
o: the loss of the Red Fort by Mughal successors
the annexation of Awadh and the proclamation of her son Birjis Qadr as ruler
the confiscation of Kunwar Singh’s estates
the denial of Baji Rao II’s pension
181.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal opposed the annexation of Awadh and had her son Birjis Qadr proclaimed ruler.
181.tq: Match the leader with the specific grievance and associated claimant.
xs: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** (Lucknow) resented the **annexation of Awadh**; her son **Birjis Qadr** was proclaimed ruler — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Red Fort** grievance was **Bahadur Shah Zafar's**; the **pension** grievance **Nana Saheb's**.
xa: ⚠ **Kanpur** = Nana Saheb; **Lucknow** = Begum Hazrat Mahal; **Jagdishpur** = Kunwar Singh; **Bareilly** = Khan Bahadur Khan.
Awadh's Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was exiled to Calcutta.

181.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Khan Bahadur Khan — proclaimed himself Nawab Nizam
Rani Lakshmibai — adopted son denied the throne
Kunwar Singh — ruined by loss of his estates
Bahadur Shah Zafar — denial of the pension of Baji Rao II
181.x: Denial of Baji Rao II’s pension was Nana Saheb’s grievance. Bahadur Shah Zafar’s grievance concerned the loss of title and the Red Fort for his successors.
181.tq: Find the swapped leader–grievance pair among closely related political grievances.
xs: **Bahadur Shah Zafar — Baji Rao II's pension** is wrong — so option **(4)** is the answer.
The pension grievance was **Nana Saheb's**; Zafar's was the **loss of title and Red Fort** for his successors.
Others are right: **Khan Bahadur Khan** proclaimed himself **Nawab Nizam**; **Rani Lakshmibai**'s adopted son was denied; **Kunwar Singh** lost his estates.
xa: Khan Bahadur Khan was a **Rohilla** chief at **Bareilly**.
Kunwar Singh was a zamindar of **Jagdishpur, Bihar**.

181.s: Which of the following states was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in spite of the presence of an adopted heir whose succession was refused?
181.x: Rani Lakshmibai’s adopted son, Damodar Rao, was not recognised as heir and Jhansi was annexed in 1853.
181.tq: Pair the adopted heir with the correct state rather than with another annexed territory.
