183.x: The revolt constituted the first great direct threat to British rule. Its heroes entered folklore and were later invoked during the Quit India and INA phases.
183.tq: Apply the historical significance to the broader political impact rather than to its immediate result.
xs: 1857 was the **first great direct threat** to British rule, and its heroes **entered folklore** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It did not create an independent government, and **urban elites stayed away**.
xa: Its heroes were invoked in the **Quit India** and **INA** phases.
It led to the **GoI Act 1858**: power to the **Crown**.

183.s: Which one of the following was NOT a major limitation of the Revolt of 1857?
o: Absence of a common programme and adequate resources
Participation of all major princes and urban elites
Lack of coordination and central leadership
183.x: Participation by all major princes and urban elites was not a limitation because many big princes and urban elites stayed away from the revolt. The other three were genuine weaknesses.
183.tq: Find the reversed comparison or participation claim among the genuine limitations.
xs: **Participation of all major princes and urban elites** was not a limitation — they in fact **stayed away** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
Real weaknesses: lack of **coordination, central leadership, programme and resources**, and a **narrow territorial and social base**.
xa: Loyal big states: **Hyderabad, Mysore, Scindia, Holkar**.
**APPSC-GS 2024**: the revolt was widespread **but failed**.

183.s: The later use of the Hindu-Muslim unity displayed during the Revolt of 1857 was significant because it was cited against the
183.x: The Hindu-Muslim unity associated with the revolt was later cited against the two-nation theory.
183.tq: Match the historical experience with the later political theory it was used to challenge.
xs: The **Hindu-Muslim unity** of 1857 was later cited against the **two-nation theory** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The unity showed in practice: rebels of both faiths fought under a common symbolic leader, **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
xa: Bahadur Shah's proclamations included a **ban on cow slaughter** and **joint commands**.
At Lucknow, **Hindus and Muslims shared offices**.

183.s: Which of the following was a major constitutional consequence of the Revolt of 1857?
o: The Act restored the authority of the East India Company over the Indian administration.
The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power to the Crown.
The Act abolished the office of Governor-General and created only provincial governments.
The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power to the elected Indian legislature.
183.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the governance of India from the East India Company to the British Crown.
183.tq: Identify the constitutional consequence while rejecting reversals of the transfer of power.
xs: The **GoI Act 1858** transferred power to the **Crown** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It kept the Governor-General, made a **Viceroy**, and created a **Secretary of State**.
xa: The Governor-General at the outbreak was **Lord Canning**.
1857 was the **first great direct threat** to British rule.

183.s: Who was the last major leader of the Revolt of 1857 to be executed?
183.x: Tantia Tope is regarded as the last major leader of the Revolt of 1857 to be executed.
183.tq: Use the LAST marker to distinguish the final major execution from other prominent leaders.
xs: **Tantia Tope** was the **last major leader executed** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Bahadur Shah Zafar** was **exiled to Rangoon**, not executed; **Azimullah Khan** was Nana Saheb's adviser.
xa: Tantia Tope fought at **Kanpur** and captured **Gwalior** with **Lakshmibai**.
⚠ **First outbreak** = **Barrackpore (29 Mar 1857)**; **great outbreak** = **Meerut (10 May 1857)**.

184.s: Which British officer is associated with the recapture of Delhi in September 1857?
184.x: John Nicholson was associated with the recapture of Delhi in September 1857 and was killed in the assault.
184.tq: Match the British officer with the centre recaptured, avoiding the Campbell–Delhi trap.
xs: **Delhi** was recaptured in **September 1857** by forces under **John Nicholson** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Nicholson** was **killed in the assault** on Delhi; **Hodson** captured the emperor.
**William Taylor** retook **Bihar** (Kunwar Singh); **Colin Campbell** retook **Kanpur**, **Lucknow** and **Bareilly**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes credit "General **Campbell**" with Delhi — Delhi was retaken by **Nicholson** and others in **Sept 1857**.
Delhi's rebel leaders: **Bahadur Shah II** (nominal) and **Bakht Khan** (real commander).
Exam angle: "Which centre was recaptured by the English?" — **Delhi** (UPPSC **2015**).

184.s: Henry Lawrence is associated with which of the following?
o: The recapture of Jhansi in April 1858
The suppression of the rising at Paralakimidi
The recapture of Delhi in September 1857
The defence of Lucknow Residency, where he was killed during the siege
184.x: Henry Lawrence was the Resident who defended Lucknow Residency and was killed during the siege.
184.tq: Identify the officer by his role at a besieged centre.
xs: **Sir Henry Lawrence** is linked with the **defence of Lucknow Residency**, where he was **killed during the siege** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He did **not** retake Lucknow; it was **relieved by Havelock-Outram and Campbell** and retaken in **March 1858**.
**Delhi** (Sept **1857**) was recaptured by **John Nicholson**, not Lawrence.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes list Henry Lawrence as Lucknow's "suppressor" — he died defending it.
Officers killed at Lucknow: **Sir Henry Lawrence**, **Gen. Neill**, **Havelock** (UPPSC **2008**).
Lucknow's rebel leader was **Begum Hazrat Mahal**.

184.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
184.x: Bihar was associated with Kunwar Singh and was recaptured by William Taylor. John Nicholson was associated with the recapture of Delhi.
184.tq: Find the swapped officer–centre pair.
xs: **Bihar — John Nicholson** is the wrong pair — so option **(4)** is the answer.
**Bihar** (Kunwar Singh) was retaken by **William Taylor**; **Nicholson** retook **Delhi** in **Sept 1857**.
**Bareilly** — **Colin Campbell** (**May 1858**) and **Kanpur** — **Sir Colin Campbell** (**Dec 1857**) are correct.
**Rani Lakshmibai** of Jhansi died fighting **Sir Hugh Rose**'s force, so Jhansi — Hugh Rose fits.
xa: Campbell's centres = **Kanpur**, **Lucknow**, **Bareilly**.
**Allahabad** and **Banaras** (Maulvi Liyakat Ali) were retaken by **Col. Neill**.
Bareilly's rebel leader was **Khan Bahadur Khan**.

184.s: Lucknow was finally retaken by the British in March 1858 after the efforts of:
184.x: Lucknow was relieved by Havelock-Outram and Campbell and was retaken in March 1858.
184.tq: Distinguish relief operations from the final recapture of a centre.
xs: Lucknow was **relieved by Havelock-Outram and Campbell** and finally retaken in **March 1858** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Nicholson** fell at **Delhi**; **William Taylor** worked in **Bihar**.
**Neill** and **Sir Henry Lawrence** were **killed at Lucknow**; they did not retake it.
xa: Lucknow's rebel leader: **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, who declared her son **Birjis Qadir** ruler.
Officers killed at Lucknow: **Henry Lawrence**, **Gen. Neill**, **Havelock** (UPPSC **2008**).
**Kanpur** was retaken by **Colin Campbell** in **Dec 1857**.

184.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sir Henry Lawrence died during the siege of Lucknow.
2. General Neill and Havelock were among the officers killed at Lucknow.
3. John Nicholson was killed at Lucknow.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: Sir Henry Lawrence, General Neill and Havelock were associated with deaths at Lucknow. Statement 3 is false because Nicholson fell during the assault on Delhi.
184.tq: Separate officers killed at Lucknow from the officer killed at Delhi.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **Sir Henry Lawrence** died **during the siege** of Lucknow.
Statement 2 is **correct**: **Gen. Neill** and **Havelock** were also among the officers killed at Lucknow.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **Nicholson fell at Delhi**, not Lucknow — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: The UPPSC **2008** key on officers killed at Lucknow: "**2, 3 and 4**" (Lawrence, Neill, Havelock).
Lucknow was retaken in **March 1858** after relief by **Havelock-Outram** and **Campbell**.
**Delhi** fell to the British in **Sept 1857**; **Hodson** captured the emperor.

184.s: Allahabad and Banaras were associated with the rebellion led by ______ and were recaptured by ______.
184.x: Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the rebellion at Allahabad and Banaras, which were recaptured by Colonel Neill.
184.tq: Match the rebel leader and British officer to the correct centres.
xs: **Allahabad** and **Banaras** were led by **Maulvi Liyakat Ali** and recaptured by **Colonel Neill** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Khan Bahadur Khan** led **Bareilly**; **Kunwar Singh** led **Bihar**; **Bakht Khan** led **Delhi**'s defence.
xa: **Neill** was later **killed at Lucknow**.
**Bihar** was retaken by **William Taylor**; **Delhi** by **John Nicholson** (**Sept 1857**).
**Bareilly** fell to **Colin Campbell** in **May 1858**.

184.s: Who among the following was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression of the revolt of 1857?
184.x: Sir Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression and later became known as Lord Clyde. He took over after General Anson died in 1857.
184.tq: Distinguish the civil head from the military commander.
xs: The **Commander-in-Chief** during the suppression was **Sir Colin Campbell** (later **Lord Clyde**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
He took over after **Gen. Anson** died in **1857**.
**Lord Canning** was the **Governor-General**, not the C-in-C.
xa: Campbell retook **Kanpur** (**Dec 1857**), **Lucknow** (with Havelock-Outram, **March 1858**) and **Bareilly** (**May 1858**).
A **Gorkha regiment** helped Campbell's suppression.
⚠ Trap: Delhi was **not** Campbell's — it was retaken by **Nicholson**.

184.s: Lord Canning was Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy from:
184.x: Lord Canning served as Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy in 1858, serving until 1862.
184.tq: Test the constitutional transition from Governor-General to Viceroy.
xs: **Lord Canning** became the **first Viceroy** in **1858** (serving till **1862**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
He had been **Governor-General** from **1856-58**.
xa: Canning formally **declared peace on 8 July 1858**.
The "**breakwaters to the storm**" label for loyal princes is credited to Canning (some notes: **Lord Elgin**).
Commander-in-Chief under him: **Sir Colin Campbell** (later **Lord Clyde**).

184.s: On which date did Canning declare peace after the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
184.x: Canning declared peace on 8 July 1858.
184.tq: Distinguish the declaration date from the dates of the main uprisings and recaptures.
xs: **Lord Canning** formally **declared peace on 8 July 1858** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**8 July 1857** is a year too early: Delhi was retaken only in **Sept 1857** and Lucknow in **March 1858**.
xa: Canning: Governor-General **1856-58** → first **Viceroy** **1858-62**.
Rani Lakshmibai **died fighting on 17 June 1858**, shortly before peace was declared.
The revolt was put down by **mid-1858**, after more than a year.

184.s: Who among the following coordinated communication among rebel leaders while serving as an adviser to Nana Saheb?
184.x: Azimullah Khan served as Nana Saheb's adviser and coordinated communication among rebel leaders.
184.tq: Distinguish adviser, military associate and political successor roles.
xs: **Azimullah Khan** served **Nana Saheb** as adviser and **coordinated communication** among rebel leaders — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Tantia Tope** was Nana Saheb's military commander; **Havelock** was a British officer; **Birjis Qadir** was Begum Hazrat Mahal's son.
xa: **Nana Saheb** (Kanpur) **escaped to Nepal**.
Other leaders: **Khan Bahadur Khan** — Rohilkhand; **Maulvi Ahmadullah** — Faizabad/Awadh.
**Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and reached **Delhi on 3 July 1857**.

184.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Tantia Tope — Nana Saheb
2. Tantia Tope — Lakshmibai
3. Birjis Qadr — Begum Hazrat Mahal
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
184.x: Tantia Tope served Nana Saheb and later fought with Lakshmibai. Birjis Qadr was the son of Begum Hazrat Mahal.
184.tq: Track an associate's changing allegiance and a family relationship together.
xs: Pair 1 is **correct**: **Tantia Tope** fought at **Kanpur** with **Nana Saheb**.
Pair 2 is **correct**: he **captured Gwalior** with **Rani Lakshmibai**.
Pair 3 is **correct**: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** declared her son **Birjis Qadir** ruler — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Tantia Tope fought on after Nana's escape; betrayed by **Man Singh**, captured and **executed** (April **1859**).
Lakshmibai **died fighting on 17 June 1858** near Gwalior against **Sir Hugh Rose**'s force.
⚠ **Nana Saheb** and **Hazrat Mahal** → **Nepal**; **Bahadur Shah** → **Rangoon**.

184.s:
Which of the following leaders and areas of operation is correctly matched?
1. Khan Bahadur Khan — Rohilkhand
2. Maulvi Ahmadullah — Faizabad
3. Kunwar Singh — Bihar
4. Tantia Tope — Central India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
184.x: All four pairs are correct. Khan Bahadur Khan operated in Rohilkhand, Ahmadullah in Faizabad, Kunwar Singh in Bihar, and Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare in Central India.
184.tq: Verify each leader–region pair before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four pairs are **correct** — option **(4)**.
**Khan Bahadur Khan** — **Rohilkhand**; **Maulvi Ahmadullah** — **Faizabad/Awadh**.
**Kunwar Singh** — **Jagdishpur/Arrah (Bihar)**; **Tantia Tope** — Kanpur, then **Central India**.
xa: Kunwar Singh was a **70-year-old zamindar** who waged guerrilla war; died April **1858**.
**Begum of Awadh** and **Maulvi Ahmadullah** quarrelled — an example of divided leadership.
**Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and commanded Delhi's defence.

184.s: Bahadur Shah II, who was the nominal leader of the revolt at Delhi, was ultimately:
o: Killed in the assault on Delhi
Executed at Delhi after a public trial
Captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon
184.x: Bahadur Shah II was captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon in Burma, where he died in 1862.
184.tq: Directly distinguish the fate of the principal rebel leaders.
xs: **Bahadur Shah II** was **captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon** (Burma) — so option **(3)** is correct.
He died there in **1862**; he was neither killed in the assault nor sent to Nepal.
xa: His **sons were shot by Hodson** and the **Mughal line ended**.
Real commander at Delhi: Gen. **Bakht Khan**.
Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to — **Rangoon**" (APPSC-G1 **2018**).
⚠ **Nana Saheb** and **Hazrat Mahal** → **Nepal**; **Tantia Tope** → executed.

184.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kunwar Singh — Took refuge at Agra
Begum Hazrat Mahal — Executed at Kanpur
184.x: Nana Saheb, the leader at Kanpur, escaped to Nepal. Tantia Tope was executed, Kunwar Singh died in Bihar, and Begum Hazrat Mahal fled to Nepal.
184.tq: Use leader–fate matching and reject swapped endings.
xs: **Nana Saheb — escaped to Nepal** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Tantia Tope** was **executed**, not exiled; **Rangoon** was **Bahadur Shah**'s exile.
**Kunwar Singh** died in **Bihar** (April **1858**); **Scindia** took refuge at **Agra**.
**Begum Hazrat Mahal** **fled to Nepal**; she was not executed.
xa: Nana Saheb's centre was **Kanpur**; his adviser was **Azimullah Khan**.
Kanpur was retaken by **Colin Campbell** in **Dec 1857**.

184.s: Tantia Tope was captured and executed after being betrayed by:
184.x: Tantia Tope was betrayed by Man Singh, captured and executed in April 1859.
184.tq: Test the specific betrayer rather than the associated British officer.
xs: **Tantia Tope** was **betrayed by Man Singh**, captured and **executed** (April **1859**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Scindia** was loyal to the British and fled to **Agra**; **Hugh Rose** and **Colin Campbell** were British commanders.
xa: Tantia Tope fought at **Kanpur**, then **Central India**, and fought on after **Nana Saheb**'s escape.
He **captured Gwalior** with **Rani Lakshmibai**.
⚠ Fates: **Bahadur Shah** → Rangoon; **Nana Saheb**, **Hazrat Mahal** → Nepal; **Tantia Tope** → executed.

184.s:
Consider the following statements about Rani Lakshmibai:
1. She captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope.
2. She died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858.
3. She died while defending Jhansi against Sir Colin Campbell.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: Rani Lakshmibai captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope and died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858 against Sir Hugh Rose's force. Statement 3 is false.
184.tq: Identify the wrong officer and location in a group of related statements.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: Lakshmibai **captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: she **died fighting on 17 June 1858** near Gwalior.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: she died near **Gwalior**, against **Sir Hugh Rose**'s force, not Campbell — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: She was proclaimed head of state on **4 June 1858** at Gwalior.
**Scindia**'s troops deserted to the Rani, and he took refuge at **Agra**.
Her centres: **Jhansi**, then **Gwalior**.

184.s: Which of the following statements regarding Kunwar Singh is correct?
o: He was a 70-year-old zamindar who waged guerrilla war in Bihar.
He was a young cavalry officer from Delhi.
He led the revolt at Kanpur and escaped to Nepal.
He was the ruler of Gwalior who joined the British.
184.x: Kunwar Singh was a 70-year-old zamindar of the Jagdishpur-Arrah region who conducted guerrilla warfare and died in April 1858.
184.tq: Combine age, social position, region and method to identify the leader.
xs: **Kunwar Singh** was a **70-year-old zamindar** who waged **guerrilla war** in **Bihar** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kanpur** and escape to **Nepal** describe **Nana Saheb**; the loyal ruler of **Gwalior** was **Scindia**.
xa: His centre: **Jagdishpur/Arrah**; he raised a fresh revolt in April **1858** and died in April **1858**.
**Bihar** was retaken by **William Taylor**.

184.s: Begum Hazrat Mahal declared her son ______ as the ruler of Lucknow and later fled to Nepal.
184.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal declared her son Birjis Qadir ruler of Lucknow and later fled to Nepal.
184.tq: Test the parent–proclaimed ruler relationship.
xs: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** declared her son **Birjis Qadir** ruler and later **fled to Nepal** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Bakht Khan** commanded **Delhi**; **Ahmadullah** led **Faizabad**; **Man Singh** betrayed **Tantia Tope**.
xa: Lucknow was relieved by **Havelock-Outram** and **Campbell**, retaken **March 1858**.
The **Begum of Awadh** quarrelled with **Maulvi Ahmadullah** — divided leadership.
⚠ **Nana Saheb** also fled to **Nepal**.

184.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the repression after the suppression of the revolt?
o: Only rebel leaders were fined, while ordinary rebels were released.
Rebels were generally pardoned without trial.
The British avoided punitive measures in Delhi.
Thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials.
184.x: The repression was harsh; thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials, and British troops also committed atrocities.
184.tq: Identify the precise description of the punitive policy.
xs: The repression was harsh: **thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials** — so option **(4)** is correct.
British troops also **committed atrocities**; there was no general pardon.
**Delhi** was punished: the emperor's **sons were shot by Hodson** and the Mughal line ended.
xa: **Bahadur Shah II** was tried and exiled to **Rangoon**.
The revolt was put down by **mid-1858** but shook British rule to its foundations.

184.s: After the recapture of Delhi, which of the following occurred?
o: Bahadur Shah was restored and his sons were pardoned.
Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, while his sons were shot by Hodson.
The Mughal line was strengthened under Birjis Qadir.
Bahadur Shah escaped to Nepal with Nana Saheb.
184.x: After Delhi was recaptured, Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, and his sons were shot by Hodson. The Mughal line consequently ended.
184.tq: Use the aftermath sequence to reject reversal and substitution traps.
xs: After Delhi's recapture, **Bahadur Shah** was **tried and deported**, and his **sons were shot by Hodson** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Mughal line ended**; Birjis Qadir was Begum Hazrat Mahal's son at **Lucknow**.
**Nana Saheb** escaped to **Nepal**; Bahadur Shah went to **Rangoon**.
xa: Delhi was retaken in **Sept 1857** by **John Nicholson**, who was killed in the assault.
Bahadur Shah died in Rangoon in **1862**.
Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to — **Rangoon**" (APPSC-G1 **2018**).

184.s: General Bakht Khan, who commanded the defence of Delhi in 1857, came to Delhi from:
184.x: Bakht Khan came from Bareilly and reached Delhi on 3 July 1857 (APPSC-GS 2023 key). Lucknow was Begum Hazrat Mahal's centre, Kanpur Nana Saheb's, and Faizabad Maulvi Ahmadullah's.
184.tq: Bakht Khan: Bareilly to Delhi, 3 July 1857.
xs: **Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and reached **Delhi on 3 July 1857** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lucknow** was **Begum Hazrat Mahal**'s centre, **Kanpur** Nana Saheb's, and **Faizabad** Maulvi Ahmadullah's.
xa: This is the APPSC-GS **2023** key.
Bakht Khan was the **real commander** at Delhi; **Bahadur Shah II** was nominal leader.
**Bareilly** itself was led by **Khan Bahadur Khan** and retaken by **Colin Campbell** (**May 1858**).

184.s: The revolt of 1857 was chiefly a revolt of the:
184.x: The revolt was chiefly of the Bengal Army; the Madras and Bombay armies largely remained loyal, while a Gorkha regiment assisted Campbell.
184.tq: Distinguish the principal rebel army from the loyal presidency armies.
xs: The revolt was chiefly one of the **Bengal Army** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Madras** and **Bombay** armies stayed **largely loyal**.
A **Gorkha regiment** actually **helped Campbell's suppression**.
xa: It was confined mostly to **North and Central India** (Doab); Bengal, Madras, Bombay regions largely peaceful.
Lack of support from the "**martial races**" of the north was a cause of failure.

184.s: Which one of the following rulers was regarded as most loyal to the British during the revolt, although his troops deserted to Rani Lakshmibai?
184.x: Scindia of Gwalior was regarded as most loyal to the British, but his troops deserted to Rani Lakshmibai.
184.tq: Separate the ruler's stand from the conduct of his troops.
xs: **Scindia of Gwalior** was the **most loyal** to the British (MPPSC **2010**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
His troops **deserted to the Rani**, and he took refuge at **Agra**.
**Holkar of Indore** also supported the British, but the "most loyal" key is Scindia; **Kunwar Singh** and **Nana Saheb** were rebels.
xa: Rani Lakshmibai and Tantia Tope **captured Gwalior**; she was proclaimed head of state there on **4 June 1858**.
Sikh chiefs of **Patiala, Nabha, Jind** actively helped the British.

184.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Holkar of Indore — Supported the British
2. Sikh chiefs of Patiala, Nabha and Jind — Actively helped the British
3. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Diwan Salar Jung I — Kept the Deccan quiet
4. Bhonsle state of Nagpur — Joined the revolt under its ruling prince
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
184.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because Nagpur had already been annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854, leaving no ruler to join the revolt.
184.tq: Use a wrong-status and wrong-timeline trap in a coded statement set.
xs: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are **correct**: **Holkar** supported the British; **Sikh chiefs** actively helped; **Nizam** and **Salar Jung I** kept the Deccan quiet.
Pair 4 is **wrong**: **Nagpur** was already annexed under the **Doctrine of Lapse** (**1854**), leaving no ruler to join — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **Scindia of Gwalior** was the most loyal (MPPSC **2010**).
Larger states — **Hyderabad**, **Mysore**, **Rajput chiefs** — ignored Bahadur Shah's appeals.
AP angle: the **Hyderabad Residency attack** (**17 July 1857**) was repulsed.

184.s: The loyal princes were described as “breakwaters to the storm” by:
184.x: The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to Lord Canning, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
184.tq: Discriminate between two authorities associated with a memorable phrase.
xs: The loyal princes were called "**breakwaters to the storm**" by **Lord Canning** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Some notes credit **Lord Elgin**, but the standard key is Canning.
xa: Big **zamindars and moneylenders** also acted as "breakwaters" to protect class interests.
Loyal princes: **Scindia**, **Holkar**, Sikh chiefs, **Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula**.
Canning: Governor-General **1856-58**, first **Viceroy** **1858-62**.

184.s: The educated middle class generally remained neutral during the revolt because it viewed it as:
o: A movement led by urban merchants
184.x: The educated middle class generally saw the revolt as a backward-looking feudal reaction and therefore remained neutral.
184.tq: Link a social class with its stated interpretation of the revolt.
xs: The **educated middle class** stayed **neutral**, seeing the revolt as a **backward-looking feudal reaction** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is a UPSC **1998** angle.
xa: **Merchants** and the **urban elite** did not support the revolt.
Participants: **sepoys**, **peasants**, **artisans**, **dispossessed rulers**.
Failure factor: **no forward-looking programme** or modern nationalist vision.

184.s: Which of the following groups acted as “breakwaters” during the revolt in order to protect their class interests?
184.x: Big zamindars and moneylenders acted as “breakwaters” because they sought to protect their class interests.
184.tq: Match the social group with its distinctive political role.
xs: **Big zamindars and moneylenders** acted as "**breakwaters**" to protect their **class interests** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Sepoys**, **peasants**, **artisans** and **dispossessed rulers** took part in the revolt.
The **educated middle class** stayed **neutral**.
xa: Canning applied "**breakwaters to the storm**" to the loyal **princes**.
Loyal princes plus big zamindars are listed among the causes of failure.

184.s: Which one of the following groups did NOT support the revolt of 1857?
184.x: Merchants and the urban elite generally did not support the revolt. Sepoys, peasants, artisans and dispossessed rulers took part in it.
184.tq: Find the social group that remained aloof among participating groups.
xs: **Merchants and the urban elite** did **not support** the revolt — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Sepoys**, **peasants** and **artisans** (with dispossessed rulers) **took part**.
xa: The **educated middle class** stayed **neutral** (UPSC **1998**).
Big **zamindars and moneylenders** acted as "breakwaters".
Hence its **limited territorial and social base** — a reason for failure.

184.s: Which one of the following regions was largely peaceful during the revolt of 1857?
184.x: The revolt was concentrated mainly in North and Central India, while Bengal, Madras and Bombay regions remained largely peaceful.
184.tq: Find the region that falls outside the principal geographical base of the revolt.
xs: **Madras Presidency** stayed **largely peaceful** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The revolt was confined mostly to **North and Central India** (the **Doab**); Bengal, Madras and Bombay regions were peaceful.
xa: The **Madras** and **Bombay armies** were largely loyal; it was chiefly a **Bengal Army** revolt.
British power intact in **East, West and South** India let them send troops north.
**Nizam** and **Salar Jung I** kept the **Deccan** quiet.

184.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the failure of the revolt of 1857:
1. It lacked an all-India character.
2. It had no unified ideology or forward-looking nationalist programme.
3. The rebels possessed superior arms and a centralised system of communication.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: The revolt lacked an all-India character and a unified modern nationalist programme. Statement 3 is false because the rebels had inferior arms and poor communication and coordination.
184.tq: Spot the reversed military and communication comparison.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the revolt had **no all-India character**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: **no unified ideology or leadership**, no modern nationalist vision.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: rebels had **swords, spears, old muskets**, while the British had **Enfield rifles** and the **electric telegraph** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Exam angle: BPSC **2023** set (military superiority, no unified programme, lack of support from all sections) — all correct.
Leaders quarrelled, e.g. **Begum of Awadh vs Maulvi Ahmadullah**.

184.s: The military disadvantage of the rebels during the revolt was mainly due to their dependence on:
184.x: The rebels generally used swords, spears and old muskets, whereas the British had Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph.
184.tq: Compare the weaponry and communication systems of the two sides.
xs: The rebels depended on **swords, spears and old muskets** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Enfield rifles** and the **electric telegraph** were **British** advantages, not the rebels'.
xa: Rebels also lacked **discipline** and **central coordination**.
British had **experienced generals** and troops sent north from East, West and South India.

184.s: Which one of the following was NOT a reason for the failure of the revolt of 1857?
o: Unified leadership under a modern nationalist programme
British ability to send troops from eastern, western and southern India
184.x: The revolt had no unified leadership or modern nationalist programme. The other options were factors contributing to its failure.
184.tq: Find the option that states the opposite of a recognised weakness.
xs: **Unified leadership under a modern nationalist programme** is the odd one — the revolt **lacked** it — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Absence of modern nationalism**, British troops from **East, West and South**, and a **limited territorial and social base** were real causes of failure.
xa: **Bahadur Shah** was old and weak; leaders quarrelled.
Rebels' **poor arms** vs British **Enfield rifles** and **telegraph**.

184.s: Which one of the following combinations contributed to the failure of the revolt of 1857?
o: A common programme for a future society
Unified central command, modern weapons and telegraph communication among rebels
Complete participation of East, West and South India
Loyal princes, loyal big zamindars and inadequate support from the martial races of the north
184.x: The revolt suffered because several princes and big zamindars remained loyal and it lacked adequate support from the martial races of the north.
184.tq: Combine political and military causes without reversing their direction.
xs: **Loyal princes**, **big zamindars** and lack of support from the north's "**martial races**" contributed to failure — so option **(4)** is correct.
The rebels had **no common programme**, **no central command**, no modern weapons or telegraph.
**East, West and South** India stayed largely **peaceful**.
xa: "**Breakwaters to the storm**" — Canning's label for the loyal princes.
**Scindia**, **Holkar**, Sikh chiefs and the **Nizam** all stood by the British.

184.s: Which one of the following best describes the historical significance of the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
o: It ended all resistance to British rule in India permanently.
It resulted in the immediate withdrawal of the British from India.
Although suppressed, it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
It strengthened British rule without causing any major impact.
184.x: The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, but its impact was profound because it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
184.tq: Choose the precise consequence while rejecting extreme claims such as ‘all’ and ‘immediate’.
xs: Though put down by **mid-1858**, the revolt **shook British rule to its foundations** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It lasted **more than a year**; it neither ended resistance nor made the British withdraw.
xa: Canning formally **declared peace on 8 July 1858**.
Later leaders such as **Bose** and **Bhagat Singh** only invoked its legacy.
Odd one out: **Bhagat Singh** not associated with 1857 (APPSC-GS **2019**).

184.s: Rani Avantibai Lodhi, remembered for her resistance during the Revolt of 1857, belonged to which place?
184.x: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was the ruler of Ramgarh in Madhya Pradesh. Mandla is only where she fought, beating Charles Waddington's force at the Battle of Kheri near Mandla; it was not her state.
184.tq: Distinguish the person’s place of association from the nearby location of the battle.
xs: **Rani Avantibai Lodhi** was of **Ramgarh** (MP) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Mandla** is only where she fought: she beat **Charles Waddington**'s force at the **Battle of Kheri** near Mandla.
xa: She **died fighting in 1858**.
She is remembered on her martyrdom day (**1 Sep 2026**).
Other women leaders: **Rani Lakshmibai** (Jhansi/Gwalior), **Begum Hazrat Mahal** (Lucknow).

184.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Hyderabad during the Revolt of 1857:
1. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula remained loyal to the British.
2. Salar Jung I remained loyal to the British.
3. The attack on the Hyderabad Residency on 17 July 1857 was repulsed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: All three statements are correct. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal, and the Hyderabad Residency attack of 17 July 1857 was repulsed.
184.tq: Combine the loyalty and event statements, checking the date and outcome separately.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: **Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula** and Diwan **Salar Jung I** stayed **loyal**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: the **Hyderabad Residency attack** (**17 July 1857**) was **repulsed** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: They **kept the Deccan quiet**.
Other large states that stayed out: **Mysore** and the **Rajput chiefs**.
**Scindia of Gwalior** was the most loyal (MPPSC **2010**).

185.s: In the British Parliament, Benjamin Disraeli characterised the uprising of 1857 primarily as which of the following?
o: A religious war confined to Awadh
A purely military mutiny without popular support
185.x: Disraeli questioned whether the event was merely a military mutiny or a national revolt, and viewed it as a national rising.
185.tq: Distinguish between closely related historiographical descriptions.
xs: **Benjamin Disraeli**, in Parliament, saw 1857 as a **national rising**, not a mere mutiny — so option **(4)** is correct.
He asked whether it was a **military mutiny** or a **national revolt**, and leaned to the latter — ruling out "purely military mutiny".
xa: **Karl Marx** also called it a **national revolt**.
The "mere **Sepoy Mutiny**" view belongs to the imperialist school: **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**, **P.E. Roberts**.
**Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** blamed the absence of Indians in the **Legislative Council**.

185.s: Which one of the following was identified by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan as the main cause of the revolt of 1857?
o: The decline of the textile industry in Bengal
The annexation of Punjab by the British
The introduction of the Subsidiary Alliance
The absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
185.x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council caused the rulers to misunderstand the ruled.
185.tq: Test the precise cause attributed by an identified contemporary observer.
xs: **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** held that the main cause was **no Indian in the Legislative Council** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Without Indians in the Council, the **rulers misunderstood the ruled**.
xa: His book: **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** (Causes of the Indian Revolt), **1859**.
Contemporaries: **Disraeli** — national rising; **Karl Marx** — national revolt.

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding interpretations of the Revolt of 1857:
1. Benjamin Disraeli regarded it as a national rising rather than a mere mutiny.
2. Karl Marx regarded it as a national revolt.
3. V.D. Savarkar regarded it as a planned First War of Indian Independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: All three statements are correct. Disraeli, Marx and Savarkar rejected the narrow interpretation of the revolt as merely a sepoy mutiny, though Savarkar gave it the specific nationalist title.
185.tq: Check each historian against the precise nationalist interpretation.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **Disraeli** saw a **national rising**, not a mere mutiny.
Statement 2 is **correct**: **Karl Marx** called it a **national revolt**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: **V.D. Savarkar** called it the planned **First War of Indian Independence** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Exam angle: "Who first called it the First Indian War of Independence?" — **Savarkar** (BPSC **2022**, **2024**).
⚠ **R.C. Majumdar**: "**Neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**" (UPPSC **2017**).
Marx and Engels' articles were compiled as **The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859**.

185.s: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' articles on the uprising were compiled under which title?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859
185.x: Karl Marx's and Friedrich Engels' articles were compiled as The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859.
185.tq: Match the compilation title with the pair of writers associated with it.
xs: **Karl Marx** and **Engels**' articles were compiled as **The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857** is **R.C. Majumdar**'s book (**1957**).
xa: **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** — **S.N. Sen** (**1957**), the Government of India-commissioned centenary history.
**Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** — **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** (**1859**).
**Awadh in Revolt** — **Rudrangshu Mukherjee**; **Discovery of India** — **Nehru**.

185.s: Which of the following historians characterised the uprising of 1857 as a purely military outbreak or a mere sepoy mutiny?
185.x: Sir John Lawrence, along with J.R. Seeley and Charles Raikes, regarded the uprising primarily as a sepoy mutiny and denied it a popular or national character.
185.tq: Match the historian with the distinctive verdict.
xs: **Sir John Lawrence** (with **J.R. Seeley** and **Charles Raikes**) saw it as a mere **Sepoy Mutiny** — a purely military outbreak — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S.N. Sen**: a fight for religion that became a **war of independence**; **Disraeli**: a **national rising**.
**T.R. Holmes**: a conflict between **civilisation and barbarism**.
xa: **P.E. Roberts**: "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over **greased cartridges**.
**L.E.R. Rees**: a war of **fanatic religionists against Christians**.
**Outram** and **W. Taylor**: a **Muslim/Hindu-Muslim conspiracy** exploiting Hindu grievances.

185.s: Which one of the following pairs of historian and interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 is correctly matched?
o: Sir James Outram — a Muslim conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances
L.E.R. Rees — a conflict between civilisation and barbarism
T.R. Holmes — a war of fanatic religionists against Christians
P.E. Roberts — a national rising against foreign rule
185.x: Outram (with W. Taylor) saw it as a Muslim (Hindu-Muslim) conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances, so A is right. B and C are swapped: Rees called it a war of fanatic religionists against Christians and Holmes a conflict between civilisation and barbarism. D is wrong: P.E. Roberts called it just a sepoy mutiny over greased cartridges.
185.tq: Outram = conspiracy; Rees = religion; Holmes = civilisation vs barbarism.
xs: **Sir James Outram** (with **W. Taylor**) saw a **Muslim conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Options 2 and 3 are **swapped**: **Rees** = fanatic religionists against Christians; **Holmes** = civilisation vs barbarism.
**P.E. Roberts** called it "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over greased cartridges, not a national rising.
xa: The imperialist "Sepoy Mutiny" school also included **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**.
The "**national rising**" view came from **Disraeli**; Marx called it a **national revolt**.

185.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Roberts — Revolt as the first war of independence
Savarkar — Revolt as a sepoy mutiny
Roberts — Revolt as a sepoy mutiny
Canning — Revolt as a peasant uprising only
185.x: Roberts described the event as a ‘sepoy mutiny’, whereas Savarkar described it as the ‘first war of independence’.
185.tq: Discriminate between similar historical interpretations by matching each label with its associated thinker.
xs: **P.E. Roberts** called it "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over **greased cartridges** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Savarkar** called it the **First War of Indian Independence**, not a sepoy mutiny — so options 1 and 2 are reversed.
xa: Others in the imperialist school: **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**.
Exam angle: **Savarkar** first called it the First Indian War of Independence (BPSC **2022**, **2024**).

185.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians is associated with:
185.x: L.E.R. Rees interpreted the revolt as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians.
185.tq: Discriminate between historians whose interpretations concern religion and mutiny.
xs: **L.E.R. Rees** called it a war of **fanatic religionists against Christians** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Charles Raikes** and **P.E. Roberts** saw a mere **Sepoy Mutiny**; **R.C. Majumdar**: "**neither first, nor national**".
xa: ⚠ Confusable: **T.R. Holmes** = conflict between **civilisation and barbarism**.
**Outram** and **W. Taylor**: a **Muslim/Hindu-Muslim conspiracy**.

185.s: Who described the Revolt of 1857 as a conflict between civilisation and barbarism?
185.x: T.R. Holmes described the revolt as a conflict between civilisation and barbarism.
185.tq: Use the exact phrase to identify the associated historian.
xs: **T.R. Holmes** called it a conflict between **civilisation and barbarism** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**L.E.R. Rees**: fanatic religionists against **Christians**; **W. Taylor** (with Outram): a **Muslim conspiracy**; **Karl Marx**: a **national revolt**.
xa: All these belong to the **British / imperialist** school, which denied it a **national character**.
**P.E. Roberts**: "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over greased cartridges.

185.s: The term 'Sepoy Mutiny' or 'Indian Mutiny' was predominantly used by which school of historians?
185.x: British or imperialist historians commonly used the labels Sepoy Mutiny or Indian Mutiny and denied the revolt a national character.
185.tq: Associate the label with the historiographical school that used it.
xs: **Sepoy Mutiny / Indian Mutiny** are the labels of **British / imperialist** historians — so option **(2)** is correct.
They blamed **religious fanaticism** and **administrative blunders** and denied a **national character**.
xa: Indian historians: **Great Rebellion**; **Savarkar**: **First War of Independence**.
Other names: **Revolt of 1857**, **Indian Insurrection**.
Imperialist names: **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**, **P.E. Roberts**.

185.s: Which one of the following labels was particularly associated with Indian nationalist interpretations of the uprising of 1857?
185.x: Indian nationalist historians commonly used the label Great Rebellion, while First War of Independence was especially associated with V.D. Savarkar.
185.tq: Distinguish a broad nationalist label from the specific Savarkar formulation.
xs: Indian nationalist historians used the label **Great Rebellion** (and **First War of Independence**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Indian Mutiny**, **religious fanaticism** and **administrative blunders** belong to the **British / imperialist** reading.
xa: **First War of Independence** is especially **Savarkar**'s label.
⚠ Trap: some tables put **R.C. Majumdar** with Savarkar and Sen — learn him as the **sceptic**.

185.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: V.D. Savarkar — First War of Independence
British or imperialist school — Sepoy Mutiny
Other names — Religious Fanaticism and Administrative Blunders
185.x: Revolt of 1857 and Indian Insurrection are listed as other names. Religious fanaticism and administrative blunders were explanations associated with the British or imperialist interpretation.
185.tq: Separate labels from explanatory causes in a school-wise classification.
xs: **Religious fanaticism and administrative blunders** are not "other names" — they are the **imperialist explanations** — so option **(4)** is the mismatch.
The real other names are **Revolt of 1857** and **Indian Insurrection**.
**Savarkar** — First War of Independence; Indian historians — **Great Rebellion**; British — **Sepoy Mutiny**: all correct.
xa: The **feudal reaction** view: dispossessed princes and taluqdars fighting to restore lost positions.
⚠ **R.C. Majumdar**'s own verdict (UPPSC **2017**) is opposite to the nationalist school.

185.s: Who first described the Revolt of 1857 as the 'First War of Indian Independence'?
185.x: V.D. Savarkar called it the First War of Indian Independence, a planned rising and not a mere mutiny. Tilak is a common distractor. R.C. Majumdar held the opposite view: 'neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence'. S.N. Sen wrote the official centenary history Eighteen Fifty-Seven.
185.tq: First War of Independence = Savarkar; Majumdar is the sceptic.
xs: **V.D. Savarkar** first called it the **First War of Indian Independence** — a planned rising, not a mere mutiny — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Tilak** is a stock distractor; **R.C. Majumdar** said "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**".
**S.N. Sen** wrote the official centenary history **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**).
xa: Exam angle: BPSC **2022**, **2024**.
**Sen**: "What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence".
Andhra nationalist writing too treated 1857 as India's first war of independence.

185.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: T.R. Holmes — Conflict between civilisation and barbarism
Benjamin Disraeli — National rising, not a mere mutiny
S.N. Sen — War of fanatic religionists against Christians
185.x: The description of the revolt as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians was given by L.E.R. Rees. S.N. Sen stated that a fight for religion ended as a war of independence.
185.tq: Find the swapped historian and verdict.
xs: **S.N. Sen — fanatic religionists against Christians** is wrong; that was **L.E.R. Rees** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
**Sen** said "what began as a **fight for religion** ended as a **war of independence**".
**Holmes** (civilisation vs barbarism), **Disraeli** (national rising) and **Marx** (national revolt) are correctly matched.
xa: ⚠ **Sen** = religion → war of independence; **Majumdar** = "neither first, nor national"; both = **embryonic** nationalism.
Sen's **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**) was the Government-commissioned centenary history.

185.s: “What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence” was the assessment of:
185.x: S.N. Sen concluded that the revolt began as a fight for religion but ultimately developed into a war of independence.
185.tq: Identify the historian from the famous concluding formulation.
xs: "What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence" is **S.N. Sen**'s verdict — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Savarkar** saw a planned **First War of Independence**; **Majumdar**: "neither first, nor national"; **Disraeli**: a **national rising**.
xa: Sen wrote **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**), the official centenary history.
Sen and Majumdar both judged mid-19th-century nationalism **embryonic** (MPPSC **2020**).

185.s: With reference to the assessment of Indian nationalism in the middle of the nineteenth century, which of the following is correct?
o: It was rejected as embryonic by both R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen.
It had already become fully developed and uniform throughout India.
It was regarded as being only embryonic by R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen.
It was confined exclusively to the British army.
185.x: R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen both regarded Indian nationalism in the mid-nineteenth century as still embryonic.
185.tq: Avoid the extreme wording in the distractors and select the qualified description.
xs: **R.C. Majumdar** and **S.N. Sen** held that Indian nationalism in the mid-19th century was only **embryonic** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They did not reject it, nor call it fully developed — it was in an **embryonic stage** (MPPSC **2020**).
xa: Majumdar: "**Neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**" (UPPSC **2017**).
Sen: began as a **fight for religion**, ended as a **war of independence**.
**Modern nationalism** had not yet emerged — a reason 1857 was not a "first war of independence".

185.s: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between S.N. Sen's and R.C. Majumdar's centenary histories?
o: Majumdar's work was Government-commissioned, whereas Sen wrote independently outside the centenary project.
Sen's work was Government-commissioned, whereas Majumdar wrote independently after parting with the official project.
Both were official Government of India volumes and reached the same conclusion about independence.
185.x: S.N. Sen's Eighteen Fifty-Seven was the Government of India-commissioned centenary history. R.C. Majumdar wrote his 1957 work independently after parting with the official project.
185.tq: Compare the commissioning status and institutional context of the two works.
xs: **S.N. Sen**'s **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** was **Government of India-commissioned**; **Majumdar** wrote independently after parting with the official project — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both came out in **1957** (centenary) and reached **different** conclusions.
xa: Majumdar's book: **The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857**.
Majumdar's verdict: "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**".
Sen's verdict: a fight for religion that ended as a **war of independence**.

185.s: R.C. Majumdar's interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 differs from the nationalist interpretation attributed to him in some classifications because he specifically argued that it was:
o: the first, national and completely successful war of independence
only a conflict between civilisation and barbarism
neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence
185.x: R.C. Majumdar's own verdict was that the revolt was neither the first nor national nor a war of independence, despite some classifications placing him in a broader nationalist school.
185.tq: Resolve the apparent contradiction by separating a school classification from the historian's own verdict.
xs: **R.C. Majumdar** argued 1857 was "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**" — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is his own verdict (UPPSC **2017**), though some tables put him in the nationalist "first war" school.
The **Hindu-Muslim conspiracy** view is **Outram**'s; **civilisation vs barbarism** is **T.R. Holmes**'.
xa: ⚠ Trap: learn Majumdar as the **sceptic**, opposite **Savarkar**.
He also judged mid-19th-century nationalism **embryonic** (with **S.N. Sen**).

185.s: Which one of the following books was written by R.C. Majumdar?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
185.x: R.C. Majumdar wrote The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857, published in 1957.
185.tq: Distinguish similar 1857 titles by their authors.
xs: **R.C. Majumdar** wrote **The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857** (**1957**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Eighteen Fifty-Seven** is **S.N. Sen**'s official centenary history.
xa: Majumdar wrote independently after **parting with the official project**.
Other books: **Awadh in Revolt** — Rudrangshu Mukherjee; **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (**1859**).

185.s: The statement that the uprising essentially represented a feudal rising was made by:
185.x: Jawaharlal Nehru described the uprising as essentially a feudal rising in The Discovery of India.
185.tq: Use the author-and-verdict association rather than the broader nationalist label.
xs: **Jawaharlal Nehru** called it essentially a **feudal rising**, in **Discovery of India** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**R.C. Majumdar** said "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**".
xa: The **feudal reaction** view: dispossessed princes and taluqdars (**Nana Saheb**, **Lakshmibai**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal**) fighting to restore lost positions.
It is seen as a **traditional uprising**, not a modern nationalist movement.

185.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a feudal reaction primarily emphasises the role of:
o: dispossessed princes and taluqdars attempting to restore their lost positions
urban middle classes demanding representative government
European merchants opposing the East India Company
185.x: The feudal-reaction interpretation highlights dispossessed princes and taluqdars such as Nana Saheb, Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal, who sought to recover lost positions.
185.tq: Apply the interpretation to the social groups and motives it highlights.
xs: The **feudal reaction** view stresses **dispossessed princes and taluqdars** trying to **restore their lost positions** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Examples: **Nana Saheb**, **Lakshmibai**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal**.
The **educated middle class** stayed **aloof**, so it was no middle-class demand.
xa: **Nehru** (Discovery of India) called it essentially a **feudal rising**.
Verdict: a **traditional uprising**, not a modern nationalist movement.

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Eric Stokes's interpretation of the revolt of 1857:
1. He emphasised local and agrarian studies.
2. He viewed the revolt as a combination of several peasant and elite risings.
3. He treated it as a single centrally directed national movement.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: Eric Stokes emphasised local agrarian studies and interpreted the revolt as multiple peasant and elite risings, not as one centrally directed movement.
185.tq: Find the statement that reverses a historian’s interpretation.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **Eric Stokes** stressed **local, agrarian studies**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: he saw **many peasant and elite risings**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: he saw them **rather than one movement** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **Rudrangshu Mukherjee**: popular resistance of **peasants and taluqdars in Awadh** (**Awadh in Revolt**).
Peasants and artisans joined in **Awadh** and **western UP**, hit by revenue burden and ruin of crafts.

185.s: Rudrangshu Mukherjee’s *Awadh in Revolt* primarily examines—
o: the military organisation of the Bombay Army
the role of the educated middle class in Bengal
the activities of Indian revolutionaries abroad
popular resistance by peasants and taluqdars in Awadh
185.x: *Awadh in Revolt* focuses on the popular resistance of peasants and taluqdars in Awadh.
185.tq: Match a historian’s work with its specific regional and social focus.
xs: **Rudrangshu Mukherjee**'s **Awadh in Revolt** studies **popular resistance by peasants and taluqdars in Awadh** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **educated middle class** stayed aloof; the book is not about it.
xa: **Eric Stokes**: local, agrarian studies — **many peasant and elite risings** rather than one movement.
**Taluqdars** and zamindars of **Awadh** joined in large numbers.

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the limitations of describing the Revolt of 1857 as the First War of Independence:
1. There was no common goal among all the participants.
2. Modern nationalism had not yet emerged.
3. The revolt was confined largely to North India.
4. Most of India remained neutral.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: All four statements are cited as limitations: the revolt lacked a common goal, modern nationalism was not yet developed, its main spread was in North India, and most of India remained neutral.
185.tq: Test the complete set of qualifications rather than selecting only the geographical limitation.
xs: All four are **correct** — option **(4)**.
**No common goal**, and **modern nationalism** had yet to emerge.
It was confined largely to **North India**, and **most of India** stayed neutral; elite and urban classes uninvolved.
xa: It began as a **military mutiny** and became a **popular rebellion**.
It was a **traditional uprising** against a common foreign enemy.
Even so it **shook British rule**.

185.s: Which one of the following best describes the initial character and subsequent spread of the revolt of 1857?
o: It began as a peasant movement and remained confined to villages
It began as a constitutional agitation and became a princely movement
It began as a religious reform movement and became an urban strike
It began as a military mutiny and rapidly developed into a popular rebellion
185.x: The revolt began among soldiers but quickly drew in rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people, becoming a wider popular rebellion.
185.tq: Test the transformation of an event from its initial to its later character.
xs: It began as a **military mutiny** and quickly became a **popular rebellion** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Rulers**, **peasants**, **soldiers** and **common people** joined in.
xa: Sepoys spearheaded at **Meerut** (**10 May 1857**); Delhi seized **11-12 May**.
It was **not a modern nationalist movement**: the idea of one Indian nation-state had not emerged.

185.s:
Consider the following statements about the national character of the revolt of 1857:
1. The idea of a single Indian nation-state had not yet emerged.
2. It was a modern nationalist movement based on a common programme for a future society.
3. It was a traditional uprising in which different classes defended local, economic and religious interests against a common foreign enemy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The revolt was not a modern nationalist movement with a common future-oriented programme, making statement 2 incorrect.
185.tq: Separate a traditional anti-foreign uprising from modern nationalism.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the idea of **one Indian nation-state** had not yet emerged.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: it was **not a modern nationalist movement**; there was **no common goal**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: a **traditional uprising** of classes defending local, economic and religious interests against a **common foreign enemy** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: **Majumdar** and **Sen**: mid-19th-century nationalism was only **embryonic**.
The revolt was confined largely to **North India**.

185.s: With reference to the consequences of the revolt of 1857, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It failed militarily but seriously shook British rule.
Its failure left British rule completely unaffected.
It succeeded in establishing a united Indian nation-state.
It resulted immediately in the withdrawal of the British from India.
185.x: Although the revolt failed, it shook British rule and later became a source of inspiration for Indian nationalism.
185.tq: Avoid the extreme conclusion that military failure means historical insignificance.
xs: The revolt **failed** but **shook British rule** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It **shattered the myth of British invincibility** and planted seeds of later nationalism.
xa: Its heroes (**Lakshmibai**, **Kunwar Singh**, **Tantia Tope**, **Zafar**) were later invoked by **Bose** and **Bhagat Singh**.
After 1857 the British turned to **divide and rule**.

185.s: The revolt at Meerut, which marked the spearhead of sepoy participation in 1857, began on—
185.x: The sepoy uprising began at Meerut on 10 May 1857.
185.tq: Discriminate between closely spaced dates in an event sequence.
xs: The sepoy rising at **Meerut** began on **10 May 1857** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**11-12 May** is when **Delhi was seized**; **29 March 1857** is **Mangal Pandey**'s act at **Barrackpore**.
xa: Sepoys were the **spearhead** of the revolt.
Mangal Pandey was **hanged/executed on 8 April 1857**.

185.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
185.x: Kunwar Singh led the revolt in Bihar, whereas Khan Bahadur Khan was associated with Bareilly.
185.tq: Find the swapped leader and centre in a regional matching question.
xs: **Kunwar Singh — Bareilly** is wrong — he led in **Bihar**; Bareilly was **Khan Bahadur Khan**'s — so option **(1)** is the answer.
**Begum Hazrat Mahal — Lucknow**, **Lakshmibai — Jhansi**, **Nana Saheb — Kanpur** are correct.
xa: These **deposed rulers** led the revolt locally.
Feudal-reaction reading: dispossessed princes fighting to **restore lost positions**.

185.s:
Consider the following statements about participation in the Revolt of 1857:
1. The taluqdars and zamindars of Awadh joined in large numbers.
2. The big zamindars of Bengal also joined the revolt in large numbers.
3. Peasants and artisans joined in Awadh and western UP, hit by the revenue burden and the ruin of crafts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
185.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the big zamindars of Bengal stayed loyal. So B; A, C and D include the false statement 2.
185.tq: Awadh landed + peasants joined; Bengal zamindars loyal.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **taluqdars and zamindars of Awadh** joined in large numbers.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: the **big zamindars of Bengal stayed loyal**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: **peasants and artisans** of **Awadh and western UP** joined — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Merchants and moneylenders** were also loyal, as were **most princes**.
**Rudrangshu Mukherjee**'s **Awadh in Revolt** studies these peasants and taluqdars.

185.s: Why did the educated middle class largely remain aloof from the revolt of 1857?
o: It considered British rule to be modernising.
It was led by the taluqdars of Awadh.
It had already established an independent national government.
It opposed all forms of education introduced by the British.
185.x: The educated middle class generally remained aloof because it viewed British rule as modernising.
185.tq: Identify the attitude of a social group rather than its formal position.
xs: The **educated middle class** **stayed aloof** because it saw British rule as **modernising** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **taluqdars of Awadh** were a separate group that joined the revolt.
xa: Elite and urban classes uninvolved — one reason 1857 is not called a "first war of independence".
Loyal too: **most princes**, **merchants and moneylenders**.

185.s: Which one of the following groups was generally loyal to the British during the revolt of 1857?
o: Most princes, including Scindia, Holkar, the Nizam and the rulers of Rajputana
185.x: Most princes, including Scindia, Holkar, the Nizam and the rulers of Rajputana, remained loyal to the British.
185.tq: Use the group-level exception to avoid assuming universal princely participation.
xs: **Most princes** — **Scindia**, **Holkar**, the **Nizam** and **Rajputana** — stayed **loyal** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Taluqdars of Awadh**, **sepoys** and **peasants and artisans** of Awadh took part.
xa: **Merchants and moneylenders** and the **big zamindars of Bengal** were also loyal.
AP: Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daulah** stayed pro-British (APHQ **2001**, **2025**).

185.s: Which one of the following statements about the Andhra region during the revolt of 1857 is NOT correct?
o: There were attempts at Kadiri and revolts associated with Korukonda Subba Reddy and Dandasena.
Turrebaz Khan was associated with a limited revolt in Hyderabad.
Andhra had no local leaders or limited revolts during the period.
185.x: The statement that Andhra had no local leaders or limited revolts is incorrect. Turrebaz Khan, the Kadiri attempt, Korukonda Subba Reddy and Dandasena are associated with such activity.
185.tq: Reject an absolute statement when several regional exceptions are identified.
xs: "**Andhra had no local leaders**" is **false** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Limited revolts: **Turrebaz Khan** (Hyderabad), an attempt at **Kadiri** (Rayalaseema), **Korukonda Subba Reddy**, **Dandasena** (Savara, Paralakimidi).
Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daulah** did stay **pro-British** (APHQ **2001**, **2025**).
xa: **Annapurnayya** ("Andhra Netaji") got **18 months RI** for his article "**Chicharapidugu**" on 1857.
Andhra nationalist writing treated 1857 as India's **first war of independence**.

185.s: What was the significance of Bahadur Shah II during the revolt of 1857?
o: He led only the sepoys of the Bengal Army.
He was accepted as the symbolic head by Hindu and Muslim rebels.
He represented the educated middle class in the revolt.
He served as the principal British commander in Delhi.
185.x: Bahadur Shah II was accepted as the symbolic head by both Hindu and Muslim rebels.
185.tq: Distinguish symbolic leadership from direct military command.
xs: **Bahadur Shah II** was accepted as **symbolic head** by **Hindu and Muslim rebels** alike — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was no British commander, nor a middle-class leader — the **educated middle class** stayed aloof.
xa: The **greased cartridges** offended both communities.
After 1857 the British turned to **divide and rule**.

185.s: The issue of greased cartridges contributed to Hindu-Muslim unity in the revolt because it—
o: offended the religious sentiments of both communities
was opposed only by Hindu rulers
abolished separate religious practices in the army
provided equal military ranks to both communities
185.x: The greased cartridges offended the religious sentiments of both Hindus and Muslims, creating a common grievance.
185.tq: Connect a common grievance with inter-community cooperation.
xs: The **greased cartridges** **offended both communities** — so option **(1)** is correct.
That common grievance fed **Hindu-Muslim cooperation** among leaders and sepoys.
xa: **P.E. Roberts** called the revolt "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over greased cartridges.
**Bahadur Shah II** was accepted as symbolic head by both.
Aftermath: **divide and rule**.

185.s: Which development after the revolt of 1857 reflected the British response to the Hindu-Muslim cooperation witnessed during the revolt?
o: Adoption of a policy of divide and rule
Withdrawal of the British Army from India
Transfer of authority to the Indian National Congress
185.x: After 1857, the British increasingly pursued a policy of divide and rule in response to the cooperation between Hindus and Muslims.
185.tq: Link a historical development with its stated political consequence.
xs: After 1857 the British turned to **divide and rule** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It answered the notable **Hindu-Muslim cooperation** among leaders and sepoys.
xa: Unity symbols: **Bahadur Shah II** as common head; the **greased cartridges** offended both.
**Outram** and **W. Taylor** painted the revolt as a **Muslim conspiracy** exploiting Hindu grievances.

185.s: Which statement best expresses the significance of the revolt of 1857 despite its failure?
o: It shattered the myth of British invincibility and planted the seeds of later nationalism.
It prevented all later nationalist movements.
It immediately ended British rule in India.
It established a modern democratic government throughout India.
185.x: The revolt damaged the belief in British invincibility and helped create the conditions for later nationalism, although it did not end British rule.
185.tq: Distinguish long-term significance from immediate political outcome.
xs: Despite failing, the revolt **shattered the myth of British invincibility** and **planted seeds of later nationalism** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It did not end British rule, but it **shook** it.
xa: Its heroes were invoked later by **Bose** and **Bhagat Singh** (Quit India, INA trials).
Debate: nationalist "**first war of independence**" vs Majumdar's "**neither first nor national**".

185.s: Annapurnayya, known as ‘Andhra Netaji’, was sentenced to 18 months’ rigorous imprisonment for which of the following?
o: Writing the article *Chicharapidugu* on the revolt of 1857
Supporting the British policy of divide and rule
Organising the RIN revolt at Bombay
185.x: Annapurnayya received 18 months’ rigorous imprisonment for his article *Chicharapidugu*, which dealt with the revolt of 1857.
185.tq: Test the association between a regional nationalist figure and his specific written work.
xs: **Annapurnayya** ("**Andhra Netaji**") got **18 months RI** for his article "**Chicharapidugu**" on **1857** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He did not lead at **Meerut** (sepoys, **10 May 1857**) or organise the **RIN revolt** (**1946**).
xa: Andhra nationalist writing treated 1857 as India's **first war of independence**.
AP during 1857: Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daulah** stayed pro-British; **Turrebaz Khan** led a limited revolt in Hyderabad.

185.s: The debate over whether an uprising was a ‘mutiny’ or a ‘revolt’ was also applied to the RIN revolt of 1946. The RIN revolt began at HMIS Talwar, Bombay, on—
185.x: The RIN revolt began at HMIS Talwar in Bombay on 18 February 1946.
185.tq: Distinguish a precise date from nearby dates associated with another event.
xs: The **RIN revolt** began at **HMIS Talwar**, **Bombay**, on **18 February 1946** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The same "**mutiny or revolt?**" debate applied to it.
xa: Its **80th anniversary** was marked on **18 Feb 2026**.
**29 March** and **8 April** are 1857 dates — **Mangal Pandey**'s attack and execution.

185.s: Mangal Pandey, who attacked British officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857, belonged to which unit?
185.x: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry at Barrackpore. He acted on 29 March 1857 and was executed on 8 April 1857. The 3rd Light Cavalry was the unit at Meerut, the 1st Cavalry of the Hyderabad Contingent was disarmed at Aurangabad in June 1857, and the 19th Native Infantry was a separate unit.
185.tq: Barrackpore, 34th BNI, 29 March 1857.
xs: **Mangal Pandey** belonged to the **34th Bengal Native Infantry** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He acted at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857** and was **hanged on 8 April 1857**.
xa: The PM paid tribute to him as an early hero of the "**1st War of Independence**".
The main sepoy rising followed at **Meerut** on **10 May 1857**.

186.s: The Government of India Act, 1858 was officially titled as the:
o: Act for the Political Settlement of India
Act for the Better Administration of India
Act for the Good Government of India
Act for the Regulation of Crown Territories
186.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 was titled the Act for the Good Government of India.
186.tq: Directly identify the exact official title of the Act.
xs: The GoI Act, **1858** was titled the **Act for the Good Government of India** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was passed after the **1857 Revolt** and **abolished Company rule**.
xa: Government, territories and revenues of India passed to the **British Crown**.
It created the **Secretary of State for India** and the title **Viceroy**.
The **1858** answer appeared in APPSC-GS **2018**, **2019** and UPPSC **2010**.

186.s: Which Act transferred the government, territories and revenues of India from the East India Company to the British Crown?
186.x: The Government of India Act, 1858, passed after the Revolt, ended Company rule and vested India in the Crown. The Charter Act 1853 and Pitt's India Act 1784 left the Company in place, and the Indian Councils Act 1861 came after the transfer.
186.tq: Crown takeover = 1858 Act; distractors are 1784, 1853, 1861.
xs: The **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred the government, territories and revenues of India to the **British Crown** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Charter Act 1853** and **Pitt's Act** left the Company in place; the **Indian Councils Act 1861** came after the transfer.
xa: Exam angle: options mix Charter Acts **1833**/**1853**, Pitt's Act and ICA **1861** — only the **1858** Act transferred power.
The East India Company was finally **dissolved in 1874**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

186.s: The year 1858 is regarded as a watershed in Indian history because it marked the transition from
186.x: The year 1858 marked the transfer of authority from the East India Company to the British Crown, beginning direct Crown rule in India.
186.tq: Distinguish the two successive systems of British administration.
xs: **1858** is the watershed between **Company rule** and **Crown rule** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It began Crown rule, which lasted **1858-1947**.
xa: Administration came to be controlled from **London** (submarine cable, **1870**).
The Proclamation fixed British policy on **princes and religion** till **1947**.
AP angle: Andhra came under **direct Crown rule**.

186.s: Under the Government of India Act, 1858, the powers of the British Crown in India were exercised through the:
o: President of the Board of Control
Chairman of the Court of Directors
186.x: The Act created the office of the Secretary of State for India, through whom the British Crown exercised its powers in India.
186.tq: Use the institutional-power clue to identify the authority concerned.
xs: The Crown's powers were exercised through the **Secretary of State for India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He was a **British cabinet minister** and could **issue orders to the Viceroy**.
xa: First SoS: **Lord Stanley**.
He was assisted (advised) by a **15-member Council of India** in London.
The Council of India was abolished by the **1935** Act.

186.s: Who was the first Secretary of State for India under the Government of India Act, 1858?
186.x: Lord Stanley was the first Secretary of State for India under the new Crown administration.
186.tq: Distinguish the first office-holder from later Viceroys and Secretaries of State.
xs: The first **Secretary of State for India** was **Lord Stanley** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Lord Canning** was the first **Viceroy**; **Kimberley** was a later SoS; **Lytton** proclaimed Victoria **Empress** in **1877**.
xa: The SoS was a **British cabinet minister** exercising the Crown's powers.
SoS **Kimberley** said an adequate number of civil servants "**shall always be Europeans**".

186.s: The Charter Act of 1833 made the East India Company:
o: an agency of the Crown headed by the Secretary of State
a body subordinate to the Board of Control in commercial matters only
186.x: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company’s remaining commercial functions and made it a purely administrative organisation.
186.tq: Use the change in the Company’s character to identify the correct Charter Act.
xs: The **Charter Act 1833** made the Company a **purely administrative** organisation — so option **(4)** is correct.
It also made the GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** (**Bentinck**).
The Company became no **agency of the Crown** under a SoS — that came only with the **1858** Act.
xa: APPSC G2 **2024** and G2 **2025** asked "GG of Bengal designated GG of India by?" — **Charter Act 1833**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

186.s: The Secretary of State for India created by the Government of India Act, 1858 was a member of the:
186.x: The Secretary of State for India was a member of the British Cabinet and exercised the powers of the Crown in relation to India.
186.tq: Match the newly created office with its constitutional position rather than with its advisory body.
xs: The **Secretary of State for India** was a **British cabinet minister** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Council of India** (**15** members) only **advised** him; he was not merely its member.
xa: He exercised the **Crown's powers** and could **issue orders to the Viceroy**.
First SoS: **Lord Stanley**.

186.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Council of India under the Government of India Act, 1858:
1. It consisted of 15 members.
2. It advised the Secretary of State for India.
3. It continued in existence until the Government of India Act, 1935.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
186.x: The Council of India consisted of 15 members and advised the Secretary of State. It was abolished by the Government of India Act, 1935, making statement 3 false.
186.tq: The time-limit statement is tested against the later abolition of the Council.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: a **15-member Council of India** in London.
Statement 2 is **correct**: it **assisted (advised) the SoS** — so the key is **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 3 is treated as wrong by the key: the Council was **abolished by the 1935 Act**.
xa: ⚠ The notes say the Council was "**abolished by the 1935 Act**" — so it did last until that Act; the key reads statement 3 strictly.
The SoS was a **British cabinet minister**; first SoS **Lord Stanley**.

186.s: Which Act changed the title to Governor-General of India?
186.x: The Charter Act of 1833 changed the title to Governor-General of India, and William Bentinck was the first holder of that title.
186.tq: Distinguish the Act changing the territorial scope of the title from the later Act creating the Viceroyship.
xs: The **Charter Act 1833** made the GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** — so option **(4)** is correct.
First holder: **Bentinck**.
The **1858** Act added the title **Viceroy**; it did not create "GG of India".
xa: APPSC G2 **2024** and G2 **2025** asked this — answer **Charter Act 1833**.
The 1833 Act also made the Company **purely administrative**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

186.s: The title ‘Viceroy and Governor-General’ was created by the:
186.x: The Government of India Act of 1858 created the title Viceroy and Governor-General. Lord Canning was its first holder.
186.tq: Match the constitutional title with the statutory change that followed the transfer of power.
xs: The title **Viceroy** was created by the **Government of India Act, 1858** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The GG (of India since **1833**) got the extra title **Viceroy**, the **Crown's representative**.
xa: First Viceroy: **Lord Canning**.
Viceroy → towards the **princely states**; Governor-General → for **British India**.
The same Act created the **Secretary of State for India** (first: **Lord Stanley**).

186.s:
Consider the following statements about the offices of Governor-General and Viceroy:
